<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_08" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 8" data-chapter="Chapter 08" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/decay,motif/home,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/vanity,character/colonel_brandon,character/edward_ferrars,character/nurse"></span>


CHAPTER VIII.





Mrs. Jennings was a widow with an ample jointure. She had only two

daughters, both of whom she had lived to see respectably married, and

she had now therefore nothing to do but to marry all the rest of the

world. In the promotion of this object she was zealously active, as far

as her ability reached; and missed no opportunity of projecting

weddings among all the young people of her acquaintance. She was

remarkably quick in the discovery of attachments, and had enjoyed the

advantage of raising the blushes and the [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] of many a young lady by

insinuations of her power over such a young man; and this kind of

discernment enabled her soon after her arrival at Barton decisively to

pronounce that [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] was very much in [[motifs/love|love]] with Marianne

Dashwood. She rather suspected it to be so, on the very first evening

of their being together, from his listening so attentively while she

sang to them; and when the visit was returned by the Middletons’ dining

at the cottage, the fact was ascertained by his listening to her again.

It must be so. She was perfectly convinced of it. It would be an

excellent match, for _he_ was rich, and _she_ was handsome. Mrs.

Jennings had been anxious to see [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] [[motifs/well|well]] married, ever

since her connection with Sir John first brought him to her knowledge;

and she was always anxious to get a good husband for every pretty girl.



The immediate advantage to herself was by no means inconsiderable, for

it supplied her with endless jokes against them both. At the park she

laughed at the colonel, and in the cottage at Marianne. To the former

her raillery was probably, as far as it regarded only himself,

perfectly indifferent; but to the latter it was at first

incomprehensible; and when its object was understood, she hardly knew

whether most to laugh at its absurdity, or censure its impertinence,

for she considered it as an unfeeling reflection on the colonel’s

advanced years, and on his forlorn condition as an old bachelor.



Mrs. Dashwood, who could not think a man five years younger than

herself, so exceedingly ancient as he appeared to the youthful fancy of

her daughter, ventured to clear Mrs. Jennings from the probability of

wishing to throw ridicule on his age.



“But at least, Mama, you cannot deny the absurdity of the accusation,

though you may not think it intentionally ill-natured. [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]

is certainly younger than Mrs. Jennings, but he is old enough to be

_my_ father; and if he were ever animated enough to be in [[motifs/love|love]], must

have long outlived every sensation of the kind. It is too ridiculous!

When is a man to be safe from such wit, if age and infirmity will not

protect him?”



“Infirmity!” said Elinor, “do you call [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] infirm? I can

easily suppose that his age may appear much greater to you than to my

mother; but you can hardly deceive yourself as to his having the use of

his limbs!”



“Did not you hear him complain of the rheumatism? and is not that the

commonest infirmity of declining life?”



“My dearest [[archetypes/child|child]],” said her mother, laughing, “at this rate you must

be in continual terror of _my_ [[motifs/decay|decay]]; and it must seem to you a miracle

that my life has been extended to the advanced age of forty.”



“Mama, you are not doing me justice. I know very [[motifs/well|well]] that Colonel

Brandon is not old enough to make his friends yet apprehensive of

losing him in the course of [[concepts/nature|nature]]. He may live twenty years longer.

But thirty-five has nothing to do with matrimony.”



“Perhaps,” said Elinor, “thirty-five and seventeen had better not have

any thing to do with matrimony together. But if there should by any

chance happen to be a woman who is single at seven and twenty, I should

not think [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s being thirty-five any objection to his

marrying _her_.”



“A woman of seven and twenty,” said Marianne, after pausing a moment,

“can never [[concepts/hope|hope]] to feel or inspire affection again, and if her [[motifs/home|home]] be

uncomfortable, or her fortune small, I can suppose that she might bring

herself to submit to the offices of a [[characters/nurse|nurse]], for the sake of the

provision and security of a wife. In his marrying such a woman

therefore there would be nothing unsuitable. It would be a compact of

convenience, and the world would be satisfied. In my eyes it would be

no [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] at all, but that would be nothing. To me it would seem only

a commercial exchange, in which each wished to be benefited at the

expense of the other.”



“It would be impossible, I know,” replied Elinor, “to convince you that

a woman of seven and twenty could feel for a man of thirty-five

anything near enough to [[motifs/love|love]], to make him a desirable companion to her.

But I must object to your dooming [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] and his wife to the

constant confinement of a sick chamber, merely because he chanced to

complain yesterday (a very cold damp day) of a slight rheumatic feel in

one of his shoulders.”



“But he talked of flannel waistcoats,” said Marianne; “and with me a

flannel waistcoat is invariably connected with aches, cramps,

rheumatisms, and every species of ailment that can afflict the old and

the feeble.”



“Had he been only in a violent fever, you would not have despised him

half so much. Confess, Marianne, is not there something interesting to

you in the flushed cheek, hollow eye, and quick pulse of a fever?”



Soon after this, upon Elinor’s leaving the room, “Mama,” said Marianne,

“I have an alarm on the subject of illness which I cannot conceal from

you. I am sure [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]] is not [[motifs/well|well]]. We have now been here almost

a fortnight, and yet he does not come. Nothing but real indisposition

could occasion this extraordinary delay. What else can detain him at

Norland?”



“Had you any idea of his coming so soon?” said Mrs. Dashwood. “_I_ had

none. On the contrary, if I have felt any anxiety at all on the

subject, it has been in recollecting that he sometimes showed a want of

pleasure and readiness in accepting my invitation, when I talked of his

coming to Barton. Does Elinor expect him already?”



“I have never mentioned it to her, but of course she must.”



“I rather think you are mistaken, for when I was talking to her

yesterday of getting a new grate for the spare bedchamber, she observed

that there was no immediate hurry for it, as it was not likely that the

room would be wanted for some [[motifs/time|time]].”



“How strange this is! what can be the meaning of it! But the whole of

their behaviour to each other has been unaccountable! How cold, how

composed were their last adieus! How languid their conversation the

last evening of their being together! In Edward’s farewell there was no

distinction between Elinor and me: it was the good wishes of an

affectionate brother to both. Twice did I leave them purposely together

in the course of the last morning, and each [[motifs/time|time]] did he most

unaccountably follow me out of the room. And Elinor, in quitting

Norland and Edward, cried not as I did. Even now her [[concepts/self|self]]-command is

invariable. When is she dejected or [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]]? When does she try to

avoid society, or appear restless and dissatisfied in it?”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO VIII.





La signora Jennings era una vedova con un cospicuo patrimonio. Aveva soltanto due…

Figlie, entrambe le quali aveva visto sposarsi in modo rispettabile…

Ora non le restava altro da fare se non sposare tutti gli altri…

Mondo… Nella promozione di questo oggetto fu estremamente attiva.

Finché le sue capacità lo permettevano, non perdeva mai l’occasione di metterle in mostra.

Matrimoni tra tutti i giovani che conosceva… Lei era…

Molto veloce nell’individuare legami affettivi… e ne aveva tratto piacere.

Il vantaggio di far arrossire le guance e suscitare la [[concepts/vanity|vanità]] di molte giovani signore.

Insinuazioni sul suo potere su un giovane così… e questo genere di cose.

La saggezza le permise, poco dopo il suo arrivo a Barton, di agire con decisione…

Si può affermare con certezza che il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] fosse profondamente [[motifs/love|innamorato]] di Marianne.

Dashwood. Già dalla prima sera, lei sospettava che fosse proprio così.

Dell’essere insieme loro due, dal modo in cui lui ascoltava con tanta attenzione mentre lei…

Cantava per loro; e quando i Middleton risposero alla visita a tavola…

Nel capanno, il fatto fu confermato ascoltandola di nuovo.

Deve essere così. Ne era assolutamente convinta: sarebbe stato perfetto…

Un matrimonio eccellente: lui era ricco, e lei era bella. La signora.

Jennings aveva sempre desiderato che [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] si sposasse bene.

Da quando il suo legame con Sir John lo ha portato per la prima volta alla sua conoscenza…

E lei era sempre ansiosa che ogni ragazza carina trovasse un buon marito.



Il vantaggio immediato per lei non era affatto trascurabile…

Le forniva infinite battute su di loro due… Nel parco, lei…

Risero del colonnello… e anche di Marianne, nella capanna. Per quanto riguarda il primo…

La sua ironia, probabilmente, riguardo a lui stesso…

Perfettamente indifferente… ma per quest’ultimo, all’inizio, era diverso.

“Incomprensibile; e quando ne fu compreso il significato, lei quasi non lo sapeva più.”

Se ridere della sua assurdità o condannarne la mancanza di pertinenza…

“Perché la considerava una riflessione insensibile riguardo al colonnello…”

Gli anni avanzati e la sua condizione desolata di vecchio scapolo.



Titolo:  
La signora Dashwood, che non riusciva a considerare un uomo di cinque anni più giovane di…

Se stessa… così antica, quanto lui apparisse alla giovane immaginazione di…

Sua figlia osò difendere la signora Jennings dalle accuse…

Desiderando mettere in ridicolo la sua età.



“Ma almeno, mamma, non puoi negare l’assurdità di questa accusa…”

Anche se potresti non considerarlo intenzionalmente malvagio, [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]].

“È certamente più giovane della signora Jennings, ma abbastanza vecchio da…”

_Mio padre; e se mai dovesse provare abbastanza sentimento da innamorarsi, sicuramente, _

Hanno da tempo superato ogni tipo di sensazione del genere. È troppo ridicolo!

Quando un uomo può essere al sicuro da tale arguzia, se né l’età né la debolezza lo proteggono?

“Proteggerlo?”



“Malattia!”, disse Elinor, “chiami davvero [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] malato? Io non credo, ”

Si può facilmente supporre che la sua età vi appaia molto più avanzata di quanto non lo sia per me.

Madre… ma è difficile ingannarsi sul fatto che lui ne abbia effettivamente bisogno.

“Le sue membra…”



“Non hai sentito lamentarsi del reumatismo? E non è forse questo il problema…”

“La più comune debolezza della vita che declina…”



“Mio caro [[archetypes/child|bambino]]”, disse sua madre ridendo, “a questo ritmo devi, ”

Vivere nel terrore costante del mio decadimento. E per voi deve sembrare un miracolo.

“Che la mia vita sia stata prolungata fino all’età avanzata di quarant’anni.”



“Mamma, non mi stai rendendo giustizia. So molto bene che il Colonnello, ”

Brandon non è abbastanza grande da far sì che i suoi amici si preoccupino per lui…

Perderlo nel corso della [[concepts/nature|natura]]. Forse potrebbe vivere ancora vent’anni.

“Ma trentacinque non ha nulla a che fare con il matrimonio.”



“Forse,” disse Elinor, “sarebbe meglio che trentacinque più diciassette non avessero mai avuto luogo…”

Titolo:  
Qualsiasi cosa abbia a che fare con il matrimonio… Ma se per qualche motivo…

Se per caso quella donna fosse single a ventisette anni…

Non credo che i trentacinque anni di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] rappresentino alcun ostacolo per lui.

“Sposare lei…”



“Una donna di ventisette anni”, disse Marianne, dopo aver fatto una breve pausa.

“Non può mai sperare di provare o ispirare affetto nuovamente; e se la sua [[motifs/home|casa]], ”

Incomoda, o forse con una fortuna limitata… Immagino che possa decidere di portare con sé…

Essa stessa si sottomise alle mansioni di una [[characters/nurse|infermiera]], per il bene di.

Provvisione e sicurezza di una moglie: nel momento in cui si sceglie di sposare una donna del genere…

Pertanto, non ci sarebbe nulla di inappropriato. Sarebbe un insieme compatto…

Convenienza… e il mondo ne sarebbe soddisfatto. Ai miei occhi, questo rappresenterebbe la soluzione ideale.

Nessun [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] affatto, ma anche così non sarebbe nulla. Per me sembrerebbe soltanto.

Un scambio commerciale in cui ognuno desiderava trarne vantaggio

“Costo dell’altro”.



“Sarebbe impossibile, lo so,” rispose Elinor, “convincervi che…”

Una donna di ventisette anni poteva comprendere un uomo di trentacinque anni

Qualsiasi cosa che fosse anche solo lontanamente paragonabile all’[[motifs/love|amore]], in modo da renderlo un compagno desiderabile per lei.

Ma devo obiettare al fatto che condanniate a morte il vostro [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] e sua moglie.

Costante reclusione in una stanza malata, soltanto perché per caso…

Ieri, in una giornata molto fredda e umida, ho lamentato un leggero mal di reumatismo…

“Su una delle sue spalle.”



“Ma parlava di gilet di flanella…”, disse Marianne; “e con me…”

Flanella gilet è inevitabilmente associata a dolori e crampi.

Reumatismi e ogni genere di malattia che può colpire gli anziani

“Il debole”.



Se solo avesse avuto una febbre violenta, non lo avreste disprezzato

“Mezzo di meno… Ammettilo, Marianne: non c’è forse qualcosa di interessante lì dentro?”

“Nel rossore delle guance, negli occhi vuoti e nel battito accelerato causati dalla febbre…”



Poco dopo, non appena Elinor lasciò la stanza, “Mamma”, disse Marianne.

Un allarme riguardo alla malattia che non posso nascondere

Tu. Sono sicura che [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]] non stia bene. Siamo ormai qui da quasi.

“Una quindicina di giorni… eppure non arriva ancora. Solo problemi di salute seri.”

Qualcosa che potrebbe causare questo ritardo insolito… Cosa altro può trattenerlo?

“Norland?”



“Avete idea che sarebbe arrivato così presto?”, chiese la signora Dashwood. “Io sì”.

Titolo:  
Nessuna ansia, al contrario… se mai ho provato qualche preoccupazione, è stata solo…

Titolo:  
Ricordando, ho notato che a volte mostrava una certa mancanza…

Felicità e disponibilità nell’accettare la mia invitazione, quando ne parlai…

“Arriverà presto a Barton… Ma Elinor se lo aspetta già?”



“Non ne ho mai parlato con lei, ma ovviamente lei deve saperlo.”



“Credo proprio che tu ti sbagli, perché quando parlavo con lei…”

Ieri, mentre acquistava una nuova grata per la camera da letto secondaria, lei osservò…

Titolo:  
Non c’era alcuna urgenza immediata in merito, poiché non era probabile che…

Sarebbe necessaria una stanza per un certo periodo di tempo.



“Che strano… Che significato può avere tutto questo? Ma l’intero…”

Il loro comportamento reciproco è stato davvero incomprensibile… Che freddezza, che distacco…

“Composti furono i loro ultimi addii… Quanto languida la loro conversazione…”

L’ultima sera in cui furono insieme… Nell’addio di Edward non c’era nulla…

La differenza tra Elinor e me: erano i buoni desideri di…

Fratello affettuoso per entrambi… Due volte li ho lasciati apposta insieme.

Nel corso della scorsa mattina, e ogni [[motifs/time|volta]] faceva esattamente così.

“Senza motivo alcuno, mi segue fuori dalla stanza… E Elinor, nel lasciare…”

Norland ed Edward non piansero come feci io. Anche ora il suo autocontrollo è.

Invariabile. Quando è depressa o [[concepts/melancholy|malinconica]]? Quando cerca di.

“Evitare la società… o apparire irrequieti e insoddisfatti al suo interno?”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_09" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 9" data-chapter="Chapter 09" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/hero,motif/clock,motif/garden,motif/hill,motif/home,motif/pain,motif/rose,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/window,concept/beauty,concept/honour,concept/imagination,concept/wonder,setting/court,character/bottom,character/speed"></span>


CHAPTER IX.





The Dashwoods were now settled at Barton with tolerable comfort to

themselves. The house and the [[motifs/garden|garden]], with all the objects surrounding

them, were now become familiar, and the ordinary pursuits which had

given to Norland half its charms were engaged in again with far greater

enjoyment than Norland had been able to afford, since the loss of their

father. Sir John Middleton, who called on them every day for the first

fortnight, and who was not in the habit of seeing much occupation at

[[motifs/home|home]], could not conceal his amazement on finding them always employed.



Their visitors, except those from Barton Park, were not many; for, in

spite of Sir John’s urgent entreaties that they would mix more in the

neighbourhood, and repeated assurances of his carriage being always at

their service, the independence of Mrs. Dashwood’s spirit overcame the

wish of society for her children; and she was resolute in declining to

visit any family beyond the distance of a walk. There were but few who

could be so classed; and it was not all of them that were attainable.

About a mile and a half from the cottage, along the narrow winding

valley of Allenham, which issued from that of Barton, as formerly

described, the girls had, in one of their earliest walks, discovered an

ancient respectable looking mansion which, by reminding them a little

of Norland, interested their [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] and made them wish to be

better acquainted with it. But they learnt, on enquiry, that its

possessor, an elderly lady of very good character, was unfortunately

too infirm to mix with the world, and never stirred from [[motifs/home|home]].



The whole country about them abounded in beautiful walks. The high

downs which invited them from almost every [[motifs/window|window]] of the cottage to

seek the exquisite enjoyment of air on their summits, were a happy

alternative when the dirt of the valleys beneath shut up their superior

beauties; and towards one of these hills did Marianne and Margaret one

memorable morning direct their steps, attracted by the partial sunshine

of a showery sky, and unable longer to bear the confinement which the

settled rain of the two preceding days had occasioned. The weather was

not tempting enough to draw the two others from their pencil and their

book, in spite of Marianne’s declaration that the day would be

lastingly fair, and that every threatening cloud would be drawn off

from their hills; and the two girls set off together.



They gaily ascended the downs, rejoicing in their own penetration at

every glimpse of blue sky; and when they caught in their faces the

animating gales of a high south-westerly [[motifs/wind|wind]], they pitied the fears

which had prevented their mother and Elinor from sharing such

delightful sensations.



“Is there a felicity in the world,” said Marianne, “superior to

this?—Margaret, we will walk here at least two hours.”



Margaret agreed, and they pursued their way against the [[motifs/wind|wind]], resisting

it with laughing delight for about twenty minutes longer, when suddenly

the clouds united over their heads, and a driving rain set full in

their face. Chagrined and surprised, they were obliged, though

unwillingly, to turn back, for no shelter was nearer than their own

house. One consolation however remained for them, to which the exigence

of the moment gave more than usual propriety,—it was that of running

with all possible [[characters/speed|speed]] down the steep side of the [[motifs/hill|hill]] which led

immediately to their [[motifs/garden|garden]] gate.



They set off. Marianne had at first the advantage, but a false step

brought her suddenly to the ground; and Margaret, unable to stop

herself to assist her, was involuntarily hurried along, and reached the

[[characters/bottom|bottom]] in safety.



A gentleman carrying a gun, with two pointers playing round him, was

passing up the [[motifs/hill|hill]] and within a few yards of Marianne, when her

accident happened. He put down his gun and ran to her assistance. She

had raised herself from the ground, but her foot had been twisted in

her fall, and she was scarcely able to stand. The gentleman offered his

services; and perceiving that her modesty declined what her situation

rendered necessary, took her up in his arms without farther delay, and

carried her down the [[motifs/hill|hill]]. Then passing through the [[motifs/garden|garden]], the gate of

which had been left open by Margaret, he bore her directly into the

house, whither Margaret was just arrived, and quitted not his hold till

he had seated her in a chair in the parlour.



Elinor and her mother [[motifs/rose|rose]] up in amazement at their entrance, and while

the eyes of both were fixed on him with an evident [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] and a secret

admiration which equally sprung from his appearance, he apologized for

his intrusion by relating its cause, in a manner so frank and so

graceful that his person, which was uncommonly handsome, received

additional charms from his voice and expression. Had he been even old,

ugly, and vulgar, the gratitude and kindness of Mrs. Dashwood would

have been secured by any act of attention to her [[archetypes/child|child]]; but the

influence of youth, [[concepts/beauty|beauty]], and elegance, gave an interest to the

action which came [[motifs/home|home]] to her feelings.



She thanked him again and again; and, with a sweetness of address which

always attended her, invited him to be seated. But this he declined, as

he was dirty and wet. Mrs. Dashwood then begged to know to whom she was

obliged. His name, he replied, was Willoughby, and his present [[motifs/home|home]] was

at Allenham, from whence he hoped she would allow him the [[concepts/honour|honour]] of

calling tomorrow to enquire after Miss Dashwood. The [[concepts/honour|honour]] was readily

granted, and he then departed, to make himself still more interesting,

in the midst of a heavy rain.



His manly [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] and more than common gracefulness were instantly the

theme of general admiration, and the laugh which his gallantry raised

against Marianne received particular spirit from his exterior

attractions. Marianne herself had seen less of his person than the

rest, for the confusion which crimsoned over her face, on his lifting

her up, had robbed her of the power of regarding him after their

entering the house. But she had seen enough of him to join in all the

admiration of the others, and with an energy which always adorned her

praise. His person and air were equal to what her fancy had ever drawn

for the [[archetypes/hero|hero]] of a favourite story; and in his carrying her into the

house with so little previous formality, there was a rapidity of

thought which particularly recommended the action to her. Every

circumstance belonging to him was interesting. His name was good, his

residence was in their favourite village, and she soon found out that

of all manly dresses a shooting-jacket was the most becoming. Her

[[concepts/imagination|imagination]] was busy, her reflections were pleasant, and the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of a

sprained ankle was disregarded.



Sir John called on them as soon as the next interval of fair weather

that morning allowed him to get out of doors; and Marianne’s accident

being related to him, he was eagerly asked whether he knew any

gentleman of the name of Willoughby at Allenham.



“Willoughby!” cried Sir John; “what, is _he_ in the country? That is

good news however; I will ride over tomorrow, and ask him to dinner on

Thursday.”



“You know him then,” said Mrs. Dashwood.



“Know him! to be sure I do. Why, he is down here every year.”



“And what sort of a young man is he?”



“As good a kind of fellow as ever lived, I assure you. A very decent

shot, and there is not a bolder rider in England.”



“And is _that_ all you can say for him?” cried Marianne, indignantly.

“But what are his manners on more intimate acquaintance? What his

pursuits, his talents, and genius?”



Sir John was rather puzzled.



“Upon my [[motifs/soul|soul]],” said he, “I do not know much about him as to all

_that_. But he is a pleasant, good humoured fellow, and has got the

nicest little black bitch of a pointer I ever saw. Was she out with him

today?”



But Marianne could no more satisfy him as to the colour of Mr.

Willoughby’s pointer, than he could describe to her the shades of his

mind.



“But who is he?” said Elinor. “Where does he come from? Has he a house

at Allenham?”



On this point Sir John could give more certain intelligence; and he

told them that Mr. Willoughby had no property of his own in the

country; that he resided there only while he was visiting the old lady

at Allenham [[settings/court|Court]], to whom he was related, and whose possessions he was

to inherit; adding, “Yes, yes, he is very [[motifs/well|well]] worth catching I can

tell you, Miss Dashwood; he has a pretty little estate of his own in

Somersetshire besides; and if I were you, I would not give him up to my

younger sister, in spite of all this tumbling down hills. Miss Marianne

must not expect to have all the men to herself. Brandon will be

jealous, if she does not take care.”



“I do not believe,” said Mrs. Dashwood, with a good humoured smile,

“that Mr. Willoughby will be incommoded by the attempts of either of

_my_ daughters towards what you call _catching him_. It is not an

employment to which they have been brought up. Men are very safe with

us, let them be ever so rich. I am glad to find, however, from what you

say, that he is a respectable young man, and one whose acquaintance

will not be ineligible.”



“He is as good a sort of fellow, I believe, as ever lived,” repeated

Sir John. “I remember last Christmas at a little hop at the park, he

danced from eight o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] till four, without once sitting down.”



“Did he indeed?” cried Marianne with sparkling eyes, “and with

elegance, with spirit?”



“Yes; and he was up again at eight to ride to covert.”



“That is what I like; that is what a young man ought to be. Whatever be

his pursuits, his eagerness in them should know no moderation, and

leave him no sense of fatigue.”



“Aye, aye, I see how it will be,” said Sir John, “I see how it will be.

You will be setting your cap at him now, and never think of poor

Brandon.”



“That is an expression, Sir John,” said Marianne, warmly, “which I

particularly dislike. I abhor every common-place phrase by which wit is

intended; and ‘setting one’s cap at a man,’ or ‘making a conquest,’ are

the most odious of all. Their tendency is gross and illiberal; and if

their construction could ever be deemed clever, [[motifs/time|time]] has long ago

destroyed all its ingenuity.”



Sir John did not much understand this reproof; but he laughed as

heartily as if he did, and then replied,



“Ay, you will make conquests enough, I dare say, one way or other. Poor

Brandon! he is quite smitten already, and he is very [[motifs/well|well]] worth setting

your cap at, I can tell you, in spite of all this tumbling about and

spraining of ankles.”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO IX.





I Dashwood si erano ora stabiliti a Barton, con una comodità più che soddisfacente…

loro stessi. La casa e il [[motifs/garden|giardino]], con tutti gli oggetti che li circondavano.

Ora que li conoscevano bene, le loro attività quotidiane…

Se solo metà dei fascini di Norland fossero stati nuovamente dedicati a qualcosa di molto più importante…

Un piacere che Norland non si era mai potuto permettere, da quando avevano perso…

Padre… Sir John Middleton, che li andava a trovare ogni giorno per la prima volta

Titolo:  
“Quindici giorni… e chi non era abituato a vedere molte attività intorno…”

A [[motifs/home|casa]], non riusciva a nascondere la sua meraviglia nel vedere che erano sempre impegnati in qualche attività.



I loro visitatori, ad eccezione di quelli provenienti da Barton Park, non erano molti; infatti…

Nonostante le insistenti suppliche di Sir John affinché si mescolassero di più…

**Quartiere… e ripetute assicurazioni che la sua carrozza fosse sempre disponibile.**

“Al servizio loro… l’indipendenza dello spirito della signora Dashwood prevalse su tutto.”

Il desiderio della società per i suoi figli… e lei fu irremovibile nel rifiutarlo.

Visita qualsiasi famiglia che si trovi al di là della distanza che può essere percorsa a piedi… C’erano poche persone che lo facessero.

Potevano essere così classificati; e non tutti erano realmente raggiungibili.

Titolo:  
A circa un miglio e mezzo dalla capanna, lungo il sentiero stretto e tortuoso…

Valle di Allenham, che si diramava da quella di Barton, come un tempo…

Come descritto, durante una delle loro prime passeggiate, le ragazze avevano scoperto…

Una antica residenza dall’aspetto rispettabile che, in qualche modo, li ricorda…

Della Norlandia, stimolavano la loro [[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]] e li facevano desiderare di essere lì.

Meglio familiari con esso… Ma, dopo averne chiesto informazioni, scoprirono che…

Una signora anziana e di ottimo carattere… sfortunatamente…

Troppo malato per mescolarsi con il mondo, e mai si allontanava da [[motifs/home|casa]].



Tutta la regione intorno a loro era ricca di bellissimi sentieri. Le alte…

Vicoli così bassi che li invitavano ad entrare da quasi ogni [[motifs/window|finestra]] della casetta.

“Cercare il piacere squisito dell’aria sulle loro cime… era una felicità.”

Un'alternativa quando la polvere delle valli sottostanti tace…

Bellezze… E verso una di queste colline si diressero Marianna e Margaret.

Una mattina indimenticabile: i loro passi sono guidati dalla luce del sole che filtra tra le nuvole.

Di un cielo tempestoso, e incapace ormai di sopportare la restrizione imposta da…

La pioggia continua dei due giorni precedenti aveva causato… Il tempo era…

Non abbastanza allettante da convincere gli altri due a prendere i loro pennelli…

Libro… nonostante la dichiarazione di Marianne secondo cui quel giorno sarebbe stato…

Eteramente bella… e che ogni nuvola minacciosa sarebbe allontanata.

Dai loro monti. E le due ragazze partirono insieme.



Salirono allegramente verso le colline, felici della loro capacità di…

Ogni barlume di cielo blu… e quando questi raggi colpivano il loro viso…

Sospinti da forti raffiche di un forte vento sud-occidentale, provavano compassione per quelle paure.

Quello che aveva impedito loro madre ed Elinor di condividere qualcosa del genere

Sensazioni deliziose.



“Esiste forse una felicità al mondo”, disse Marianne, “che sia superiore a…”

“Questo posto? — Margaret, cammineremo qui per almeno due ore.”



Margaret acconsentì, e continuarono il loro cammino contro il [[motifs/wind|vento]], resistendone.

Continuando a ridere felicemente per altri venti minuti circa, all’improvviso…

Le nuvole si unirono sopra le loro teste, e iniziò a piovere forte.

Il loro viso… Riluttanti e sorpresi, dovettero comunque farlo.

Con riluttanza, dovettero tornare indietro: non esisteva nessun rifugio più vicino del loro.

La casa. Tuttavia, rimaneva loro un conforto, a cui faceva appello l'esigenza.

In quel momento, l’azione presa fu più appropriata del solito: si trattava di correre.

A tutta la velocità possibile, lungo il ripido versante della [[motifs/hill|collina]] che conduceva.

Immediatamente verso il cancello del loro [[motifs/garden|giardino]].



Partirono. All’inizio Marianne aveva il vantaggio, ma commise un errore.

La fece cadere improvvisamente a terra; e Margaret, incapace di fermarsi…

Si affrettò involontariamente per aiutarla e arrivò…

[[characters/bottom|Parte inferiore]] al sicuro.



Un gentiluomo armato di pistola, con due canne puntate contro di lui…

Superando la [[motifs/hill|collina]] e a pochi metri da Marianne, quando lei.

Un incidente è avvenuto. Ha messo giù la pistola e si è precipitato ad aiutarla. Lei…

Si era alzata da terra, ma il suo piede si era distorto…

La sua caduta… e lei faticava a reggersi in piedi. Il gentiluomo le offrì il suo aiuto.

Servizi… e rendendosi conto che la sua modestia diminuiva man mano che la sua situazione peggiorava…

La prese tra le braccia senza indugiare

La portò giù per la [[motifs/hill|collina]]. Poi, attraversando il [[motifs/garden|giardino]], passarono dalla porta.

Che era stato lasciato aperto da Margaret, la portò direttamente lì dentro.

La casa, dove Margaret era appena arrivata, e non lasciò la sua presa fino a.

L’aveva fatta sedere su una sedia nel salotto.



Elinor e sua madre si alzarono in piedi, stupite, al loro ingresso, e mentre.

Gli occhi di entrambi erano fissi su di lui, pieni di evidente [[concepts/wonder|stupore]] e di un segreto.

Un'ammirazione che nasceva tanto dal suo aspetto… si scusò per questo.

La sua intrusione, spiegata attraverso le sue cause, in modo così franco e aperto…

Elegante nella sua figura, insolitamente attraente…

Altri fascini derivanti dalla sua voce e dal suo modo di esprimersi… Anche se fosse stato anziano,

“Bella ma volgare: la gratitudine e la gentilezza della signora Dashwood…”

Sono state garantite da qualsiasi atto di attenzione rivolto a suo [[archetypes/child|bambino]]; ma.

L’influenza della gioventù, della [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e dell’eleganza conferiva un certo fascino a.

Un'azione che rispecchiava appieno i suoi sentimenti.



Gli ringraziò ancora e ancora; e con una dolcezza nel modo in cui si rivolgeva a lui…

Sempre le era accanto, lo invitò a sedersi… Ma lui rifiutò.

Era sporco e bagnato… La signora Dashwood chiese allora a chi appartenesse

Obbligato. Il suo nome, rispose, era Willoughby, e la sua attuale [[motifs/home|casa]] era.

Ad Allenham, da dove sperava che lei gli concedesse l’onore di.

Chiamerò domani per chiedere notizie di Miss Dashwood. Quell’[[concepts/honour|'onore]] fu prontamente concesso.

“Concesso questo, se ne andò per rendersi ancora più interessante…”

nel mezzo di una pioggia battente.



La sua mascolina [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e una grazia ben al di sopra della norma attirarono immediatamente l’attenzione.

Ammirazione generale e le risate suscitate dalla sua galanteria

“Contro Marianne ricevette uno spirito particolare dal suo aspetto esteriore”

Attrazioni… Anche Marianna lo aveva visto meno di quanto avesse voluto…

Titolo:  
Il suo viso si tinse di rosso per la confusione… e tutto dipendeva dal suo gesto di alzare…

Ridotta in condizioni di impotenza… privata della capacità di considerarlo come prima

Entrando nella casa. Ma aveva già visto abbastanza di lui per partecipare a tutto.

Ampia ammirazione da parte degli altri, e con quell’energia che sempre la caratterizzava…

Elogi… Il suo aspetto e il suo portamento corrispondevano esattamente a ciò che la sua immaginazione aveva sempre fantasticato.

Per l’[[archetypes/hero|eroe]] di una storia che mi piace molto. E mentre la portava dentro.

Casa priva di qualsiasi formalità precedente, c'era una certa velocità nel procedere.

Un pensiero che in particolare le suggeriva di agire. Ogni…

Il nome che portava era interessante… Il suo nome stesso era significativo.

La loro residenza si trovava nel villaggio che amavano di più, e lei scoprì presto…

Tra tutti i vestiti da uomo, il giubbotto da caccia era quello che le donava di più. Lei…

La [[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]] era attiva; i suoi pensieri erano piacevoli, e il [[motifs/pain|)dolore]] di una.

La distorsione alla caviglia fu ignorata.



Sir John li andò a trovare non appena tornò il bel tempo

Quella mattina gli permise di uscire all’aperto; e l’incidente di Marianne…

Essendo imparentato con lui, gli fu chiesto con ansia se sapesse qualcosa al riguardo.

Un gentiluomo di nome Willoughby, residente ad Allenham.



“Willoughby!”, esclamò Sir John; “Ma… è lui qui in campagna? Che strano…”

Buone notizie: passerò da lui domani e lo inviterò a cena.

“Giovedì”.



“Allora lo conosci,” disse la signora Dashwood.



“Lo conosco bene, sì… Ogni anno è qui.”



“E che tipo di giovane uomo è?”



“Un uomo davvero gentile, ve lo assicuro… Molto rispettabile.”

“Colpito… e non c’è nessun cavaliere più coraggioso in Inghilterra.”



“E questo è tutto quello che puoi dire di lui?” esclamò Marianne, indignata.

“Ma come si comporta in situazioni di conoscenza più intima? E quale è il suo…?”

“Le sue passioni, i suoi talenti e il suo genio…”



Sir John era piuttosto perplesso.



“Per la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]],” disse, “non so molto su di lui, in realtà, ”

Quell’uomo… Ma è davvero una persona piacevole e di buon umore, e possiede anche…

“La più bella cagnolina nera che abbia mai visto… Era con lui?”

“Oggi?”



Ma Marianne non riusciva più a soddisfarlo riguardo al colore del signor.

Il dito di Willoughby… che lui stesso non riusciva a descriverle con precisione

mente.



“Ma chi è?” disse Elinor. “Da dove viene? Ha una casa?”

“Ad Allenham?”



Su questo punto, Sir John poteva fornire informazioni più precise; e lui…

Disse loro che il signor Willoughby non possedeva alcuna proprietà personale.

Paese… dove risiedeva soltanto durante le visite alla vecchia signora.

Ad Allenham [[settings/court|Courtyard]], dove aveva parenti e le cui proprietà erano sue.

Per ereditare. Aggiungo: “Sì, sì, vale davvero la pena catturarlo.”

Ve lo dico io, signorina Dashwood: possiede una piccola tenuta tutta sua…

Titolo:  
“Somersetshire… e se fossi in te, non lo lascerei mai andare.”

Sorella minore… nonostante tutto questo caos e difficoltà… Miss Marianne

Non si può certo aspettare di avere tutti gli uomini per sé… Brandon sarà tra loro.

“Invidioso… se lei non si prende cura di me.”



“Non ci credo”, disse la signora Dashwood, con un sorriso cordiale.

Titolo:  
“Che il signor Willoughby possa rimanere disturbato dai tentativi di entrambi…”

Le mie figlie e quella che voi chiamate “la sua cattura”. Non è affatto…

Titolo:  
L’occupazione per la quale sono stati educati… Gli uomini sono molto al sicuro in questo ambito.

“Che siano pure molto ricchi… Tuttavia, sono felice di scoprire, da quanto mi dite…”

Diciamo che sia un giovane rispettabile, e una persona con cui vale la pena fare conoscenza…

“Non sarà considerato inadeguato.”



“Credo che sia davvero una brava persona, come poche altre ci siano state nella storia”, ripeté più volte.

Sir John. “Ricordo il Natale scorso in quel piccolo pub nel parco… Lui…”

Ballò dalle otto di sera fino alle quattro del mattino, senza mai sedersi nemmeno per un attimo.



“Davvero lo ha fatto?” esclamò Marianne con gli occhi scintillanti, “e con…”

Eleganza… con spirito?



“Sì; ed era già in piedi alle otto per andare a cavalcare nella brughiera.”



“Ecco ciò che mi piace; ecco come dovrebbe essere un giovane uomo… Qualunque cosa accada…”

Le sue attività, la sua determinazione nel perseguirle non dovrebbero conoscer limiti alcuni…

“Non lasciargli alcuna sensazione di stanchezza.”



“Sì, sì, ora capisco come andranno le cose,” disse Sir John. “Ora capisco.”

Ora stabilirai tu il limite per lui… e mai pensare al povero…

“Brandon.”



“Quella è davvero un’espressione appropriata, signor John”, disse Marianne con calore, “che io…”

Disprezzo profondo. Odio ogni frase banale con cui si cerca di esprimere ingegno.

Inteso; e “mettersi come obiettivo una persona” o “raggiungere un successo con lei”, sono…

Il più odioso di tutti. La loro tendenza è disgustosa e illiberale; e se…

La loro costruzione non potrebbe mai essere considerata ingegnosa; il [[motifs/time|tempo]], ormai da molto.

“Distrusse tutta la sua ingegnosità.”



Sir John non capì molto bene questo rimprovero; ma rise lo stesso.

Rispose con entusiasmo, come se davvero lo pensasse.



“Ah, sicuramente riuscirai a ottenere delle vittorie, in un modo o nell’altro… Povero…”

Brandon! È già molto innamorato, e vale davvero la pena impegnarsi con lui.

Mai arrenderti, nonostante tutto questo caos…

“Distorsione degli ankle”.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_10--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 10 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 10" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/imagination,concept/truth"></span>


CHAPTER X.





Marianne’s preserver, as Margaret, with more elegance than precision,

styled Willoughby, called at the cottage early the next morning to make

his personal enquiries. He was received by Mrs. Dashwood with more than

politeness; with a kindness which Sir John’s account of him and her own

gratitude prompted; and every thing that passed during the visit tended

to assure him of the sense, elegance, mutual affection, and domestic

comfort of the family to whom accident had now introduced him. Of their

personal charms he had not required a second interview to be convinced.



Miss Dashwood had a delicate complexion, regular features, and a

remarkably pretty figure. Marianne was still handsomer. Her form,

though not so correct as her sister’s, in having the advantage of

height, was more striking; and her face was so lovely, that when in the

common cant of praise, she was called a beautiful girl, [[concepts/truth|truth]] was less

violently outraged than usually happens. Her skin was very brown, but,

from its transparency, her complexion was uncommonly brilliant; her

features were all good; her smile was sweet and attractive; and in her

eyes, which were very dark, there was a life, a spirit, an eagerness,

which could hardly be seen without delight. From Willoughby their

expression was at first held back, by the embarrassment which the

remembrance of his assistance created. But when this passed away, when

her spirits became collected, when she saw that to the perfect

good-breeding of the gentleman, he united frankness and vivacity, and

above all, when she heard him declare, that of music and dancing he was

passionately fond, she gave him such a look of approbation as secured

the largest share of his discourse to herself for the rest of his stay.



It was only necessary to mention any favourite amusement to engage her

to talk. She could not be silent when such points were introduced, and

she had neither shyness nor reserve in their discussion. They speedily

discovered that their enjoyment of dancing and music was mutual, and

that it arose from a general conformity of judgment in all that related

to either. Encouraged by this to a further examination of his opinions,

she proceeded to question him on the subject of books; her favourite

authors were brought forward and dwelt upon with so rapturous a

delight, that any young man of five and twenty must have been

insensible indeed, not to become an immediate convert to the excellence

of such works, however disregarded before. Their taste was strikingly

alike. The same books, the same passages were idolized by each—or if

any difference appeared, any objection arose, it lasted no longer than

till the force of her arguments and the brightness of her eyes could be

displayed. He acquiesced in all her decisions, caught all her

enthusiasm; and long before his visit concluded, they conversed with

the familiarity of a long-established acquaintance.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], Marianne,” said Elinor, as soon as he had left them, “for _one_

morning I think you have done pretty [[motifs/well|well]]. You have already ascertained

Mr. Willoughby’s opinion in almost every matter of importance. You know

what he thinks of Cowper and Scott; you are certain of his estimating

their beauties as he ought, and you have received every assurance of

his admiring Pope no more than is proper. But how is your acquaintance

to be long supported, under such extraordinary despatch of every

subject for discourse? You will soon have exhausted each favourite

topic. Another meeting will suffice to explain his sentiments on

picturesque [[concepts/beauty|beauty]], and second marriages, and then you can have nothing

farther to ask.”



“Elinor,” cried Marianne, “is this fair? is this just? are my ideas so

scanty? But I see what you mean. I have been too much at my ease, too

happy, too frank. I have erred against every common-place notion of

decorum; I have been open and sincere where I ought to have been

reserved, spiritless, dull, and deceitful—had I talked only of the

weather and the roads, and had I spoken only once in ten minutes, this

reproach would have been spared.”



“My [[motifs/love|love]],” said her mother, “you must not be offended with Elinor—she

was only in jest. I should scold her myself, if she were capable of

wishing to check the delight of your conversation with our new friend.”

Marianne was softened in a moment.



Willoughby, on his side, gave every proof of his pleasure in their

acquaintance, which an evident wish of improving it could offer. He

came to them every day. To enquire after Marianne was at first his

excuse; but the encouragement of his reception, to which every day gave

greater kindness, made such an excuse unnecessary before it had ceased

to be possible, by Marianne’s perfect recovery. She was confined for

some days to the house; but never had any confinement been less

irksome. Willoughby was a young man of good abilities, quick

[[concepts/imagination|imagination]], lively spirits, and open, affectionate manners. He was

exactly formed to engage Marianne’s heart, for with all this, he joined

not only a captivating person, but a natural ardour of mind which was

now roused and increased by the example of her own, and which

recommended him to her affection beyond every thing else.



His society became gradually her most exquisite enjoyment. They read,

they talked, they sang together; his musical talents were considerable;

and he read with all the sensibility and spirit which Edward had

unfortunately wanted.



In Mrs. Dashwood’s estimation he was as faultless as in Marianne’s; and

Elinor saw nothing to censure in him but a propensity, in which he

strongly resembled and peculiarly delighted her sister, of saying too

much what he thought on every occasion, without attention to persons or

circumstances. In hastily forming and giving his opinion of other

people, in sacrificing general politeness to the enjoyment of undivided


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO X.





Il salvatore di Marianne… come Margaret, con più eleganza che precisione.

Willoughby lo stilevole, arrivato alla capanna all’alba del giorno seguente per…

Le sue indagini personali. Fu accolto dalla signora Dashwood con grande cordialità…

Cortesia… e una gentilezza che rispecchiava sia il racconto di Sir John che le sue stesse qualità.

Gratitudine ispirata; e tutto ciò che accadde durante la visita contribuì…

Per assicurargli che ci sia senso, eleganza, affetto reciproco e armonia domestica…

Il conforto della famiglia a cui l’incidente lo aveva ora introdotto… Di loro.

Grazie ai suoi fascini personali, non ebbe bisogno di un secondo colloquio per essere convinto.



La signorina Dashwood aveva una pelle delicata, tratti regolari e…

“Una figura straordinariamente bella… Marianne era ancora più attraente. La sua forma…”

Sebbene non sia altrettanto corretto quanto quello di sua sorella, presenta il vantaggio di…

Il suo portamento era ancora più affascinante; e il suo viso così incantevole, che quando…

Un comune canto di lode: veniva chiamata una ragazza bella; la [[concepts/truth|verità]], invece, era meno evidente.

Profondamente indignata, più di quanto avvenga di solito… La sua pelle era molto scura, ma…

Dalla sua trasparenza, il suo incarnato era insolitamente luminoso; lei…

Le caratteristiche fisiche erano tutte positive: il suo sorriso era dolce e attraente…

Occhi molto scuri… in essi c’era vita, spirito, desiderio.

Che difficilmente si poteva guardare senza provare gioia… Da Willoughby loro

Il suo atteggiamento inizialmente era contenuto, a causa dell’imbarazzo che provava…

Il ricordo del suo aiuto rimase… Ma quando lui morì, allora…

Il suo spirito si rasserenò quando vide che tutto era perfetto.

La buona educazione del gentiluomo si manifestava nella sua franchezza e vivacità…

Soprattutto quando lo sentì dichiarare che, per lui, la musica e la danza erano…

Con passione e affetto, gli rivolse uno sguardo pieno di approvazione che lo rese sicuro…

La maggior parte del suo discorso lo rivolgeva a se stessa per il resto del suo soggiorno.



Bastava menzionare qualsiasi divertimento preferito da lei per attirarne l’attenzione.

Parlare… Non poteva rimanere in silenzio quando venivano sollevati argomenti del genere.

Nella loro discussione, lei non mostrava né timidezza né reticenza. Conversavano con facilità.

Scoprirono che il loro piacere per la danza e la musica era reciproco…

Titolo:  
Che derivi da un accordo generale di giudizio su tutto ciò che è correlato.

“… incoraggiato da ciò ad esaminare più approfonditamente le sue opinioni.”

Continuò a interrogarlo sull’argomento dei libri: il suo preferito

Gli autori furono menzionati e analizzati con tale entusiasmo…

Che gioia per qualsiasi giovane di venticinque anni…

Veramente insensibile, non era certo il caso che diventasse immediatamente un convinto sostenitore di tale eccellenza.

Titolo:  
Di opere del genere, per quanto precedentemente trascurate… Il loro gusto era straordinariamente…

Simili… Gli stessi libri, gli stessi passaggi venivano adorati da entrambi… o forse no?

Qualsiasi differenza si manifestasse, qualsiasi obiezione sorgesse, non durava più a lungo di…

Fino a quando la forza delle sue argomentazioni e lo splendore dei suoi occhi non potessero prevalere…

Accettava senza obiezioni tutte le sue decisioni, seguendo fedelmente ogni sua indicazione.

Entusiasmo… E molto prima che la sua visita terminasse, continuarono a conversare con grande entusiasmo.

La familiarità derivante da un'amicizia consolidata da tempo.



“Beh, Marianne,” disse Elinor non appena lui se ne fu andato, “per _una_ volta, ”

Penso che questa mattina tu abbia fatto davvero molto bene. Hai già accertato.

L’opinione del signor Willoughby su quasi ogni questione importante… Lo sai.

Cosa pensa di Cowper e Scott… sei sicuro che li apprezzi molto?

“Le loro bellezze vengono apprezzate come meritano, e avete ricevuto ogni garanzia al riguardo.”

Il suo ammirato Papa… non più di quanto sia appropriato. Ma com’è la tua conoscenza con lui?

Per essere sostenuto a lungo termine, con un tale impegno e rapidità da parte di tutti…

Un argomento di discussione? Presto esaurirai tutti i tuoi preferiti…

Titolo: Un’altra riunione sarà sufficiente per spiegare i suoi sentimenti su…

Bellezze pittoresche, matrimoni successivi, ma poi potresti non avere più nulla.

“Non c’è bisogno di chiedere altro.”



“Elinor”, esclamò Marianne, “è questo giusto? è questa equo? I miei pensieri sono davvero così…”

Scarno? Capisco cosa intendi… Sono stato troppo a mio agio, troppo rilassato…

Felice… troppo franco. Ho commesso errori contro ogni nozione comune e convenzionale…

Decoro; Sono stato aperto e sincero lì dove avrei dovuto esserlo.

Triste, privo di spirito, noioso e ingannevole… se solo avessi parlato solo di questo

“Meteo e strade… E se avessi parlato una sola volta in dieci minuti…”

“Non ci sarebbe stata alcuna rimprovera.”



“Mio [[motifs/love|amore]]”, disse sua madre, “non devi offenderti per Elinor, lei, ”

“Era solo uno scherzo… Dovrei rimproverarla io stesso, se solo fosse in grado di farlo.”

“Desidero assaporare la gioia della vostra conversazione con il nostro nuovo amico.”

Marianne si addolcì all’istante.



Willoughby, da parte sua, dimostrò apertamente quanto fosse felice della loro…

Conoscenza che, se accompagnata da un reale desiderio di migliorarla, potrebbe portare a grandi risultati. Lui…

Ogni giorno andava da loro per chiedere notizie di Marianne… All’inizio, il suo scopo era proprio quello.

Scusa… ma l’incoraggiamento ricevuto per la sua accoglienza, che aumentava ogni giorno…

Una gentilezza ancora maggiore rendeva inutile quell’excuse, prima ancora che venisse pronunciata

Per poter realizzare questo sogno, era necessario che Marianne si riprendesse completamente. Lei fu costretta a rimanere confinata…

Alcuni giorni in quella casa; ma mai nessuna reclusione è stata così poco restrittiva.

“Fastidioso… Willoughby era un giovane dotato di buone capacità, veloce nell’agire.”

[[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]], spirito vivace e modi aperti e affettuosi. Lui era così.

Un cuore destinato a conquistare quello di Marianne

Non solo una persona affascinante, ma anche una passione naturale e intensa…

Ora risvegliato e intensificato dall’esempio stesso di lei…

Glielo raccomandò con tutto il proprio affetto, più di qualsiasi altra cosa.



La sua compagnia divenne gradualmente il suo più grande piacere. Leggevano insieme…

Cantavano insieme; i suoi talenti musicali erano notevoli.

E lesse con tutta la sensibilità e lo spirito che caratterizzavano Edward.

Purtroppo era desiderato, ma non ottenuto.



Nel giudizio della signora Dashwood, era altrettanto impeccabile quanto nel giudizio di Marianne; e…

Elinor non vedeva nulla di criticabile in lui, se non una certa tendenza…

Assomigliava molto a sua sorella e le piaceva particolarmente il fatto che lei dicesse anche…

Quello che pensava in ogni occasione, senza prestare attenzione alle persone o…

Circostanze… Nella fretta di formarsi un’opinione sugli altri

Gente che, sacrificando la cortesia generale per godere di qualcosa di esclusivo…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_10--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 10 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 10" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/imagination,concept/nature,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


attention where his heart was engaged, and in slighting too easily the

forms of worldly propriety, he displayed a want of caution which Elinor

could not approve, in spite of all that he and Marianne could say in

its support.



Marianne began now to perceive that the desperation which had seized

her at sixteen and a half, of ever seeing a man who could satisfy her

ideas of perfection, had been rash and unjustifiable. Willoughby was

all that her fancy had delineated in that unhappy hour and in every

brighter period, as capable of attaching her; and his behaviour

declared his wishes to be in that respect as earnest, as his abilities

were strong.



Her mother too, in whose mind not one speculative thought of their

[[motifs/marriage|marriage]] had been raised, by his prospect of riches, was led before the

end of a week to [[concepts/hope|hope]] and expect it; and secretly to congratulate

herself on having gained two such sons-in-law as Edward and Willoughby.



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s partiality for Marianne, which had so early been

discovered by his friends, now first became perceptible to Elinor, when

it ceased to be noticed by them. Their attention and wit were drawn off

to his more fortunate rival; and the raillery which the other had

incurred before any partiality arose, was removed when his feelings

began really to call for the ridicule so justly annexed to sensibility.

Elinor was obliged, though unwillingly, to believe that the sentiments

which Mrs. Jennings had assigned him for her own satisfaction, were now

actually excited by her sister; and that however a general resemblance

of disposition between the parties might forward the affection of Mr.

Willoughby, an equally striking opposition of character was no

hindrance to the regard of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]. She saw it with concern;

for what could a silent man of five and thirty [[concepts/hope|hope]], when opposed to a

very lively one of five and twenty? and as she could not even wish him

successful, she heartily wished him indifferent. She liked him—in spite

of his gravity and reserve, she beheld in him an object of interest.

His manners, though serious, were mild; and his reserve appeared rather

the result of some oppression of spirits than of any natural gloominess

of temper. Sir John had dropped hints of past injuries and

disappointments, which justified her belief of his being an unfortunate

man, and she regarded him with respect and compassion.



Perhaps she pitied and esteemed him the more because he was slighted by

Willoughby and Marianne, who, prejudiced against him for being neither

lively nor young, seemed resolved to undervalue his merits.



“Brandon is just the kind of man,” said Willoughby one day, when they

were talking of him together, “whom every [[concepts/body|body]] speaks [[motifs/well|well]] of, and

nobody cares about; whom all are delighted to see, and nobody remembers

to talk to.”



“That is exactly what I think of him,” cried Marianne.



“Do not boast of it, however,” said Elinor, “for it is injustice in

both of you. He is highly esteemed by all the family at the park, and I

never see him myself without taking pains to converse with him.”



“That he is patronised by _you_,” replied Willoughby, “is certainly in

his favour; but as for the esteem of the others, it is a reproach in

itself. Who would submit to the indignity of being approved by such a

woman as Lady Middleton and Mrs. Jennings, that could command the

indifference of any [[concepts/body|body]] else?”



“But perhaps the abuse of such people as yourself and Marianne will

make amends for the regard of Lady Middleton and her mother. If their

praise is censure, your censure may be praise, for they are not more

undiscerning, than you are prejudiced and unjust.”



“In defence of your _protégé_ you can even be saucy.”



“My _protégé_, as you call him, is a sensible man; and sense will

always have attractions for me. Yes, Marianne, even in a man between

thirty and forty. He has seen a great deal of the world; has been

abroad, has read, and has a thinking mind. I have found him capable of

giving me much information on various subjects; and he has always

answered my inquiries with readiness of good-breeding and good [[concepts/nature|nature]].”



“That is to say,” cried Marianne contemptuously, “he has told you, that

in the East Indies the climate is hot, and the mosquitoes are

troublesome.”



“He _would_ have told me so, I [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] not, had I made any such

inquiries, but they happened to be points on which I had been

previously informed.”



“Perhaps,” said Willoughby, “his observations may have extended to the

existence of nabobs, gold mohrs, and palanquins.”



“I may venture to say that _his_ observations have stretched much

further than _your_ candour. But why should you dislike him?”



“I do not dislike him. I consider him, on the contrary, as a very

respectable man, who has every [[concepts/body|body]]’s good word, and nobody’s notice;

who has more money than he can spend, more [[motifs/time|time]] than he knows how to

employ, and two new coats every year.”



“Add to which,” cried Marianne, “that he has neither genius, taste, nor

spirit. That his understanding has no brilliancy, his feelings no

ardour, and his voice no expression.”



“You decide on his imperfections so much in the mass,” replied Elinor,

“and so much on the strength of your own [[concepts/imagination|imagination]], that the

commendation _I_ am able to give of him is comparatively cold and

insipid. I can only pronounce him to be a sensible man, [[motifs/well|well]]-bred,

[[motifs/well|well]]-informed, of gentle address, and, I believe, possessing an amiable

heart.”



“Miss Dashwood,” cried Willoughby, “you are now using me unkindly. You

are endeavouring to disarm me by reason, and to convince me against my

will. But it will not do. You shall find me as stubborn as you can be

artful. I have three unanswerable reasons for disliking Colonel

Brandon; he threatened me with rain when I wanted it to be fine; he has

found fault with the hanging of my curricle, and I cannot persuade him

to buy my brown mare. If it will be any satisfaction to you, however,

to be told, that I believe his character to be in other respects

irreproachable, I am ready to confess it. And in return for an

acknowledgment, which must give me some [[motifs/pain|pain]], you cannot deny me the

privilege of disliking him as much as ever.”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Osservazione attenta verso ciò che realmente lo interessava… e troppa leggerezza nel sottovalutare il resto

"#Forme di decoro mondaniero… ma lui dimostrò una mancanza di prudenza che Elinor…"

Non poteva approvare, nonostante tutto ciò che lui e Marianne avessero potuto dire…

il suo sostegno.



Marianne iniziò ora a rendersi conto della disperazione che l’aveva assalita…

A sedici anni e mezzo, non aveva mai incontrato un uomo in grado di soddisfarla…

“Idee di perfezione… erano avventate e ingiustificate. Willoughby era…”

Tutto ciò che la sua immaginazione aveva descritto in quell’ora infelice… e in ogni altra occasione simile.

Un periodo più luminoso, capace di legarla a lui… e il suo comportamento.

Un ostacolo per gli occhi di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]]. Lo vedeva con preoccupazione.

Perché un uomo silenzioso di cinquantatré anni poteva sperare in qualcosa, quando si trovava di fronte a.

A causa della sua gravità e riservatezza, lei vedeva in lui un oggetto di interesse.

I suoi modi, sebbene seri, erano gentili; e la sua riservatezza sembrava piuttosto…

“Brandon è proprio il tipo d’uomo che…” disse un giorno Willoughby, mentre erano insieme…

Stavano parlando di lui insieme: “di colui di cui tutti parlano bene, ”

Nessuno se ne cura; tutti sono felici di vederlo, ma nessuno se lo ricorda.

Rimediare al disprezzo di Lady Middleton e sua madre

All'estero, ha letto molto e possiede una mente pensante. Ho ritenuto che fosse capace di…

fornendomi molte informazioni su svariati argomenti; e lui lo ha sempre fatto

Un uomo rispettabile, che gode della stima di tutti, ma che non attira l’attenzione di nessuno.

“Assumere personale e acquistare due nuovi cappotti ogni anno.”

Titolo:  
La lode che posso fargli è piuttosto fredda…

Cuore.

“Il privilegio di odiarlo ancora quanto prima.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 11" data-chapter="Chapter 11" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/memory,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/water,concept/body,concept/friendship,concept/history,concept/imagination,concept/melancholy,concept/self,form/history,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER XI.





Little had Mrs. Dashwood or her daughters imagined when they first came

into Devonshire, that so many engagements would arise to occupy their

[[motifs/time|time]] as shortly presented themselves, or that they should have such

frequent invitations and such constant visitors as to leave them little

leisure for serious employment. Yet such was the case. When Marianne

was recovered, the schemes of amusement at [[motifs/home|home]] and abroad, which Sir

John had been previously forming, were put into execution. The private

balls at the park then began; and parties on the [[motifs/water|water]] were made and

accomplished as often as a showery October would allow. In every

meeting of the kind Willoughby was included; and the ease and

familiarity which naturally attended these parties were exactly

calculated to give increasing intimacy to his acquaintance with the

Dashwoods, to afford him opportunity of witnessing the excellencies of

Marianne, of marking his animated admiration of her, and of receiving,

in her behaviour to himself, the most pointed assurance of her

affection.



Elinor could not be surprised at their attachment. She only wished that

it were less openly shown; and once or twice did venture to suggest the

propriety of some [[concepts/self|self]]-command to Marianne. But Marianne abhorred all

concealment where no real disgrace could attend unreserve; and to aim

at the restraint of sentiments which were not in themselves illaudable,

appeared to her not merely an unnecessary effort, but a disgraceful

subjection of reason to common-place and mistaken notions. Willoughby

thought the same; and their behaviour at all times, was an illustration

of their opinions.



When he was present she had no eyes for any one else. Every thing he

did, was right. Every thing he said, was clever. If their evenings at

the park were concluded with cards, he cheated himself and all the rest

of the party to get her a good hand. If dancing formed the amusement of

the [[motifs/night|night]], they were partners for half the [[motifs/time|time]]; and when obliged to

separate for a couple of dances, were careful to stand together and

scarcely spoke a word to any [[concepts/body|body]] else. Such conduct made them of

course most exceedingly laughed at; but ridicule could not shame, and

seemed hardly to provoke them.



Mrs. Dashwood entered into all their feelings with a warmth which left

her no inclination for checking this excessive display of them. To her

it was but the natural consequence of a strong affection in a young and

ardent mind.



This was the season of happiness to Marianne. Her heart was devoted to

Willoughby, and the fond attachment to Norland, which she brought with

her from Sussex, was more likely to be softened than she had thought it

possible before, by the charms which his society bestowed on her

present [[motifs/home|home]].



Elinor’s happiness was not so great. Her heart was not so much at ease,

nor her satisfaction in their amusements so pure. They afforded her no

companion that could make amends for what she had left behind, nor that

could teach her to think of Norland with less regret than ever. Neither

Lady Middleton nor Mrs. Jennings could supply to her the conversation

she missed; although the latter was an everlasting talker, and from the

first had regarded her with a kindness which ensured her a large share

of her discourse. She had already repeated her own [[concepts/history|history]] to Elinor

three or four times; and had Elinor’s [[motifs/memory|memory]] been equal to her means of

improvement, she might have known very early in their acquaintance all

the particulars of Mr. Jennings’s last illness, and what he said to his

wife a few minutes before he died. Lady Middleton was more agreeable

than her mother only in being more silent. Elinor needed little

observation to perceive that her reserve was a mere calmness of manner

with which sense had nothing to do. Towards her husband and mother she

was the same as to them; and intimacy was therefore neither to be

looked for nor desired. She had nothing to say one day that she had not

said the day before. Her insipidity was invariable, for even her

spirits were always the same; and though she did not oppose the parties

arranged by her husband, provided every thing were conducted in style

and her two eldest children attended her, she never appeared to receive

more enjoyment from them than she might have experienced in sitting at

[[motifs/home|home]];—and so little did her presence add to the pleasure of the others,

by any share in their conversation, that they were sometimes only

reminded of her being amongst them by her solicitude about her

troublesome boys.



In [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] alone, of all her new acquaintance, did Elinor find

a person who could in any degree claim the respect of abilities, excite

the interest of [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], or give pleasure as a companion. Willoughby

was out of the question. Her admiration and regard, even her sisterly

regard, was all his own; but he was a [[archetypes/lover|lover]]; his attentions were wholly

Marianne’s, and a far less agreeable man might have been more generally

pleasing. [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], unfortunately for himself, had no such

encouragement to think only of Marianne, and in conversing with Elinor

he found the greatest consolation for the indifference of her sister.



Elinor’s compassion for him increased, as she had reason to suspect

that the misery of disappointed [[motifs/love|love]] had already been known to him.

This suspicion was given by some words which accidentally dropped from

him one evening at the park, when they were sitting down together by

mutual consent, while the others were dancing. His eyes were fixed on

Marianne, and, after a [[motifs/silence|silence]] of some minutes, he said, with a faint

smile, “Your sister, I understand, does not approve of second

attachments.”



“No,” replied Elinor, “her opinions are all romantic.”



“Or rather, as I believe, she considers them impossible to exist.”



“I believe she does. But how she contrives it without reflecting on the

character of her own father, who had himself two wives, I know not. A

few years however will settle her opinions on the reasonable basis of

common sense and observation; and then they may be more easy to define

and to justify than they now are, by any [[concepts/body|body]] but herself.”



“This will probably be the case,” he replied; “and yet there is

something so amiable in the prejudices of a young mind, that one is

sorry to see them give way to the reception of more general opinions.”



“I cannot agree with you there,” said Elinor. “There are inconveniences

attending such feelings as Marianne’s, which all the charms of

enthusiasm and ignorance of the world cannot atone for. Her systems

have all the unfortunate tendency of setting propriety at nought; and a

better acquaintance with the world is what I look forward to as her

greatest possible advantage.”



After a short pause he resumed the conversation by saying,—



“Does your sister make no distinction in her objections against a

second attachment? or is it equally criminal in every [[concepts/body|body]]? Are those

who have been disappointed in their first choice, whether from the

inconstancy of its object, or the perverseness of circumstances, to be

equally indifferent during the rest of their lives?”



“Upon my word, I am not acquainted with the minutiae of her principles.

I only know that I never yet heard her admit any instance of a second

attachment’s being pardonable.”



“This,” said he, “cannot hold; but a change, a total change of

sentiments—No, no, do not [[motifs/desire|desire]] it; for when the romantic refinements

of a young mind are obliged to give way, how frequently are they

succeeded by such opinions as are but too common, and too dangerous! I

speak from experience. I once knew a lady who in temper and mind

greatly resembled your sister, who thought and judged like her, but who

from an enforced change—from a series of unfortunate circumstances—”

Here he stopt suddenly; appeared to think that he had said too much,

and by his countenance gave rise to conjectures, which might not

otherwise have entered Elinor’s head. The lady would probably have

passed without suspicion, had he not convinced Miss Dashwood that what

concerned her ought not to escape his lips. As it was, it required but

a slight effort of fancy to connect his emotion with the tender

recollection of past regard. Elinor attempted no more. But Marianne, in

her place, would not have done so little. The whole story would have

been speedily formed under her active [[concepts/imagination|imagination]]; and every thing

established in the most [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] order of disastrous [[motifs/love|love]].
