Da un cambiamento imposto… da una serie di circostanze sfortunate…

Qui si fermò improvvisamente; sembrava pensare di aver detto troppo.

Dal suo volto si potevano fare varie congetture… che forse non erano del tutto corrette.

Altrimenti, questi pensieri sarebbero entrati nella mente di Elinor… Probabilmente, la signora avrebbe…

Passò inosservato, se non fosse riuscito a convincere la signorina Dashwood che…

“Ciò che la riguardava non avrebbe dovuto uscire dalle sue labbra… In realtà, bastava solo…”

Un lieve sforzo di immaginazione per collegare le sue emozioni con quella tenerezza…

Recuerdo di un affetto passato… Elinor non cercò più di intervenire. Ma Marianne, invece…

Il suo posto… non avrebbe fatto così poco. L’intera storia sarebbe stata diversa.

Fu creato rapidamente grazie alla sua attiva [[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]]; e tutto ciò.

Sistemato nell’ordine più [[concepts/melancholy|malinconico]] di un disastroso [[motifs/love|amore]].



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_12" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 12" data-chapter="Chapter 12" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/home,motif/horse,motif/night,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,character/colonel_brandon,character/queen"></span>


CHAPTER XII.





As Elinor and Marianne were walking together the next morning the

latter communicated a piece of news to her sister, which in spite of

all that she knew before of Marianne’s imprudence and want of thought,

surprised her by its extravagant testimony of both. Marianne told her,

with the greatest delight, that Willoughby had given her a [[motifs/horse|horse]], one

that he had bred himself on his estate in Somersetshire, and which was

exactly calculated to carry a woman. Without considering that it was

not in her mother’s plan to keep any [[motifs/horse|horse]], that if she were to alter

her resolution in favour of this gift, she must buy another for the

servant, and keep a servant to ride it, and after all, build a stable

to receive them, she had accepted the present without hesitation, and

told her sister of it in raptures.



“He intends to send his groom into Somersetshire immediately for it,”

she added, “and when it arrives we will ride every day. You shall share

its use with me. Imagine to yourself, my dear Elinor, the delight of a

gallop on some of these downs.”



Most unwilling was she to awaken from such a dream of felicity to

comprehend all the unhappy truths which attended the affair; and for

some [[motifs/time|time]] she refused to submit to them. As to an additional servant,

the expense would be a trifle; Mama she was sure would never object to

it; and any [[motifs/horse|horse]] would do for _him;_ he might always get one at the

park; as to a stable, the merest shed would be sufficient. Elinor then

ventured to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] the propriety of her receiving such a present from a

man so little, or at least so lately known to her. This was too much.



“You are mistaken, Elinor,” said she warmly, “in supposing I know very

little of Willoughby. I have not known him long indeed, but I am much

better acquainted with him, than I am with any other creature in the

world, except yourself and mama. It is not [[motifs/time|time]] or opportunity that is

to determine intimacy;—it is disposition alone. Seven years would be

insufficient to make some people acquainted with each other, and seven

days are more than enough for others. I should hold myself guilty of

greater impropriety in accepting a [[motifs/horse|horse]] from my brother, than from

Willoughby. Of John I know very little, though we have lived together

for years; but of Willoughby my judgment has long been formed.”



Elinor thought it wisest to touch that point no more. She knew her

sister’s temper. Opposition on so tender a subject would only attach

her the more to her own opinion. But by an appeal to her affection for

her mother, by representing the inconveniences which that indulgent

mother must draw on herself, if (as would probably be the case) she

consented to this increase of establishment, Marianne was shortly

subdued; and she promised not to tempt her mother to such imprudent

kindness by mentioning the offer, and to tell Willoughby when she saw

him next, that it must be declined.



She was faithful to her word; and when Willoughby called at the

cottage, the same day, Elinor heard her express her disappointment to

him in a low voice, on being obliged to forego the acceptance of his

present. The reasons for this alteration were at the same [[motifs/time|time]] related,

and they were such as to make further entreaty on his side impossible.

His concern however was very apparent; and after expressing it with

earnestness, he added, in the same low voice,—“But, Marianne, the [[motifs/horse|horse]]

is still yours, though you cannot use it now. I shall keep it only till

you can claim it. When you leave Barton to form your own establishment

in a more lasting [[motifs/home|home]], [[characters/queen|Queen]] Mab shall receive you.”



This was all overheard by Miss Dashwood; and in the whole of the

sentence, in his manner of pronouncing it, and in his addressing her

sister by her Christian name alone, she instantly saw an intimacy so

decided, a meaning so direct, as marked a perfect agreement between

them. From that moment she doubted not of their being engaged to each

other; and the belief of it created no other surprise than that she, or

any of their friends, should be left by tempers so frank, to discover

it by accident.



Margaret related something to her the next day, which placed this

matter in a still clearer light. Willoughby had spent the preceding

evening with them, and Margaret, by being left some [[motifs/time|time]] in the parlour

with only him and Marianne, had had opportunity for observations,

which, with a most important face, she communicated to her eldest

sister, when they were next by themselves.



“Oh, Elinor!” she cried, “I have such a secret to tell you about

Marianne. I am sure she will be married to Mr. Willoughby very soon.”



“You have said so,” replied Elinor, “almost every day since they first

met on High-church Down; and they had not known each other a week, I

believe, before you were certain that Marianne wore his picture round

her neck; but it turned out to be only the miniature of our great

uncle.”



“But indeed this is quite another thing. I am sure they will be married

very soon, for he has got a lock of her hair.”



“Take care, Margaret. It may be only the hair of some great uncle of

_his_.”



“But, indeed, Elinor, it is Marianne’s. I am almost sure it is, for I

saw him cut it off. Last [[motifs/night|night]] after tea, when you and mama went out of

the room, they were whispering and talking together as fast as could

be, and he seemed to be begging something of her, and presently he took

up her scissors and cut off a long lock of her hair, for it was all

tumbled down her back; and he kissed it, and folded it up in a piece of

white paper; and put it into his pocket-book.”



For such particulars, stated on such authority, Elinor could not

withhold her credit; nor was she disposed to it, for the circumstance

was in perfect unison with what she had heard and seen herself.



Margaret’s sagacity was not always displayed in a way so satisfactory

to her sister. When Mrs. Jennings attacked her one evening at the park,

to give the name of the young man who was Elinor’s particular

favourite, which had been long a matter of great curiosity to her,

Margaret answered by looking at her sister, and saying, “I must not

tell, may I, Elinor?”



This of course made every [[concepts/body|body]] laugh; and Elinor tried to laugh too.

But the effort was painful. She was convinced that Margaret had fixed

on a person whose name she could not bear with composure to become a

standing joke with Mrs. Jennings.



Marianne felt for her most sincerely; but she did more harm than good

to the cause, by turning very red and saying in an angry manner to

Margaret,



“Remember that whatever your conjectures may be, you have no right to

repeat them.”



“I never had any conjectures about it,” replied Margaret; “it was you

who told me of it yourself.”



This increased the mirth of the company, and Margaret was eagerly

pressed to say something more.



“Oh! pray, Miss Margaret, let us know all about it,” said Mrs.

Jennings. “What is the gentleman’s name?”



“I must not tell, ma’am. But I know very [[motifs/well|well]] what it is; and I know

where he is too.”



“Yes, yes, we can guess where he is; at his own house at Norland to be

sure. He is the curate of the parish I dare say.”



“No, _that_ he is not. He is of no profession at all.”



“Margaret,” said Marianne with great warmth, “you know that all this is

an invention of your own, and that there is no such person in

existence.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], then, he is lately dead, Marianne, for I am sure there was such

a man once, and his name begins with an F.”



Most grateful did Elinor feel to Lady Middleton for observing, at this

moment, “that it rained very hard,” though she believed the

interruption to proceed less from any attention to her, than from her

ladyship’s great dislike of all such inelegant subjects of raillery as

delighted her husband and mother. The idea however started by her, was

immediately pursued by [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], who was on every occasion

mindful of the feelings of others; and much was said on the subject of

rain by both of them. Willoughby opened the piano-forte, and asked

Marianne to sit down to it; and thus amidst the various endeavours of

different people to quit the topic, it fell to the ground. But not so

easily did Elinor recover from the alarm into which it had thrown her.



A party was formed this evening for going on the following day to see a

very fine place about twelve miles from Barton, belonging to a

brother-in-law of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], without whose interest it could not

be seen, as the proprietor, who was then abroad, had left strict orders

on that head. The grounds were declared to be highly beautiful, and Sir

John, who was particularly warm in their praise, might be allowed to be

a tolerable judge, for he had formed parties to visit them, at least,

twice every [[motifs/summer|summer]] for the last ten years. They contained a noble piece

of [[motifs/water|water]]; a sail on which was to form a great part of the morning’s

amusement; cold provisions were to be taken, open carriages only to be

employed, and every thing conducted in the usual style of a complete

party of pleasure.



To some few of the company it appeared rather a bold undertaking,

considering the [[motifs/time|time]] of year, and that it had rained every day for the

last fortnight;—and Mrs. Dashwood, who had already a cold, was

persuaded by Elinor to stay at [[motifs/home|home]].


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XII.





Mentre Elinor e Marianne camminavano insieme la mattina seguente…

L’ultima comunicò una notizia alla sua sorella, che, nonostante…

Tutto ciò che sapeva riguardo all’imprudenza e alla mancanza di riflessione di Marianne…

La sorprese con la sua testimonianza eccessiva su entrambi gli argomenti. Marianne le disse…

Con grande gioia, Willoughby le aveva regalato un [[motifs/horse|cavallo]], uno in particolare.

Che si era nutrito delle risorse della sua tenuta nel Somersetshire… e che erano…

Calcolato appositamente per portare una donna… Senza considerare che…

Non faceva parte dei piani di sua madre tenere alcun [[motifs/horse|cavallo]]; se avesse voluto cambiare idea.

La sua determinazione a favore di questo dono la spinge ad acquistare un altro…

Servitore… e procurati anche un servitore che lo monti; in fondo, costruisci pure uno stallo per lui.

Per riceverli, aveva accettato il dono senza esitazione…

Ne parlò con sua sorella, estasiato.



“Intende inviare immediatamente il suo sposo nel Somersetshire per farlo.”

“E quando arriverà, cavalcheremo ogni giorno… Tu ne farai parte anche tu.”

Il suo uso con me… Immagina, cara Elinor, la gioia che può procurare…

“Galoppa su queste colline…”



Con estrema riluttanza, lei era disposta ad uscire da un simile sogno di felicità, per ritrovarsi nella realtà.

Comprendere tutte le verità sgradevoli che accompagnarono quell’evento… e per questo.

A volte rifiutava di sottomettersi a loro. Per quanto riguarda un altro servitore.

L’spesa sarebbe stata irrisoria; Mama, ne era sicura, non avrebbe mai obiettato.

Qualsiasi [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] andasse bene per lui; poteva sempre trovarne uno.

“Parco… Per quanto riguarda un stallo, anche la più semplice capanna sarebbe sufficiente. Elinor allora…”

Osò [[concepts/doubt|mettere in dubbio]] la convenienza che lei ricevesse un tale regalo da parte di.

Un uomo che lei conosceva così poco, o almeno che aveva conosciuto solo di recente. Era troppo.



“Ti sbagli, Elinor”, disse lei con calore, “a pensare che io sappia molto…”

Poco di Willoughby… Non lo conosco da molto tempo, ma…

Conoscerlo meglio di qualsiasi altra creatura…

Il mondo, tranne te e mamma. Non è la [[motifs/time|ora]] o l’[[motifs/time|opportunità]] il problema.

Per determinare l’intimità. È soltanto la disposizione personale. Sette anni sarebbero sufficienti.

Inadeguato per far conoscere alcune persone tra loro, e sette

“Giorni più che sufficienti per gli altri… Io dovrei considerarmi colpevole…”

Accettare un [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] dal mio fratello rappresenterebbe una maggior scorrettezza rispetto ad accettarlo da qualcun altro.

Willoughby: Di John so poco so che abbiamo vissuto insieme

“Da anni… ma riguardo a Willoughby, la mia opinione è ormai definita da tempo.”



“Elinor pensò fosse la cosa più saggia non toccare più quell’argomento. Sapeva che…”

Titolo:  
Il carattere irascibile della sorella… Opposizioni su un argomento così delicato non farebbero altro che rafforzare la situazione.

Più ancora, si atteneva alla propria opinione. Ma facendo appello al suo affetto…

Titolo:  
Sua madre, rappresentando i disagi che quella indulgenza comportava…

“La madre deve attingere alle proprie risorse interne, se… come probabilmente accadrà.”

Consentì a questo aumento delle strutture organizzative; poco dopo…

Trattenuta… e promise di non tentare sua madre a compiere azioni così imprudenti

Titolo:  
La gentilezza di menzionare l’offerta… e dirlo a Willoughby non appena lo vedrà.

Dopo di lui, deve essere rifiutato.



Lei mantenne la sua parola; e quando Willoughby venne a…

Cottage: lo stesso giorno, Elinor la sentì esprimere il proprio disappunto…

A bassa voce, quando fu costretto ad abbandonare l’idea di accettarlo…

Attualmente. Le ragioni di questo cambiamento erano, allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]], collegate tra loro.

E erano tali che rendevano impossibile qualsiasi ulteriore supplica da parte sua.

La sua preoccupazione, tuttavia, era evidente; e dopo averla espressa…

Con serietà, aggiunse, sempre a bassa voce: “Ma, Marianna, il [[motifs/horse|cavallo]], ”

“È ancora tuo, anche se al momento non puoi usarlo. Lo terrò con me solo fino a…”

Puoi rivendicarlo… Quando lascerai Barton per fondare la tua propria attività.

In un rifugio più stabile, la [[characters/queen|Regina]] Mab vi accoglierà.



Tutto questo fu sentito da Miss Dashwood; e per tutta la durata…

Il modo in cui lo pronunciava e il modo in cui le si rivolgeva…

Sorella, con il suo nome cristiano sola, percepì immediatamente un'intimità tale.

Titolo:  
Deciso, un significato così diretto, che segnava un perfetto accordo tra…

Da quel momento, non ebbe più dubbi che fossero fidanzati.

Altro… E la credenza in ciò non suscitò alcuna sorpresa, se non il fatto che lei…

Titolo:  
Qualsiasi dei loro amici, se lasciato alle proprie reazioni spontanee, potrebbe scoprire…

In modo accidentale.



Il giorno dopo, Margaret le raccontò qualcosa che cambiò completamente la situazione.

Il quadro diventa ancora più chiaro. Willoughby aveva trascorso il periodo precedente…

Trascorrendo la serata con loro, e poiché a Margaret veniva lasciato un po’ di [[motifs/time|tempo]] nel salotto.

Solo lui e Marianne avevano avuto l’opportunità di osservare.

“Con un’espressione molto seria, glielo comunicò il suo figlio maggiore.”

Sorella, quando erano soli insieme.



“Oh, Elinor!”, esclamò, “Devo raccontarti un segreto…”

“Marianne… Sono sicura che presto sposerà il signor Willoughby.”



“È vero,” rispose Elinor, “quasi ogni giorno da quando tutto è iniziato…”

Si incontrarono a High-church Down; e non si conoscevano nemmeno da una settimana…

"Credere, prima di essere sicuri che Marianna portasse con sé la sua immagine..."

Il suo collo… ma in realtà era solo una miniatura del nostro grande…

“Zio…”



“Ma davvero, questa è un’altra storia… Sono sicura che si sposeranno.”

“Molto presto, perché possiede una ciocca dei suoi capelli.”



“Stai attenta, Margaret… Potrebbe trattarsi soltanto dei capelli di qualche tuo lontano antenato…”

Il suo “segreto”.



“Ma davvero, Elinor, appartiene a Marianne… Sono quasi sicura che sia così.”

Lo vidi tagliarla via. L’ultima [[motifs/night|notte]], dopo il tè, quando tu e mamma siete uscite.

La stanza: sussurravano e parlavano insieme il più velocemente possibile

Sembrava che stesse chiedendole qualcosa… e poi prese…

Si tagliò una lunga ciocca di capelli… perché era tutto ciò che aveva.

Le cadde sul dorso; lui la baciò e la ripiegò in un pezzo di…

“Un documento tecnico… e lo mise nel suo portafoglio.”



Per tali particolari, dichiarati su tale autorità, Elinor non poteva…

Non le fu concesso il credito che meritava; inoltre, lei stessa non era disposta ad accettarlo, data quella particolare circostanza.

Corrispondeva perfettamente a ciò che lei stessa aveva sentito e visto.



La saggezza di Margaret non veniva sempre dimostrata in modo soddisfacente.

“Per sua sorella… Quando una sera la signora Jennings l’attaccò nel parco…”

Il giovane che era particolarmente legato a Elinor

Il preferito… qualcosa che da tempo suscitava in lei una grande curiosità.

“Devo proprio non farlo”, rispose Margaret guardando sua sorella.

“Posso dirtelo, Elinor?”



Questo, naturalmente, fece ridere tutti; anche Elinor cercò di ridere.

Un sforzo doloroso… Era convinta che Margaret ci avesse messo lo zampino.

Su una persona il cui nome lei non riusciva nemmeno a pronunciare senza provare disagio…

Una barzelletta ricorrente con la signora Jennings.



Compassione sincera… ma più danno che beneficio

“Per la causa…”, dicendo con il viso molto rosso e in tono arrabbiato…”

Margaret



"Ricorda che, per quanto possano essere le tue congetture, non hai alcun diritto..."

“Ripetili.”



“Non ho mai fatto alcuna congettura al riguardo”, rispose Margaret; “eri tu…”

“Chi me ne ha parlato è stato tu stesso.”



Questo aumentò l’allegria del gruppo, e Margaret era molto felice…

Costretto a dire qualcos’altro ancora.



“Oh! per favore, signorina Margaret, raccontateci tutto in dettaglio,” disse la signora.

Jennings. “Come si chiama questo signore?”



“Non devo dirlo, signora. Ma so molto bene di cosa si tratta; e lo so con certezza.”

“Anche lui è lì.”



“Sì, sì, possiamo indovinare dove si trova: sicuramente nella sua stessa casa a Norland.”

“Certo… Direi che sia il curato della parrocchia.”



"No, non è affatto così. Lui non ha alcuna professione."



“Margaret,” disse Marianne con grande calore, “tu sai che tutto questo…”

Un’invenzione tutta tua… e in realtà non esiste nessuna persona del genere.

"Esistenza."



“Allora, beh, di recente è morto, Marianne, perché ne sono sicura.”

“Un uomo una volta… il cui nome inizia con la lettera F.”



“Elinor era davvero molto grata a Lady Middleton per aver osservato, in quel momento…”

Titolo:  
“In quel momento, pioveva molto forte”, anche se lei credeva…

Interruzione che non derivava da alcuna attenzione verso di lei, ma da…

Il grande disprezzo della signora per tutti questi argomenti di scherzo poco raffinati…

Rallegrò molto suo marito e sua madre. Tuttavia, l’idea era nata proprio da lei.

Subito inseguito da [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], che era sempre presente in ogni occasione.

Con attenzione ai sentimenti altrui; e si discusse molto sull’argomento.

“La pioggia cade su entrambi… Willoughby aprì il pianoforte e chiese…”

Marianne si siederà a occuparsene; e così, tra le varie attività che la impegnano…

Persone diverse… per abbandonare l’argomento… ma non così semplicemente.

Elinor si riprese facilmente dall'allarme in cui era caduta.



Una festa è stata organizzata stasera per partire il giorno dopo e andare a…

Un luogo meraviglioso, situato a circa dodici miglia da Barton, di proprietà di…

Soggiunto del [[characters/colonel-brandon|-Colonnello Brandon]], senza il cui interessamento nulla sarebbe stato possibile.

Si diceva che, poiché il proprietario, che in quel momento si trovava all’estero, aveva impartito ordini severi…

Su quel punto… I terreni furono dichiarati di estrema bellezza, e Sir…

John, il cui elogio fu particolarmente caloroso, potrebbe essere…

Un giudice tollerabile… almeno perché aveva formato dei gruppi per andarle a trovare.

Due volte ogni [[motifs/summer|estate]], negli ultimi dieci anni. Contenevano pezzi davvero nobili.

Dell’[[motifs/water|acqua]]; una vela che avrebbe costituito la maggior parte della mattina.

Divertimento… ma solo provviste fredde da prendere, e carrozze aperte soltanto per…

Impiegati e tutto svolto nel solito stile di un’organizzazione efficiente

Festa di piacere.



Per alcuni membri del gruppo, sembrava davvero un’impresa audace.

Considerando la [[motifs/time|epoca]] dell’anno, e il fatto che aveva piovuto ogni giorno.

L’ultima quindicina… e la signora Dashwood, che già soffriva di raffreddore,

Convinto da Elinor a rimanere a [[motifs/home|casa]].



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_13--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 13 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 13" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/journey,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,motif/winter,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/truth,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER XIII.





Their intended excursion to Whitwell turned out very different from

what Elinor had expected. She was prepared to be wet through, fatigued,

and frightened; but the event was still more unfortunate, for they did

not go at all.



By ten o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] the whole party was assembled at the park, where they

were to breakfast. The morning was rather favourable, though it had

rained all [[motifs/night|night]], as the clouds were then dispersing across the sky,

and the sun frequently appeared. They were all in high spirits and good

humour, eager to be happy, and determined to submit to the greatest

inconveniences and hardships rather than be otherwise.



While they were at breakfast the letters were brought in. Among the

rest there was one for [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]];—he took it, looked at the

direction, changed colour, and immediately left the room.



“What is the matter with Brandon?” said Sir John.



Nobody could tell.



“I [[concepts/hope|hope]] he has had no bad news,” said Lady Middleton. “It must be

something extraordinary that could make [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] leave my

breakfast table so suddenly.”



In about five minutes he returned.



“No bad news, Colonel, I [[concepts/hope|hope]];” said Mrs. Jennings, as soon as he

entered the room.



“None at all, ma’am, I thank you.”



“Was it from Avignon? I [[concepts/hope|hope]] it is not to say that your sister is

worse.”



“No, ma’am. It came from town, and is merely a letter of business.”



“But how came the hand to discompose you so much, if it was only a

letter of business? Come, come, this won’t do, Colonel; so let us hear

the [[concepts/truth|truth]] of it.”



“My dear madam,” said Lady Middleton, “recollect what you are saying.”



“Perhaps it is to tell you that your cousin Fanny is married?” said

Mrs. Jennings, without attending to her daughter’s reproof.



“No, indeed, it is not.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], then, I know who it is from, Colonel. And I [[concepts/hope|hope]] she is [[motifs/well|well]].”



“Whom do you mean, ma’am?” said he, colouring a little.



“Oh! you know who I mean.”



“I am particularly sorry, ma’am,” said he, addressing Lady Middleton,

“that I should receive this letter today, for it is on business which

requires my immediate attendance in town.”



“In town!” cried Mrs. Jennings. “What can you have to do in town at

this [[motifs/time|time]] of year?”



“My own loss is great,” he continued, “in being obliged to leave so

agreeable a party; but I am the more concerned, as I [[concepts/fear|fear]] my presence

is necessary to gain your admittance at Whitwell.”



What a blow upon them all was this!



“But if you write a note to the housekeeper, Mr. Brandon,” said

Marianne, eagerly, “will it not be sufficient?”



He shook his head.



“We must go,” said Sir John.—“It shall not be put off when we are so

near it. You cannot go to town till tomorrow, Brandon, that is all.”



“I wish it could be so easily settled. But it is not in my power to

delay my [[motifs/journey|journey]] for one day!”



“If you would but let us know what your business is,” said Mrs.

Jennings, “we might see whether it could be put off or not.”



“You would not be six hours later,” said Willoughby, “if you were to

defer your [[motifs/journey|journey]] till our return.”



“I cannot afford to lose _one_ hour.”



Elinor then heard Willoughby say, in a low voice to Marianne, “There

are some people who cannot bear a party of pleasure. Brandon is one of

them. He was afraid of catching cold I dare say, and invented this

trick for getting out of it. I would lay fifty guineas the letter was

of his own writing.”



“I have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of it,” replied Marianne.



“There is no persuading you to change your mind, Brandon, I know of

old,” said Sir John, “when once you are determined on anything. But,

however, I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you will think better of it. Consider, here are the two

Miss Careys come over from Newton, the three Miss Dashwoods walked up

from the cottage, and Mr. Willoughby got up two hours before his usual

[[motifs/time|time]], on purpose to go to Whitwell.”



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] again repeated his sorrow at being the cause of

disappointing the party; but at the same [[motifs/time|time]] declared it to be

unavoidable.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], then, when will you come back again?”



“I [[concepts/hope|hope]] we shall see you at Barton,” added her ladyship, “as soon as

you can conveniently leave town; and we must put off the party to

Whitwell till you return.”



“You are very obliging. But it is so uncertain, when I may have it in

my power to return, that I dare not engage for it at all.”



“Oh! he must and shall come back,” cried Sir John. “If he is not here

by the end of the week, I shall go after him.”



“Ay, so do, Sir John,” cried Mrs. Jennings, “and then perhaps you may

find out what his business is.”



“I do not want to pry into other men’s concerns. I suppose it is

something he is ashamed of.”



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s horses were announced.



“You do not go to town on horseback, do you?” added Sir John.



“No. Only to Honiton. I shall then go post.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], as you are resolved to go, I wish you a good [[motifs/journey|journey]]. But you

had better change your mind.”



“I assure you it is not in my power.”



He then took leave of the whole party.



“Is there no chance of my seeing you and your sisters in town this

[[motifs/winter|winter]], Miss Dashwood?”



“I am afraid, none at all.”



“Then I must bid you farewell for a longer [[motifs/time|time]] than I should wish to

do.”



To Marianne, he merely bowed and said nothing.



“Come Colonel,” said Mrs. Jennings, “before you go, do let us know what

you are going about.”



He wished her a good morning, and, attended by Sir John, left the room.



The complaints and lamentations which politeness had hitherto

restrained, now burst forth universally; and they all agreed again and

again how provoking it was to be so disappointed.



“I can guess what his business is, however,” said Mrs. Jennings

exultingly.



“Can you, ma’am?” said almost every [[concepts/body|body]].

CAPITOLO XIII.





La loro prevista gita a Whitwell si rivelò molto diversa da quanto previsto…

Esattamente ciò che Elinor si aspettava: era pronta ad essere bagnata fradicia e stanca.

Spaventati e atterriti; ma l’evento risultò ancora più sfortunato, poiché…

Assolutamente no.



Alle dieci in punto, l'intero gruppo si riunì nel parco, dove.

Se ci fosse stato il tempo per colazione… La mattina era abbastanza favorevole, anche se…

Piovve tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]; mentre le nuvole si disperdevano nel cielo.

E il sole spesso splendeva… Erano tutti di ottimo umore e felici.

umorismo, desideroso di essere felice e deciso a sottomettersi al più grande.

Incomodi e difficoltà, piuttosto che fare altrimenti.



Mentre erano a colazione, arrivarono le lettere. Tra queste…

La direzione cambiò, il colore cambiò, e immediatamente lasciarono la stanza.

Nessuno poteva dirlo.

“La tavola per la colazione… così all’improvviso.”



Dopo circa cinque minuti tornò indietro.



“Nessune cattive notizie, Colonnello, spero,” disse la signora Jennings non appena lui.

Entrò nella stanza.



"Niente affatto, signora, la ringrazio."



“È arrivato da Avignone? Spero di no, altrimenti significherebbe che tua sorella, ”

“Peggio ancora.”



"No, signora. È arrivato dalla città e si tratta semplicemente di una lettera d’affari."



“Ma come mai quella mano riuscì a turbarvi così tanto, se in realtà era solo…”

Lettera di intenti? Ma no, colonnello, questo non va affatto… Allora, sentiamo cosa ha da dire.

La [[concepts/truth|verità]] su questo argomento.



“Mia cara signora,” disse Lady Middleton, “ricordi bene ciò che stai dicendo.”



“Forse è per dirvi che vostra cugina Fanny si è sposata…” disse

La signora Jennings, ignorando le rimproveri di sua figlia.



"No, indeed, it is not."



“Allora, so da chi proviene, Colonnello. E spero che stia bene.”



“A chi vi riferite, signora?” disse lui, arrossendo leggermente.



“Ah, capite di chi parlo…”



“Mi dispiace molto, signora”, disse rivolgendosi a Lady Middleton.

“Che io debba ricevere questa lettera oggi… perché riguarda una questione di lavoro.”

“Richiede la mia immediata presenza in città.”



“Sono in città!”, esclamò la signora Jennings. “Cosa potresti mai avere da fare in città…”

“In questa stagione dell’anno, ”



“La mia stessa perdita è enorme“, continuò, “perché sono costretto ad andarmene in questo modo…“

Adatto per una festa. Ma sono ancora più preoccupato, perché temo che la mia presenza possa creare problemi.

“È necessario scrivere questa lettera per ottenere l’ammissione a Whitwell.”



Che colpo terribile fu questo per tutti loro!



“Ma se scriveste una nota alla cameriera, signor Brandon…”, disse

“Marianne, con impazienza: ‘Non sarà sufficiente?’”



Scosse la testa.



“Dobbiamo andare”, disse Sir John. “Non possiamo rimandare, soprattutto ora che siamo così vicini…”

“Non puoi andare in città fino a domani, Brandon… È tutto qui.”



“Vorrei che potesse essere risolto così facilmente… Ma non è nelle mie possibilità.”

“Rinviate il mio [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] di un giorno!”



“Se solo ci diceste di cosa si tratta,” disse la signora.

“Jennings, potremmo vedere se sia possibile rimandarlo o meno.”



“Non saresti qui sei ore dopo”, disse Willoughby, “se avessi fatto così”.

“Rinvia il tuo [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] fino al nostro ritorno.”



“Non posso permettermi di perdere nemmeno un’ora.”



“Elinor allora sentì Willoughby dire, a bassa voce, a Marianne: ‘Ci…’”

Ci sono alcune persone che non riescono a sopportare le feste e le occasioni di divertimento… Brandon è uno di loro.

Loro… Probabilmente temeva di prendere freddo, quindi inventò questa scusa.

Titolo:  
“Un trucco per uscirne… Scommetterei cinquanta ghinee che quella lettera…”

“Della sua stessa scrittura.”



“Non ne ho alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]],” rispose Marianne.



"Non c’è modo di farti cambiare idea, Brandon… lo so."

“Vecchio”, disse Sir John, “quando una volta si è presa una decisione riguardo a qualcosa… Ma…”

Tuttavia, [[concepts/hope|spero]] che tu cambi idea. Riflettici: ecco qui le due opzioni.

Le tre signorine Dashwood si avvicinarono

Dalla capanna, e il signor Willoughby si alzò due ore prima del solito.

[[motifs/time|In quel momento]], con l’intento di andare a Whitwell.



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] ripeté ancora una volta il suo dolore per essere la causa di.

Deludere la compagnia, ma allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] dichiarare che.

Inevitabile.

“Spero di vedervi a Barton,” aggiunse la sua signoria, “non appena, ”

Puoi tranquillamente lasciare la città; e dobbiamo rimandare la festa…

“Whitwell… fino al tuo ritorno.”



“Sei molto gentile… Ma è davvero incerto quando potrò riceverlo.”

“Oh! Deve e tornerà indietro”, esclamò Sir John. “Se non è qui…”

“Entro la fine della settimana, andrò a cercarlo.”



“Ah sì, proprio così, signor John”, esclamò la signora Jennings, “e forse allora potrete…”

Scopri di che si occupa.



“Non voglio immischiarmi nelle faccende altrui… Immagino che sia così.”

“Qualcosa di cui si vergogna.”



I cavalli di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] furono annunciati.

“Meglio che cambi idea.”



“Vi assicuro che non è nelle mie possibilità.”



Poi si congedò da tutta la compagnia.



“Non c’è alcuna possibilità che io possa vedervi voi e le vostre sorelle in città questa volta?”

“[[motifs/winter|Inverno]], signorina Dashwood?”



“Temo di no, affatto.”



“Allora devo salutarvi per un periodo più lungo di quanto desidererei, ”

do.”



Di fronte a Marianne, si limitò ad inchinarsi senza dire nulla.



“Prima di andarsene, colonnello”, disse la signora Jennings, “per favore dicaci cosa…”

“Come stai procedendo…”



Le augurò buongiorno e, accompagnato da Sir John, lasciò la stanza.



Le lamentele e i rimpianti che la cortesia aveva fino ad allora…

Riservate fino ad ora, ora esplodono ovunque; e tutti concordano di nuovo…

Ancora una volta, quanto fosse frustrante essere così delusi.



“Posso indovinare di che si tratta”, disse la signora Jennings.

con esultanza.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_13--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 13 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 13" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/dance,motif/garden,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/fear,concept/hope"></span>


“Yes; it is about Miss Williams, I am sure.”



“And who is Miss Williams?” asked Marianne.



“What! do not you know who Miss Williams is? I am sure you must have

heard of her before. She is a relation of the Colonel’s, my dear; a

very near relation. We will not say how near, for [[concepts/fear|fear]] of shocking the

young ladies.” Then, lowering her voice a little, she said to Elinor,

“She is his natural daughter.”



“Indeed!”



“Oh, yes; and as like him as she can stare. I dare say the Colonel will

leave her all his fortune.”



When Sir John returned, he joined most heartily in the general regret

on so unfortunate an event; concluding however by observing, that as

they were all got together, they must do something by way of being

happy; and after some consultation it was agreed, that although

happiness could only be enjoyed at Whitwell, they might procure a

tolerable composure of mind by driving about the country. The carriages

were then ordered; Willoughby’s was first, and Marianne never looked

happier than when she got into it. He drove through the park very fast,

and they were soon out of sight; and nothing more of them was seen till

their return, which did not happen till after the return of all the

rest. They both seemed delighted with their drive; but said only in

general terms that they had kept in the lanes, while the others went on

the downs.



It was settled that there should be a [[motifs/dance|dance]] in the evening, and that

every [[concepts/body|body]] should be extremely merry all day long. Some more of the

Careys came to dinner, and they had the pleasure of sitting down nearly

twenty to table, which Sir John observed with great contentment.

Willoughby took his usual place between the two elder Miss Dashwoods.

Mrs. Jennings sat on Elinor’s right hand; and they had not been long

seated, before she leant behind her and Willoughby, and said to

Marianne, loud enough for them both to hear, “I have found you out in

spite of all your tricks. I know where you spent the morning.”



Marianne coloured, and replied very hastily, “Where, pray?”



“Did not you know,” said Willoughby, “that we had been out in my

curricle?”



“Yes, yes, Mr. Impudence, I know that very [[motifs/well|well]], and I was determined

to find out _where_ you had been to. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you like your house, Miss

Marianne. It is a very large one, I know; and when I come to see you, I

[[concepts/hope|hope]] you will have new-furnished it, for it wanted it very much when I

was there six years ago.”



Marianne turned away in great confusion. Mrs. Jennings laughed

heartily; and Elinor found that in her resolution to know where they

had been, she had actually made her own woman enquire of Mr.

Willoughby’s groom; and that she had by that method been informed that

they had gone to Allenham, and spent a considerable [[motifs/time|time]] there in

walking about the [[motifs/garden|garden]] and going all over the house.



Elinor could hardly believe this to be true, as it seemed very unlikely

that Willoughby should propose, or Marianne consent, to enter the house

while Mrs. Smith was in it, with whom Marianne had not the smallest

acquaintance.



As soon as they left the dining-room, Elinor enquired of her about it;

and great was her surprise when she found that every circumstance

related by Mrs. Jennings was perfectly true. Marianne was quite angry

with her for doubting it.



“Why should you imagine, Elinor, that we did not go there, or that we

did not see the house? Is not it what you have often wished to do

yourself?”



“Yes, Marianne, but I would not go while Mrs. Smith was there, and with

no other companion than Mr. Willoughby.”



“Mr. Willoughby however is the only person who can have a right to show

that house; and as he went in an open carriage, it was impossible to

have any other companion. I never spent a pleasanter morning in my

life.”



“I am afraid,” replied Elinor, “that the pleasantness of an employment

does not always evince its propriety.”



“On the contrary, nothing can be a stronger proof of it, Elinor; for if

there had been any real impropriety in what I did, I should have been

sensible of it at the [[motifs/time|time]], for we always know when we are acting

wrong, and with such a conviction I could have had no pleasure.”



“But, my dear Marianne, as it has already exposed you to some very

impertinent remarks, do you not now begin to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] the discretion of

your own conduct?”



“If the impertinent remarks of Mrs. Jennings are to be the proof of

impropriety in conduct, we are all offending every moment of our lives.

I value not her censure any more than I should do her commendation. I

am not sensible of having done anything wrong in walking over Mrs.

Smith’s grounds, or in seeing her house. They will one day be Mr.

Willoughby’s, and—”



“If they were one day to be your own, Marianne, you would not be

justified in what you have done.”



She blushed at this hint; but it was even visibly gratifying to her;

and after a ten minutes’ interval of earnest thought, she came to her

sister again, and said with great good humour, “Perhaps, Elinor, it

_was_ rather ill-judged in me to go to Allenham; but Mr. Willoughby

wanted particularly to show me the place; and it is a charming house, I

assure you.—There is one remarkably pretty sitting room up stairs; of a

nice comfortable size for constant use, and with modern furniture it

would be delightful. It is a corner room, and has windows on two sides.

On one side you look across the bowling-green, behind the house, to a

beautiful hanging wood, and on the other you have a view of the church

and village, and, beyond them, of those fine bold hills that we have so

often admired. I did not see it to advantage, for nothing could be more

forlorn than the furniture,—but if it were newly fitted up—a couple of

hundred pounds, Willoughby says, would make it one of the pleasantest

[[motifs/summer|summer]]-rooms in England.”



Could Elinor have listened to her without interruption from the others,

she would have described every room in the house with equal delight.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Sì; si tratta sicuramente di Miss Williams.”



“E chi è la signorina Williams?” chiese Marianne.



“Ma che! Non sapete chi sia la signorina Williams? Sono sicura che debba esservi familiare…”

L’ho già sentita parlare… È una parente del Colonnello, cara mia.

Una parentela molto stretta. Non diremo quanto stretta, per paura di scioccare qualcuno.

“Giovani signore…” Poi, abbassando un po’ la voce, disse a Elinor:

“È sua figlia biologica.”



“Certamente!”



“Ah sì… E lo guarda proprio come lui vorrebbe essere visto. Scommetto che il Colonnello sarà contento…”

“Lasciarle tutta la sua fortuna.”



Quando Sir John tornò, si unì con grande partecipazione al generale rammarico.

Su un evento così sfortunato; concludendo tuttavia osservando che…

Erano tutti riuniti, dovevano pur fare qualcosa per reagire

Felici… e dopo alcune consultazioni si decise che, nonostante…

Felicità che si può gustare solo a Whitwell… forse lì riusciranno ad ottenerla.

"Composizione mentale tollerabile grazie ai viaggi in campagna… Le carrozze."

Fu allora che vennero serviti; quello di Willoughby fu il primo, e Marianne non lo guardò mai.

Più felice di quando ci era entrata… Guidava molto velocemente attraverso il parco.

E presto scomparvero dalla vista; non si seppe più nulla di loro fino a…

Il loro ritorno, che non avvenne fino a quando tutti gli altri non furono tornati.

Rest… Entrambi sembravano molto soddisfatti della loro gita; ma dissero solo…

Titolo:  
Termini generali che avevano mantenuto nei loro percorsi, mentre gli altri proseguivano…

Le difficoltà.



Fu deciso che quella sera ci sarebbe stata una [[motifs/dance|danza]], e che.

Ogni [[concepts/body|-corpo]] dovrebbe essere estremamente felice per tutto il giorno. Ancora un po’ di questo.

“Careys vennero a cena e ebbero il piacere di sedersi insieme…”

Venti persone al tavolo, cosa che Sir John osservò con grande soddisfazione.

Willoughby prese il suo solito posto tra le due più anziane signorine Dashwood.

La signora Jennings sedeva alla destra di Elinor; e non erano trascorsi molti minuti…

“Seduta, si appoggiò indietro contro di lui e disse…”

“Marianne, abbastanza forte perché entrambi possano sentire: ‘Ti ho scoperta…’”

Nonostante tutti i tuoi trucchi… So dove hai trascorso la mattina.



“Dove, per favore?” rispose Marianne arrossendo e in fretta.



“Non lo sapevi?” disse Willoughby, “che eravamo stati fuori, nella mia…”

“La carrozzina?”



“Sì, sì, signor Sfrontatezza, lo so molto bene, e ero decisa, ”

Volevo sapere _dove_ eri stata. Spero che ti piaccia la tua casa, signorina.

Marianne… È un titolo molto lungo, lo so; e quando verrò a trovarti, io…

Spero che tu l’abbia arredata con mobili nuovi, perché ne aveva davvero bisogno quando io.

“C’era sei anni fa…”



Marianne si allontanò, profondamente confusa. La signora Jennings rise.

Con entusiasmo; ed Elinor si rese conto che nella sua determinazione di scoprire dove si trovassero…

Essendo stata così, aveva effettivamente fatto sì che la sua donna chiedesse informazioni al signor.

Il fidanzato di Willoughby; e che in quel modo era stata informata…

Erano andati ad Allenham e avevano trascorso lì un considerevole [[motifs/time|tempo]].

Camminare per il [[motifs/garden|giardino]] e visitare tutta la casa.



Elinor faticava a credere che fosse vero, sembrava davvero improbabile.

Che Willoughby facesse la proposta, o che Marianne acconsentisse a entrare in quella casa.

Mentre la signora Smith era lì dentro, con cui Marianne non aveva il minimo.

conoscenza.



Non appena lasciarono la sala da pranzo, Elinor le chiese cosa fosse successo.

E grande fu la sua sorpresa quando scoprì che ogni circostanza…

Il titolo “Related by Mrs. Jennings” era assolutamente vero: Marianne era davvero arrabbiata.

Per averlo messo in dubbio.



Perché dovresti pensare, Elinor, che non siamo andati lì, o che…

Non hai visto quella casa? Non è forse quello che hai sempre desiderato fare?

“Te stesso?”



“Sì, Marianne, ma non vorrei andare mentre la signora Smith è lì, ”

“Nessun altro compagno se non il signor Willoughby.”



“Tuttavia, il signor Willoughby è l’unica persona che possa avere il diritto di manifestare…”

Quella casa; e poiché vi entrava in una carrozza scoperta, era impossibile.

Nessun altro compagno… Non ho mai trascorso una mattina più piacevole della mia…

“La vita”.



“Temo”, rispose Elinor, “che la piacevolezza di un certo incarico…”

“Non sempre dimostra di essere appropriato.”



"#Contrariamente, nulla potrebbe essere una prova più evidente di ciò, Elinor; perché se..."

Se ci fosse stata davvero qualche irregolarità nelle mie azioni, avrei dovuto…

Ne eravamo consapevoli in quel momento, perché sappiamo sempre quando stiamo agendo.

“Errato… e con una tale convinzione che non avrei potuto provare alcun piacere.”



“Ma, mia cara Marianne, poiché ciò ha già esposto te a dei pericoli…”

Commenti impertinenti. Ora non inizi a [[concepts/doubt|dubitare]] della discrezione di,?

“La tua stessa condotta…”



Titolo:  
“Se le osservazioni impertinenti della signora Jennings devono costituire la prova…”

Con comportamenti inappropriati, tutti noi commettiamo errori in ogni momento della nostra vita.

Non valorizzo le sue critiche né più di quanto dovrei apprezzare i suoi elogi.

Non mi rendo conto di aver fatto nulla di sbagliato nell’aver calpestato la signora.

I terreni di Smith, o l’abitazione di lei. Un giorno diventeranno quelle del signor.

“Willoughby’s, e…”



“Se un giorno diventassero tuoi, Marianne, non saresti…”

“Giustificato da ciò che hai fatto.”



Arrossì di fronte a questo suggerimento; ma in realtà ne fu visibilmente compiaciuta.

Dopo dieci minuti di profonda riflessione, giunse a una conclusione…

Di nuovo la sorella, e con grande buon umorismo, disse: “Forse, Elinor, è, ”

Andare ad Allenham è stato davvero un errore da parte mia… ma il signor Willoughby…

Voleva particolarmente mostrarmi quel posto; ed è davvero una casa incantevole.

Vi assicuriamo… C’è un salotto al piano di sopra davvero molto bello; di una certa… eleganza.

Dimensioni comode e adatte all’uso frequente; in abbinamento con mobili moderni…

Sarebbe delizioso. È una stanza angolare, con finestre su entrambi i lati.

Da un lato, si può guardare attraverso il prato del bowling, dietro la casa, fino a.

Bello legno appeso… e dall’altra parte si ha la vista della chiesa.

Villaggio e campagna, e al di là di essi, quelle belle colline maestose che abbiamo sempre ammirato…

Spesso ammirato… Ma non lo ritenevo un vantaggio: nulla potrebbe essere di più…

Più desolato dei mobili… ma se fossero stati appena acquistati e sistemati…

“Cento sterline”, dice Willoughby, “farebbero di essa una delle case più piacevoli in cui vivere”.

“Stanze estive in Inghilterra.”



Avrebbe Elinor potuto ascoltarla senza interruzioni da parte degli altri?

Avrebbe descritto ogni stanza della casa con lo stesso entusiasmo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_14" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 14" data-chapter="Chapter 14" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/clock,motif/home,motif/marriage,motif/silence,motif/spring,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/melancholy,concept/poverty,concept/truth,concept/wonder,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER XIV.





The sudden termination of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s visit at the park, with his

steadiness in concealing its cause, filled the mind, and raised the

[[concepts/wonder|wonder]] of Mrs. Jennings for two or three days; she was a great

wonderer, as every one must be who takes a very lively interest in all

the comings and goings of all their acquaintance. She wondered, with

little intermission what could be the reason of it; was sure there must

be some bad news, and thought over every kind of distress that could

have befallen him, with a fixed determination that he should not escape

them all.



“Something very [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] must be the matter, I am sure,” said she. “I

could see it in his face. Poor man! I am afraid his circumstances may

be bad. The estate at Delaford was never reckoned more than two

thousand a year, and his brother left everything sadly involved. I do

think he must have been sent for about money matters, for what else can

it be? I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] whether it is so. I would give anything to know the

[[concepts/truth|truth]] of it. Perhaps it is about Miss Williams and, by the bye, I dare

say it is, because he looked so conscious when I mentioned her. May be

she is ill in town; nothing in the world more likely, for I have a

notion she is always rather sickly. I would lay any wager it is about

Miss Williams. It is not so very likely he should be distressed in his

circumstances _now_, for he is a very prudent man, and to be sure must

have cleared the estate by this [[motifs/time|time]]. I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] what it can be! May be

his sister is worse at Avignon, and has sent for him over. His setting

off in such a hurry seems very like it. [[motifs/well|Well]], I wish him out of all his

trouble with all my heart, and a good wife into the bargain.”



So wondered, so talked Mrs. Jennings. Her opinion varying with every

fresh conjecture, and all seeming equally probable as they arose.

Elinor, though she felt really interested in the welfare of Colonel

Brandon, could not bestow all the [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] on his going so suddenly away,

which Mrs. Jennings was desirous of her feeling; for besides that the

circumstance did not in her opinion justify such lasting amazement or

variety of speculation, her [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] was otherwise disposed of. It was

engrossed by the extraordinary [[motifs/silence|silence]] of her sister and Willoughby on

the subject, which they must know to be peculiarly interesting to them

all. As this [[motifs/silence|silence]] continued, every day made it appear more strange

and more incompatible with the disposition of both. Why they should not

openly acknowledge to her mother and herself, what their constant

behaviour to each other declared to have taken place, Elinor could not

imagine.



She could easily conceive that [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] might not be immediately in

their power; for though Willoughby was independent, there was no reason

to believe him rich. His estate had been rated by Sir John at about six

or seven hundred a year; but he lived at an expense to which that

income could hardly be equal, and he had himself often complained of

his [[concepts/poverty|poverty]]. But for this strange kind of secrecy maintained by them

relative to their engagement, which in fact concealed nothing at all,

she could not account; and it was so wholly contradictory to their

general opinions and practice, that a [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] sometimes entered her mind

of their being really engaged, and this [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] was enough to prevent her

making any inquiry of Marianne.



Nothing could be more expressive of attachment to them all, than

Willoughby’s behaviour. To Marianne it had all the distinguishing

tenderness which a [[archetypes/lover|lover]]’s heart could give, and to the rest of the

family it was the affectionate attention of a son and a brother. The

cottage seemed to be considered and loved by him as his [[motifs/home|home]]; many more

of his hours were spent there than at Allenham; and if no general

engagement collected them at the park, the exercise which called him

out in the morning was almost certain of ending there, where the rest

of the day was spent by himself at the side of Marianne, and by his

favourite pointer at her feet.



One evening in particular, about a week after [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] left the

country, his heart seemed more than usually open to every feeling of

attachment to the objects around him; and on Mrs. Dashwood’s happening

to mention her design of improving the cottage in the [[motifs/spring|spring]], he warmly

opposed every alteration of a place which affection had established as

perfect with him.



“What!” he exclaimed—“Improve this dear cottage! No. _That_ I will

never consent to. Not a stone must be added to its walls, not an inch

to its size, if my feelings are regarded.”



“Do not be alarmed,” said Miss Dashwood, “nothing of the kind will be

done; for my mother will never have money enough to attempt it.”



“I am heartily glad of it,” he cried. “May she always be poor, if she

can employ her riches no better.”



“Thank you, Willoughby. But you may be assured that I would not

sacrifice one sentiment of local attachment of yours, or of any one

whom I loved, for all the improvements in the world. Depend upon it

that whatever unemployed sum may remain, when I make up my accounts in

the [[motifs/spring|spring]], I would even rather lay it uselessly by than dispose of it

in a manner so painful to you. But are you really so attached to this

place as to see no defect in it?”



“I am,” said he. “To me it is faultless. Nay, more, I consider it as

the only form of building in which happiness is attainable, and were I

rich enough I would instantly pull Combe down, and build it up again in

the exact plan of this cottage.”



“With dark narrow stairs and a kitchen that smokes, I suppose,” said

Elinor.



“Yes,” cried he in the same eager tone, “with all and every thing

belonging to it;—in no one convenience or inconvenience about it,

should the least variation be perceptible. Then, and then only, under

such a roof, I might perhaps be as happy at Combe as I have been at

Barton.”



“I flatter myself,” replied Elinor, “that even under the disadvantage

of better rooms and a broader staircase, you will hereafter find your

own house as faultless as you now do this.”



“There certainly are circumstances,” said Willoughby, “which might

greatly endear it to me; but this place will always have one claim of

my affection, which no other can possibly share.”



Mrs. Dashwood looked with pleasure at Marianne, whose fine eyes were

fixed so expressively on Willoughby, as plainly denoted how [[motifs/well|well]] she

understood him.



“How often did I wish,” added he, “when I was at Allenham this [[motifs/time|time]]

twelvemonth, that Barton cottage were inhabited! I never passed within

view of it without admiring its situation, and grieving that no one

should live in it. How little did I then think that the very first news

I should hear from Mrs. Smith, when I next came into the country, would

be that Barton cottage was taken: and I felt an immediate satisfaction

and interest in the event, which nothing but a kind of prescience of

what happiness I should experience from it, can account for. Must it

not have been so, Marianne?” speaking to her in a lowered voice. Then

continuing his former tone, he said, “And yet this house you would

spoil, Mrs. Dashwood? You would rob it of its simplicity by imaginary

improvement! and this dear parlour in which our acquaintance first

began, and in which so many happy hours have been since spent by us

together, you would degrade to the condition of a common entrance, and

every [[concepts/body|body]] would be eager to pass through the room which has hitherto

contained within itself more real accommodation and comfort than any

other apartment of the handsomest dimensions in the world could

possibly afford.”



Mrs. Dashwood again assured him that no alteration of the kind should

be attempted.



“You are a good woman,” he warmly replied. “Your promise makes me easy.

Extend it a little farther, and it will make me happy. Tell me that not

only your house will remain the same, but that I shall ever find you

and yours as unchanged as your dwelling; and that you will always

consider me with the kindness which has made everything belonging to

you so dear to me.”



The promise was readily given, and Willoughby’s behaviour during the

whole of the evening declared at once his affection and happiness.



“Shall we see you tomorrow to dinner?” said Mrs. Dashwood, when he was

leaving them. “I do not ask you to come in the morning, for we must

walk to the park, to call on Lady Middleton.”



He engaged to be with them by four o’[[motifs/clock|clock]].

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_15--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 15 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 15" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/home,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/nature,concept/solitude,concept/suffering,setting/london"></span>


CHAPTER XV.





Mrs. Dashwood’s visit to Lady Middleton took place the next day, and

two of her daughters went with her; but Marianne excused herself from

being of the party, under some trifling pretext of employment; and her

mother, who concluded that a promise had been made by Willoughby the

[[motifs/night|night]] before of calling on her while they were absent, was perfectly

satisfied with her remaining at [[motifs/home|home]].



On their return from the park they found Willoughby’s curricle and

servant in waiting at the cottage, and Mrs. Dashwood was convinced that

her conjecture had been just. So far it was all as she had foreseen;

but on entering the house she beheld what no foresight had taught her

to expect. They were no sooner in the passage than Marianne came

hastily out of the parlour apparently in violent affliction, with her

handkerchief at her eyes; and without noticing them ran up stairs.

Surprised and alarmed they proceeded directly into the room she had

just quitted, where they found only Willoughby, who was leaning against

the mantel-piece with his back towards them. He turned round on their

coming in, and his countenance showed that he strongly partook of the

emotion which over-powered Marianne.



“Is anything the matter with her?” cried Mrs. Dashwood as she

entered—“is she ill?”



“I [[concepts/hope|hope]] not,” he replied, trying to look cheerful; and with a forced

smile presently added, “It is I who may rather expect to be ill—for I

am now [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] under a very heavy disappointment!”



“Disappointment?”



“Yes, for I am unable to keep my engagement with you. Mrs. Smith has

this morning exercised the privilege of riches upon a poor dependent

cousin, by sending me on business to [[settings/london|London]]. I have just received my

dispatches, and taken my farewell of Allenham; and by way of

exhilaration I am now come to take my farewell of you.”



“To [[settings/london|London]]!—and are you going this morning?”



“Almost this moment.”



“This is very unfortunate. But Mrs. Smith must be obliged;—and her

business will not detain you from us long I [[concepts/hope|hope]].”



He coloured as he replied, “You are very kind, but I have no idea of

returning into Devonshire immediately. My visits to Mrs. Smith are

never repeated within the twelvemonth.”



“And is Mrs. Smith your only friend? Is Allenham the only house in the

neighbourhood to which you will be welcome? For shame, Willoughby, can

you wait for an invitation here?”



His colour increased; and with his eyes fixed on the ground he only

replied, “You are too good.”



Mrs. Dashwood looked at Elinor with surprise. Elinor felt equal

amazement. For a few moments every one was silent. Mrs. Dashwood first

spoke.



“I have only to add, my dear Willoughby, that at Barton cottage you

will always be welcome; for I will not press you to return here

immediately, because you only can judge how far _that_ might be

pleasing to Mrs. Smith; and on this head I shall be no more disposed to

question your judgment than to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] your inclination.”



“My engagements at present,” replied Willoughby, confusedly, “are of

such a [[concepts/nature|nature]]—that—I dare not flatter myself—”



He stopped. Mrs. Dashwood was too much astonished to speak, and another

pause succeeded. This was broken by Willoughby, who said with a faint

smile, “It is folly to linger in this manner. I will not torment myself

any longer by remaining among friends whose society it is impossible

for me now to enjoy.”



He then hastily took leave of them all and left the room. They saw him

step into his carriage, and in a minute it was out of sight.



Mrs. Dashwood felt too much for speech, and instantly quitted the

parlour to give way in [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] to the concern and alarm which this

sudden departure occasioned.



Elinor’s uneasiness was at least equal to her mother’s. She thought of

what had just passed with anxiety and distrust. Willoughby’s behaviour

in taking leave of them, his embarrassment, and affectation of

cheerfulness, and, above all, his unwillingness to accept her mother’s

invitation, a backwardness so unlike a [[archetypes/lover|lover]], so unlike himself,

greatly disturbed her. One moment she feared that no serious design had

ever been formed on his side; and the next that some unfortunate

quarrel had taken place between him and her sister;—the distress in

which Marianne had quitted the room was such as a serious quarrel could

most reasonably account for, though when she considered what Marianne’s

[[motifs/love|love]] for him was, a quarrel seemed almost impossible.



But whatever might be the particulars of their separation, her sister’s

affliction was indubitable; and she thought with the tenderest

compassion of that violent sorrow which Marianne was in all probability

not merely giving way to as a relief, but feeding and encouraging as a

duty.



In about half an hour her mother returned, and though her eyes were

red, her countenance was not uncheerful.



“Our dear Willoughby is now some miles from Barton, Elinor,” said she,

as she sat down to work, “and with how heavy a heart does he travel?”



“It is all very strange. So suddenly to be gone! It seems but the work

of a moment. And last [[motifs/night|night]] he was with us so happy, so cheerful, so

affectionate? And now, after only ten minutes notice—Gone too without

intending to return!—Something more than what he owned to us must have

happened. He did not speak, he did not behave like himself. _You_ must

have seen the difference as [[motifs/well|well]] as I. What can it be? Can they have

quarrelled? Why else should he have shown such unwillingness to accept

your invitation here?”



“It was not inclination that he wanted, Elinor; I could plainly see

_that_. He had not the power of accepting it. I have thought it all

over I assure you, and I can perfectly account for every thing that at

first seemed strange to me as [[motifs/well|well]] as to you.”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XV.





La visita della signora Dashwood alla lady Middleton ebbe luogo il giorno seguente.

Due delle sue figlie la accompagnarono; ma Marianna si scusò e non partecipò.

Essendo una delle partecipanti alla festa, si è presentata con qualche pretesto banale legato al lavoro… e lei…

Titolo:  
“Madre… che concluse che Willoughby avesse fatto una promessa…”

La [[motifs/night|notte]] prima di andare a trovarla mentre loro non c'erano, tutto era perfettamente.

Risolta nel sapere che sarebbe rimasta a [[motifs/home|casa]].



Al loro ritorno dal parco, trovarono la carrozza di Willoughby…

Il servitore di guardia nella capanna… e la signora Dashwood ne era convinta.

La sua congettura si era rivelata corretta. Finora tutto stava andando esattamente come aveva previsto.

Ma entrando nella casa, vide qualcosa che nessuna previsione le aveva potuto rivelare.

Non si poteva certo aspettarselo… Non erano ancora entrati nel corridoio che Marianne arrivò.

"Fuori dalla sala in fretta e furia, chiaramente colta da un dolore violento… con lei."

Un fazzoletto sugli occhi; e senza accorgersene salì le scale.

Sorpresi e allarmati, entrarono direttamente nella stanza in cui lei si trovava

Appena lasciati, trovarono solo Willoughby, che era appoggiato contro…

Con le spalle rivolte verso di loro… Si girò verso di loro.

Entrando, il suo volto mostrava chiaramente che condivideva pienamente quell’opinione.

Un’emozione che sopraffaceva Marianne.



“C’è qualcosa che non va con lei?” esclamò la signora Dashwood mentre…

“È malata?”



“Non lo spero,” rispose, cercando di sembrare allegro; e con un tono forzato.

“Sorridi pure… Sono io, in realtà, quello che dovrebbe aspettarsi di ammalarsi… Perché…”

Ora sto soffrendo a causa di una delusione molto grande!



Delusione?



“Sì, perché non sono in grado di mantenere il nostro impegno. La signora Smith ha, ”

Questa mattina ho esercitato il privilegio della ricchezza su un povero dipendente

Cugino, mandandomi in viaggio d'affari a [[settings/london|Londra]]. Ho appena ricevuto il mio.

Dispacci e addio ad Allenham; per la strada di…

“Esultanza… Ora sono giunto al momento di dire addio a te.”



“A [[settings/london|Londra]]!. Partirai questa mattina?”



“Quasi in questo stesso istante.”



“È molto sfortunato. Ma la signora Smith deve essere obbligata a farlo, e anche lei.”

Spero che gli affari non ti trattenano lontano da noi a lungo.



“Siete molto gentili, ma non ne ho la minima idea”, rispose arrossendo.

Tornando immediatamente in Devonshire. Le mie visite a Madame Smith sono.

“Non mai ripetuto entro i dodici mesi successivi.”



“E la signora Smith è l’unica tua amica? È Allenham l’unico casa nella, ”

“Can you, indeed!”

“I can hardly tell myself. But suspicion of something unpleasant is the

But it would have been more like Willoughby to acknowledge them at

“Do not blame him, however, for departing from his character, where the

present. But this is no excuse for their concealing it from us.”



“Concealing it from us! my dear [[archetypes/child|child]], do you accuse Willoughby and

Marianne of concealment? This is strange indeed, when your eyes have

been reproaching them every day for incautiousness.”



“I want no proof of their affection,” said Elinor; “but of their

engagement I do.”



“I am perfectly satisfied of both.”



“Yet not a syllable has been said to you on the subject, by either of

them.”



“I have not wanted syllables where actions have spoken so plainly. Has

not his behaviour to Marianne and to all of us, for at least the last

wife, and that he felt for us the attachment of the nearest relation?

Have we not perfectly understood each other? Has not my consent been

daily asked by his looks, his manner, his attentive and affectionate

such a thought occur to you? How is it to be supposed that Willoughby,

persuaded as he must be of your sister’s [[motifs/love|love]], should leave her, and

“I confess,” replied Elinor, “that every circumstance except _one_ is

“How strange this is! You must think wretchedly indeed of Willoughby,

“No, I cannot think that. He must and does [[motifs/love|love]] her I am sure.”

“You must remember, my dear mother, that I have never considered this

matter as certain. I have had my doubts, I confess; but they are

fainter than they were, and they may soon be entirely done away. If we

find they correspond, every [[concepts/fear|fear]] of mine will be removed.”



“A mighty concession indeed! If you were to see them at the altar, you
