CHAPTER XVI.





Marianne would have thought herself very inexcusable had she been able

to [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] at all the first [[motifs/night|night]] after parting from Willoughby. She

would have been ashamed to look her family in the face the next

morning, had she not risen from her bed in more need of repose than

when she lay down in it. But the feelings which made such composure a

disgrace, left her in no danger of incurring it. She was awake the

whole [[motifs/night|night]], and she wept the greatest part of it. She got up with a

headache, was unable to talk, and unwilling to take any nourishment;

giving [[motifs/pain|pain]] every moment to her mother and sisters, and forbidding all

attempt at consolation from either. Her sensibility was potent enough!



When breakfast was over she walked out by herself, and wandered about

the village of Allenham, indulging the recollection of past enjoyment

and crying over the present reverse for the chief of the morning.



The evening passed off in the equal indulgence of feeling. She played

over every favourite song that she had been used to play to Willoughby,

every air in which their voices had been oftenest joined, and sat at

the instrument gazing on every line of music that he had written out

for her, till her heart was so heavy that no farther sadness could be

gained; and this nourishment of grief was every day applied. She spent

whole hours at the pianoforte alternately singing and crying; her voice

often totally suspended by her [[motifs/tears|tears]]. In books too, as [[motifs/well|well]] as in

music, she courted the misery which a contrast between the past and

present was certain of giving. She read nothing but what they had been

used to read together.



Such violence of affliction indeed could not be supported for ever; it

sunk within a few days into a calmer [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]]; but these employments,

to which she daily recurred, her solitary walks and silent meditations,

still produced occasional effusions of sorrow as lively as ever.



No letter from Willoughby came; and none seemed expected by Marianne.

Her mother was surprised, and Elinor again became uneasy. But Mrs.

Dashwood could find explanations whenever she wanted them, which at

least satisfied herself.



“Remember, Elinor,” said she, “how very often Sir John fetches our

letters himself from the post, and carries them to it. We have already

agreed that secrecy may be necessary, and we must acknowledge that it

could not be maintained if their correspondence were to pass through

Sir John’s hands.”



Elinor could not deny the [[concepts/truth|truth]] of this, and she tried to find in it a

motive sufficient for their [[motifs/silence|silence]]. But there was one method so

direct, so simple, and in her opinion so eligible of knowing the real

state of the affair, and of instantly removing all mystery, that she

could not help suggesting it to her mother.



“Why do you not ask Marianne at once,” said she, “whether she is or she

is not engaged to Willoughby? From you, her mother, and so kind, so

indulgent a mother, the question could not give offence. It would be

the natural result of your affection for her. She used to be all

unreserve, and to you more especially.”



“I would not ask such a question for the world. Supposing it possible

that they are not engaged, what distress would not such an enquiry

inflict! At any rate it would be most ungenerous. I should never

deserve her confidence again, after forcing from her a confession of

what is meant at present to be unacknowledged to any one. I know

Marianne’s heart: I know that she dearly loves me, and that I shall not

be the last to whom the affair is made known, when circumstances make

the revealment of it eligible. I would not attempt to force the

confidence of any one; of a [[archetypes/child|child]] much less; because a sense of duty

would prevent the denial which her wishes might direct.”



Elinor thought this generosity overstrained, considering her sister’s

youth, and urged the matter farther, but in vain; common sense, common

care, common prudence, were all sunk in Mrs. Dashwood’s romantic

delicacy.



It was several days before Willoughby’s name was mentioned before

Marianne by any of her family; Sir John and Mrs. Jennings, indeed, were

not so nice; their witticisms added [[motifs/pain|pain]] to many a painful hour;—but

one evening, Mrs. Dashwood, accidentally taking up a volume of

Shakespeare, exclaimed,



“We have never finished [[characters/hamlet|Hamlet]], Marianne; our dear Willoughby went away

before we could get through it. We will put it by, that when he comes

again...But it may be months, perhaps, before _that_ happens.”



“Months!” cried Marianne, with strong surprise. “No—nor many weeks.”



Mrs. Dashwood was sorry for what she had said; but it gave Elinor

pleasure, as it produced a reply from Marianne so expressive of

confidence in Willoughby and knowledge of his intentions.



One morning, about a week after his leaving the country, Marianne was

prevailed on to join her sisters in their usual walk, instead of

wandering away by herself. Hitherto she had carefully avoided every

companion in her rambles. If her sisters intended to walk on the downs,

she directly stole away towards the lanes; if they talked of the

valley, she was as speedy in climbing the hills, and could never be

found when the others set off. But at length she was secured by the

exertions of Elinor, who greatly disapproved such continual seclusion.

They walked along the [[motifs/road|road]] through the valley, and chiefly in [[motifs/silence|silence]],

for Marianne’s _mind_ could not be controlled, and Elinor, satisfied

with gaining one point, would not then attempt more. Beyond the

entrance of the valley, where the country, though still rich, was less

wild and more open, a long stretch of the [[motifs/road|road]] which they had travelled

on first coming to Barton, lay before them; and on reaching that point,

they stopped to look around them, and examine a prospect which formed

the distance of their view from the cottage, from a spot which they had

never happened to reach in any of their walks before.



Amongst the objects in the scene, they soon discovered an animated one;

it was a man on horseback riding towards them. In a few minutes they

could distinguish him to be a gentleman; and in a moment afterwards

Marianne rapturously exclaimed,



“It is he; it is indeed;—I know it is!”—and was hastening to meet him,

when Elinor cried out,



“Indeed, Marianne, I think you are mistaken. It is not Willoughby. The

person is not tall enough for him, and has not his air.”



“He has, he has,” cried Marianne, “I am sure he has. His air, his coat,

his [[motifs/horse|horse]]. I knew how soon he would come.”



She walked eagerly on as she spoke; and Elinor, to screen Marianne from

particularity, as she felt almost certain of its not being Willoughby,

quickened her pace and kept up with her. They were soon within thirty

yards of the gentleman. Marianne looked again; her heart sunk within

her; and abruptly turning round, she was hurrying back, when the voices

of both her sisters were raised to detain her; a third, almost as [[motifs/well|well]]

known as Willoughby’s, joined them in begging her to stop, and she

turned round with surprise to see and welcome [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]].



He was the only person in the world who could at that moment be

forgiven for not being Willoughby; the only one who could have gained a

smile from her; but she dispersed her [[motifs/tears|tears]] to smile on _him_, and in

her sister’s happiness forgot for a [[motifs/time|time]] her own disappointment.



He dismounted, and giving his [[motifs/horse|horse]] to his servant, walked back with

them to Barton, whither he was purposely coming to visit them.



He was welcomed by them all with great cordiality, but especially by

Marianne, who showed more warmth of regard in her reception of him than

even Elinor herself. To Marianne, indeed, the meeting between Edward

and her sister was but a continuation of that unaccountable coldness

which she had often observed at Norland in their mutual behaviour. On

Edward’s side, more particularly, there was a deficiency of all that a

[[archetypes/lover|lover]] ought to look and say on such an occasion. He was confused,

seemed scarcely sensible of pleasure in seeing them, looked neither

rapturous nor gay, said little but what was forced from him by

questions, and distinguished Elinor by no mark of affection. Marianne

saw and listened with increasing surprise. She began almost to feel a

dislike of Edward; and it ended, as every feeling must end with her, by

carrying back her thoughts to Willoughby, whose manners formed a

contrast sufficiently striking to those of his brother elect.



After a short [[motifs/silence|silence]] which succeeded the first surprise and enquiries

of meeting, Marianne asked Edward if he came directly from [[settings/london|London]]. No,

he had been in Devonshire a fortnight.



“A fortnight!” she repeated, surprised at his being so long in the same

county with Elinor without seeing her before.



He looked rather distressed as he added, that he had been staying with

some friends near Plymouth.



“Have you been lately in Sussex?” said Elinor.



“I was at Norland about a month ago.”



“And how does dear, dear Norland look?” cried Marianne.



“Dear, dear Norland,” said Elinor, “probably looks much as it always

does at this [[motifs/time|time]] of the year. The woods and walks thickly covered with

dead [[motifs/leaves|leaves]].”



“Oh,” cried Marianne, “with what transporting sensation have I formerly

seen them fall! How have I delighted, as I walked, to see them driven

in showers about me by the [[motifs/wind|wind]]! What feelings have they, the season,

the air altogether inspired! Now there is no one to regard them. They

are seen only as a nuisance, swept hastily off, and driven as much as

possible from the sight.”



“It is not every one,” said Elinor, “who has your passion for dead

[[motifs/leaves|leaves]].”



“No; my feelings are not often shared, not often understood. But

_sometimes_ they are.”—As she said this, she sunk into a reverie for a

few moments;—but rousing herself again, “Now, Edward,” said she,

calling his attention to the prospect, “here is Barton valley. Look up

to it, and be tranquil if you can. Look at those hills! Did you ever

see their equals? To the left is Barton park, amongst those woods and

plantations. You may see the end of the house. And there, beneath that

farthest [[motifs/hill|hill]], which rises with such grandeur, is our cottage.”



“It is a beautiful country,” he replied; “but these bottoms must be

dirty in [[motifs/winter|winter]].”



“How can you think of dirt, with such objects before you?”



“Because,” replied he, smiling, “among the rest of the objects before

me, I see a very dirty lane.”



“How strange!” said Marianne to herself as she walked on.



“Have you an agreeable neighbourhood here? Are the Middletons pleasant

people?”



“No, not all,” answered Marianne; “we could not be more unfortunately

situated.”



“Marianne,” cried her sister, “how can you say so? How can you be so

unjust? They are a very respectable family, Mr. Ferrars; and towards us

have behaved in the friendliest manner. Have you forgot, Marianne, how

many pleasant days we have owed to them?”



“No,” said Marianne, in a low voice, “nor how many painful moments.”



Elinor took no notice of this; and directing her attention to their

visitor, endeavoured to support something like discourse with him, by

talking of their present residence, its conveniences, &c. extorting

from him occasional questions and remarks. His coldness and reserve

mortified her severely; she was vexed and half angry; but resolving to

regulate her behaviour to him by the past rather than the present, she

avoided every appearance of resentment or displeasure, and treated him

as she thought he ought to be treated from the family connection.

CAPITOLO XVI.





Marianne avrebbe pensato di non avere alcuna scusa se fosse stata in grado…

Non riusciva a [[motifs/sleep|)dormire]] nemmeno la prima [[motifs/night|notte]] dopo essersi separata da Willoughby. Lei.

Avrebbe avuto vergogna di guardare in faccia la sua famiglia il giorno dopo

“Mattina… se solo non si fosse alzata dal letto, avendo più bisogno di riposo che…”

Quando vi si sdraiò… Ma i sentimenti che rendevano possibile tale compostezza…

Disgrazia… che non la mise mai in pericolo di subirla. Era sveglia…

Per tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], pianse quasi senza sosta. Si alzò il mattino seguente con.

Mal di testa, impossibilità di parlare e riluttanza ad assumere qualsiasi alimento.

Causando continuo [[motifs/pain|dolore]] a sua madre e alle sue sorelle, e vietando loro tutto.

Un tentativo di conforto da parte di entrambi. La sua sensibilità era davvero forte abbastanza!



Dopo colazione, uscì da sola e iniziò a girovagare per le strade.

Il villaggio di Allenham, immerso nei ricordi dei piaceri passati

e piangendo per la sfortuna attuale del capo della mattina.



La serata trascorse in un’atmosfera di totale abbandono alle emozioni. Lei suonò…

su ogni canzone preferita che lei era abituata a suonare per Willoughby.

In ogni luogo dove le loro voci si univano più spesso…

L'strumento che osserva ogni nota di musica che ha scritto

Per lei, fino a quando il suo cuore non divenne così pesante da non poter contenere più alcuna tristezza…

Acquisita… e questa “nutrizione del dolore” veniva applicata ogni giorno. Lei trascorreva il suo tempo…

Ore intere trascorse al pianoforte, alternando canti e pianti… La sua voce…

Spesso completamente sommersa dalle sue [[motifs/tears|lacrime]]. Anche nei libri, come ben si sa.

Musica… Lei cercò deliberatamente quella sofferenza che derivava dal contrasto tra il passato e il presente.

Certezza di dare… Lei leggeva soltanto ciò che era stato stabilito.

Erano soliti leggere insieme.



Una violenza così intensa di sofferenze non poteva certamente durare per sempre; era insostenibile…

In pochi giorni cadde in una più tranquilla [[concepts/melancholy|melancolia]]; ma questi impegni.

Alle sue solitarie passeggiate e silenziose meditazioni, a cui ricorreva ogni giorno…

Continuava ancora a provare, di tanto in tanto, momenti di tristezza altrettanto intensi quanto prima.



Non arrivò alcuna lettera da Willoughby; e sembrava che nemmeno Marianne se l’aspettasse.

Sua madre rimase sorpresa, ed Elinor si sentì di nuovo a disagio. Ma la signora.

Dashwood poteva trovare spiegazioni ogni volta che ne aveva bisogno…

Nemmeno lei era del tutto soddisfatta.



“Ricorda, Elinor,” disse lei, “quanto spesso Sir John venga a prendere noi…”

“Si ritira le lettere dalla cassetta della posta e le porta subito lì. Lo abbiamo già fatto…”

Si è concordato sul fatto che la segretezza possa essere necessaria, e dobbiamo ammetterlo.

Non potrebbe essere mantenuto se la loro corrispondenza dovesse essere trasmessa…

“Le mani di Sir John”.



Elinor non poteva negare la [[concepts/truth|verità]] di ciò, e cercò di trovarvi qualcosa di.

Motivi sufficienti per il loro [[motifs/silence|silenzio]]. Ma c'era un metodo in particolare.

Diretta, così semplice… e, secondo lei, perfettamente idonea a conoscere la verità

Lo stato delle cose… e la necessità di eliminare immediatamente ogni mistero.

Non potei fare a meno di suggerirlo a sua madre.



“Perché non chiedi subito a Marianne se lei è… o se non lo è”, disse.

“Non è fidanzata con Willoughby? Da te, sua madre… così gentile e premurosa…”

“Una madre indulgente… Una domanda che non poteva offendere nessuno.”

Il risultato naturale del tuo affetto per lei… Un tempo era tutta…

“Senza riserve, e soprattutto per te.”



“Non chiederei mai una cosa del genere, nemmeno per tutto l’oro del mondo… Anche se fosse possibile.”

Che non siano fidanzati… Quanta angoscia potrebbe causare una domanda del genere

“Inflicted! Comunque sarebbe estremamente ingiusto… Non dovrei mai farlo.”

Riscattare la sua fiducia, dopo averla costretta a confessare…

Ciò che attualmente viene ignorato da tutti… Lo so.

Il cuore di Marianne: So che mi ama profondamente, e so che non…

Essere gli ultimi a venire informati, quando le circostanze lo richiedono

La rivelazione di ciò che è idoneo… Non cercherei mai di forzarlo.

La fiducia di chiunque; figuriamoci quella di un [[archetypes/child|bambino]]; perché c'è sempre un senso del dovere.

“Ciò che avrebbe impedito il rifiuto che i suoi desideri potessero comportare.”



Elinor riteneva che tale generosità fosse eccessiva, considerando le circostanze della sua sorella…

“Giovinezza… e si cercò di approfondire la questione, ma invano; il buon senso, semplicemente, prevalse.”

“Cura, buon senso comune… tutto venne dimenticato nella natura romantica della signora Dashwood.”

Delicatezza.



Trascorsero diversi giorni prima che il nome di Willoughby venisse menzionato di nuovo.

Marianne… da nessuno della sua famiglia; anzi, Sir John e la signora Jennings…

Niente di così piacevole; i loro scherzi aggiungevano [[motifs/pain|dolore]] a molte ore difficili, ma.

Un sera, la signora Dashwood, prendendo per errore un volume…

“Shakespeare!”, esclamò.



“Non abbiamo mai finito di leggere [[characters/hamlet|Amleto]], Marianne; il nostro caro Willoughby se n’è andato, ”

Prima che riuscissimo a risolverlo… Lo metteremo da parte, fino al suo arrivo.

Di nuovo… Ma forse passeranno mesi prima che ciò accada.



“Mesi!”, esclamò Marianne, sorpresa. “No… nemmeno molte settimane.”



Mrs. Dashwood si pentì di ciò che aveva detto; ma questo fece sì che Elinor…

Piacere, poiché suscitò da parte di Marianne una risposta così espressiva…

Fiducia in Willoughby e conoscenza delle sue intenzioni.



Un mattino, circa una settimana dopo la sua partenza dal paese, Marianne…

Preferì unirsi alle sue sorelle nella loro solita passeggiata, invece di…

Perduta da sola… Fino ad allora aveva sempre evitato con cura ogni situazione che potesse portarla in quella condizione.

Compagno delle sue escursioni… Se le sue sorelle intendevano camminare lungo quelle colline…

Si diresse direttamente verso i viali; se ne parlavano…

Velocissima nelle salite…

Trovata quando gli altri se ne andarono… Ma alla fine fu recuperata.

Gli sforzi di Elinor, che disapprovava profondamente tale costante isolamento.

Camminarono lungo la [[motifs/road|strada]] attraverso la valle, per lo più in [[motifs/silence|silenzio]].

Perché la mente di Marianne non poteva essere controllata… e Elinor, soddisfatta.

Con l’acquisizione di un punto, non si cercherebbe più nulla in più. Oltre a questo…

Entrata nella valle, dove la terra, sebbene ancora rigogliosa, appariva meno…

Deserto e più aperto, un lungo tratto di [[motifs/road|strada]] che avevano percorso.

Al loro arrivo a Barton, si presentò davanti a loro; e una volta raggiunto quel punto…

Si fermarono per guardarsi intorno e esaminare il paesaggio che si apriva davanti a loro.

La distanza del loro punto di osservazione dal capanno

Non era mai successo che, durante le loro passeggiate, provassero ad infilare la mano all’interno di nulla.



Tra gli oggetti presenti nella scena, trovarono presto uno che era animato.

Un uomo a cavallo si stava avvicinando a loro. In pochi minuti…

Si poteva distinguere che era un gentiluomo; e poco dopo…

“Marianne esclamò con entusiasmo…”



“È lui; davvero è lui… Lo so con certezza!” – e si affrettava ad andargli incontro.

Quando Elinor gridò



“Infatti, Marianne, penso che ti sbagli. Non è Willoughby.”

“Quella persona non è abbastanza alta per lui, e non ha lo stesso fascino…”



“Lo ha, lo ha,” gridò Marianna, “Sono sicura che lo abbia. Il suo modo di comportarsi, il suo cappotto…”

Il suo [[motifs/horse|cavallo]]. Sapevo che sarebbe arrivato presto.



Continuò ad avanzare con impazienza mentre parlava; e Elinor, per proteggere Marianne…

“Particolariità… poiché era quasi certa che non si trattasse di Willoughby.”

Aumentò il passo per raggiungerla; in poco tempo si trovarono entrambe a meno di trenta metri di distanza l’una dall’altra.

“Iarde del gentiluomo… Marianna guardò di nuovo; il suo cuore si spezzò.”

Lei… e all’improvviso si girò di scatto, tornando di corsa indietro, mentre quelle voci…

Entrambe le sue sorelle erano state educate per trattenerla; una terza, quasi altrettanto [[motifs/well|benestante,]]

Conosciuta come quella di Willoughby, si unì a loro nel supplicarla di smettere…

Si girò sorpreso per vedere e salutare [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]].



L’unico al mondo in grado di farlo in quel momento

“Perdonato per non essere Willoughby… l’unico che avrebbe potuto vincere.”

Lei sorrise, ma asciugò le sue [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] per poter sorridere a _lui_.

La felicità di sua sorella le fece dimenticare, per un [[motifs/time|momento]], la propria delusione.



Scese da cavallo e, affidando il suo [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] al suo servitore, tornò a piedi.

Li portò a Barton, dove era appunto andato apposta per far loro visita.



Fu accolto da tutti loro con grande cordialità, ma soprattutto da…

Marianne, che dimostrò un calore maggiore nel suo accogliimento verso di lui…

Anche Elinor stessa… Per Marianne, invece, l’incontro tra Edward…

E sua sorella non era altro che una continuazione di quella fredda indifferenza inspiegabile.

Quello che spesso aveva notato a Norland nel loro comportamento reciproco…

Il lato di Edward… in particolare, mancava tutto ciò che è necessario

Un [[archetypes/lover|innamorato]] dovrebbe sapere cosa dire in una situazione del genere. Lui, invece, era confuso.

Sembrava quasi incapace di provare piacere nel vederli; non mostrava alcuna reazione positiva.

Né estasiato né gioioso, diceva poco, e solo ciò che gli veniva imposto di dire…

Domande… e nessun segno di affetto da parte di Elinor verso Marianne.

Ascoltava e guardava con sempre maggiore sorpresa… Iniziò quasi a provare…

Disprezzo per Edward… E tutto finì, come deve finire ogni sentimento con lei…

Portando i suoi pensieri a Willoughby, il cui comportamento rappresentava…

Un contrasto abbastanza evidente rispetto a quello di suo fratello eletto.



Dopo un breve [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] che seguì la prima sorpresa e le prime domande.

Durante l’incontro, Marianne chiese a Edward se fosse venuto direttamente da [[settings/london|Londra]]. No.

Era stato nel Devonshire per due settimane.



“Due settimane!”, ripeté, sorpresa dal fatto che fosse rimasto nello stesso posto per così tanto tempo.

Una contea con Elinor, senza averla mai vista prima.



Sembrava piuttosto preoccupato mentre aggiungeva che aveva soggiornato da…

Alcuni amici vicino a Plymouth.



“Sei stato recentemente nel Sussex?” chiese Elinor.



"Ero a Norland circa un mese fa."



“E come sta il caro, adorato Norland?” esclamò Marianne.



“Caro, caro Norland,” disse Elinor, “probabilmente sembra esattamente come sempre…”

Vengono considerati soltanto un fastidio, spazzati via in fretta e…

“Possibile a prima vista…”

“[[motifs/leaves|Le foglie]].”



"No; i miei sentimenti spesso non vengono condivisi, spesso non vengono compresi. Ma..."

“A volte lo sono…” Mentre pronunciava queste parole, si immerse in una sorta di riflessione.

“Solo qualche momento… ma poi si riprese e disse: ‘Ora, Edward’.”

“Ecco la valle di Barton – guardate in alto”, disse, attirando la sua attenzione su quella vista.

Aggrappati a ciò che hai e cerca di rimanere sereno… Guarda quelle colline! L’hai mai fatto prima?

“Vedere i propri pari… A sinistra c’è Barton Park, tra quei boschi…”

Le piantagioni. Si può vedere la fine di quella casa. E lì, sotto quel.

La più lontana delle [[motifs/hill|colline]], quella che si erge con tale maestosità, è la nostra capanna.



“È un bel paese,” rispose; “ma questi fondali devono essere…”

“Sporco nell’[[motifs/winter|inverno]].”



"#Come puoi pensare a cose volgari, con oggetti del genere davanti ai tuoi occhi?"



“Perché,” rispose lui sorridendo, “tra tutti gli altri oggetti presenti…”

“Vedo una strada molto sporca…”



“Che strano!” pensò Marianne mentre continuava a camminare.



Titolo: “Avete un quartiere piacevole qui? I Middleton sono persone gentili?”

“Gente?”



“No, non tutti,” rispose Marianne; “non potremmo essere più sfortunati…”

“Situato in una posizione strategica.”



“Marianne”, gridò sua sorella, “come puoi dire una cosa del genere? Come può essere così…”

“Ingiusto? Sono una famiglia molto rispettabile, signor Ferrars… E nei nostri confronti…”

Si sono comportati nel modo più amichevole possibile… Hai dimenticato, Marianne, come?

“Quanti bei giorni abbiamo trascorso insieme a loro…”



“No,” disse Marianne, a bassa voce, “né per quanti momenti dolorosi possano esserci.”



Elinor non prestò attenzione a questo; e rivolse la sua attenzione verso di loro…

Visitatore: cercò di avviare una sorta di conversazione con lui, attraverso…

Parlando della loro attuale residenza, dei suoi comodi, ecc., estorcendo…

Domande e osservazioni occasionali da parte sua… La sua freddezza e riservatezza.

La umiliò profondamente; era irritata e quasi arrabbiata; ma decise di…

Regola il suo comportamento nei suoi confronti in base al passato e non al presente…

Evitò qualsiasi segno di risentimento o disappunto e lo trattò con gentilezza.

Poiché riteneva che dovesse essere trattato in base ai legami familiari.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_17" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 17" data-chapter="Chapter 17" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/grave,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/ambition,concept/body,concept/deception,concept/doubt,concept/greatness,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/wonder,form/novel,setting/london"></span>


CHAPTER XVII.





Mrs. Dashwood was surprised only for a moment at seeing him; for his

coming to Barton was, in her opinion, of all things the most natural.

Her joy and expression of regard long outlived her [[concepts/wonder|wonder]]. He received

the kindest welcome from her; and shyness, coldness, reserve could not

stand against such a reception. They had begun to fail him before he

entered the house, and they were quite overcome by the captivating

manners of Mrs. Dashwood. Indeed a man could not very [[motifs/well|well]] be in [[motifs/love|love]]

with either of her daughters, without extending the passion to her; and

Elinor had the satisfaction of seeing him soon become more like

himself. His affections seemed to reanimate towards them all, and his

interest in their welfare again became perceptible. He was not in

spirits, however; he praised their house, admired its prospect, was

attentive, and kind; but still he was not in spirits. The whole family

perceived it, and Mrs. Dashwood, attributing it to some want of

liberality in his mother, sat down to table indignant against all

selfish parents.



“What are Mrs. Ferrars’s views for you at present, Edward?” said she,

when dinner was over and they had drawn round the [[motifs/fire|fire]]; “are you still

to be a great orator in spite of yourself?”



“No. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] my mother is now convinced that I have no more talents than

inclination for a public life!”



“But how is your fame to be established? for famous you must be to

satisfy all your family; and with no inclination for expense, no

affection for strangers, no profession, and no assurance, you may find

it a difficult matter.”



“I shall not attempt it. I have no wish to be distinguished; and have

every reason to [[concepts/hope|hope]] I never shall. Thank Heaven! I cannot be forced

into genius and eloquence.”



“You have no [[concepts/ambition|ambition]], I [[motifs/well|well]] know. Your wishes are all moderate.”



“As moderate as those of the rest of the world, I believe. I wish as

[[motifs/well|well]] as every [[concepts/body|body]] else to be perfectly happy; but, like every [[concepts/body|body]]

else it must be in my own way. [[concepts/greatness|Greatness]] will not make me so.”



“Strange that it would!” cried Marianne. “What have wealth or grandeur

to do with happiness?”



“Grandeur has but little,” said Elinor, “but wealth has much to do with

it.”



“Elinor, for shame!” said Marianne, “money can only give happiness

where there is nothing else to give it. Beyond a competence, it can

afford no real satisfaction, as far as mere [[concepts/self|self]] is concerned.”



“Perhaps,” said Elinor, smiling, “we may come to the same point. _Your_

competence and _my_ wealth are very much alike, I dare say; and without

them, as the world goes now, we shall both agree that every kind of

external comfort must be wanting. Your ideas are only more noble than

mine. Come, what is your competence?”



“About eighteen hundred or two thousand a year; not more than _that_.”



Elinor laughed. “_two_ thousand a year! _one_ is my wealth! I guessed

how it would end.”



“And yet two thousand a-year is a very moderate income,” said Marianne.

“A family cannot [[motifs/well|well]] be maintained on a smaller. I am sure I am not

extravagant in my demands. A proper establishment of servants, a

carriage, perhaps two, and hunters, cannot be supported on less.”



Elinor smiled again, to hear her sister describing so accurately their

future expenses at Combe Magna.



“Hunters!” repeated Edward—“but why must you have hunters? Every [[concepts/body|body]]

does not hunt.”



Marianne coloured as she replied, “But most people do.”



“I wish,” said Margaret, striking out a [[forms/novel|novel]] thought, “that somebody

would give us all a large fortune apiece!”



“Oh that they would!” cried Marianne, her eyes sparkling with

animation, and her cheeks glowing with the delight of such imaginary

happiness.



“We are all unanimous in that wish, I suppose,” said Elinor, “in spite

of the insufficiency of wealth.”



“Oh dear!” cried Margaret, “how happy I should be! I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] what I

should do with it!”



Marianne looked as if she had no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] on that point.



“I should be puzzled to spend so large a fortune myself,” said Mrs.

Dashwood, “if my children were all to be rich without my help.”



“You must begin your improvements on this house,” observed Elinor, “and

your difficulties will soon vanish.”



“What magnificent orders would travel from this family to [[settings/london|London]],” said

Edward, “in such an event! What a happy day for booksellers,

music-sellers, and print-shops! You, Miss Dashwood, would give a

general commission for every new print of merit to be sent you—and as

for Marianne, I know her [[concepts/greatness|greatness]] of [[motifs/soul|soul]], there would not be music

enough in [[settings/london|London]] to content her. And books!—Thomson, Cowper, Scott—she

would buy them all over and over again: she would buy up every copy, I

believe, to prevent their falling into unworthy hands; and she would

have every book that tells her how to admire an old twisted tree.

Should not you, Marianne? Forgive me, if I am very saucy. But I was

willing to show you that I had not forgot our old disputes.”



“I [[motifs/love|love]] to be reminded of the past, Edward—whether it be [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] or

gay, I [[motifs/love|love]] to recall it—and you will never offend me by talking of

former times. You are very right in supposing how my money would be

spent—some of it, at least—my loose cash would certainly be employed in

improving my collection of music and books.”



“And the bulk of your fortune would be laid out in annuities on the

authors or their heirs.”



“No, Edward, I should have something else to do with it.”



“Perhaps, then, you would bestow it as a reward on that person who

wrote the ablest defence of your favourite maxim, that no one can ever

be in [[motifs/love|love]] more than once in their life—your opinion on that point is

unchanged, I presume?”



“Undoubtedly. At my [[motifs/time|time]] of life opinions are tolerably fixed. It is

not likely that I should now see or hear any thing to change them.”



“Marianne is as steadfast as ever, you see,” said Elinor, “she is not

at all altered.”



“She is only grown a little more [[motifs/grave|grave]] than she was.”



“Nay, Edward,” said Marianne, “_you_ need not reproach me. You are not

very gay yourself.”



“Why should you think so!” replied he, with a sigh. “But gaiety never

was a part of _my_ character.”



“Nor do I think it a part of Marianne’s,” said Elinor; “I should hardly

call her a lively girl—she is very earnest, very eager in all she

does—sometimes talks a great deal and always with animation—but she is

not often really merry.”



“I believe you are right,” he replied, “and yet I have always set her

down as a lively girl.”



“I have frequently detected myself in such kind of mistakes,” said

Elinor, “in a total misapprehension of character in some point or

other: fancying people so much more gay or [[motifs/grave|grave]], or ingenious or

stupid than they really are, and I can hardly tell why or in what the

[[concepts/deception|deception]] originated. Sometimes one is guided by what they say of

themselves, and very frequently by what other people say of them,

without giving oneself [[motifs/time|time]] to deliberate and judge.”



“But I thought it was right, Elinor,” said Marianne, “to be guided

wholly by the opinion of other people. I thought our judgments were

given us merely to be subservient to those of neighbours. This has

always been your doctrine, I am sure.”



“No, Marianne, never. My doctrine has never aimed at the subjection of

the understanding. All I have ever attempted to influence has been the

behaviour. You must not confound my meaning. I am guilty, I confess, of

having often wished you to treat our acquaintance in general with

greater attention; but when have I advised you to adopt their

sentiments or to conform to their judgment in serious matters?”



“You have not been able to bring your sister over to your plan of

general civility,” said Edward to Elinor, “Do you gain no ground?”



“Quite the contrary,” replied Elinor, looking expressively at Marianne.



“My judgment,” he returned, “is all on your side of the question; but I

am afraid my practice is much more on your sister’s. I never wish to

offend, but I am so foolishly shy, that I often seem negligent, when I

am only kept back by my natural awkwardness. I have frequently thought

that I must have been intended by [[concepts/nature|nature]] to be fond of low company, I

am so little at my ease among strangers of gentility!”



“Marianne has not shyness to excuse any inattention of hers,” said

Elinor.



“She knows her own worth too [[motifs/well|well]] for false shame,” replied Edward.

“Shyness is only the effect of a sense of inferiority in some way or

other. If I could persuade myself that my manners were perfectly easy

and graceful, I should not be shy.”



“But you would still be reserved,” said Marianne, “and that is worse.”



Edward started—“Reserved! Am I reserved, Marianne?”



“Yes, very.”



“I do not understand you,” replied he, colouring. “Reserved!—how, in

what manner? What am I to tell you? What can you suppose?”



Elinor looked surprised at his emotion; but trying to laugh off the

subject, she said to him, “Do not you know my sister [[motifs/well|well]] enough to

understand what she means? Do not you know she calls every one reserved

who does not talk as fast, and admire what she admires as rapturously

as herself?”



Edward made no answer. His gravity and thoughtfulness returned on him

in their fullest extent—and he sat for some [[motifs/time|time]] silent and dull.

“Verso il genio e l’eloquenza”.

felicità.

Elinor sembrò sorpresa dalla sua reazione; ma cercò di riderci sopra

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_18" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 18" data-chapter="Chapter 18" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/dance,motif/grave,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/forgiveness,concept/hope,concept/nature"></span>


CHAPTER XVIII.





Elinor saw, with great uneasiness the low spirits of her friend. His

visit afforded her but a very partial satisfaction, while his own

enjoyment in it appeared so imperfect. It was evident that he was

unhappy; she wished it were equally evident that he still distinguished

her by the same affection which once she had felt no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of

inspiring; but hitherto the continuance of his preference seemed very

uncertain; and the reservedness of his manner towards her contradicted

one moment what a more animated look had intimated the preceding one.



He joined her and Marianne in the breakfast-room the next morning

before the others were down; and Marianne, who was always eager to

promote their happiness as far as she could, soon left them to

themselves. But before she was half way upstairs she heard the parlour

door open, and, turning round, was astonished to see Edward himself

come out.



“I am going into the village to see my horses,” said he, “as you are

not yet ready for breakfast; I shall be back again presently.”





Edward returned to them with fresh admiration of the surrounding

country; in his walk to the village, he had seen many parts of the

valley to advantage; and the village itself, in a much higher situation

than the cottage, afforded a general view of the whole, which had

exceedingly pleased him. This was a subject which ensured Marianne’s

attention, and she was beginning to describe her own admiration of

these scenes, and to question him more minutely on the objects that had

particularly struck him, when Edward interrupted her by saying, “You

must not enquire too far, Marianne—remember I have no knowledge in the

picturesque, and I shall offend you by my ignorance and want of taste

if we come to particulars. I shall call hills steep, which ought to be

bold; surfaces strange and uncouth, which ought to be irregular and

rugged; and distant objects out of sight, which ought only to be

indistinct through the soft medium of a hazy atmosphere. You must be

satisfied with such admiration as I can honestly give. I call it a very

fine country—the hills are steep, the woods seem full of fine timber,

and the valley looks comfortable and snug—with rich meadows and several

neat farm houses scattered here and there. It exactly answers my idea

of a fine country, because it unites [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] with utility—and I dare say

it is a picturesque one too, because you admire it; I can easily

believe it to be full of rocks and promontories, grey moss and brush

wood, but these are all lost on me. I know nothing of the picturesque.”



“I am afraid it is but too true,” said Marianne; “but why should you

boast of it?”



“I suspect,” said Elinor, “that to avoid one kind of affectation,

Edward here falls into another. Because he believes many people pretend

to more admiration of the beauties of [[concepts/nature|nature]] than they really feel, and

is disgusted with such pretensions, he affects greater indifference and

less discrimination in viewing them himself than he possesses. He is

fastidious and will have an affectation of his own.”



“It is very true,” said Marianne, “that admiration of landscape scenery

is become a mere jargon. Every [[concepts/body|body]] pretends to feel and tries to

describe with the taste and elegance of him who first defined what

picturesque [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] was. I detest jargon of every kind, and sometimes I

have kept my feelings to myself, because I could find no language to

describe them in but what was worn and hackneyed out of all sense and

meaning.”



“I am convinced,” said Edward, “that you really feel all the delight in

a fine prospect which you profess to feel. But, in return, your sister

must allow me to feel no more than I profess. I like a fine prospect,

but not on picturesque principles. I do not like crooked, twisted,

blasted trees. I admire them much more if they are tall, straight, and

flourishing. I do not like ruined, tattered cottages. I am not fond of

nettles or thistles, or heath blossoms. I have more pleasure in a snug

farm-house than a watch-tower—and a troop of tidy, happy villagers

please me better than the finest banditti in the world.”



Marianne looked with amazement at Edward, with compassion at her

sister. Elinor only laughed.



The subject was continued no farther; and Marianne remained

thoughtfully silent, till a new object suddenly engaged her attention.

She was sitting by Edward, and in taking his tea from Mrs. Dashwood,

his hand passed so directly before her, as to make a ring, with a plait

of hair in the centre, very conspicuous on one of his fingers.



“I never saw you wear a ring before, Edward,” she cried. “Is that

Fanny’s hair? I remember her promising to give you some. But I should

have thought her hair had been darker.”



Marianne spoke inconsiderately what she really felt—but when she saw

how much she had pained Edward, her own vexation at her want of thought

could not be surpassed by his. He coloured very deeply, and giving a

momentary glance at Elinor, replied, “Yes; it is my sister’s hair. The

setting always casts a different shade on it, you know.”



Elinor had met his eye, and looked conscious likewise. That the hair

was her own, she instantaneously felt as [[motifs/well|well]] satisfied as Marianne;

the only difference in their conclusions was, that what Marianne

considered as a free gift from her sister, Elinor was conscious must

have been procured by some theft or contrivance unknown to herself. She

was not in a humour, however, to regard it as an affront, and affecting

to take no notice of what passed, by instantly talking of something

else, she internally resolved henceforward to catch every opportunity

of eyeing the hair and of satisfying herself, beyond all [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], that it

was exactly the shade of her own.



Edward’s embarrassment lasted some [[motifs/time|time]], and it ended in an absence of

mind still more settled. He was particularly [[motifs/grave|grave]] the whole morning.

Marianne severely censured herself for what she had said; but her own

[[concepts/forgiveness|forgiveness]] might have been more speedy, had she known how little

offence it had given her sister.



Before the middle of the day, they were visited by Sir John and Mrs.

Jennings, who, having heard of the arrival of a gentleman at the

cottage, came to take a survey of the guest. With the assistance of his

mother-in-law, Sir John was not long in discovering that the name of

Ferrars began with an F. and this prepared a future mine of raillery

against the devoted Elinor, which nothing but the newness of their

acquaintance with Edward could have prevented from being immediately

sprung. But, as it was, she only learned, from some very significant

looks, how far their penetration, founded on Margaret’s instructions,

extended.



Sir John never came to the Dashwoods without either inviting them to

dine at the park the next day, or to drink tea with them that evening.

On the present occasion, for the better entertainment of their visitor,

towards whose amusement he felt himself bound to contribute, he wished

to engage them for both.



“You _must_ drink tea with us to [[motifs/night|night]],” said he, “for we shall be

quite alone—and tomorrow you must absolutely dine with us, for we shall

be a large party.”



Mrs. Jennings enforced the necessity. “And who knows but you may raise

a [[motifs/dance|dance]],” said she. “And that will tempt _you_, Miss Marianne.”



“A [[motifs/dance|dance]]!” cried Marianne. “Impossible! Who is to [[motifs/dance|dance]]?”



“Who! why yourselves, and the Careys, and Whitakers to be sure.—What!

you thought nobody could [[motifs/dance|dance]] because a certain person that shall be

nameless is gone!”



“I wish with all my [[motifs/soul|soul]],” cried Sir John, “that Willoughby were among

us again.”



This, and Marianne’s blushing, gave new suspicions to Edward. “And who

is Willoughby?” said he, in a low voice, to Miss Dashwood, by whom he

was sitting.



She gave him a brief reply. Marianne’s countenance was more

communicative. Edward saw enough to comprehend, not only the meaning of

others, but such of Marianne’s expressions as had puzzled him before;

and when their visitors left them, he went immediately round her, and

said, in a whisper, “I have been guessing. Shall I tell you my guess?”



“What do you mean?”



“Shall I tell you?”



“Certainly.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]] then; I guess that Mr. Willoughby hunts.”



Marianne was surprised and confused, yet she could not help smiling at

the quiet archness of his manner, and after a moment’s [[motifs/silence|silence]], said,



“Oh, Edward! How can you?—But the [[motifs/time|time]] will come I [[concepts/hope|hope]]...I am sure you

will like him.”



“I do not [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] it,” replied he, rather astonished at her earnestness

and warmth; for had he not imagined it to be a joke for the good of her

acquaintance in general, founded only on a something or a nothing

between Mr. Willoughby and herself, he would not have ventured to

mention it.

CAPITOLO XVIII.





Elinor osservava con grande preoccupazione lo stato di depressione del suo amico. Lui…

La visita le procurò solo una soddisfazione parziale, mentre per lui…

L’godimento che ne traeva sembrava così imperfetto… Era evidente che lui…

Insoddisfatta; avrebbe voluto che fosse altrettanto evidente che lui continuasse a distinguerla…

con lo stesso affetto che un tempo le aveva fatto provare assolutamente nessun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]].

Inspirante… ma fino ad ora la persistenza di questa sua preferenza sembrava davvero insolita.

Titolo: Incerto… e la riservatezza del suo comportamento verso di lei erano in contraddizione.

Un attimo prima, uno sguardo molto più vivace aveva già lasciato intendere ciò che sarebbe accaduto dopo.



Il giorno seguente, si unì a lei e a Marianne nella sala da pranzo.

Prima che gli altri cadessero; e Marianne, che era sempre pronta…

Promuovere la loro felicità nel modo possibile… Poi li lasciò da soli.

Si sentirono soli… Ma prima ancora di raggiungere metà della scala, udì il suono provenire dal salotto.

La porta era aperta e, voltandosi, rimase sorpresa nel vedere Edward in persona.

Uscire allo scoperto.



“Sto andando nel villaggio per vedere i miei cavalli”, disse, “proprio come voi…”

“Non sono ancora pronto per la colazione; tornerò tra poco.”





Edward tornò da loro con un nuovo senso di ammirazione per ciò che lo circondava

Paese; nel suo cammino verso il villaggio, aveva visto molte parti di esso…

Valle vantaggiosa; e il villaggio stesso, situato in una posizione molto più elevata.

Più della capanna stessa, offriva una vista d’insieme su tutto il luogo.

Lo soddisfece enormemente. Questo era un argomento che garantiva la felicità di Marianne.

Attenzione… e iniziava a descrivere la propria ammirazione per…

Queste scene, e per interrogarlo più dettagliatamente sugli oggetti che aveva…

Lo colpì particolarmente quando Edward la interruppe dicendo: “Tu…”

“Non devi indagare troppo a fondo, Marianne… Ricorda che io non ne so nulla.”

“ pittoresco… ma la mia ignoranza e la mancanza di gusto potrebbero offendervi”

Se dobbiamo entrare nei dettagli… chiamerò “ripide” quelle colline che in realtà non lo sono.

Titolo:  
Superfici strane e grezze, che dovrebbero essere irregolari…

Titolo:  
Oggetti ruvidi e lontani, fuori dalla vista… che invece dovrebbero essere visibili.

“Indistinto attraverso la nebbiosa atmosfera… Devi essere…”

“Soddisfatto di tale ammirazione, che posso sinceramente provare… La definisco davvero grande.”

Un paesaggio incantevole: le colline sono ripide, i boschi sembrano pieni di legname pregiato.

E la valle appare accogliente e confortevole, con praterie rigogliose e diversi…

Case agricole ordinate sparse qua e là… Esattamente ciò che immaginavo.

Di un paese meraviglioso, perché unisce la [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] all’utilità. E oso dire che.

“È anche un luogo pittoresco, perché tu lo ammiri… Posso facilmente…”

Un luogo pieno di rocce e promontori, muschio grigio e cespugli

“Legno… ma tutto questo non ha alcun significato per me. Non so nulla di ciò che è pittoresco o bello da vedere.”



“Temo che sia davvero troppo vero,” disse Marianne; “ma perché dovresti…”

“Di cosa andare fieri?”



“Sospetto,” disse Elinor, “che per evitare un certo tipo di affettazione…”

Edward cade in un’altra trappola… perché crede che molte persone fingano.

Per ammirare ancora di più le bellezze della [[concepts/nature|natura]] di quanto in realtà provino, e

È disgustato da tali pretese, ma finge di essere ancora più indifferente.

Meno discriminazione nel giudicarli di quanto ne abbia lui stesso. Lui…

“Fastidioso e incline ad ostentare le proprie affettazioni.”



“È assolutamente vero”, disse Marianne, “che l’ammirazione per i paesaggi naturali…”

È diventato soltanto un gergo. Ogni [[concepts/body|individuo]] finge di provare certe emozioni e cerca di farlo credere agli altri.

Descrivere con il gusto ed l’eleganza di colui che per primo definì ciò…

La bellezza pittoresca era davvero incantevole. Detesto ogni tipo di gergo, e a volte.

Ho tenuto per me i miei sentimenti, perché non riuscivo a trovare le parole giuste per esprimerli.

Descrivili… ma in termini di ciò che era indossato, e di ciò che era ormai logoro e privo di ogni significato.

Il significato delle parole



“Sono convinto,” disse Edward, “che tu provi davvero tutta questa gioia…”

“Una prospettiva allettante, che affermi di apprezzare… Ma in cambio, tua sorella…”

“Deve permettermi di provare esattamente ciò che dichiaro… Mi piacciono le belle viste.”

Ma non seguendo principi pittoreschi… Non mi piacciono le cose storte e contorte.

Alberi spezzati… Li ammiro ancora di più se sono alti, dritti…

“Florire… Non mi piacciono le capanne in rovina, strappate e logore. Non mi attraggono affatto.”

“Nettles o cardi, o fiori di brughiera… Mi dà più piacere qualcosa di confortevole.”

Una fattoria-casa è molto più utile di una torre di guardia, e anche di un gruppo di villaggi tranquilli e felici.

“Pregami meglio dei migliori briganti del mondo.”



Marianne lo guardò con meraviglia, con compassione verso di lui

Sorella. Elinor si limitò a ridere.



Il soggetto non fu più approfondito; e Marianne rimase…

In silenzio, assorta nei suoi pensieri, fino a quando un nuovo oggetto attirò improvvisamente la sua attenzione.

Era seduta accanto a Edward e, mentre prendeva il tè che le porgeva la signora Dashwood…

“La sua mano le passò così vicino da formare quasi un cerchio, insieme alla sua treccia…”

Un ciuffo di capelli al centro, molto visibile su uno dei suoi dita.



“Non ti ho mai visto indossare un anello, Edward… È vero?” gridò lei. “È così?”

La chioma di Fanny? Ricordo che aveva promesso di dartene un po’. Ma forse…

“Ho pensato che i suoi capelli fossero più scuri…”



Marianne disse ciò che realmente pensava, senza riflettere… ma quando se ne rese conto…

“Quanto dolore abbia causato a Edward… e quanto lei stessa si tormentasse per la propria mancanza di riflessione…”

Un talento insuperabile

“Un’occhiata fugace a Elinor… e rispose: ‘Sì, è i capelli di mia sorella.’”

“L’ambientazione, sai, dà sempre un significato diverso alle cose.”



“Elinor incrociò il suo sguardo e sembrava altrettanto consapevole… Quel capello…”

Era tutta sua, e immediatamente si sentì altrettanto soddisfatta quanto Marianne.

L’unica differenza nelle loro conclusioni era che… quello che Marianne…

Considerata un regalo gratuito da parte di sua sorella, Elinor era consapevole che…

Quegli oggetti sono stati ottenuti attraverso furti o metodi sconosciuti a lei stessa.

Tuttavia, non era dell'umore giusto per considerarlo un affronto, e fece finta di nulla.

Ignorare completamente ciò che è accaduto, passando immediatamente a parlare di qualcos’altro.

Altrimenti, si ripromise in cuor suo di cogliere ogni opportunità che le si presentasse da allora in poi.

Guardando i propri capelli e assicurandosi, senza alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], che fossero.

Aveva esattamente lo stesso colore del suo.



L’imbarazzo di Edward durò per un po’ di tempo, e finì con la sua assenza.

Il suo stato d’animo era ancora più sereno; per tutta la mattina è stato particolarmente [[motifs/grave|serio]].

Marianne si rimproverò severamente per ciò che aveva detto; ma lei stessa…

La [[concepts/forgiveness|perdono]] avrebbe potuto arrivare più rapidamente, se lei avesse saputo quanto poco.

L’offesa che aveva arrecato a sua sorella.



Prima di mezzogiorno, furono visitati da Sir John e dalla signora.

Jennings, che aveva sentito parlare dell’arrivo di un gentiluomo…

Cottage: una visita per effettuare un sopralluogo del soggiorno degli ospiti. Con l’aiuto di…

Titolo:  
La suocera… Sir John non impiegò molto ad scoprire il nome di…

“Il cognome Ferrars iniziava con la lettera ‘F’, e questo, in futuro, sarebbe diventato motivo di molte battute ironiche…”

Titolo:  
Contro la devota Elinor… che nulla, se non la novità della loro relazione, poteva mettere in pericolo.

Conoscere Edward avrebbe potuto evitare che ciò accadesse immediatamente.

Scattata in piedi… Ma, in realtà, seppe solo in seguito, da alcune informazioni molto importanti…

Quanto sia profonda la loro penetrazione, basata sulle istruzioni di Margaret…

esteso.



Sir John non veniva mai dai Dashwood senza invitarli prima.

Cenare nel parco il giorno dopo, o bere il tè con loro quella sera.

In questa occasione, al fine di intrattenere meglio il loro ospite…

Per il divertimento di chiunque, sentiva di dover contribuire…

Per assumerli entrambi.



“Devi assolutamente bere il tè con noi stasera,” disse lui, “perché, ”.

Del tutto solo. E domani devi assolutamente cenare con noi, perché.

“Sarà una grande festa.”



Titolo:  
La signora Jennings sottolineò l’importanza di farlo. “E chi sa… forse riuscirete addirittura a…”

“Una [[motifs/dance|danza]]”, disse lei. “E questo sicuramente ti attirerà, signorina Marianne.”



“Una [[motifs/dance|danza]]!” gridò Marianne. “Impossibile! Chi sarà a [[motifs/dance|danzare]]?”



“Chi! Perché proprio voi, e anche i Carey e i Whitaker, naturalmente. Che cosa!”

Pensavi che nessuno potesse [[motifs/dance|danzare]] perché c'era una certa persona.

“Il nomeless se n’è andato…”



“Desidero con tutta la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]],” gridò Sir John, “che Willoughby fosse tra loro.”

“Di nuovo con noi…”



“Questo, e il rossore di Marianne, suscitarono nuove sospetti in Edward. ‘E chi…’”

“È davvero Willoughby?”, chiese sottovoce alla signorina Dashwood, accanto a cui si trovava.

Stava seduto.



Una breve risposta… Il volto di Marianne era più…

Comunicativo. Edward vide abbastanza per capire, non solo il significato di…

Altre espressioni di Marianne, quelle che prima lo avevano confuso…

E quando i loro visitatori se ne furono andati, lui si avvicinò immediatamente a lei…

Disse, sussurrando: “Stavo facendo delle congetture… Devo raccontarti quale è la mia ipotesi?”



“Cosa intendi dire?”



"#Devo dirtelo?"



"Certo."



“Allora, immagino che il signor Willoughby vada a caccia.”



Marianne rimase sorpresa e confusa, ma non poté fare a meno di sorridere.

La tranquilla grazia del suo modo di comportarsi. Dopo un momento di [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], disse:



“Oh, Edward! Come puoi farlo?. Ma spero che arrivi quel momento. Sono sicura che tu, ”

“Gli piacerà molto.”



“Non ne dubito affatto,” rispose lui, piuttosto sorpreso dalla sua serietà.

E calore… perché altrimenti avrebbe pensato che si trattasse di una battuta fatta per il suo bene.

Conoscenza superficiale, basata soltanto su piccoli dettagli o nulla in realtà

Tra il signor Willoughby e lei, non avrebbe mai osato…

Menzionalo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_19--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 19 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 19" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/education,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,concept/self,setting/london,setting/oxford"></span>


CHAPTER XIX.





Edward remained a week at the cottage; he was earnestly pressed by Mrs.

Dashwood to stay longer; but, as if he were bent only on

[[concepts/self|self]]-mortification, he seemed resolved to be gone when his enjoyment

among his friends was at the height. His spirits, during the last two

or three days, though still very unequal, were greatly improved—he grew

more and more partial to the house and environs—never spoke of going

away without a sigh—declared his [[motifs/time|time]] to be wholly disengaged—even

doubted to what place he should go when he left them—but still, go he

must. Never had any week passed so quickly—he could hardly believe it

to be gone. He said so repeatedly; other things he said too, which

marked the turn of his feelings and gave the lie to his actions. He had

no pleasure at Norland; he detested being in town; but either to

Norland or [[settings/london|London]], he must go. He valued their kindness beyond any

thing, and his greatest happiness was in being with them. Yet, he must

leave them at the end of a week, in spite of their wishes and his own,

and without any restraint on his [[motifs/time|time]].



Elinor placed all that was astonishing in this way of acting to his

mother’s account; and it was happy for her that he had a mother whose

character was so imperfectly known to her, as to be the general excuse

for every thing strange on the part of her son. Disappointed, however,

and vexed as she was, and sometimes displeased with his uncertain

behaviour to herself, she was very [[motifs/well|well]] disposed on the whole to regard

his actions with all the candid allowances and generous qualifications,

which had been rather more painfully extorted from her, for

Willoughby’s service, by her mother. His want of spirits, of openness,

and of consistency, were most usually attributed to his want of

independence, and his better knowledge of Mrs. Ferrars’s disposition

and designs. The shortness of his visit, the steadiness of his purpose

in leaving them, originated in the same fettered inclination, the same

inevitable necessity of temporizing with his mother. The old

[[motifs/well|well]]-established grievance of duty against will, parent against [[archetypes/child|child]],

was the cause of all. She would have been glad to know when these

difficulties were to cease, this opposition was to yield,—when Mrs.

Ferrars would be reformed, and her son be at liberty to be happy. But

from such vain wishes she was forced to turn for comfort to the renewal

of her confidence in Edward’s affection, to the remembrance of every

mark of regard in look or word which fell from him while at Barton, and

above all to that flattering proof of it which he constantly wore round

his finger.



“I think, Edward,” said Mrs. Dashwood, as they were at breakfast the

last morning, “you would be a happier man if you had any profession to

engage your [[motifs/time|time]] and give an interest to your plans and actions. Some

inconvenience to your friends, indeed, might result from it—you would

not be able to give them so much of your [[motifs/time|time]]. But (with a smile) you

would be materially benefited in one particular at least—you would know

where to go when you left them.”



“I do assure you,” he replied, “that I have long thought on this point,

as you think now. It has been, and is, and probably will always be a

heavy misfortune to me, that I have had no necessary business to engage

me, no profession to give me employment, or afford me any thing like

independence. But unfortunately my own nicety, and the nicety of my

friends, have made me what I am, an idle, helpless being. We never

could agree in our choice of a profession. I always preferred the

church, as I still do. But that was not smart enough for my family.

They recommended the army. That was a great deal too smart for me. The

law was allowed to be genteel enough; many young men, who had chambers

in the Temple, made a very good appearance in the first circles, and

drove about town in very knowing gigs. But I had no inclination for the

law, even in this less abstruse study of it, which my family approved.

As for the navy, it had fashion on its side, but I was too old when the

subject was first started to enter it—and, at length, as there was no

necessity for my having any profession at all, as I might be as dashing

and expensive without a red coat on my back as with one, idleness was

pronounced on the whole to be most advantageous and honourable, and a

young man of eighteen is not in general so earnestly bent on being busy

as to resist the solicitations of his friends to do nothing. I was

therefore entered at [[settings/oxford|Oxford]] and have been properly idle ever since.”



“The consequence of which, I suppose, will be,” said Mrs. Dashwood,

“since leisure has not promoted your own happiness, that your sons will

be brought up to as many pursuits, employments, professions, and trades

as Columella’s.”



“They will be brought up,” said he, in a serious accent, “to be as

unlike myself as is possible. In feeling, in action, in condition, in

every thing.”



“Come, come; this is all an effusion of immediate want of spirits,

Edward. You are in a [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] humour, and fancy that any one unlike

yourself must be happy. But remember that the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of parting from

friends will be felt by every [[concepts/body|body]] at times, whatever be their

[[concepts/education|education]] or state. Know your own happiness. You want nothing but

patience—or give it a more fascinating name, call it [[concepts/hope|hope]]. Your mother

will secure to you, in [[motifs/time|time]], that independence you are so anxious for;

it is her duty, and it will, it must ere long become her happiness to

prevent your whole youth from being wasted in discontent. How much may

not a few months do?”



“I think,” replied Edward, “that I may defy many months to produce any

good to me.”



This desponding turn of mind, though it could not be communicated to

Mrs. Dashwood, gave additional [[motifs/pain|pain]] to them all in the parting, which


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XIX.





Edward rimase una settimana nella capanna; la signora insisteva molto affinché lo facesse.

Dashwood rimarrà più a lungo… ma sembra che abbia un obiettivo preciso in mente.

Autodisciplina e mortificazione: sembrava deciso a andarsene quando il suo piacere.

Tra i suoi amici… era al culmine della sua felicità. Il suo umore, negli ultimi due giorni…

O tre giorni… anche se ancora molto disuguali, le cose migliorarono notevolmente: lui crebbe.

Sempre più affezionato a quella casa e ai suoi dintorni. Non parlava mai di andarsene.

Andando via senza un sospiro, dichiarò che il suo [[motifs/time|tempo]] era ormai completamente libero.

Non sapeva proprio dove andare dopo averli lasciati… ma comunque, doveva andare.

Non c’era mai stata una settimana che passasse così in fretta… A malapena riusciva a crederci.

È sparito… Lo ripeteva continuamente; diceva anche altre cose, ma…

Cambiò il corso dei suoi sentimenti, ma le sue azioni dimostravano il contrario. Lui…

Nessun piacere a Norland; odiava stare in città… ma forse per qualche motivo…

Che si tratti di Norland o di [[settings/london|Londra]], deve andare. Apprezzava la loro gentilezza più di qualsiasi altra cosa.

“La cosa più importante per lui era stare con loro… Eppure, doveva…”

Lasciali alla fine della settimana, nonostante i loro desideri e i suoi stessi.

e senza alcuna restrizione riguardo al suo [[motifs/time|tempo]].



Elinor attribuì tutto ciò che era sorprendente nel suo modo di comportarsi a…

“La testimonianza di una madre… E fu un bene per lei che lui avesse una madre del genere.”

Il carattere di quell’uomo le era così poco noto da costituire una scusa generale per non comprenderlo appieno.

Per ogni cosa strana che faceva suo figlio… Delusa, tuttavia.

Nonostante fosse così turbata e a volte insoddisfatta della sua incertezza…

Il suo comportamento verso se stessa era tale che, nel complesso, aveva una buona disposizione ad considerarla in questo modo.

Le sue azioni, considerate con tutta onestà e generosità…

Un titolo che le era stato estorto in modo particolarmente doloroso…

Il servizio di Willoughby, fornito da sua madre… La mancanza in lui di spirito, di apertura…

Titolo:  
E la coerenza, spesso venivano attribuite alla sua mancanza di…

**Indipendenza… e la sua maggiore conoscenza del carattere della signora Ferrars**

Brevità della sua visita, fermezza delle sue intenzioni

Nella loro partenza, tutto derivava dalla stessa inclinazione vincolata, dalla stessa…

“L’inevitabile necessità di temporeggiare con sua madre… La vecchia…”

Un diritto legittimo e affermato contro la volontà altrui: un genitore contro il proprio [[archetypes/child|figlio]].

“Era la causa di tutto. Le sarebbe piaciuto saperlo quando queste cose…”

Le difficoltà non avrebbero smesso, questa opposizione non si sarebbe arresa, quando la signora.

I Ferrars sarebbero stati riformati, e suo figlio avrebbe potuto vivere felice. Ma…

Da tali vane speranze, fu costretta a cercare conforto nella rinascita…

La fiducia nella sua affezione per Edward, al ricordo di ogni cosa…

Un segno di considerazione, espresso nel suo sguardo o nelle sue parole durante il soggiorno a Barton…

Soprattutto per quella lusinghiera dimostrazione di ciò che portava sempre con sé…

Il suo dito.



“Credo che… Edward”, disse la signora Dashwood mentre erano a colazione.

“Se avessi una qualche professione, saresti un uomo più felice…”

Impiega il tuo [[motifs/time|tempo]] e dedica attenzione ai tuoi piani e alle tue azioni. Alcuni.

Certo, potrebbe causare qualche disagio ai vostri amici…

Non essere in grado di dedicare loro così tanto del tuo [[motifs/time|tempo]]. Ma, (con un sorriso) tu.

Ne trarresti un beneficio concreto, almeno… lo sapresti.

“Dove andare quando li hai lasciati…”



“Vi assicuro sinceramente”, rispose, “che ho riflettuto a lungo su questo argomento”.

Come pensi ora… È sempre stato così, è ancora così, e probabilmente lo sarà per sempre.

Una grave sfortuna per me… non aver mai avuto bisogno di impegnarmi in nulla di necessario.

Senza una professione che mi permetta di trovare lavoro o di disporre di qualcosa…

“Indipendenza… Ma purtroppo, sia la mia stessa delicatezza che quella delle altre persone…”

Amici… sono stati quelli che mi hanno reso ciò che sono: un essere inutile e impotente. Mai…

Potremmo essere d’accordo sulla scelta della nostra professione… Io ho sempre preferito…

La chiesa, proprio come faccio ancora oggi. Ma per la mia famiglia, quella non era un’opzione abbastanza intelligente.

“Consigliarono l’esercito… Una mossa davvero troppo astuta per me.”

Il diritto poteva essere abbastanza raffinato… Molti giovani uomini, che possedevano studi…

“Nel Tempio, fece una molto buona impressione nei primi circoli…”

Vagabondaggi per la città… con intenti ben precisi. Ma non ne avevo alcuna voglia.

La legge, anche in questo studio meno astratto di essa, che fu approvato dalla mia famiglia.

Per quanto riguarda la marina, aveva il favore della moda… ma ero troppo vecchio quando ciò accadde.

Il soggetto fu inizialmente introdotto… e, alla fine, poiché non c’era nulla…

La necessità di avere una qualche professione… anche se potrei essere altrettanto affascinante senza di essa

“E costoso… senza un mantello rosso addosso, proprio come con uno: l’ozio…”

Ritenuto nel complesso il più vantaggioso e onorevole…

Un giovane di diciotto anni non è necessariamente così assiduamente impegnato nella sua attività…

Non riusciva a resistere alle insistenze dei suoi amici che lo esortavano a non fare nulla. Io…

Pertanto entrò a [[settings/oxford|Oxford]] e da allora ha vissuto tranquillamente senza fare nulla.



“La conseguenza di ciò, immagino, sarà…”, disse la signora Dashwood.

“Poiché il tempo libero non ha aumentato la tua felicità, allora i tuoi figli…”

Essere educati per intraprendere molteplici attività, occupazioni, professioni e mestieri.

“Come quello di Columella.”



“Verranno educati”, disse con un tono serio, “per diventare come…”

“Non come me, nel modo possibile… Nel sentire, nell’agire, nello stato in cui mi trovo…”

"Tutto quanto."



“Ah, ah… tutto questo non è altro che un segno di evidente mancanza di spirito…”

Edward. Sei di un umore [[concepts/melancholy|malinconico]] e pensi che qualcuno diverso da te possa capirti.

Dovresti essere felice tu stesso. Ma ricorda che il [[motifs/pain|dolore]] di separarsi da.

Gli amici vengono sentiti da ogni [[concepts/body|-corpo]] in alcuni momenti, indipendentemente dalle circostanze.

L’[[concepts/education|istruzione]] o lo stato. Conosci la tua propria felicità. Non desideri nulla di più.

La pazienza, o forse un nome più affascinante: chiamiamola [[concepts/hope|speranza]]. Tua madre.

Vi assicurerà, nel [[motifs/time|tempo]], quella indipendenza di cui desiderate ardentemente.

“È suo dovere… e presto diventerà anche la sua felicità.”

Impedisce che tutta la tua giovinezza venga sprecata nel discontento… Quanto potrebbe valere?

“Non sono passati pochi mesi, vero?”



“Credo”, rispose Edward, “che possa riuscire a fare qualcosa anche senza mesi di lavoro”.

“Buono per me.”



Questo atteggiamento disperato, sebbene non potesse essere comunicato…

La signora Dashwood causò loro ancora più [[motifs/pain|dolore]] nel momento dell’addio.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_19--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 19 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 19" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/grave,motif/memory,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/doubt,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/solitude,setting/court,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


shortly took place, and left an uncomfortable impression on Elinor’s

feelings especially, which required some trouble and [[motifs/time|time]] to subdue.

But as it was her determination to subdue it, and to prevent herself

from appearing to suffer more than what all her family suffered on his

going away, she did not adopt the method so judiciously employed by

Marianne, on a similar occasion, to augment and fix her sorrow, by

seeking [[motifs/silence|silence]], [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] and idleness. Their means were as different

as their objects, and equally suited to the advancement of each.



Elinor sat down to her drawing-table as soon as he was out of the

house, busily employed herself the whole day, neither sought nor

avoided the mention of his name, appeared to interest herself almost as

much as ever in the general concerns of the family, and if, by this

conduct, she did not lessen her own grief, it was at least prevented

from unnecessary increase, and her mother and sisters were spared much

solicitude on her account.



Such behaviour as this, so exactly the reverse of her own, appeared no

more meritorious to Marianne, than her own had seemed faulty to her.

The business of [[concepts/self|self]]-command she settled very easily;—with strong

affections it was impossible, with calm ones it could have no merit.

That her sister’s affections _were_ calm, she dared not deny, though

she blushed to acknowledge it; and of the strength of her own, she gave

a very striking proof, by still loving and respecting that sister, in

spite of this mortifying conviction.



Without shutting herself up from her family, or leaving the house in

determined [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] to avoid them, or lying awake the whole [[motifs/night|night]] to

indulge meditation, Elinor found every day afforded her leisure enough

to think of Edward, and of Edward’s behaviour, in every possible

variety which the different state of her spirits at different times

could produce,—with tenderness, pity, approbation, censure, and [[concepts/doubt|doubt]].

There were moments in abundance, when, if not by the absence of her

mother and sisters, at least by the [[concepts/nature|nature]] of their employments,

conversation was forbidden among them, and every effect of [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] was

produced. Her mind was inevitably at liberty; her thoughts could not be

chained elsewhere; and the past and the future, on a subject so

interesting, must be before her, must force her attention, and engross

her [[motifs/memory|memory]], her reflection, and her fancy.



From a reverie of this kind, as she sat at her drawing-table, she was

roused one morning, soon after Edward’s leaving them, by the arrival of

company. She happened to be quite alone. The closing of the little

gate, at the entrance of the green [[settings/court|court]] in front of the house, drew

her eyes to the [[motifs/window|window]], and she saw a large party walking up to the

door. Amongst them were Sir John and Lady Middleton and Mrs. Jennings,

but there were two others, a gentleman and lady, who were quite unknown

to her. She was sitting near the [[motifs/window|window]], and as soon as Sir John

perceived her, he left the rest of the party to the ceremony of

knocking at the door, and stepping across the turf, obliged her to open

the casement to speak to him, though the space was so short between the

door and the [[motifs/window|window]], as to make it hardly possible to speak at one

without being heard at the other.



“[[motifs/well|Well]],” said he, “we have brought you some strangers. How do you like

them?”



“Hush! they will hear you.”



“Never mind if they do. It is only the Palmers. Charlotte is very

pretty, I can tell you. You may see her if you look this way.”



As Elinor was certain of seeing her in a couple of minutes, without

taking that liberty, she begged to be excused.



“Where is Marianne? Has she run away because we are come? I see her

instrument is open.”



“She is walking, I believe.”



They were now joined by Mrs. Jennings, who had not patience enough to

wait till the door was opened before she told _her_ story. She came

hallooing to the [[motifs/window|window]], “How do you do, my dear? How does Mrs.

Dashwood do? And where are your sisters? What! all alone! you will be

glad of a little company to sit with you. I have brought my other son

and daughter to see you. Only think of their coming so suddenly! I

thought I heard a carriage last [[motifs/night|night]], while we were drinking our tea,

but it never entered my head that it could be them. I thought of

nothing but whether it might not be [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] come back again; so

I said to Sir John, I do think I hear a carriage; perhaps it is Colonel

Brandon come back again—”



Elinor was obliged to turn from her, in the middle of her story, to

receive the rest of the party; Lady Middleton introduced the two

strangers; Mrs. Dashwood and Margaret came down stairs at the same

[[motifs/time|time]], and they all sat down to look at one another, while Mrs. Jennings

continued her story as she walked through the passage into the parlour,

attended by Sir John.



Mrs. Palmer was several years younger than Lady Middleton, and totally

unlike her in every respect. She was short and plump, had a very pretty

face, and the finest expression of good humour in it that could

possibly be. Her manners were by no means so elegant as her sister’s,

but they were much more prepossessing. She came in with a smile, smiled

all the [[motifs/time|time]] of her visit, except when she laughed, and smiled when she

went away. Her husband was a [[motifs/grave|grave]] looking young man of five or six and

twenty, with an air of more fashion and sense than his wife, but of

less willingness to please or be pleased. He entered the room with a

look of [[concepts/self|self]]-consequence, slightly bowed to the ladies, without

speaking a word, and, after briefly surveying them and their

apartments, took up a newspaper from the table, and continued to read

it as long as he staid.

Molto più meritevole per Marianne, di quanto ciò che era suo le fosse sembrato difettoso.

Nonostante questa umiliante condanna.

Madre e sorelle, almeno per la natura dei loro compiti.

Attirare l’attenzione, essere il primo nella sua mente… e catturare completamente la sua attenzione.

La sua [[motifs/memory|memoria]], il suo riflessione e la sua fantasia.

La porta, all’ingresso del verde [[settings/court|giardino]] di fronte alla casa, fu aperta.

A lei. Era seduta vicino alla [[motifs/window|finestra]], e non appena Sir John.

La vide, e lasciò il resto dei partecipanti alla cerimonia…

Bussando alla porta e attraversando il prato, fu costretta ad aprirla

senza che l'altro potesse sentirlo.

Come Elinor era certa di rivederla entro pochi minuti…
