to speak, and to speak cautiously, she said, with calmness of manner,

which tolerably [[motifs/well|well]] concealed her surprise and solicitude—“May I ask

if your engagement is of long standing?”



“We have been engaged these four years.”



“Four years!”



“Yes.”



Elinor, though greatly shocked, still felt unable to believe it.



“I did not know,” said she, “that you were even acquainted till the

other day.”



“Our acquaintance, however, is of many years date. He was under my

uncle’s care, you know, a considerable while.”



“Your uncle!”



“Yes; Mr. Pratt. Did you never hear him talk of Mr. Pratt?”



“I think I have,” replied Elinor, with an exertion of spirits, which

increased with her increase of emotion.



“He was four years with my uncle, who lives at Longstaple, near

Plymouth. It was there our acquaintance begun, for my sister and me was

often staying with my uncle, and it was there our engagement was

formed, though not till a year after he had quitted as a pupil; but he

was almost always with us afterwards. I was very unwilling to enter

into it, as you may imagine, without the knowledge and approbation of

his mother; but I was too young, and loved him too [[motifs/well|well]], to be so

prudent as I ought to have been. Though you do not know him so [[motifs/well|well]] as

me, Miss Dashwood, you must have seen enough of him to be sensible he

is very capable of making a woman sincerely attached to him.”



“Certainly,” answered Elinor, without knowing what she said; but after

a moment’s reflection, she added, with revived security of Edward’s

[[concepts/honour|honour]] and [[motifs/love|love]], and her companion’s falsehood—“Engaged to Mr. Edward

Ferrars!—I confess myself so totally surprised at what you tell me,

that really—I beg your pardon; but surely there must be some mistake of

person or name. We cannot mean the same Mr. Ferrars.”



“We can mean no other,” cried Lucy, smiling. “Mr. [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]], the

eldest son of Mrs. Ferrars, of Park Street, and brother of your

sister-in-law, Mrs. John Dashwood, is the person I mean; you must allow

that I am not likely to be deceived as to the name of the man on who

all my happiness depends.”



“It is strange,” replied Elinor, in a most painful perplexity, “that I

should never have heard him even mention your name.”



“No; considering our situation, it was not strange. Our first care has

been to keep the matter secret. You knew nothing of me, or my family,

and, therefore, there could be no _occasion_ for ever mentioning my

name to you; and, as he was always particularly afraid of his sister’s

suspecting any thing, _that_ was reason enough for his not mentioning

it.”



She was silent.—Elinor’s security sunk; but her [[concepts/self|self]]-command did not

sink with it.



“Four years you have been engaged,” said she with a firm voice.



“Yes; and heaven knows how much longer we may have to wait. Poor

Edward! It puts him quite out of heart.” Then taking a small miniature

from her pocket, she added, “To prevent the possibility of mistake, be

so good as to look at this face. It does not do him justice, to be

sure, but yet I think you cannot be deceived as to the person it was

drew for.—I have had it above these three years.”



She put it into her hands as she spoke; and when Elinor saw the

painting, whatever other doubts her [[concepts/fear|fear]] of a too hasty decision, or

her wish of detecting falsehood might suffer to linger in her mind, she

could have none of its being Edward’s face. She returned it almost

instantly, acknowledging the likeness.



“I have never been able,” continued Lucy, “to give him my picture in

return, which I am very much vexed at, for he has been always so

anxious to get it! But I am determined to set for it the very first

opportunity.”



“You are quite in the right,” replied Elinor calmly. They then

proceeded a few paces in [[motifs/silence|silence]]. Lucy spoke first.



“I am sure,” said she, “I have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] in the world of your faithfully

keeping this secret, because you must know of what importance it is to

us, not to have it reach his mother; for she would never approve of it,

I dare say. I shall have no fortune, and I fancy she is an exceeding

proud woman.”



“I certainly did not seek your confidence,” said Elinor; “but you do me

no more than justice in imagining that I may be depended on. Your

secret is safe with me; but pardon me if I express some surprise at so

unnecessary a communication. You must at least have felt that my being

acquainted with it could not add to its safety.”



As she said this, she looked earnestly at Lucy, hoping to discover

something in her countenance; perhaps the falsehood of the greatest

part of what she had been saying; but Lucy’s countenance suffered no

change.

not a creature whose advice I can ask. Anne is the only person that

have suffered for Edward’s sake these last four years. Every thing in

meet above twice a-year. I am sure I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] my heart is not quite

Here she took out her handkerchief; but Elinor did not feel very

“Sometimes.” continued Lucy, after wiping her eyes, “I think whether it

would not be better for us both to break off the matter entirely.” As

she said this, she looked directly at her companion. “But then at other

times I have not resolution enough for it. I cannot bear the thoughts

of making him so miserable, as I know the very mention of such a thing

would do. And on my own account too—so dear as he is to me—I don’t

think I could be equal to it. What would you advise me to do in such a

case, Miss Dashwood? What would you do yourself?”



“Pardon me,” replied Elinor, startled by the question; “but I can give

you no advice under such circumstances. Your own judgment must direct

you.”



“To be sure,” continued Lucy, after a few minutes [[motifs/silence|silence]] on both

sides, “his mother must provide for him sometime or other; but poor

Edward is so cast down by it! Did you not think him dreadful

low-spirited when he was at Barton? He was so miserable when he left us

at Longstaple, to go to you, that I was afraid you would think him

quite ill.”



“Did he come from your uncle’s, then, when he visited us?”



“Oh, yes; he had been staying a fortnight with us. Did you think he

came directly from town?”



“No,” replied Elinor, most feelingly sensible of every fresh

circumstance in favour of Lucy’s veracity; “I remember he told us, that

he had been staying a fortnight with some friends near Plymouth.” She

remembered too, her own surprise at the [[motifs/time|time]], at his mentioning nothing

farther of those friends, at his total [[motifs/silence|silence]] with respect even to

their names.



“Did not you think him sadly out of spirits?” repeated Lucy.



“We did, indeed, particularly so when he first arrived.”



“I begged him to exert himself for [[concepts/fear|fear]] you should suspect what was the

matter; but it made him so [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]], not being able to stay more than

a fortnight with us, and seeing me so much affected. Poor fellow! I am

filled the sheet to me as full as possible.”



Elinor saw that it _was_ his hand, and she could [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] no longer. This

picture, she had allowed herself to believe, might have been

struggled so resolutely against the oppression of her feelings, that

pocket, “is the only comfort we have in such long separations. Yes, _I_

have one other comfort in his picture, but poor Edward has not even

_that_. If he had but my picture, he says he should be easy. I gave him

a lock of my hair set in a ring when he was at Longstaple last, and

that was some comfort to him, he said, but not equal to a picture.

Perhaps you might notice the ring when you saw him?”



“I did,” said Elinor, with a composure of voice, under which was

concealed an emotion and distress beyond any thing she had ever felt

before. She was mortified, shocked, confounded.



Fortunately for her, they had now reached the cottage, and the

conversation could be continued no farther. After sitting with them a

few minutes, the Miss Steeles returned to the Park, and Elinor was then

at liberty to think and be wretched.



END OF THE FIRST VOLUME


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Senza un soldo.”



Qui tirò fuori il fazzoletto; ma Elinor non si sentiva molto…

comprensiva.



“A volte,” continuò Lucy, dopo essersi asciugata gli occhi, “penso che…”

“Forse sarebbe meglio per entrambi interrompere del tutto questa relazione.”

“Ma poi, in altri momenti…” disse, guardando direttamente il suo compagno.

Molte volte non ho la determinazione necessaria… Non riesco a sopportare quei pensieri.

Farlo soffrire così tanto… poiché conosco bene quanto possa essere terribile anche solo menzionare una cosa del genere

“Non andrebbe affatto bene… E anche per motivi personali: per quanto lui sia caro per me, non è possibile.”

Credo di potercela fare… Che consiglio mi dareste in una situazione del genere?

“Cosa fareste voi, signorina Dashwood? In quale situazione vi trovereste?”



“Scusi,” rispose Elinor, sorpresa dalla domanda; “ma non posso dare…”

In tali circostanze, non esiste alcun consiglio da seguire: è la tua stessa valutazione a dover guidarti.

“Tu, davvero.”



“Con certezza,” continuò Lucy, dopo alcuni minuti di [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] da entrambe le parti.

Titolo:  
“Dai suoi discorsi si capisce che sua madre dovrà pur provvedere a lui prima o poi… Ma poveretto…”

Edward è davvero distrutto per questo… Non vi è sembrato terribile?

Mentre era a Barton, era di cattivo umore… Se ne è andato in uno stato di profonda tristezza.

A Longstaple, per dirvelo… temevo che poteste pensare che lui…

“Molto malato.”



“Quindi è venuto da tuo zio quando ci ha visitati?”



“Oh, sì; era rimasto da noi per due settimane. Pensavi che…”

“È arrivato direttamente dalla città?”



“No,” rispose Elinor, con profonda sensibilità verso ogni nuova situazione che si presentava.

Circostanza a favore della veridicità di Lucy; “Ricordo che ci disse…”

“Era rimasto per due settimane con alcuni amici vicino a Plymouth.” Lei

Ricordava anche la propria sorpresa in quel momento, quando lui non aveva menzionato nulla.

Più lontano di quegli amici, nel suo totale [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], persino rispetto a.

I loro nomi.



“Non pensavi che fosse tristemente depresso?” ripeté Lucy.



“Lo abbiamo fatto davvero, soprattutto quando è arrivato per la prima volta.”



“Gli ho supplicato di fare del suo meglio, per paura che poteste sospettare cosa fosse realmente, ”

Non era importante; ma lo rese molto [[concepts/melancholy|malinconico]], non riuscendo a trattenersi oltre.

“Una quindicina di giorni con noi… e vedermi così commosso… Povero ragazzo!”

Temo che anche per lui sia la stessa cosa ora; scrive in modo davvero pessimo…

“Spirit… Ne ho ricevuto una lettera proprio prima di lasciare Exeter.”

Dalla sua tasca, e mostrando con noncuranza la direzione a Elinor… “Tu”

Conosce bene le sue capacità, oserei dire… Una mano davvero affascinante; ma questo non è tutto.

Scritto come al solito, in modo davvero eccellente. Direi che fosse stanco, perché aveva appena.

“Riempì il foglio il più completamente possibile.”



Elinor vide che era davvero la sua mano, e non poté più [[concepts/doubt|dubitarne]]. Questo.

Titolo:  
Quella immagine, si era permessa di credere, forse avrebbe potuto…

Ottenuto per caso… Forse non era un regalo di Edward… Ma…

La corrispondenza tra di loro, attraverso lettere, poteva esistere soltanto sotto determinate condizioni…

Un coinvolgimento positivo, che non potrebbe essere autorizzato da nulla altro… per pochi.

In quei momenti, stava per essere sopraffatta: il suo cuore sembrava affondare dentro di lei…

Non riusciva quasi a reggersi in piedi; ma lo sforzo era assolutamente necessario… e lei lo fece.

Lottò con tale determinazione contro l’oppressione dei propri sentimenti…

Il suo successo fu rapido e, per quella volta, completo.



“Ci scriviamo a vicenda”, disse Lucy, riponendo la lettera nella sua busta.

“La tasca… è l’unico conforto che abbiamo nelle lunghe separazioni. Sì, _io_…”

Un’altra consolazione nella sua immagine… ma povero Edward non ne ha nemmeno una.

Che se avesse solo la mia foto… dice che tutto sarebbe più facile. Gliel’ho data.

“Una ciocca dei miei capelli incastonata in un anello… quando lui era l’ultima volta a Longstaple…”

“Quello rappresentava un certo conforto per lui,” disse, “ma non era paragonabile a un dipinto.”

“Forse noterai quell’anello quando lo vedrai…”



“Lo feci,” disse Elinor con voce calma, ma sotto quella calma…

Nascose un’emozione e un dolore mai provati prima.

Prima. Era mortificata, scioccata, confusa.



Fortunatamente per lei, erano ormai arrivati alla capanna.

La conversazione non poté proseguire oltre. Dopo essere rimasto con loro per un po’,…

Dopo pochi minuti, la signorina Steeles tornò al Parco, e in quel momento Elinor…

Libero di pensare, e di soffrire.



Fine del primo volume



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_23--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 23 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 23" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/education,concept/fear,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/temptation,concept/truth,concept/vanity,character/lucy_steele"></span>


CHAPTER XXIII.





However small Elinor’s general dependence on Lucy’s veracity might be,

it was impossible for her on serious reflection to suspect it in the

present case, where no [[concepts/temptation|temptation]] could be answerable to the folly of

inventing a falsehood of such a description. What Lucy had asserted to

be true, therefore, Elinor could not, dared not longer [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]; supported

as it was too on every side by such probabilities and proofs, and

contradicted by nothing but her own wishes. Their opportunity of

acquaintance in the house of Mr. Pratt was a foundation for the rest,

at once indisputable and alarming; and Edward’s visit near Plymouth,

his [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] state of mind, his dissatisfaction at his own prospects,

his uncertain behaviour towards herself, the intimate knowledge of the

Miss Steeles as to Norland and their family connections, which had

often surprised her, the picture, the letter, the ring, formed

altogether such a [[concepts/body|body]] of evidence, as overcame every [[concepts/fear|fear]] of

condemning him unfairly, and established as a fact, which no partiality

could set aside, his ill-treatment of herself.—Her resentment of such

behaviour, her indignation at having been its dupe, for a short [[motifs/time|time]]

made her feel only for herself; but other ideas, other considerations,

soon arose. Had Edward been intentionally deceiving her? Had he feigned

a regard for her which he did not feel? Was his engagement to Lucy an

engagement of the heart? No; whatever it might once have been, she

could not believe it such at present. His affection was all her own.

She could not be deceived in that. Her mother, sisters, Fanny, all had

been conscious of his regard for her at Norland; it was not an illusion

of her own [[concepts/vanity|vanity]]. He certainly loved her. What a softener of the heart

was this persuasion! How much could it not tempt her to forgive! He had

been blamable, highly blamable, in remaining at Norland after he first

felt her influence over him to be more than it ought to be. In that, he

could not be defended; but if he had injured her, how much more had he

injured himself; if her case were pitiable, his was hopeless. His

imprudence had made her miserable for a while; but it seemed to have

deprived himself of all chance of ever being otherwise. She might in

[[motifs/time|time]] regain tranquillity; but _he_, what had he to look forward to?

Could he ever be tolerably happy with [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]]; could he, were his

affection for herself out of the question, with his integrity, his

delicacy, and [[motifs/well|well]]-informed mind, be satisfied with a wife like

her—illiterate, artful, and selfish?



The youthful infatuation of nineteen would naturally blind him to every

thing but her [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] and good [[concepts/nature|nature]]; but the four succeeding

years—years, which if rationally spent, give such improvement to the

understanding, must have opened his eyes to her defects of [[concepts/education|education]],

while the same period of [[motifs/time|time]], spent on her side in inferior society

and more frivolous pursuits, had perhaps robbed her of that simplicity

which might once have given an interesting character to her [[concepts/beauty|beauty]].



If in the supposition of his seeking to marry herself, his difficulties

from his mother had seemed great, how much greater were they now likely

to be, when the object of his engagement was undoubtedly inferior in

connections, and probably inferior in fortune to herself. These

difficulties, indeed, with a heart so alienated from Lucy, might not

press very hard upon his patience; but [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] was the state of the

person by whom the expectation of family opposition and unkindness,

could be felt as a relief!



As these considerations occurred to her in painful succession, she wept

for him, more than for herself. Supported by the conviction of having

done nothing to merit her present unhappiness, and consoled by the

belief that Edward had done nothing to forfeit her esteem, she thought

she could even now, under the first smart of the heavy blow, command

herself enough to guard every suspicion of the [[concepts/truth|truth]] from her mother

and sisters. And so [[motifs/well|well]] was she able to answer her own expectations,

that when she joined them at dinner only two hours after she had first

suffered the extinction of all her dearest hopes, no one would have

supposed from the appearance of the sisters, that Elinor was mourning

in secret over obstacles which must divide her for ever from the object

of her [[motifs/love|love]], and that Marianne was internally dwelling on the

perfections of a man, of whose whole heart she felt thoroughly

possessed, and whom she expected to see in every carriage which drove

near their house.



The necessity of concealing from her mother and Marianne, what had been

entrusted in confidence to herself, though it obliged her to unceasing

exertion, was no aggravation of Elinor’s distress. On the contrary it

was a relief to her, to be spared the communication of what would give

such affliction to them, and to be saved likewise from hearing that

condemnation of Edward, which would probably flow from the excess of

their partial affection for herself, and which was more than she felt

equal to support.



From their counsel, or their conversation, she knew she could receive

no assistance, their tenderness and sorrow must add to her distress,

while her [[concepts/self|self]]-command would neither receive encouragement from their

example nor from their praise. She was stronger alone, and her own good

sense so [[motifs/well|well]] supported her, that her firmness was as unshaken, her

appearance of cheerfulness as invariable, as with regrets so poignant

and so fresh, it was possible for them to be.



Much as she had suffered from her first conversation with Lucy on the

subject, she soon felt an earnest wish of renewing it; and this for

more reasons than one. She wanted to hear many particulars of their


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XXIII.





Per quanto piccola possa essere la dipendenza generale di Elinor dalla veridicità di Lucy…

Era impossibile, se ci si pensava seriamente, che lei potesse sospettarlo.

Nel caso attuale, in cui nessuna [[concepts/temptation|tentazione]] potrebbe essere ritenuta responsabile della follia di.

Inventare una falsità di tale natura… Quello che Lucy aveva affermato…

Se quindi era vero, Elinor non poteva, non osava più [[concepts/doubt|dubitare]]; era convinta.

Come era evidente da tutte le parti, a causa di tali probabilità e prove…

Contraddetto soltanto dai suoi stessi desideri… La loro opportunità di…

La conoscenza nella casa del signor Pratt fu la base per tutto il resto.

Allo stesso tempo indiscutibile e allarmante… E la visita di Edward vicino a Plymouth.

Il suo stato d'animo melanconico, il suo disappunto riguardo alle proprie prospettive future.

Il suo comportamento incerto nei suoi confronti, la conoscenza intima di…

Titolo:  
Le relazioni familiari di Miss Steeles con Norland e la loro storia

Spesso la sorprendevano: quell’immagine, quella lettera, quel anello…

Un insieme così completo di prove eliminò ogni timore riguardo a.

Condannandolo ingiustamente, e stabilendo tale fatto come incontrovertibile, senza alcuna prevenzione…

Il suo maltrattamento verso se stessa… e il risentimento che ne derivava.

Il suo comportamento, la sua indignazione per essere stata vittima di una simile situazione, per un breve [[motifs/time|periodo]] di tempo.

Le fece pensare solo a se stessa; ma altre idee, altri considerazioni…

Presto emersero dei dubbi. Stava Edward ingannandola intenzionalmente? Aveva forse finto…

Un sentimento che non provava davvero? Il suo fidanzamento con Lucy…

Il coinvolgimento del cuore? No… Qualunque cosa fosse una volta, lei…

Non riusciva a crederci in quel momento. Quel suo affetto apparteneva esclusivamente a lei.

Non poteva essere ingannata su quel punto. Sua madre, sue sorelle, Fanny… tutte avevano fatto lo stesso.

Aveva sempre avuto consapevolezza del suo interesse per lei a Norland… Non era un’illusione.

A causa della sua stessa [[concepts/vanity|vanità]]. Lui la amava davvero. Che modo meraviglioso per addolcire il cuore.

Che convincimento. Quanto non doveva essere forte per spingerla a perdonare! Lui aveva.

Assai biasimabile… rimanere a Norland dopo averlo lasciato la prima volta.

Percepiva che il suo ascendente su di lui fosse maggiore di quanto sarebbe dovuto essere… In questo senso, lui…

Non poteva essere difeso; ma se l’aveva ferita, quanto di più allora…

Si è ferito da solo; se il suo caso fosse degno di compassione, il suo sarebbe senza speranza. Il suo…

L'imprudenza l'aveva resa infelice per un po'; ma sembrava che ora…

Si privò di ogni possibilità di cambiare la sua situazione. Forse avrebbe potuto…

Il [[motifs/time|tempo]] ritrovò la sua tranquillità; ma lui, cosa aveva davanti a sé?

Potrebbe mai essere veramente felice con [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]]? Potrebbe, se le sue.

Un affetto per sé stessa è fuori discussione… con la sua integrità, la sua…

Delicatezza e mente ben informata, si potrà essere soddisfatti con una moglie del genere.

Lei, analfabeta, astuta e egoista?



La giovane passione dei diciannove anni lo avrebbe naturalmente reso cieco di fronte a tutto…

Nient'altro che la sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e la sua buona [[concepts/nature|natura]]; ma i quattro successivi.

Titolo:  
Anni… anni che, se trascorsi in modo razionale, possono portare a grandi miglioramenti.

Con questa comprensione, doveva essersi reso conto dei difetti legati alla sua [[concepts/education|educazione]].

Nello stesso lasso di [[motifs/time|tempo]], trascorso dal suo lato, in una società inferiore.

E altre attività frivole forse le avevano fatto perdere quella semplicità…

Qualcosa che un tempo avrebbe potuto conferire un carattere interessante alla sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]].



Se si ipotizza che lui voglia sposarla… le sue difficoltà

Il dono ricevuto da sua madre sembrava già enorme; quanto più grande doveva essere ora…

Titolo:  
Essere… quando l’oggetto del suo fidanzamento era senza dubbio inferiore…

Connessioni… e probabilmente anche inferiore a lei per fortuna. Queste…

Difficoltà, certamente, per un cuore così allontanato da Lucy… potrebbero non essere facilmente superabili.

Esigeva molto dalla sua pazienza; ma lo stato d’animo di quella persona era quello della [[concepts/melancholy|melancolia]].

Colui che sa di doversi aspettare l’opposizione e la cattiveria della famiglia

Poteva essere considerato un vero sollievo!



Mentre queste considerazioni le attraversavano la mente una dopo l’altra, con dolore, lei pianse.

Per lui, più che per sé stessa. Sostenuta dalla convinzione di aver…

Non ha fatto nulla per meritarsi la sua attuale infelicità, e si consola…

Credette fermamente che Edward non avesse fatto nulla per meritarsi la sua disapprovazione.

Ora ancora, nonostante il primo impatto violento di quel colpo potente, lei era in grado di comandare…

abbastanza sicura di sé da tenere sua madre lontana da qualsiasi sospetto riguardo alla [[concepts/truth|_verità]].

E anche le sorelle. E così, in qualche modo, riuscì a soddisfare le proprie aspettative.

Titolo:  
Quando si unì a loro per la cena, solo due ore dopo essere arrivata…

Tutte le sue speranze più care andarono perdute… nessuno avrebbe potuto fare nulla al riguardo.

Dalla loro apparenza, si poteva dedurre che Elinor fosse in lutto.

In segreto, attraverso ostacoli che la separeranno per sempre dall’oggetto dei suoi desideri…

A causa del suo [[motifs/love|amore]], e Marianne continuava a riflettere su questo nel profondo di sé.

Perfezioni di un uomo, di cui sentiva profondamente tutto il cuore

Possed… e di cui si aspettava di vedere l’immagine in ogni carrozza che passasse.

vicino alla loro casa.



La necessità di nascondere a sua madre e a Marianne ciò che era accaduto

Con fiducia affidato a lei stessa, anche se ciò la costringeva ad agire senza sosta…

Lo sforzo non aumentò affatto la sofferenza di Elinor; anzi…

Per lei fu un sollievo essere risparmiata dalla comunicazione di ciò che avrebbe significato…

Una tale sofferenza per loro… e allo stesso tempo la possibilità di essere salvati dal dover ascoltare quelle cose.

Condanna di Edward, che probabilmente deriverebbe dall’eccesso…

Il loro affetto parziale per lei… un sentimento che andava oltre ciò che lei provava.

Uguale a sostegno.



Dalle loro parole o dai loro discorsi, lei capì di poter ricevere…

Senza alcun aiuto, la loro tenerezza e il loro dolore non fanno che aumentare la sua sofferenza.

Mentre il suo autocontrollo non riceveva alcun incoraggiamento da parte loro.

Né gli esempi né i loro elogi potevano influenzarla. Era più forte da sola, e il suo valore proveniva soltanto da sé stessa.

Il sostegno ricevuto da lei era così forte che la sua determinazione rimase incrollabile.

Apparenza di allegria come qualcosa di immutabile, così come i rimpianti profondamente dolorosi

E così freschi, era possibile che fossero così.



“Nonostante abbia sofferto molto durante la sua prima conversazione con Lucy…”

Titolo:  
Ben presto provò un sincero desiderio di rinnovarlo… e questo per…

Più motivi di uno… Voleva conoscere tutti i dettagli riguardo a loro.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_23--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 23 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 23" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/love,motif/rose,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/charity,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/solitude,concept/wonder,character/lucy_steele"></span>


engagement repeated again, she wanted more clearly to understand what

Lucy really felt for Edward, whether there were any sincerity in her

declaration of tender regard for him, and she particularly wanted to

convince Lucy, by her readiness to enter on the matter again, and her

calmness in conversing on it, that she was no otherwise interested in

it than as a friend, which she very much feared her involuntary

agitation, in their morning discourse, must have left at least

doubtful. That Lucy was disposed to be jealous of her appeared very

probable: it was plain that Edward had always spoken highly in her

praise, not merely from Lucy’s assertion, but from her venturing to

trust her on so short a personal acquaintance, with a secret so

confessedly and evidently important. And even Sir John’s joking

intelligence must have had some weight. But indeed, while Elinor

remained so [[motifs/well|well]] assured within herself of being really beloved by

Edward, it required no other consideration of probabilities to make it

natural that Lucy should be jealous; and that she was so, her very

confidence was a proof. What other reason for the disclosure of the

affair could there be, but that Elinor might be informed by it of

Lucy’s superior claims on Edward, and be taught to avoid him in future?

She had little difficulty in understanding thus much of her rival’s

intentions, and while she was firmly resolved to act by her as every

principle of [[concepts/honour|honour]] and honesty directed, to combat her own affection

for Edward and to see him as little as possible; she could not deny

herself the comfort of endeavouring to convince Lucy that her heart was

unwounded. And as she could now have nothing more painful to hear on

the subject than had already been told, she did not mistrust her own

ability of going through a repetition of particulars with composure.



But it was not immediately that an opportunity of doing so could be

commanded, though Lucy was as [[motifs/well|well]] disposed as herself to take

advantage of any that occurred; for the weather was not often fine

enough to allow of their joining in a walk, where they might most

easily separate themselves from the others; and though they met at

least every other evening either at the park or cottage, and chiefly at

the former, they could not be supposed to meet for the sake of

conversation. Such a thought would never enter either Sir John or Lady

Middleton’s head; and therefore very little leisure was ever given for

a general chat, and none at all for particular discourse. They met for

the sake of eating, drinking, and laughing together, playing at cards,

or consequences, or any other game that was sufficiently noisy.



One or two meetings of this kind had taken place, without affording

Elinor any chance of engaging Lucy in private, when Sir John called at

the cottage one morning, to beg, in the name of [[concepts/charity|charity]], that they

would all dine with Lady Middleton that day, as he was obliged to

attend the club at Exeter, and she would otherwise be quite alone,

except her mother and the two Miss Steeles. Elinor, who foresaw a

fairer opening for the point she had in view, in such a party as this

was likely to be, more at liberty among themselves under the tranquil

and [[motifs/well|well]]-bred direction of Lady Middleton than when her husband united

them together in one noisy purpose, immediately accepted the

invitation; Margaret, with her mother’s permission, was equally

compliant, and Marianne, though always unwilling to join any of their

parties, was persuaded by her mother, who could not bear to have her

seclude herself from any chance of amusement, to go likewise.



The young ladies went, and Lady Middleton was happily preserved from

the frightful [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] which had threatened her. The insipidity of the

meeting was exactly such as Elinor had expected; it produced not one

novelty of thought or expression, and nothing could be less interesting

than the whole of their discourse both in the dining parlour and

drawing room: to the latter, the children accompanied them, and while

they remained there, she was too [[motifs/well|well]] convinced of the impossibility of

engaging Lucy’s attention to attempt it. They quitted it only with the

removal of the tea-things. The card-table was then placed, and Elinor

began to [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at herself for having ever entertained a [[concepts/hope|hope]] of

finding [[motifs/time|time]] for conversation at the park. They all [[motifs/rose|rose]] up in

preparation for a round game.



“I am glad,” said Lady Middleton to Lucy, “you are not going to finish

poor little Annamaria’s basket this evening; for I am sure it must hurt

your eyes to work filigree by candlelight. And we will make the dear

little [[motifs/love|love]] some amends for her disappointment to-morrow, and then I

[[concepts/hope|hope]] she will not much mind it.”



This hint was enough, Lucy recollected herself instantly and replied,

“Indeed you are very much mistaken, Lady Middleton; I am only waiting

to know whether you can make your party without me, or I should have

been at my filigree already. I would not disappoint the little angel

for all the world: and if you want me at the card-table now, I am

resolved to finish the basket after supper.”



“You are very good, I [[concepts/hope|hope]] it won’t hurt your eyes—will you ring the

bell for some working candles? My poor little girl would be sadly

disappointed, I know, if the basket was not finished tomorrow, for

though I told her it certainly would not, I am sure she depends upon

having it done.”



Lucy directly drew her work table near her and reseated herself with an

alacrity and cheerfulness which seemed to infer that she could taste no

greater delight than in making a filigree basket for a spoilt [[archetypes/child|child]].



Lady Middleton proposed a rubber of Casino to the others. No one made

any objection but Marianne, who with her usual inattention to the forms

of general civility, exclaimed, “Your Ladyship will have the goodness

to excuse _me_—you know I detest cards. I shall go to the piano-forte;

I have not touched it since it was tuned.” And without farther

ceremony, she turned away and walked to the instrument.



Lady Middleton looked as if she thanked heaven that _she_ had never

made so rude a speech.



“Marianne can never keep long from that instrument you know, ma’am,”

said Elinor, endeavouring to smooth away the offence; “and I do not

much [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at it; for it is the very best toned piano-forte I ever

heard.”



The remaining five were now to draw their cards.



“Perhaps,” continued Elinor, “if I should happen to cut out, I may be

of some use to Miss [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]], in rolling her papers for her; and

there is so much still to be done to the basket, that it must be

impossible I think for her labour singly, to finish it this evening. I

should like the work exceedingly, if she would allow me a share in it.”



“Indeed I shall be very much obliged to you for your help,” cried Lucy,

“for I find there is more to be done to it than I thought there was;

and it would be a shocking thing to disappoint dear Annamaria after

all.”



“Oh! that would be terrible, indeed,” said Miss Steele. “Dear little

[[motifs/soul|soul]], how I do [[motifs/love|love]] her!”



“You are very kind,” said Lady Middleton to Elinor; “and as you really

like the work, perhaps you will be as [[motifs/well|well]] pleased not to cut in till

another rubber, or will you take your chance now?”



Elinor joyfully profited by the first of these proposals, and thus by a

little of that address which Marianne could never condescend to

practise, gained her own end, and pleased Lady Middleton at the same

[[motifs/time|time]]. Lucy made room for her with ready attention, and the two fair

rivals were thus seated side by side at the same table, and, with the

utmost harmony, engaged in forwarding the same work. The pianoforte at

which Marianne, wrapped up in her own music and her own thoughts, had

by this [[motifs/time|time]] forgotten that any [[concepts/body|body]] was in the room besides herself,

was luckily so near them that Miss Dashwood now judged she might

safely, under the shelter of its noise, introduce the interesting

subject, without any risk of being heard at the card-table.

L’impegno fu ripetuto ancora una volta; lei voleva capire più chiaramente di cosa si trattasse.

Lucy provava davvero compassione per Edward, anche se non si sapeva quanto fosse sincera…

Dichiarazione di profondo rispetto per lui… e lei voleva particolarmente…

Convinci Lucy: dalla sua prontezza nel riprendere l’argomento, e dal suo…

fidati di lei dopo una conoscenza così breve, per un segreto del genere…

Natural che Lucy fosse gelosa… E infatti lo era davvero.

Qualsiasi relazione potesse esistere, ma che Elinor ne venisse a conoscenza…

Le fu abbastanza facile comprendere gran parte di ciò che la sua rivale aveva detto.

Intenzioni… e mentre era fermamente decisa ad agire secondo esse.

Il principio di [[concepts/honour|onore]] e onestà, utilizzato per contrastare i propri stessi sentimenti.

“Per Edward… e per vederlo il meno possibile possibile; non poteva negarlo.”

Il conforto di cercare di convincere Lucy che il suo cuore…

Innocua… E poiché ormai non poteva più sentire nulla di più doloroso…

La capacità di affrontare ripetutamente degli elementi specifici con tranquillità.



Ma non fu subito che si presentò l’opportunità di farlo.

Ordinò che fosse fatto, anche se Lucy era altrettanto disposta a collaborare quanto lei stessa.

Il vantaggio di qualsiasi cosa fosse accaduta… poiché il tempo non era spesso bello.

Abbastanza per permettere loro di unirsi a una passeggiata, dove potrebbero divertirsi di più

Si distinguono facilmente dagli altri; e sebbene si siano incontrati…

Almeno ogni altro venerdì sera, sia nel parco che nella capanna… e soprattutto lì.

Il primo, non si poteva certo pensare che si incontrassero per quel motivo…

Conversazione… Un pensiero del genere non sarebbe mai passato per la mente né di Sir John né di Lady…

La testa di Middleton; e quindi molto poco tempo libero le veniva mai concesso…

Una chiacchierata generale, senza alcun argomento specifico. Si sono incontrati per…

Per il gusto di mangiare, bere e ridere insieme, giocando a carte…

O le conseguenze, o qualsiasi altro gioco che fosse abbastanza rumoroso.



Uno o due incontri di questo tipo si erano già tenuti, ma senza portare a nessun risultato concreto.

Qualche possibilità di parlare in privato con Lucy, quando Sir John è venuto a far visita?

Una mattina, nella capanna, andarono a chiedere l’elemosina, in nome della [[concepts/charity|carità]], affinché loro.

Quel giorno, tutti avrebbero pranzato con la signora Middleton, poiché lui era costretto ad andarci.

Aspettare il club a Exeter. Altrimenti sarebbe davvero molto sola.

“Ad eccezione di sua madre e delle due signorine Steele… Elinor, che se ne rese conto in anticipo…”

Un’occasione migliore per esporre il punto che aveva in mente, in una serata come questa…

Probabilmente erano più liberi tra loro, in quell’atmosfera di tranquillità…

E la buona educazione e le maniere raffinate di Lady Middleton erano ancora più evidenti dopo che suo marito si era unito a loro.

Uniti da uno scopo comune e deciso, furono immediatamente accettati…

Invito: Con il permesso di sua madre, Margaret…

“Compliant… e Marianne, sebbene sempre riluttante ad unirsi a loro…”

Le feste… fu convinta da sua madre, che non riusciva a sopportare l’idea di vederla partecipare.

Si allontana da qualsiasi possibilità di divertimento, per andare allo stesso modo.



Le giovani signore se ne andarono, e Lady Middleton rimase felicemente al sicuro…

La terribile [[concepts/solitude|solitudine]] che l’aveva minacciata. L’insipidità di tutto ciò.

La riunione fu esattamente come Elinor si aspettava; non produsse nulla di significativo.

Un’originalità di pensiero o di espressione… ma niente potrebbe essere meno interessante.

Più di tutto il loro discorso, sia nella sala da pranzo che altrove…

Sala da pranzo: i bambini li accompagnarono, e mentre…

Rimasero lì; lei era troppo [[motifs/well|convinta]] dell’impossibilità di.

Attirare l’attenzione di Lucy per provare… Lo abbandonarono solo quando…

La rimozione degli oggetti legati al tè… Poi fu posizionato il tavolo da gioco, e Elinor…

Incominciò a [[concepts/wonder|chiedersi]] come avesse mai potuto nutrire una [[concepts/hope|speranza]] del genere.

Trovarono il [[motifs/time|tempo]] per chiacchierare nel parco. Tutti si alzarono insieme.

Preparazione per una partita a turno.



“Sono contenta”, disse Lady Middleton a Lucy, “che tu non intenda finire…”

La cesta di povera piccola Annamaria stasera… perché sono sicura che debba farle male.

"#Lavorare con gli occhi alla luce delle candele… E creeremo qualcosa di prezioso."

La piccola [[motifs/love|amore]] farà qualche tentativo per rimediare alla sua delusione domani, e poi io.

“Spero che non le dispiaccia troppo.”



“Questo indizio è stato sufficiente”, si ricordò immediatamente Lucy e rispose.

“Infatti, si sbaglia di grosso, signora Middleton: sto semplicemente aspettando.”

Titolo:  
Per capire se riuscite a organizzare la vostra festa senza di me… o forse sarebbe stato meglio che io non ci fossi.

Ho già provato con i miei sforzi… Non vorrei deludere quel piccolo angelo.

Per tutto il mondo… E se ora volete che io sia al tavolo da gioco, eccomi qui.

“Deciso a finire il lavoro dopo cena.”



“Sei molto brava, spero che non ti faccia male agli occhi, vuoi suonare il, ”

“Una candela per il lavoro… Mia povera piccola ragazza ne avrebbe bisogno…”

Deluso, lo so… se il cesto non fosse finito entro domani…

“Anche se le ho detto che sicuramente non sarebbe successo, sono certo che lei ci conta comunque…”

“Riuscirci davvero.”



Lucy portò immediatamente il suo tavolo da lavoro vicino a sé e si risedette.

Allegria e vivacità che sembravano indicare che non apprezzasse affatto…

Nessuna gioia maggiore di quella di creare un cestino intrecciato per un bambino viziato.



Una partita al casinò proposta da Lady Middleton… ma nessuno accettò

“Nessuna obiezione… tranne che da parte di Marianne, la quale, come al solito, non presta attenzione alle formalità…”

“Di una generale cortesia…”, esclamò, “Spero che Vostra Signoria abbia la gentilezza…”

“Per scusarmi… sapete che odio le carte. Andrò al pianoforte.”

“Non l’ho più toccato da quando è stato accordato…” E senza aggiungere altro.

Durante la cerimonia, lei si girò e si avvicinò all’strumento.



Lady Middleton sembrava ringraziare il cielo per non aver mai…

Tenne un discorso così scortese.



“Marianne non riesce mai a stare lontana da quell’instrumento, sa?”

“E così,” disse Elinor, cercando di alleviare l’offesa; “e non penso affatto…”

Ero davvero molto [[concepts/wonder|meravigliato]] di fronte ad esso; perché era il pianoforte a coda con il suono più squisito che avessi mai sentito.

“Sentito.”



I restanti cinque avrebbero ora dovuto tirare le loro carte.



“Forse,” proseguì Elinor, “se dovesse capitarmi di tagliarmi via qualcosa…”

Doveva essere di qualche utilità per la signorina [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]], aiutandola a impilare i suoi documenti; e.

C’è ancora molto da fare su quel cesto… deve essere sistemato completamente.

“Impossibile, penso… Per lei, da sola, non riuscirà a finirlo stasera.”

“Le piacerebbe molto il lavoro, se solo mi permettesse di parteciparvi.”



“Certamente vi sarò molto grata per il vostro aiuto,” esclamò Lucy.

“Perché mi rendo conto che ci sono ancora molte cose da fare, più di quanto pensassi.”

E sarebbe davvero spiacevole deludere cara Annamaria…

“Tutto.”



“Oh! sarebbe terribile davvero,” disse la signorina Steele. “Caro piccolo…”

“Anima mia, quanto la amo!”



“Siete molto gentile,” disse Lady Middleton a Elinor; “e poiché davvero…”

Se ti piace il lavoro, forse sarai altrettanto soddisfatto se non interrompi fino a.

“Un’altra possibilità… o deciderai di cogliere l’occasione ora?”



Elinor trasse grande beneficio dal primo di questi suggerimenti

Poco di quella cortesia che Marianne non avrebbe mai avuto la pretesa di usare

"Pratica che portò i suoi frutti e, al contempo, soddisfece Lady Middleton."

[[motifs/time|tempo]]. Lucy le fece spazio con grande attenzione, e le due giovani donne.

I rivali furono così seduti uno accanto all’altro allo stesso tavolo, e…

Massima armonia, uniti nel perseguire lo stesso obiettivo: il pianoforte…

Che Marianna, immersa nella propria musica e nei propri pensieri, aveva…

"Al sicuro, sotto il riparo del suo rumore, introdurre ciò che è interessante..."

CHAPTER XXIV.





In a firm, though cautious tone, Elinor thus began.



“I should be undeserving of the confidence you have honoured me with,

if I felt no [[motifs/desire|desire]] for its continuance, or no farther curiosity on its

subject. I will not apologize therefore for bringing it forward again.”



“Thank you,” cried Lucy warmly, “for breaking the ice; you have set my

heart at ease by it; for I was somehow or other afraid I had offended

you by what I told you that Monday.”



“Offended me! How could you suppose so? Believe me,” and Elinor spoke

it with the truest sincerity, “nothing could be farther from my

intention than to give you such an idea. Could you have a motive for

the trust, that was not honourable and flattering to me?”



“And yet I do assure you,” replied Lucy, her little sharp eyes full of

meaning, “there seemed to me to be a coldness and displeasure in your

manner that made me quite uncomfortable. I felt sure that you was angry

with me; and have been quarrelling with myself ever since, for having

took such a liberty as to trouble you with my affairs. But I am very

glad to find it was only my own fancy, and that you really do not blame

me. If you knew what a consolation it was to me to relieve my heart

speaking to you of what I am always thinking of every moment of my

life, your compassion would make you overlook every thing else I am

sure.”



“Indeed, I can easily believe that it was a very great relief to you,

to acknowledge your situation to me, and be assured that you shall

never have reason to repent it. Your case is a very unfortunate one;

you seem to me to be surrounded with difficulties, and you will have

need of all your mutual affection to support you under them. Mr.

Ferrars, I believe, is entirely dependent on his mother.”



“He has only two thousand pounds of his own; it would be [[concepts/madness|madness]] to

marry upon that, though for my own part, I could give up every prospect

of more without a sigh. I have been always used to a very small income,

and could struggle with any [[concepts/poverty|poverty]] for him; but I [[motifs/love|love]] him too [[motifs/well|well]] to

be the selfish means of robbing him, perhaps, of all that his mother

might give him if he married to please her. We must wait, it may be for

many years. With almost every other man in the world, it would be an

alarming prospect; but Edward’s affection and constancy nothing can

deprive me of I know.”



“That conviction must be every thing to you; and he is undoubtedly

supported by the same trust in your’s. If the strength of your

reciprocal attachment had failed, as between many people, and under

many circumstances it naturally would during a four years’ engagement,

your situation would have been pitiable, indeed.”



Lucy here looked up; but Elinor was careful in guarding her countenance

from every expression that could give her words a suspicious tendency.



“Edward’s [[motifs/love|love]] for me,” said Lucy, “has been pretty [[motifs/well|well]] put to the

test, by our long, very long absence since we were first engaged, and

it has stood the trial so [[motifs/well|well]], that I should be unpardonable to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]

it now. I can safely say that he has never gave me one moment’s alarm

on that account from the first.”



Elinor hardly knew whether to smile or sigh at this assertion.



Lucy went on. “I am rather of a jealous temper too by [[concepts/nature|nature]], and from

our different situations in life, from his being so much more in the

world than me, and our continual separation, I was enough inclined for

suspicion, to have found out the [[concepts/truth|truth]] in an instant, if there had been

the slightest alteration in his behaviour to me when we met, or any

lowness of spirits that I could not account for, or if he had talked

more of one lady than another, or seemed in any respect less happy at

Longstaple than he used to be. I do not mean to say that I am

particularly observant or quick-sighted in general, but in such a case

I am sure I could not be deceived.”



“All this,” thought Elinor, “is very pretty; but it can impose upon

neither of us.”



“But what,” said she after a short [[motifs/silence|silence]], “are your views? or have

you none but that of waiting for Mrs. Ferrars’s [[motifs/death|death]], which is a

[[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] and shocking extremity?—Is her son determined to submit to

this, and to all the tediousness of the many years of suspense in which

it may involve you, rather than run the risk of her displeasure for a

while by owning the [[concepts/truth|truth]]?”



“If we could be certain that it would be only for a while! But Mrs.

Ferrars is a very headstrong proud woman, and in her first fit of anger

upon hearing it, would very likely secure every thing to Robert, and

the idea of that, for Edward’s sake, frightens away all my inclination

for hasty measures.”



“And for your own sake too, or you are carrying your disinterestedness

beyond reason.”



Lucy looked at Elinor again, and was silent.



“Do you know Mr. Robert Ferrars?” asked Elinor.



“Not at all—I never saw him; but I fancy he is very unlike his

brother—silly and a great coxcomb.”



“A great coxcomb!” repeated Miss Steele, whose ear had caught those

words by a sudden pause in Marianne’s music. “Oh, they are talking of

their favourite beaux, I dare say.”



“No sister,” cried Lucy, “you are mistaken there, our favourite beaux

are _not_ great coxcombs.”



“I can answer for it that Miss Dashwood’s is not,” said Mrs. Jennings,

laughing heartily; “for he is one of the modestest, prettiest behaved

young men I ever saw; but as for Lucy, she is such a sly little

creature, there is no finding out who _she_ likes.”



“Oh,” cried Miss Steele, looking significantly round at them, “I dare

say Lucy’s beau is quite as modest and pretty behaved as Miss

Dashwood’s.”



Elinor blushed in spite of herself. Lucy bit her lip, and looked

angrily at her sister. A mutual [[motifs/silence|silence]] took place for some [[motifs/time|time]]. Lucy

CAPITOLO XXIV.





Con un tono deciso ma cauto, Elinor iniziò così.



"#Non merito affatto la fiducia che mi avete concesso."

Se non provassi alcun [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] che si continuasse, né più curiosità riguardo ad esso.

“Non mi scuserò quindi per sollevare di nuovo questa questione.”



“Grazie,” esclamò Lucy con calore, “per aver rotto il ghiaccio… Mi avete aiutato molto.”

Cuore in pace… perché in qualche modo temevo di aver offeso qualcuno.

“Ricorda ciò che ti ho detto quel lunedì…”



“Mi avete offeso! Come avete potuto pensarlo? Credetemi,” disse Elinor.

Con la più sincera sincerità, “niente potrebbe essere più lontano dai miei intenti”.

Titolo:  
Non avevo alcuna intenzione di farvi pensare una cosa del genere… Potreste avere qualche motivo nascosto?

“La fiducia che non era né onorevole né lusinghiera per me…”



“Eppure vi assicuro,” rispose Lucy, i suoi piccoli occhi acuti pieni di…

Titolo:  
“Mi è sembrato che ci fosse freddezza e disappunto nel tuo comportamento…”

Un modo che mi ha messo molto a disagio… Ero sicuro che fossi arrabbiato.

Con me… E da allora continuo a litigare con me stesso per averlo fatto.

“Ho osato disturbarti con le mie faccende… Ma sono davvero molto…”

Felice di scoprire che era solo una mia fantasia e che tu davvero non mi biasimi.

“Me… Se solo sapessi quanto sia stato un conforto per me poter sfogare i miei sentimenti.”

Di ciò a cui penso costantemente in ogni momento della mia vita

Titolo:  
La tua compassione ti farebbe ignorare tutto il resto di ciò che sono…

“Certo.”



“Certamente, posso facilmente credere che sia stato un grande sollievo per te…”

Condividere la tua situazione con me, e farti certo che io sarò al tuo fianco

Non c’è mai motivo di pentirsi. Il tuo caso è davvero sfortunato.

Mi sembra che tu sia circondato da difficoltà… e ne avrai molte ancora.

Hai bisogno di tutto il vostro affetto reciproco per superare queste difficoltà. Signore.

“Credo che Ferrars dipenda interamente da sua madre.”



“Ha soltanto duemila sterline personali; sarebbe una [[concepts/madness|follezza]] investirle, ”

Titolo:  
E su questo, per quanto riguarda me, sarei disposto ad abbandonare qualsiasi possibilità…

“Di più… senza un sospiro. Sono sempre stato abituato a un reddito molto limitato.”

E avrebbe potuto affrontare qualsiasi tipo di [[concepts/poverty|povertà]] per lui; ma lo [[motifs/love|amo]] troppo bene per farlo.

Titolo:  
Forse, agire in modo egoistico significa derubarlo di tutto ciò che sua madre gli ha dato…

“Potremmo darglielo se si sposasse per compiacerla… Dobbiamo aspettare; forse ci vorrà del tempo.”

Molti anni… Come per quasi tutti gli uomini del mondo, anche per lui sarebbe stato lo stesso.

Prospettiva allarmante… ma l’affetto e la fedeltà di Edward sono qualcosa che nulla può distruggere.

“Privami di ciò che so…”



“Quella condanna deve essere tutto per te… E lui, senza dubbio…”

Titolo:  
Sostenuto dalla stessa fiducia nel vostro… Se la forza del vostro…

L’attaccamento reciproco era fallito, come per molte persone, e in quelle circostanze…

In molte circostanze, è naturale che ciò accada durante un fidanzamento di quattro anni.

“La tua situazione sarebbe stata davvero deplorevole.”



“Lucy alzò lo sguardo; ma Elinor fece attenzione a nascondere le proprie emozioni.”

Da ogni espressione che potesse dare alle sue parole un significato sospetto.



“L’amore di Edward per me”, disse Lucy, “è stato espresso in modo davvero molto bello.”

Una lunga assenza…

Ha resistito alla prova in modo così [[motifs/well|buono]] che sarebbe imperdonabile da parte mia dubitarne.

Ora posso dire con certezza che non mi ha mai causato il minimo preoccupazione.

“Per quel motivo, fin dall’inizio…”



Di fronte a questa affermazione, Elinor non sapeva quasi se sorridere o sospirare.



Lucy continuò: “Per natura, ho anche un carattere piuttosto geloso, e a causa di questo, ”

Le nostre diverse situazioni nella vita, dato che lui si trova in una posizione molto più vantaggiosa…

Titolo:  
Più di chiunque altro al mondo, e a causa della nostra costante separazione, ero particolarmente incline…

Sospetto, se solo fosse stato possibile scoprire la [[concepts/truth|verità]] in un istante.

Qualsiasi minima variazione nel suo comportamento verso di me quando ci siamo incontrati…

Un umore cupo che non riuscivo a spiegarmi… o se avesse parlato…

Più da una signora che da un’altra… o sembrava meno felice in ogni senso…

“Più rigido di una volta… Non intendo dire che io…”

Particolarmente attento o perspicace in generale, ma in quel caso…

“Sono sicuro di non poter essere ingannato.”



“Tutto questo,” pensò Elinor, “è molto bello; ma può risultare oppressivo…”

“Nessuno di noi due.”



“Ma quale,” disse lei dopo un breve [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], “è la tua opinione? O forse, ”

Non vi resta altro che aspettare la [[motifs/death|morte]] della signora Ferrars, il che è.

Melanconia e estremità scioccanti. Il suo figlio è davvero deciso a sottomettersi a tutto ciò?

Questo, e tutta la noia dei molti anni di attesa…

Potrebbe coinvolgerti… piuttosto che correre il rischio di farla arrabbiare.

Mentre possedendo la [[concepts/truth|_verità]],?



“Se solo potessimo essere certi che durerà solo per un po’. Ma la signora, ”

Ferrars è una donna molto testarda e orgogliosa; nel suo primo attacco di rabbia…

Al sentirlo, molto probabilmente avrebbe assicurato tutto a Robert…

L’idea stessa, per l’amor di Dio, spaventa via ogni mia tentazione

“Per misure affrettate…”



“E anche per il tuo stesso bene… altrimenti stai dimostrando di non essere affatto imparziale.”

“Al di là della ragione.”



Lucy guardò di nuovo Elinor e rimase in silenzio.



“Conosci il signor Robert Ferrars?” chiese Elinor.



"Assolutamente no: non l’ho mai visto; ma immagino che sia molto diverso da..."

“Un fratello… sciocco e un vero vanitoso.”



“Un vero vanitoso!”, ripeté la signorina Steele, che aveva sentito quelle parole.

Una pausa improvvisa nella musica di Marianne… “Oh, stanno parlando di…”

“Senza dubbio, i loro amanti preferiti…”



“Nessuna sorella”, gridò Lucy, “ti sbagli: i nostri preferiti sono loro”.

“Non sono certo individui eccezionali…”



“Posso garantirvi che quello di Miss Dashwood non lo è”, disse la signora Jennings.

Ride forte di cuore; “perché è uno dei più umili e dai modi più gentili”.

“Giovani come quelli che ho mai visto… Ma per quanto riguarda Lucy, è davvero una ragazzina astuta…”

“Creatura… non c’è modo di scoprire chi le piaccia.”



“Oh,” esclamò la signorina Steele, guardandoli intorno con aria significativa, “Oso dire…”

Il fidanzato di Lucy è altrettanto modesto e ben comportato quanto la signorina…

“Dashwood’s”.



Elinor arrossì suo malgrado. Lucy morse il labbro e guardò…

Con rabbia, verso sua sorella. Un reciproco [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] durò per un po’. Lucy

then giving them the powerful protection of a very magnificent

concerto,—



“I will honestly tell you of one scheme which has lately come into my

head, for bringing matters to bear; indeed I am bound to let you into

the secret, for you are a party concerned. I dare say you have seen

enough of Edward to know that he would prefer the church to every other

profession; now my plan is that he should take orders as soon as he

can, and then through your interest, which I am sure you would be kind

enough to use out of [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] for him, and I [[concepts/hope|hope]] out of some regard

to me, your brother might be persuaded to give him Norland living;

which I understand is a very good one, and the present incumbent not

likely to live a great while. That would be enough for us to marry

upon, and we might trust to [[motifs/time|time]] and chance for the rest.”



“I should always be happy,” replied Elinor, “to show any mark of my

esteem and [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] for Mr. Ferrars; but do you not perceive that my

interest on such an occasion would be perfectly unnecessary? He is

brother to Mrs. John Dashwood—_that_ must be recommendation enough to

her husband.”



“But Mrs. John Dashwood would not much approve of Edward’s going into

orders.”



“Then I rather suspect that my interest would do very little.”



They were again silent for many minutes. At length Lucy exclaimed with

a deep sigh,



“I believe it would be the wisest way to put an end to the business at

once by dissolving the engagement. We seem so beset with difficulties

on every side, that though it would make us miserable for a [[motifs/time|time]], we

should be happier perhaps in the end. But you will not give me your

advice, Miss Dashwood?”



“No,” answered Elinor, with a smile, which concealed very agitated

feelings, “on such a subject I certainly will not. You know very [[motifs/well|well]]

that my opinion would have no weight with you, unless it were on the

side of your wishes.”



“Indeed you wrong me,” replied Lucy, with great solemnity; “I know

nobody of whose judgment I think so highly as I do of yours; and I do

really believe, that if you was to say to me, ‘I advise you by all

means to put an end to your engagement with [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]], it will be

more for the happiness of both of you,’ I should resolve upon doing it

immediately.”



Elinor blushed for the insincerity of Edward’s future wife, and

replied, “This compliment would effectually frighten me from giving any

opinion on the subject had I formed one. It raises my influence much

too high; the power of dividing two people so tenderly attached is too

much for an indifferent person.”



“’Tis because you are an indifferent person,” said Lucy, with some

pique, and laying a particular stress on those words, “that your

judgment might justly have such weight with me. If you could be

supposed to be biased in any respect by your own feelings, your opinion

would not be worth having.”



Elinor thought it wisest to make no answer to this, lest they might

provoke each other to an unsuitable increase of ease and unreserve; and

was even partly determined never to mention the subject again. Another

pause therefore of many minutes’ duration, succeeded this speech, and

Lucy was still the first to end it.



“Shall you be in town this [[motifs/winter|winter]], Miss Dashwood?” said she with all

her accustomary complacency.



“Certainly not.”



“I am sorry for that,” returned the other, while her eyes brightened at

the information, “it would have gave me such pleasure to meet you

there! But I dare say you will go for all that. To be sure, your

brother and sister will ask you to come to them.”



“It will not be in my power to accept their invitation if they do.”



“How unlucky that is! I had quite depended upon meeting you there. Anne

and me are to go the latter end of January to some relations who have

been wanting us to visit them these several years! But I only go for

the sake of seeing Edward. He will be there in February, otherwise

[[settings/london|London]] would have no charms for me; I have not spirits for it.”



Elinor was soon called to the card-table by the conclusion of the first

rubber, and the confidential discourse of the two ladies was therefore

at an end, to which both of them submitted without any reluctance, for

nothing had been said on either side to make them dislike each other

less than they had done before; and Elinor sat down to the card table

with the [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] persuasion that Edward was not only without

affection for the person who was to be his wife; but that he had not

even the chance of being tolerably happy in [[motifs/marriage|marriage]], which sincere

affection on _her_ side would have given, for [[concepts/self|self]]-interest alone could

induce a woman to keep a man to an engagement, of which she seemed so

thoroughly aware that he was weary.



From this [[motifs/time|time]] the subject was never revived by Elinor, and when

entered on by Lucy, who seldom missed an opportunity of introducing it,

and was particularly careful to inform her confidante, of her happiness

whenever she received a letter from Edward, it was treated by the

former with calmness and caution, and dismissed as soon as civility

would allow; for she felt such conversations to be an indulgence which

Lucy did not deserve, and which were dangerous to herself.



The visit of the Miss Steeles at Barton Park was lengthened far beyond

what the first invitation implied. Their favour increased; they could

not be spared; Sir John would not hear of their going; and in spite of

their numerous and long arranged engagements in Exeter, in spite of the

absolute necessity of returning to fulfill them immediately, which was

in full force at the end of every week, they were prevailed on to stay

nearly two months at the park, and to assist in the due celebration of

that festival which requires a more than ordinary share of private

balls and large dinners to proclaim its importance.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_25" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 25" data-chapter="Chapter 25" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/death,motif/home,motif/time,motif/well,motif/winter,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/mercy,concept/truth,setting/london,character/edward_ferrars"></span>


CHAPTER XXV.





Though Mrs. Jennings was in the habit of spending a large portion of

the year at the houses of her children and friends, she was not without

a settled habitation of her own. Since the [[motifs/death|death]] of her husband, who

had traded with success in a less elegant part of the town, she had

resided every [[motifs/winter|winter]] in a house in one of the streets near Portman

Square. Towards this [[motifs/home|home]], she began on the approach of January to turn

her thoughts, and thither she one day abruptly, and very unexpectedly

by them, asked the elder Misses Dashwood to accompany her. Elinor,

without observing the varying complexion of her sister, and the

animated look which spoke no indifference to the plan, immediately gave

a grateful but absolute denial for both, in which she believed herself

to be speaking their united inclinations. The reason alleged was their

determined resolution of not leaving their mother at that [[motifs/time|time]] of the

year. Mrs. Jennings received the refusal with some surprise, and

repeated her invitation immediately.



“Oh, Lord! I am sure your mother can spare you very [[motifs/well|well]], and I _do_

beg you will favour me with your company, for I’ve quite set my heart

upon it. Don’t fancy that you will be any inconvenience to me, for I

shan’t put myself at all out of my way for you. It will only be sending

Betty by the coach, and I [[concepts/hope|hope]] I can afford _that_. We three shall be

able to go very [[motifs/well|well]] in my chaise; and when we are in town, if you do

not like to go wherever I do, [[motifs/well|well]] and good, you may always go with one

of my daughters. I am sure your mother will not object to it; for I

have had such good luck in getting my own children off my hands that

she will think me a very fit person to have the charge of you; and if I

don’t get one of you at least [[motifs/well|well]] married before I have done with you,

it shall not be my fault. I shall speak a good word for you to all the

young men, you may depend upon it.”



“I have a notion,” said Sir John, “that Miss Marianne would not object

to such a scheme, if her elder sister would come into it. It is very

hard indeed that she should not have a little pleasure, because Miss

Dashwood does not wish it. So I would advise you two, to set off for

town, when you are tired of Barton, without saying a word to Miss

Dashwood about it.”



“Nay,” cried Mrs. Jennings, “I am sure I shall be monstrous glad of

Miss Marianne’s company, whether Miss Dashwood will go or not, only the

more the merrier say I, and I thought it would be more comfortable for

them to be together; because, if they got tired of me, they might talk

to one another, and laugh at my odd ways behind my back. But one or the

other, if not both of them, I must have. Lord bless me! how do you

think I can live poking by myself, I who have been always used till

this [[motifs/winter|winter]] to have Charlotte with me. Come, Miss Marianne, let us

strike hands upon the bargain, and if Miss Dashwood will change her

mind by and bye, why so much the better.”



“I thank you, ma’am, sincerely thank you,” said Marianne, with warmth:

“your invitation has insured my gratitude for ever, and it would give

me such happiness, yes, almost the greatest happiness I am capable of,

to be able to accept it. But my mother, my dearest, kindest mother,—I

feel the justice of what Elinor has urged, and if she were to be made

less happy, less comfortable by our absence—Oh! no, nothing should

tempt me to leave her. It should not, must not be a struggle.”



Mrs. Jennings repeated her assurance that Mrs. Dashwood could spare

them perfectly [[motifs/well|well]]; and Elinor, who now understood her sister, and saw

to what indifference to almost every thing else she was carried by her

eagerness to be with Willoughby again, made no farther direct

opposition to the plan, and merely referred it to her mother’s

decision, from whom however she scarcely expected to receive any

support in her endeavour to prevent a visit, which she could not

approve of for Marianne, and which on her own account she had

particular reasons to avoid. Whatever Marianne was desirous of, her

mother would be eager to promote—she could not expect to influence the

latter to cautiousness of conduct in an affair respecting which she had

never been able to inspire her with distrust; and she dared not explain

the motive of her own disinclination for going to [[settings/london|London]]. That

Marianne, fastidious as she was, thoroughly acquainted with Mrs.

Jennings’ manners, and invariably disgusted by them, should overlook

every inconvenience of that kind, should disregard whatever must be

most wounding to her irritable feelings, in her pursuit of one object,

was such a proof, so strong, so full, of the importance of that object

to her, as Elinor, in spite of all that had passed, was not prepared to

witness.



On being informed of the invitation, Mrs. Dashwood, persuaded that such

an excursion would be productive of much amusement to both her

daughters, and perceiving through all her affectionate attention to

herself, how much the heart of Marianne was in it, would not hear of

their declining the offer upon _her_ account; insisted on their both

accepting it directly; and then began to foresee, with her usual

cheerfulness, a variety of advantages that would accrue to them all,

from this separation.



“I am delighted with the plan,” she cried, “it is exactly what I could

wish. Margaret and I shall be as much benefited by it as yourselves.

When you and the Middletons are gone, we shall go on so quietly and

happily together with our books and our music! You will find Margaret

so improved when you come back again! I have a little plan of

alteration for your bedrooms too, which may now be performed without

any inconvenience to any one. It is very right that you _should_ go to

town; I would have every young woman of your condition in life

acquainted with the manners and amusements of [[settings/london|London]]. You will be under

the care of a motherly good sort of woman, of whose kindness to you I

can have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]. And in all probability you will see your brother,

and whatever may be his faults, or the faults of his wife, when I

consider whose son he is, I cannot bear to have you so wholly estranged

from each other.”



“Though with your usual anxiety for our happiness,” said Elinor, “you

have been obviating every impediment to the present scheme which

occurred to you, there is still one objection which, in my opinion,

cannot be so easily removed.”



Marianne’s countenance sunk.



“And what,” said Mrs. Dashwood, “is my dear prudent Elinor going to

suggest? What formidable obstacle is she now to bring forward? Do not

let me hear a word about the expense of it.”



“My objection is this; though I think very [[motifs/well|well]] of Mrs. Jennings’s

heart, she is not a woman whose society can afford us pleasure, or

whose protection will give us consequence.”



“That is very true,” replied her mother, “but of her society,

separately from that of other people, you will scarcely have any thing

at all, and you will almost always appear in public with Lady

Middleton.”



“If Elinor is frightened away by her dislike of Mrs. Jennings,” said

Marianne, “at least it need not prevent MY accepting her invitation. I

have no such scruples, and I am sure I could put up with every

unpleasantness of that kind with very little effort.”



Elinor could not help smiling at this display of indifference towards

the manners of a person, to whom she had often had difficulty in

persuading Marianne to behave with tolerable politeness; and resolved

within herself, that if her sister persisted in going, she would go

likewise, as she did not think it proper that Marianne should be left

to the sole guidance of her own judgment, or that Mrs. Jennings should

be abandoned to the [[concepts/mercy|mercy]] of Marianne for all the comfort of her

domestic hours. To this determination she was the more easily

reconciled, by recollecting that [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]], by Lucy’s account, was

not to be in town before February; and that their visit, without any

unreasonable abridgement, might be previously finished.



“I will have you _both_ go,” said Mrs. Dashwood; “these objections are

nonsensical. You will have much pleasure in being in [[settings/london|London]], and

especially in being together; and if Elinor would ever condescend to

anticipate enjoyment, she would foresee it there from a variety of

sources; she would, perhaps, expect some from improving her

acquaintance with her sister-in-law’s family.”



Elinor had often wished for an opportunity of attempting to weaken her

mother’s dependence on the attachment of Edward and herself, that the

shock might be less when the whole [[concepts/truth|truth]] were revealed, and now on this

attack, though almost hopeless of success, she forced herself to begin

her design by saying, as calmly as she could, “I like [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]]

very much, and shall always be glad to see him; but as to the rest of

the family, it is a matter of perfect indifference to me, whether I am

ever known to them or not.”



Mrs. Dashwood smiled, and said nothing. Marianne lifted up her eyes in

astonishment, and Elinor conjectured that she might as [[motifs/well|well]] have held

her tongue.



After very little farther discourse, it was finally settled that the

invitation should be fully accepted. Mrs. Jennings received the

information with a great deal of joy, and many assurances of kindness

and care; nor was it a matter of pleasure merely to her. Sir John was

delighted; for to a man, whose prevailing anxiety was the dread of

being alone, the acquisition of two, to the number of inhabitants in

[[settings/london|London]], was something. Even Lady Middleton took the trouble of being

delighted, which was putting herself rather out of her way; and as for

the Miss Steeles, especially Lucy, they had never been so happy in

their lives as this intelligence made them.



Elinor submitted to the arrangement which counteracted her wishes with

less reluctance than she had expected to feel. With regard to herself,

it was now a matter of unconcern whether she went to town or not, and

when she saw her mother so thoroughly pleased with the plan, and her

sister exhilarated by it in look, voice, and manner, restored to all

her usual animation, and elevated to more than her usual gaiety, she

could not be dissatisfied with the cause, and would hardly allow

herself to distrust the consequence.



Marianne’s joy was almost a degree beyond happiness, so great was the

perturbation of her spirits and her impatience to be gone. Her

unwillingness to quit her mother was her only restorative to calmness;

and at the moment of parting her grief on that score was excessive. Her

mother’s affliction was hardly less, and Elinor was the only one of the

three, who seemed to consider the separation as any thing short of

eternal.



Their departure took place in the first week in January. The Middletons

were to follow in about a week. The Miss Steeles kept their station at

the park, and were to quit it only with the rest of the family.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XXV.





Sebbene la signora Jennings avesse l’abitudine di spendere una grande parte…

L'anno trascorso nelle case dei suoi figli e amici… non fu affatto privo di momenti significativi.

Una dimora stabile tutta sua. Dalla [[motifs/death|morte]] di suo marito.

Aveva fatto affari con successo in una zona meno elegante della città.

Ogni [[motifs/winter|inverno]], risiedeva in una casa situata in una delle strade vicino a Portman.

Dritto verso questa [[motifs/home|casa]], iniziò ad orientarsi verso gennaio per poi svoltare.

I suoi pensieri… e un giorno, improvvisamente e in modo del tutto inaspettato, si diresse verso di loro.

“By them, the older Miss Dashwood was asked to accompany her. Elinor…”

Senza notare il cambiamento di colore del viso di sua sorella, e…

Uno sguardo pieno di interesse, che non lasciava dubbi sulla sua approvazione del piano…

Titolo:  
Una negazione grata ma assoluta per entrambi, nella quale lei credeva in se stessa.

Per esprimere le loro tendenze condivise… La ragione addotta fu…

Una risoluzione decisa di non abbandonare la propria madre in quel [[motifs/time|momento]].

Anno. La signora Jennings ricevette il rifiuto con una certa sorpresa…

Ripeté immediatamente la sua invito.



“Oh, Signore! Sono sicura che tua madre possa permettersi di darti molto bene, e io _davvero_, ”

"Vi prego, concedetemi la vostra compagnia: ho davvero deciso di farlo."

Su di esso. Non pensare nemmeno che possa rappresentare un problema per me, perché…

Non mi darò affatto la pena per te… Sarà solo uno spreco di tempo.

Betty vicino al vagone, e io [[concepts/hope|spero]] di potermelo permettere. Noi tre saremo.

Posso muovermi molto bene nella mia sedia a rotelle; e quando siamo in città, se tu lo fai.

Non mi piace andare dove vado io, ma va bene, comunque puoi sempre accompagnarmi.

“Delle mie figlie… Sono certo che vostra madre non avrà obiezioni; infatti…”

Ho avuto davvero molta fortuna nel riuscire a liberarmi dei miei figli…

“Lei penserà che io sia la persona adatta per prendersi cura di te; e se io…”

Che nessuno di voi si sposi almeno [[motifs/well|benissimo]] prima che io abbia finito con voi.

“Non sarà colpa mia… Parlerò bene di te a tutti.”

“Giovani uomini, potete contarci su.”



“Ho un’idea”, disse Sir John, “che Miss Marianne non avrebbe obiezioni…”

“Se sua sorella maggiore partecipasse a questo piano… Sarebbe davvero molto importante.”

Davvero difficile non concedersi un po’ di piacere, solo perché la signorina…

Dashwood non lo desidera… Quindi vi consiglio entrambi di partire subito.

Città… quando ti stanchi di Barton, senza dire una parola alla signorina…

“Dashwood al riguardo…”



“No,” esclamò la signora Jennings, “sono sicura che sarò immensamente felice…”
