<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 26 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/fire,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/nature,motif/silence,motif/soul,motif/time,concept/beauty,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/nature,setting/london"></span>


CHAPTER XXVI.





Elinor could not find herself in the carriage with Mrs. Jennings, and

beginning a [[motifs/journey|journey]] to [[settings/london|London]] under her protection, and as her guest,

without wondering at her own situation, so short had their acquaintance

with that lady been, so wholly unsuited were they in age and

disposition, and so many had been her objections against such a measure

only a few days before! But these objections had all, with that happy

ardour of youth which Marianne and her mother equally shared, been

overcome or overlooked; and Elinor, in spite of every occasional [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]

of Willoughby’s constancy, could not witness the rapture of delightful

expectation which filled the whole [[motifs/soul|soul]] and beamed in the eyes of

Marianne, without feeling how blank was her own prospect, how cheerless

her own state of mind in the comparison, and how gladly she would

engage in the solicitude of Marianne’s situation to have the same

animating object in view, the same possibility of [[concepts/hope|hope]]. A short, a very

short [[motifs/time|time]] however must now decide what Willoughby’s intentions were;

in all probability he was already in town. Marianne’s eagerness to be

gone declared her dependence on finding him there; and Elinor was

resolved not only upon gaining every new light as to his character

which her own observation or the intelligence of others could give her,

but likewise upon watching his behaviour to her sister with such

zealous attention, as to ascertain what he was and what he meant,

before many meetings had taken place. Should the result of her

observations be unfavourable, she was determined at all events to open

the eyes of her sister; should it be otherwise, her exertions would be

of a different [[concepts/nature|nature]]—she must then learn to avoid every selfish

comparison, and banish every regret which might lessen her satisfaction

in the happiness of Marianne.



They were three days on their [[motifs/journey|journey]], and Marianne’s behaviour as they

travelled was a happy specimen of what future complaisance and

companionableness to Mrs. Jennings might be expected to be. She sat in

[[motifs/silence|silence]] almost all the way, wrapt in her own meditations, and scarcely

ever voluntarily speaking, except when any object of picturesque [[concepts/beauty|beauty]]

within their view drew from her an exclamation of delight exclusively

addressed to her sister. To atone for this conduct therefore, Elinor

took immediate possession of the post of civility which she had

assigned herself, behaved with the greatest attention to Mrs. Jennings,

talked with her, laughed with her, and listened to her whenever she

could; and Mrs. Jennings on her side treated them both with all

possible kindness, was solicitous on every occasion for their ease and

enjoyment, and only disturbed that she could not make them choose their

own dinners at the inn, nor extort a confession of their preferring

salmon to cod, or boiled fowls to veal cutlets. They reached town by

three o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] the third day, glad to be released, after such a [[motifs/journey|journey]],

from the confinement of a carriage, and ready to enjoy all the luxury

of a good [[motifs/fire|fire]].



The house was handsome, and handsomely fitted up, and the young ladies

were immediately put in possession of a very comfortable apartment. It

had formerly been Charlotte’s, and over the mantelpiece still hung a

landscape in coloured silks of her performance, in proof of her having

spent seven years at a great school in town to some effect.



As dinner was not to be ready in less than two hours from their

arrival, Elinor determined to employ the interval in writing to her

mother, and sat down for that purpose. In a few moments Marianne did

the same. “_I_ am writing [[motifs/home|home]], Marianne,” said Elinor; “had not you

better defer your letter for a day or two?”



“I am _not_ going to write to my mother,” replied Marianne, hastily,

and as if wishing to avoid any farther inquiry. Elinor said no more; it

immediately struck her that she must then be writing to Willoughby; and

the conclusion which as instantly followed was, that, however

mysteriously they might wish to conduct the affair, they must be

engaged. This conviction, though not entirely satisfactory, gave her

pleasure, and she continued her letter with greater alacrity.

Marianne’s was finished in a very few minutes; in length it could be no

more than a note; it was then folded up, sealed, and directed with

eager rapidity. Elinor thought she could distinguish a large W in the

direction; and no sooner was it complete than Marianne, ringing the

bell, requested the footman who answered it to get that letter conveyed

for her to the two-penny post. This decided the matter at once.



Her spirits still continued very high; but there was a flutter in them

which prevented their giving much pleasure to her sister, and this

agitation increased as the evening drew on. She could scarcely eat any

dinner, and when they afterwards returned to the drawing room, seemed

anxiously listening to the sound of every carriage.



It was a great satisfaction to Elinor that Mrs. Jennings, by being much

engaged in her own room, could see little of what was passing. The tea

things were brought in, and already had Marianne been disappointed more

than once by a rap at a neighbouring door, when a loud one was suddenly

heard which could not be mistaken for one at any other house, Elinor

felt secure of its announcing Willoughby’s approach, and Marianne,

starting up, moved towards the door. Every thing was silent; this could

not be borne many seconds; she opened the door, advanced a few steps

towards the stairs, and after listening half a minute, returned into

the room in all the agitation which a conviction of having heard him

would naturally produce; in the ecstasy of her feelings at that instant

she could not help exclaiming, “Oh, Elinor, it is Willoughby, indeed it

is!” and seemed almost ready to throw herself into his arms, when

Intitolato a sua sorella. Per espiare questo comportamento, dunque, Elinor…

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 26 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/journey,motif/pain,motif/rose,motif/secrets,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,setting/london,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] appeared.



It was too great a shock to be borne with calmness, and she immediately

left the room. Elinor was disappointed too; but at the same [[motifs/time|time]] her

regard for [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] ensured his welcome with her; and she felt

particularly hurt that a man so partial to her sister should perceive

that she experienced nothing but grief and disappointment in seeing

him. She instantly saw that it was not unnoticed by him, that he even

observed Marianne as she quitted the room, with such astonishment and

concern, as hardly left him the recollection of what civility demanded

towards herself.



“Is your sister ill?” said he.



Elinor answered in some distress that she was, and then talked of

head-aches, low spirits, and over fatigues; and of every thing to which

she could decently attribute her sister’s behaviour.



He heard her with the most earnest attention, but seeming to recollect

himself, said no more on the subject, and began directly to speak of

his pleasure at seeing them in [[settings/london|London]], making the usual inquiries about

their [[motifs/journey|journey]], and the friends they had left behind.



In this calm kind of way, with very little interest on either side,

they continued to talk, both of them out of spirits, and the thoughts

of both engaged elsewhere. Elinor wished very much to ask whether

Willoughby were then in town, but she was afraid of giving him [[motifs/pain|pain]] by

any enquiry after his rival; and at length, by way of saying something,

she asked if he had been in [[settings/london|London]] ever since she had seen him last.

“Yes,” he replied, with some embarrassment, “almost ever since; I have

been once or twice at Delaford for a few days, but it has never been in

my power to return to Barton.”



This, and the manner in which it was said, immediately brought back to

her remembrance all the circumstances of his quitting that place, with

the uneasiness and suspicions they had caused to Mrs. Jennings, and she

was fearful that her question had implied much more curiosity on the

subject than she had ever felt.



Mrs. Jennings soon came in. “Oh! Colonel,” said she, with her usual

noisy cheerfulness, “I am monstrous glad to see you—sorry I could not

come before—beg your pardon, but I have been forced to look about me a

little, and settle my matters; for it is a long while since I have been

at [[motifs/home|home]], and you know one has always a world of little odd things to do

after one has been away for any [[motifs/time|time]]; and then I have had Cartwright to

settle with. Lord, I have been as busy as a bee ever since dinner! But

pray, Colonel, how came you to conjure out that I should be in town

today?”



“I had the pleasure of hearing it at Mr. Palmer’s, where I have been

dining.”



“Oh, you did; [[motifs/well|well]], and how do they all do at their house? How does

Charlotte do? I warrant you she is a fine size by this [[motifs/time|time]].”



“Mrs. Palmer appeared quite [[motifs/well|well]], and I am commissioned to tell you,

that you will certainly see her to-morrow.”



“Ay, to be sure, I thought as much. [[motifs/well|Well]], Colonel, I have brought two

young ladies with me, you see—that is, you see but one of them now, but

there is another somewhere. Your friend, Miss Marianne, too—which you

will not be sorry to hear. I do not know what you and Mr. Willoughby

will do between you about her. Ay, it is a fine thing to be young and

handsome. [[motifs/well|Well]]! I was young once, but I never was very handsome—worse

luck for me. However, I got a very good husband, and I don’t know what

the greatest [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] can do more. Ah! poor man! he has been dead these

eight years and better. But Colonel, where have you been to since we

parted? And how does your business go on? Come, come, let’s have no

[[motifs/secrets|secrets]] among friends.”



He replied with his accustomary mildness to all her inquiries, but

without satisfying her in any. Elinor now began to make the tea, and

Marianne was obliged to appear again.



After her entrance, [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] became more thoughtful and silent

than he had been before, and Mrs. Jennings could not prevail on him to

stay long. No other visitor appeared that evening, and the ladies were

unanimous in agreeing to go early to bed.



Marianne [[motifs/rose|rose]] the next morning with recovered spirits and happy looks.

The disappointment of the evening before seemed forgotten in the

expectation of what was to happen that day. They had not long finished

their breakfast before Mrs. Palmer’s barouche stopped at the door, and

in a few minutes she came laughing into the room: so delighted to see

them all, that it was hard to say whether she received most pleasure

from meeting her mother or the Miss Dashwoods again. So surprised at

their coming to town, though it was what she had rather expected all

along; so angry at their accepting her mother’s invitation after having

declined her own, though at the same [[motifs/time|time]] she would never have forgiven

them if they had not come!



“Mr. Palmer will be so happy to see you,” said she; “What do you think

he said when he heard of your coming with Mama? I forget what it was

now, but it was something so droll!”



After an hour or two spent in what her mother called comfortable chat,

or in other words, in every variety of inquiry concerning all their

acquaintance on Mrs. Jennings’s side, and in laughter without cause on

Mrs. Palmer’s, it was proposed by the latter that they should all

accompany her to some shops where she had business that morning, to

which Mrs. Jennings and Elinor readily consented, as having likewise

some purchases to make themselves; and Marianne, though declining it at

first was induced to go likewise.



Wherever they went, she was evidently always on the watch. In Bond

Street especially, where much of their business lay, her eyes were in

constant inquiry; and in whatever shop the party were engaged, her mind

was equally abstracted from every thing actually before them, from all


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] apparve.



Un colpo troppo forte da sopportare con calma… Lei reagì immediatamente.

Uscì dalla stanza. Anche Elinor era delusa; ma allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] lei.

Il rispetto che tutti provavano per il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] garantì che fosse accolto con favore da lei; e lei ne fu consapevole.

Particolarmente ferita dal fatto che un uomo così favorevole verso sua sorella possa percepire…

Titolo:  
Che non provò altro che dolore e delusione nel vedere…

Lui se ne accorse immediatamente. Lei vide subito che non gli era sfuggito, anzi…

“Osservai Marianne mentre lasciava la stanza, con tale stupore…”

Con preoccupazione, poiché gli rimanevano appena i ricordi di ciò che la cortesia richiedeva…

Verso se stessa.



“Tua sorella è malata?” chiese lui.



Elinor rispose con evidente preoccupazione che lo era, e poi continuò a parlare…

Mal di testa, malumore e estrema stanchezza… e di tutto ciò che ne consegue

Poteva attribuire in modo plausibile il comportamento di sua sorella a determinate cause.



La ascoltava con la massima attenzione, ma sembrava ricordare qualcosa…

Lui stesso non disse più nulla sull’argomento e iniziò subito a parlare di altro.

La sua gioia nel vederli a [[settings/london|Londra]], facendo le solite domande su.

Il loro [[motifs/journey|viaggio]], e gli amici che avevano lasciato indietro.



Con questa calma e distacco, senza alcun interesse da parte di entrambe le parti…

Continuarono a parlare, entrambi senza molta energia, e i loro pensieri…

Titolo:  
“Entrambi impegnati altrove… Elinor avrebbe voluto molto chiedere…”

A quel tempo Willoughby si trovava in città, ma lei aveva paura di causargli[[motifs/pain|dolore]].

Qualsiasi domanda riguardo al suo rivale… e alla fine, come se volesse dire qualcosa…

Gli chiese se fosse mai stato a [[settings/london|Londra]] da quando lo aveva visto l'ultima volta.

“Sì”, rispose lui, con un certo imbarazzo, “quasi da allora; ho…”

Mai stato a Delaford nemmeno una volta, per pochi giorni che fossero…

“Il mio potere di tornare a Barton”.



Questo, e il modo in cui fu detto, mi fecero immediatamente ricordare…

Il suo ricordo di tutte le circostanze relative al suo lascio di quel luogo…

L’ansia e i sospetti che avevano suscitato in Mrs. Jennings… e lei.

Titolo:  
Temeva che la sua domanda implicasse una curiosità molto più profonda…

Un senso di soggezione più forte di qualsiasi altro avesse mai provato.



La signora Jennings entrò subito dopo. “Oh! Colonnello”, disse, con il suo solito tono…

“Allegria chiassosa… Sono davvero felicissimo di vederti… Mi dispiace di non essere potuto…”

“Come prima… scusate, ma sono stato costretto a guardarmi intorno.”

"Risolvere le mie faccende in fretta… perché è da molto tempo che non lo faccio."

A [[motifs/home|casa]], e sai bene che ci sono sempre un sacco di piccole cose strane da fare.

Dopo che uno è stato via per qualsiasi periodo di tempo. E poi ho avuto Cartwright a.

“Accettare la situazione… Signore, da dopo cena sono stata davvero molto impegnata!”

“Per favore, colonnello… come ha fatto a indovinare che fossi in città?”

“Oggi?”



“Ho avuto il piacere di ascoltarlo a casa del signor Palmer, dove sono stato…”

“Cena”.



“Ah, l’hai fatto davvero; bene, e come stanno tutti nella loro casa? Come va, ”

Charlotte, vero? Scommetto che ormai sia diventata davvero formosa.



“La signora Palmer sembrava davvero in buona salute, e sono stato incaricato di comunicarvelo.”

“Ne sono sicuro: la vedrai senz’altro domani.”



“Ah, certo, anch'io ho pensato lo stesso. [[motifs/well|Beh]], Colonnello, ho portato con me due, ”

“Donne giovani con me… beh, insomma, al momento ne vedete solo una…”

C’è un’altra persona da qualche parte… Anche la tua amica, Miss Marianne…

Non mi dispiacerà affatto sentirlo… Non so cosa tu e il signor Willoughby abbiate in mente.

“Cosa potete fare voi due al riguardo… Ah, essere giovani è davvero una bella cosa…”

Attraente. Beh! Anche io ero giovane una volta, ma non sono mai stato molto attraente, anzi, peggio ancora.

Fortuna per me… Tuttavia, ho un marito davvero meraviglioso, e non so proprio cosa dire al riguardo.

La più grande [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] può fare di più. Ah! Poveruomo. È morto da molto tempo.

Otto anni… e di più. Ma Colonnello, dove è stato da allora?

“Partito? E come va avanti la tua attività? Dai, non parliamone più…”

“[[motifs/secrets|Segreti]] tra amici, ”



Rispose con la sua solita dolcezza a tutte le sue domande, ma…

“Senza riuscire a soddisfarla in alcun modo… Elinor iniziò quindi a preparare il tè.”

Marianne fu costretta a comparire di nuovo.



Dopo il suo ingresso, [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] divenne più pensieroso e silenzioso.

Più di prima, e la signora Jennings non riuscì a convincerlo a…

Aspetta ancora un po’. Quella sera non arrivò nessun altro visitatore, e le signore…

Unanimità nel decidere di andare a letto presto.



Il giorno dopo, Marianne fiorì di nuovo, con lo spirito ripreso e un'espressione felice sul viso.

La delusione della sera precedente sembrava essere stata dimenticata…

Aspettative riguardo a ciò che sarebbe accaduto quel giorno… Non erano ancora trascorsi molti minuti da quando tutto era finito.

Il loro pasto mattutino… prima che la berlina della signora Palmer si fermasse davanti alla porta.

In pochi minuti entrò nella stanza ridendo, felicissima di vedermi.

Tutti quanti… era difficile dire se lei ne traggesse maggior piacere

Mai più incontrare sua madre o la signorina Dashwood… Così sorpreso…

Il loro arrivo in città… anche se era esattamente ciò che si aspettava.

Arrabbiatissimi perché hanno accettato l’invito di sua madre…

Rifiutò la sua stessa offerta, anche se allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] non avrebbe mai potuto perdonare.

Se non fossero venuti.



“Il signor Palmer sarà molto felice di vedervi,” disse lei; “Che ne pensate?”

Cosa ha detto quando ha saputo che saresti arrivata con mamma? Non ricordo esattamente cosa fosse…

“Ora… ma era davvero qualcosa di così divertente!”



Dopo un’ora o due trascorse in quelle che sua madre definiva “conversazioni piacevoli”,

In altre parole, in ogni tipo di indagine relativa a tutto ciò che riguarda loro

Conoscenza del lato della signora Jennings… e risate senza motivo

La proposta di Mrs. Palmer

Acompagnarla in alcuni negozi dove aveva degli affari quella mattina…

Titolo:  
Il che la signora Jennings ed Elinor accettarono volentieri, poiché anch’esse…

Alcune compere da fare… E Marianne, sebbene le rifiutasse…

Prima di lui, anche un altro fu indotto a fare lo stesso.



Ovunque andassero, lei era evidentemente sempre all’erta. In Bond

Via particolare, dove si svolgeva gran parte del loro lavoro… i suoi occhi erano lì.

Costante curiosità… E in qualsiasi negozio si trovassero, la sua mente rimaneva sempre attenta e interessata.

Era altrettanto distaccato da tutto ciò che realmente si trovava davanti a loro, da ogni cosa…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_26--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 26 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 26" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/window"></span>


that interested and occupied the others. Restless and dissatisfied

every where, her sister could never obtain her opinion of any article

of purchase, however it might equally concern them both: she received

no pleasure from anything; was only impatient to be at [[motifs/home|home]] again, and

could with difficulty govern her vexation at the tediousness of Mrs.

Palmer, whose eye was caught by every thing pretty, expensive, or new;

who was wild to buy all, could determine on none, and dawdled away her

[[motifs/time|time]] in rapture and indecision.



It was late in the morning before they returned [[motifs/home|home]]; and no sooner had

they entered the house than Marianne flew eagerly up stairs, and when

Elinor followed, she found her turning from the table with a sorrowful

countenance, which declared that no Willoughby had been there.



“Has no letter been left here for me since we went out?” said she to

the footman who then entered with the parcels. She was answered in the

negative. “Are you quite sure of it?” she replied. “Are you certain

that no servant, no porter has left any letter or note?”



The man replied that none had.



“How very odd!” said she, in a low and disappointed voice, as she

turned away to the [[motifs/window|window]].



“How odd, indeed!” repeated Elinor within herself, regarding her sister

with uneasiness. “If she had not known him to be in town she would not

have written to him, as she did; she would have written to Combe Magna;

and if he is in town, how odd that he should neither come nor write!

Oh! my dear mother, you must be wrong in permitting an engagement

between a daughter so young, a man so little known, to be carried on in

so doubtful, so mysterious a manner! _I_ long to inquire; and how will

_my_ interference be borne.”



She determined, after some consideration, that if appearances continued

many days longer as unpleasant as they now were, she would represent in

the strongest manner to her mother the necessity of some serious

enquiry into the affair.



Mrs. Palmer and two elderly ladies of Mrs. Jennings’s intimate

acquaintance, whom she had met and invited in the morning, dined with

them. The former left them soon after tea to fulfill her evening

engagements; and Elinor was obliged to assist in making a whist table

for the others. Marianne was of no use on these occasions, as she would

never learn the game; but though her [[motifs/time|time]] was therefore at her own

disposal, the evening was by no means more productive of pleasure to

her than to Elinor, for it was spent in all the anxiety of expectation

and the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of disappointment. She sometimes endeavoured for a few

minutes to read; but the book was soon thrown aside, and she returned

to the more interesting employment of walking backwards and forwards

across the room, pausing for a moment whenever she came to the [[motifs/window|window]],

in hopes of distinguishing the long-expected rap.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Quello che interessava e occupava gli altri… Inquieti e insoddisfatti.

Dappertutto, sua sorella non riusciva mai a ottenere il suo parere su nessun articolo.

Titolo:  
Di acquisto… tuttavia potrebbe riguardarli entrambi allo stesso modo: lei l’ha ricevuto.

Nessun piacere in nulla; voleva solo tornare a [[motifs/home|casa]] il prima possibile.

Aveva difficoltà a controllare la propria irritazione per la noia causata dalla signora.

Palmer, il cui sguardo era attratto da tutto ciò che era bello, costoso o nuovo…

Chi era così folle da voler comprare tutto, non riusciva a decidere nulla e finì per perdere tempo inutilmente…

[[motifs/time|tempo]] tra estasi e incertezza.



Era già tardi nella mattinata quando tornarono a [[motifs/home|casa]]; e non appena.

Entrarono nella casa, quando Marianne salì di corsa le scale.

Elinor lo seguì; lo trovò mentre si allontanava dal tavolo con un’espressione triste.

Il suo volto esprimeva chiaramente che nessun Willoughby era stato lì.



“Non è stata lasciata nessuna lettera per me da quando siamo usciti?” disse lei.

Il valletto che entrò poi con i pacchi… Le risposero…

“Negativo… ‘Ne sei davvero sicura?’ rispose lei. ‘Sei certa?’”

“Che nessun servitore, nessun portiere abbia lasciato alcuna lettera o biglietto?”



L’uomo rispose che nessuno l’aveva.



“Che strano davvero!”, disse lei con voce bassa e delusa.

Si girò verso la [[motifs/window|finestra]].



“Che strano davvero!”, ripeté tra sé Elinor, osservando sua sorella.

Con ansia… “Se non avesse saputo che si trovava in città, non lo avrebbe cercato.”

Ha scritto a lui, proprio come ha fatto; avrebbe anche scritto a Combe Magna.

E se si trova in città, che strano che non venga né scriva!

“Oh! mia cara madre, devi sbagliarti ad aver permesso questo fidanzamento…”

Tra una figlia così giovane e un uomo così poco conosciuto… continuare la vita insieme.

Un modo così dubioso, così misterioso… Vorrei tanto chiedere spiegazioni; ma come farò?

“Che la mia interferenza venga tollerata.”



Dopo averci pensato attentamente, decise che, se le apparenze continuavano così…

Se quei giorni fossero stati ancora più sgradevoli di quelli attuali, lei li avrebbe rappresentati…

Il modo più deciso per far comprendere a sua madre l’urgenza di una decisione seria

Indagine sull’incidente.



La signora Palmer e due anziane dame intime della signora Jennings

Conoscenza che aveva incontrato quella mattina e invitato a cena…

Loro… La prima li lasciò poco dopo il tè per andare a svolgere i suoi impegni serali.

Imprese varie… e Elinor dovette aiutare a preparare un tavolo da whist.

“Per gli altri… In queste occasioni, Marianne non era di alcuna utilità, poiché…”

Non imparò mai le regole del gioco; ma poiché così era, il suo [[motifs/time|tempo]] apparteneva soltanto a lei.

Disposizione… Quella sera non fu affatto più piacevole di altre…

Più che con Elinor, poiché fu trascorsa nell’ansia e nell’attesa incessante…

E il [[motifs/pain|dolore]] della delusione. A volte cercava di raggiungere qualcosa.

Minuti da leggere… ma il libro fu presto abbandonato, e lei tornò indietro.

All'occupazione più interessante di camminare avanti e indietro

Dall'altra parte della stanza, si fermava per un momento ogni volta che arrivava vicino alla [[motifs/window|finestra]].

Nella speranza di ascoltare finalmente quel rap tanto atteso.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_27--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 27 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 27" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/city,motif/fire,motif/frost,motif/home,motif/night,motif/time,motif/wind,motif/window,concept/truth,setting/london,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER XXVII.





“If this open weather holds much longer,” said Mrs. Jennings, when they

met at breakfast the following morning, “Sir John will not like leaving

Barton next week; ’tis a sad thing for sportsmen to lose a day’s

pleasure. Poor souls! I always pity them when they do; they seem to

take it so much to heart.”



“That is true,” cried Marianne, in a cheerful voice, and walking to the

[[motifs/window|window]] as she spoke, to examine the day. “I had not thought of _that_.

This weather will keep many sportsmen in the country.”



It was a lucky recollection, all her good spirits were restored by it.

“It is charming weather for _them_ indeed,” she continued, as she sat

down to the breakfast table with a happy countenance. “How much they

must enjoy it! But” (with a little return of anxiety) “it cannot be

expected to last long. At this [[motifs/time|time]] of the year, and after such a

series of rain, we shall certainly have very little more of it. Frosts

will soon set in, and in all probability with severity. In another day

or two perhaps; this extreme mildness can hardly last longer—nay,

perhaps it may freeze tonight!”



“At any rate,” said Elinor, wishing to prevent Mrs. Jennings from

seeing her sister’s thoughts as clearly as she did, “I dare say we

shall have Sir John and Lady Middleton in town by the end of next

week.”



“Ay, my dear, I’ll warrant you we do. Mary always has her own way.”



“And now,” silently conjectured Elinor, “she will write to Combe by

this day’s post.”



But if she _did_, the letter was written and sent away with a privacy

which eluded all her watchfulness to ascertain the fact. Whatever the

[[concepts/truth|truth]] of it might be, and far as Elinor was from feeling thorough

contentment about it, yet while she saw Marianne in spirits, she could

not be very uncomfortable herself. And Marianne was in spirits; happy

in the mildness of the weather, and still happier in her expectation of

a [[motifs/frost|frost]].



The morning was chiefly spent in leaving cards at the houses of Mrs.

Jennings’s acquaintance to inform them of her being in town; and

Marianne was all the [[motifs/time|time]] busy in observing the direction of the [[motifs/wind|wind]],

watching the variations of the sky and imagining an alteration in the

air.



“Don’t you find it colder than it was in the morning, Elinor? There

seems to me a very decided difference. I can hardly keep my hands warm

even in my muff. It was not so yesterday, I think. The clouds seem

parting too, the sun will be out in a moment, and we shall have a clear

afternoon.”



Elinor was alternately diverted and pained; but Marianne persevered,

and saw every [[motifs/night|night]] in the brightness of the [[motifs/fire|fire]], and every morning in

the appearance of the atmosphere, the certain symptoms of approaching

[[motifs/frost|frost]].



The Miss Dashwoods had no greater reason to be dissatisfied with Mrs.

Jennings’s style of living, and set of acquaintance, than with her

behaviour to themselves, which was invariably kind. Every thing in her

household arrangements was conducted on the most liberal plan, and

excepting a few old [[motifs/city|city]] friends, whom, to Lady Middleton’s regret, she

had never dropped, she visited no one to whom an introduction could at

all discompose the feelings of her young companions. Pleased to find

herself more comfortably situated in that particular than she had

expected, Elinor was very willing to compound for the want of much real

enjoyment from any of their evening parties, which, whether at [[motifs/home|home]] or

abroad, formed only for cards, could have little to amuse her.



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], who had a general invitation to the house, was with

them almost every day; he came to look at Marianne and talk to Elinor,

who often derived more satisfaction from conversing with him than from

any other daily occurrence, but who saw at the same [[motifs/time|time]] with much

concern his continued regard for her sister. She feared it was a

strengthening regard. It grieved her to see the earnestness with which

he often watched Marianne, and his spirits were certainly worse than

when at Barton.



About a week after their arrival, it became certain that Willoughby was

also arrived. His card was on the table when they came in from the

morning’s drive.



“Good God!” cried Marianne, “he has been here while we were out.”

Elinor, rejoiced to be assured of his being in [[settings/london|London]], now ventured to

say, “Depend upon it, he will call again tomorrow.” But Marianne seemed

hardly to hear her, and on Mrs. Jennings’s entrance, escaped with the

precious card.



This event, while it raised the spirits of Elinor, restored to those of

her sister all, and more than all, their former agitation. From this

moment her mind was never quiet; the expectation of seeing him every

hour of the day, made her unfit for any thing. She insisted on being

left behind, the next morning, when the others went out.



Elinor’s thoughts were full of what might be passing in Berkeley Street

during their absence; but a moment’s glance at her sister when they

returned was enough to inform her, that Willoughby had paid no second

visit there. A note was just then brought in, and laid on the table.



“For me!” cried Marianne, stepping hastily forward.



“No, ma’am, for my mistress.”



But Marianne, not convinced, took it instantly up.



“It is indeed for Mrs. Jennings; how provoking!”



“You are expecting a letter, then?” said Elinor, unable to be longer

silent.



“Yes, a little—not much.”



After a short pause. “You have no confidence in me, Marianne.”



“Nay, Elinor, this reproach from _you_—you who have confidence in no

one!”



“Me!” returned Elinor in some confusion; “indeed, Marianne, I have

nothing to tell.”



“Nor I,” answered Marianne with energy, “our situations then are alike.

We have neither of us any thing to tell; you, because you do not

communicate, and I, because I conceal nothing.”



Elinor, distressed by this charge of reserve in herself, which she was


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XXVII.





“Se questo bel tempo dura ancora a lungo…”, disse la signora Jennings, mentre loro…

Si incontrarono a colazione la mattina seguente: “A Sir John non piacerà dover andarsene”.

Barton la prossima settimana… È davvero triste per gli atleti perdere una giornata così importante.

Poveri esseri… Sempre provo compassione per loro quando lo fanno; sembrano davvero…

“Prenditela davvero molto a cuore.”



“È vero,” esclamò Marianne con voce allegra, avvicinandosi…

Mentre parlava, [[motifs/window|finestra]] osservava il corso della giornata. “Non ci avevo pensato affatto.”

“Con questo tempo, molti atleti rimarranno nel paese.”



Fu un ricordo fortunato: grazie ad esso, tutto il suo buon umore tornò.

“Che tempo incantevole per loro, davvero,” continuò lei, mentre sedeva…

“Giunto al tavolo della colazione con un viso felice… Quanto devono essere contenti…”

“Deve piacergli molto… Ma”, con un’ombra di ansia, “non può essere…”

Si prevede che duri a lungo. A questa [[motifs/time|epoca]] dell’anno, e dopo tutto ciò che è accaduto.

"Una serie di piogge… sicuramente ne avremo ancora molto poco. E poi arriveranno le gelate."

Il freddo arriverà presto, e molto probabilmente con intensità. Tra un giorno…

“Forse uno o due… Questa estrema dolcezza difficilmente potrà durare ancora a lungo… No,…”

“Forse stasera farà freddo abbastanza da congelare tutto…”



“Comunque sia,” disse Elinor, desiderando impedire alla signora Jennings di…

“Vedendo i pensieri di sua sorella con la stessa chiarezza con cui li vedeva lei, ‘Oso dire che noi…’”

“Sir John e Lady Middleton saranno in città entro la fine del prossimo mese.”

“Settimana”.



“Ah, cara mia, te lo assicuro: lo facciamo davvero. Mary ha sempre la sua testa dura.”



“E ora”, pensò silenziosamente Elinor, “scriverà a Combe…”

“La pubblicazione di oggi”.



Ma se lo avesse fatto, la lettera sarebbe stata scritta e inviata mantenendo il rispetto della privacy…

Ciò che sfuggì a ogni sua attenzione per scoprire la verità… Qualunque cosa fosse.

La verità potrebbe essere proprio questa; e per quanto riguarda Elinor, lei non provava affatto un sentimento profondo.

Senza alcuna soddisfazione al riguardo, tuttavia, mentre vedeva che Marianne era di buon umore, riusciva…

Marianne era di buon umore e felice.

Nella dolcezza del clima, e ancora più felice nell’attesa di…

al [[motifs/frost|freddo gelido]].



La mattina fu principalmente trascorsa lasciando biglietti alle case della signora.

L’acquaintanza di Jennings li avvisò che si trovava in città; e…

Marianne era sempre impegnata a osservare la direzione del [[motifs/wind|vento]].

Osservando le variazioni del cielo e immaginando un cambiamento…

aria.



“Non trovi che faccia più freddo rispetto a stamattina, Elinor?…”

A mio parere, c’è una differenza abbastanza marcata… Faccio fatica persino a tenere le mani calde.

Nemmeno nel mio muffin… Ieri non era così, credo. Le nuvole sembrano…

Anche il sole sorgerà presto, e ci sarà luce chiara intorno a noi…

“Pomeriggio.”



Elinor provava alternativamente distrazione e dolore; ma Marianne persisteva.

E vedeva ogni [[motifs/night|notte]] nella luce del [[motifs/fire|fuoco]], e ogni mattina.

L’aspetto dell’atmosfera, i segni certi dell’avvicinamento…

[[motifs/frost|brina]].



Le signorine Dashwood non avevano alcun motivo maggiore per essere insoddisfatte della signora.

Il modo di vivere di Jennings e il suo giro di conoscenze, piuttosto che lei stessa…

Comportamento sempre gentile verso se stessa… Ogni aspetto della sua persona rifletteva questa bontà.

Gli accordi domestici venivano gestiti secondo i principi più liberali possibile.

Ad eccezione di alcuni vecchi amici della [[motifs/city|città]], che, a dispiacere di Lady Middleton, lei.

Non aveva mai perso contatto con nessuno, e non andava a trovare nessuno che potesse aiutarla a farsi conoscere…

“Tutto questo sconvolge i sentimenti dei suoi giovani compagni… Felice di scoprire…”

Si trovava in quella situazione molto più a suo agio di quanto avesse mai immaginato.

Come era prevedibile, Elinor fu molto disposta a compensare per la mancanza di qualcosa di concreto…

Godimento derivante da qualsiasi delle loro feste serali, che si svolgano in [[motifs/home|casa]] o altrove.

All’estero, un ambiente creato esclusivamente per il gioco delle carte, probabilmente non avrebbe potuto offrirle molto di divertente.



Il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], che aveva ricevuto un invito generale per la casa, era lì con loro.

Li vedeva quasi ogni giorno; veniva a guardare Marianne e a parlare con Elinor.

Chi spesso traeva maggiore soddisfazione nel conversare con lui che in altro

Qualsiasi altra cosa accada ogni giorno, ma chi l’ha vista nello stesso [[motifs/time|momento]], con tanta chiarezza.

Il suo continuo interesse per sua sorella… Lei temeva che fosse qualcosa di più…

Rafforzare il rispetto… Le dispiaceva vedere con quanta sincerità lui lo facesse.

Spesso la osservava, e il suo umore era sicuramente peggiore di prima

quando era a Barton.



Circa una settimana dopo il loro arrivo, divenne certo che Willoughby…

Anche lui è arrivato. La sua carta era sul tavolo quando sono entrati.

La gita mattutina.



“Mio Dio!”, esclamò Marianne, “dev’essere stato qui mentre noi eravamo fuori”.

Elinor, felice di aver la certezza che si trovasse a [[settings/london|Londra]], osò ora dire.

"Ma forse, chissà..." sembrava dire Marianne."

A malapena si riusciva a sentirla; non appena entrò la signora Jennings, lei fuggì via…

Carta preziosa.



Questo evento, sebbene rinvigorisse lo spirito di Elinor, restituì la serenità anche agli altri

“Sua sorella… e soprattutto, tutta quell’agitazione precedente.”

Non appena il suo pensiero si soffermava su di lui, la sua mente non trovava mai pace; l’attesa di rivederlo era costante…

L’ora del giorno la rendeva incapace di fare qualsiasi cosa… Insisteva comunque nel voler…

Lasciato indietro, la mattina seguente, quando gli altri uscirono.



I pensieri di Elinor erano pieni di ciò che probabilmente stava accadendo in Berkeley Street.

Durante la loro assenza… ma un’occhiata fugace alla sorella quando arrivarono…

“Tornato indietro fu sufficiente per farle capire che Willoughby non aveva pagato nulla.”

Visita lì. Proprio in quel momento fu portata dentro una nota, che venne posata sul tavolo.



“Per me!” gridò Marianne, avvicinandosi in fretta.



"No, signora, per la mia padrona."



Ma Marianne, non convinta, la prese immediatamente in mano.



“È davvero per la signora Jennings… Che fastidio!”



“Quindi stai aspettando una lettera, vero?”, disse Elinor, senza riuscire a trattenersi oltre.

Silenzioso.



“Sì, un po’… non molto.”



Dopo una breve pausa: “Non hai fiducia in me, Marianne”.



“No, Elinor… questa accusa da parte tua… tu che non hai fiducia in nessuno…”

“Uno!”



“Me!”, rispose Elinor con un po’ di confusione; “davvero, Marianne, io ho…”

“Niente da dire.”



“Nemmeno io,” rispose Marianne con energia, “quindi le nostre situazioni sono simili.”

Titolo:  
Nessuno di noi ha nulla da dire… tu, perché non hai nulla.

“Comunicare… e io, perché non nascondo nulla.”



Elinor, angosciata da questa accusa di riservatezza che le veniva mossa…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_27--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 27 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 27" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/dance,motif/fire,motif/grave,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/melancholy,concept/truth,setting/london,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


not at liberty to do away, knew not how, under such circumstances, to

press for greater openness in Marianne.



Mrs. Jennings soon appeared, and the note being given her, she read it

aloud. It was from Lady Middleton, announcing their arrival in Conduit

Street the [[motifs/night|night]] before, and requesting the company of her mother and

cousins the following evening. Business on Sir John’s part, and a

violent cold on her own, prevented their calling in Berkeley Street.

The invitation was accepted; but when the hour of appointment drew

near, necessary as it was in common civility to Mrs. Jennings, that

they should both attend her on such a visit, Elinor had some difficulty

in persuading her sister to go, for still she had seen nothing of

Willoughby; and therefore was not more indisposed for amusement abroad,

than unwilling to run the risk of his calling again in her absence.



Elinor found, when the evening was over, that disposition is not

materially altered by a change of abode, for although scarcely settled

in town, Sir John had contrived to collect around him, nearly twenty

young people, and to amuse them with a ball. This was an affair,

however, of which Lady Middleton did not approve. In the country, an

unpremeditated [[motifs/dance|dance]] was very allowable; but in [[settings/london|London]], where the

reputation of elegance was more important and less easily attained, it

was risking too much for the gratification of a few girls, to have it

known that Lady Middleton had given a small [[motifs/dance|dance]] of eight or nine

couple, with two violins, and a mere side-board collation.



Mr. and Mrs. Palmer were of the party; from the former, whom they had

not seen before since their arrival in town, as he was careful to avoid

the appearance of any attention to his mother-in-law, and therefore

never came near her, they received no mark of recognition on their

entrance. He looked at them slightly, without seeming to know who they

were, and merely nodded to Mrs. Jennings from the other side of the

room. Marianne gave one glance round the apartment as she entered: it

was enough—_he_ was not there—and she sat down, equally ill-disposed to

receive or communicate pleasure. After they had been assembled about an

hour, Mr. Palmer sauntered towards the Miss Dashwoods to express his

surprise on seeing them in town, though [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] had been first

informed of their arrival at his house, and he had himself said

something very droll on hearing that they were to come.



“I thought you were both in Devonshire,” said he.



“Did you?” replied Elinor.



“When do you go back again?”



“I do not know.” And thus ended their discourse.



Never had Marianne been so unwilling to [[motifs/dance|dance]] in her life, as she was

that evening, and never so much fatigued by the exercise. She

complained of it as they returned to Berkeley Street.



“Aye, aye,” said Mrs. Jennings, “we know the reason of all that very

[[motifs/well|well]]; if a certain person who shall be nameless, had been there, you

would not have been a bit tired: and to say the [[concepts/truth|truth]] it was not very

pretty of him not to give you the meeting when he was invited.”



“Invited!” cried Marianne.



“So my daughter Middleton told me, for it seems Sir John met him

somewhere in the street this morning.” Marianne said no more, but

looked exceedingly hurt. Impatient in this situation to be doing

something that might lead to her sister’s relief, Elinor resolved to

write the next morning to her mother, and hoped by awakening her fears

for the health of Marianne, to procure those inquiries which had been

so long delayed; and she was still more eagerly bent on this measure by

perceiving after breakfast on the morrow, that Marianne was again

writing to Willoughby, for she could not suppose it to be to any other

person.



About the middle of the day, Mrs. Jennings went out by herself on

business, and Elinor began her letter directly, while Marianne, too

restless for employment, too anxious for conversation, walked from one

[[motifs/window|window]] to the other, or sat down by the [[motifs/fire|fire]] in [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] meditation.

Elinor was very earnest in her application to her mother, relating all

that had passed, her suspicions of Willoughby’s inconstancy, urging her

by every plea of duty and affection to demand from Marianne an account

of her real situation with respect to him.



Her letter was scarcely finished, when a rap foretold a visitor, and

[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] was announced. Marianne, who had seen him from the

[[motifs/window|window]], and who hated company of any kind, left the room before he

entered it. He looked more than usually [[motifs/grave|grave]], and though expressing

satisfaction at finding Miss Dashwood alone, as if he had somewhat in

particular to tell her, sat for some [[motifs/time|time]] without saying a word.

Elinor, persuaded that he had some communication to make in which her

sister was concerned, impatiently expected its opening. It was not the

first [[motifs/time|time]] of her feeling the same kind of conviction; for, more than

once before, beginning with the observation of “your sister looks

unwell to-day,” or “your sister seems out of spirits,” he had appeared

on the point, either of disclosing, or of inquiring, something

particular about her. After a pause of several minutes, their [[motifs/silence|silence]]

was broken, by his asking her in a voice of some agitation, when he was

to congratulate her on the acquisition of a brother? Elinor was not

prepared for such a question, and having no answer ready, was obliged

to adopt the simple and common expedient, of asking what he meant? He

tried to smile as he replied, “your sister’s engagement to Mr.

Willoughby is very generally known.”



“It cannot be generally known,” returned Elinor, “for her own family do

not know it.”



He looked surprised and said, “I beg your pardon, I am afraid my

inquiry has been impertinent; but I had not supposed any secrecy


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Non aveva la libertà di eliminarlo; non sapeva nemmeno come farlo, in tali circostanze…

Pressare affinché Marianne diventi più aperta.



La signora Jennings arrivò presto e, dopo aver ricevuto il biglietto, lo lesse.

“Alto”, diceva la lettera. Era di Lady Middleton e annunciava il loro arrivo a Conduit.

La sera prima, per strada, chiese di essere accompagnata da sua madre.

“Cugini… la sera seguente. Affari da parte di Sir John…”

Il freddo intenso li impedì di chiamare da Berkeley Street.

L’invito fu accettato; ma quando arrivò l’ora dell’appuntamento…

“Essendo qualcosa di quasi indispensabile nella normale cortesia, per la signora Jennings…”

“Dovrebbero entrambi accompagnarla in una visita del genere… Elinor ebbe qualche difficoltà nel farlo.”

Nella tentativa di convincere sua sorella ad andare, poiché lei ancora non aveva visto nulla…

Willoughby; e quindi non era affatto contrario ad divertirsi all’estero.

Piuttosto che correre il rischio che la sua chiamata si ripresentasse di nuovo in sua assenza.



Titolo:  
Alla fine della serata, Elinor si rese conto che quel carattere non era affatto…

Titolo: Modificato in modo significativo a causa del cambio di residenza, poiché ancora poco stabile…

In città, Sir John riuscì a radunare intorno a sé quasi venti persone.

“Giovani persone… e divertirli con un ballo: questa era l’idea.”

Tuttavia, cosa che Lady Middleton non approvò affatto. In campagna…

Una danza non premeditata era del tutto accettabile; ma a [[settings/london|Londra]], dove.

La reputazione di eleganza era più importante e più difficile da ottenere…

Rischiare troppo per il piacere di poche ragazze… non ne vale la pena.

Si sapeva che Lady Middleton aveva organizzato un piccolo [[motifs/dance|ballo]] di otto o nove persone.

Un duo, con due violini, e un semplice accompagnamento musicale.



Il signor e la signora Palmer erano tra i partecipanti; in particolare il primo…

Da quando sono arrivati in città, non è mai stato visto prima… perché lui faceva attenzione a evitarli.

Nessun segno di attenzione verso la suocera… e quindi…

Non le si avvicinarono mai; non ricevettero alcun segno di riconoscimento da parte sua.

Entrata. Li guardò appena, come se non sapesse chi fossero.

Erano lì, e si limitarono ad annuire alla signora Jennings dall’altra parte…

“Room…”. Non appena entrò nell’appartamento, Marianne gettò un’occhiata intorno a sé: era una stanza ordinata e pulita.

Non era abbastanza… Lui non c’era, e lei si sedette, altrettanto indisposta…

Provare piacere o condividere gioie. Dopo essersi riuniti intorno…

Ore… Il signor Palmer si avvicinò alle signorine Dashwood per esprimere il suo…

Sorpresa nel vederli in città, anche se [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] era arrivato prima di loro.

Informato del loro arrivo a casa sua, lui stesso aveva detto.

Qualcosa di davvero divertente, quando si seppe che sarebbero venuti.



“Pensavo che foste entrambi a Devonshire,” disse lui.



“L’hai fatto davvero?” rispose Elinor.



“Quando tornerai di nuovo?”



“Non lo so.” E così terminò il loro dialogo.



Marianne non era mai stata così riluttante a [[motifs/dance|)danzare]] in tutta la sua vita.

Quella sera, mai così stanca per lo sforzo appena compiuto… Lei

Ne lamentarono l’assenza mentre tornavano in Berkeley Street.



“Ah sì, ah sì,” disse la signora Jennings, “conosciamo benissimo il motivo di tutto questo.”

[[motifs/well|Beh]]; se quella certa persona, la cui identità non verrà rivelata, fosse stata lì, tu.

Non sarei stato affatto stanco. E, per dire la [[concepts/truth|verità]], non è stato nemmeno molto faticoso.

Che gentile da parte sua non farti partecipare all’incontro, nonostante fosse stato invitato anche lui…



“Invitata!”, esclamò Marianne.



“Mia figlia Middleton mi ha detto che, a quanto pare, Sir John lo ha incontrato…”

“Da qualche parte per strada questa mattina…” Marianna non aggiunse altro.

Sembrava davvero ferito… In una situazione del genere, essere impazienti è comprensibile.

Decise che qualcosa potesse portare al sollievo di sua sorella.

Scrisse la mattina seguente a sua madre, nella speranza di suscitare in lei paura.

Per il bene di Marianne, effettuare quelle indagini che erano state necessarie…

Dopo tante ritardi, lei era ancora più decisa ad attuare questa misura.

"#Percepire, la mattina seguente dopo colazione, che Marianne era di nuovo..."

Scrivendo a Willoughby, poiché non poteva pensare che fosse indirizzata a nessun altro.

persona.



Intorno a mezzogiorno, la signora Jennings uscì da sola…

Business… Elinor iniziò la sua lettera subito, mentre anche Marianne lo fece allo stesso modo.

In cerca di lavoro, troppo ansioso per conversare, camminava da un posto all’altro…

Si spostava da una [[motifs/window|finestra]] all'altra, oppure si sedeva accanto al [[motifs/fire|focolare]] immerso in meditazioni [[concepts/melancholy|malinconiche]].

Elinor era molto seria nella sua richiesta rivolta alla madre, raccontandole tutto nei dettagli.

Quei sospetti riguardo all’infedeltà di Willoughby continuavano ad assillarla…

Con ogni richiesta dovuta al dovere e all'affetto, chiedere a Marianne una spiegazione

Della sua vera situazione rispetto a lui.



Appena aveva finito di scrivere la sua lettera, un colpo alla porta annunciò l’arrivo di un visitatore.

Fu annunciato l’arrivo di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]]. Marianne, che lo aveva visto da.

La [[motifs/window|finestra]], che odiava la compagnia di qualsiasi tipo, lasciò la stanza prima che.

Entrò dentro. Sembrava più [[motifs/grave|serio]] del solito, e sebbene esprimesse.

Soddisfazione nel trovare la signorina Dashwood da sola, come se avesse ottenuto qualcosa.

Era così particolare da non dire una parola per un po'.

Elinor, convinta che avesse qualcosa da dirle…

La sorella era preoccupata e aspettava con impazienza che iniziasse… Ma non era quello che sperava.

Per la prima volta nella sua vita provava lo stesso tipo di convinzione; infatti, più di.

Titolo:  
Una volta, a partire dall’osservazione che “tua sorella sembra…”

“Non si sente bene oggi”, o “sua sorella sembra giù di morale”, ecco cosa aveva detto.

Sul punto di rivelare o di chiedere qualcosa

Era molto particolare riguardo a lei. Dopo un pausa di diversi minuti, il loro [[motifs/silence|silenzio]].

Era rotto… quando le chiese di sposarlo con voce agitata.

Congratularla per l’acquisizione di un fratello? Elinor non era d’accordo.

Impreparato a una tale domanda e senza una risposta pronta, fu costretto…

“Adottare la semplice e comune soluzione di chiedere cosa intendesse…?”

Cercò di sorridere mentre rispondeva: “La promessa di tua sorella con il signor, ”

“Willoughby è molto conosciuto in generale.”



“Non può essere reso noto a tutti”, rispose Elinor, “perché la sua stessa famiglia…”.

“Non lo so.”



“Sembrava sorpreso e disse: ‘Mi scusi, temo che io…’”

L’indagine risultava inopportuna; ma non avevo immaginato che ci fosse alcun segreto da proteggere.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_27--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 27 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 27" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/rose,motif/time,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


intended, as they openly correspond, and their [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] is universally

talked of.”



“How can that be? By whom can you have heard it mentioned?”



“By many—by some of whom you know nothing, by others with whom you are

most intimate, Mrs. Jennings, Mrs. Palmer, and the Middletons. But

still I might not have believed it, for where the mind is perhaps

rather unwilling to be convinced, it will always find something to

support its doubts, if I had not, when the servant let me in today,

accidentally seen a letter in his hand, directed to Mr. Willoughby in

your sister’s writing. I came to inquire, but I was convinced before I

could ask the question. Is every thing finally settled? Is it

impossible to—? But I have no right, and I could have no chance of

succeeding. Excuse me, Miss Dashwood. I believe I have been wrong in

saying so much, but I hardly know what to do, and on your prudence I

have the strongest dependence. Tell me that it is all absolutely

resolved on, that any attempt, that in short concealment, if

concealment be possible, is all that remains.”



These words, which conveyed to Elinor a direct avowal of his [[motifs/love|love]] for

her sister, affected her very much. She was not immediately able to say

anything, and even when her spirits were recovered, she debated for a

short [[motifs/time|time]], on the answer it would be most proper to give. The real

state of things between Willoughby and her sister was so little known

to herself, that in endeavouring to explain it, she might be as liable

to say too much as too little. Yet as she was convinced that Marianne’s

affection for Willoughby, could leave no [[concepts/hope|hope]] of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s

success, whatever the event of that affection might be, and at the same

[[motifs/time|time]] wished to shield her conduct from censure, she thought it most

prudent and kind, after some consideration, to say more than she really

knew or believed. She acknowledged, therefore, that though she had

never been informed by themselves of the terms on which they stood with

each other, of their mutual affection she had no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], and of their

correspondence she was not astonished to hear.



He listened to her with silent attention, and on her ceasing to speak,

[[motifs/rose|rose]] directly from his seat, and after saying in a voice of emotion,

“to your sister I wish all imaginable happiness; to Willoughby that he

may endeavour to deserve her,”—took leave, and went away.



Elinor derived no comfortable feelings from this conversation, to

lessen the uneasiness of her mind on other points; she was left, on the

contrary, with a [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] impression of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s

unhappiness, and was prevented even from wishing it removed, by her

anxiety for the very event that must confirm it.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Inteso appunto così, poiché comunicano apertamente tra loro, e il loro [[motifs/marriage|mattrimono]] è riconosciuto universalmente.

Di cui si è parlato.



“Come è possibile? Da chi hai sentito menzionare questa cosa?”



Titolo:  
“Da molti… alcuni dei quali non conosci affatto, altri invece che conosci bene…”

Le più intime: la signora Jennings, la signora Palmer e i Middleton… Ma

Ancora oggi potrei non crederci, perché dove la mente…

Piuttosto riluttante ad essere convinta, troverà sempre qualcosa per…

Non avrei potuto confermare i miei dubbi, se non fosse stato per quanto è accaduto oggi quando il servitore mi ha fatto entrare…

Per caso ho visto una lettera nelle sue mani, indirizzata al signor Willoughby…

“La scrittura di tua sorella… Sono venuto per chiedere informazioni, ma sono rimasto convinto già prima…”

“Potrebbe porre questa domanda: è tutto davvero risolto, ormai?”

Impossibile… Ma non ho alcun diritto, e comunque non avrei alcuna possibilità.

“Successivo… Scusi, signorina Dashwood… Credo di aver sbagliato…”

Detto questo, non so davvero cosa fare… E confido nella tua saggezza per prendere una decisione.

La dipendenza più forte… Dimmi che tutto questo è assolutamente necessario.

Deciso che qualsiasi tentativo di nascondere…

“Se la nascondigione è possibile, questo è tutto ciò che rimane.”



Queste parole, che trasmettevano a Elinor una dichiarazione diretta del suo [[motifs/love|amore]] per.

Sua sorella la colpì profondamente; non riuscì subito a dire nulla…

Qualsiasi cosa… E anche quando il suo umore si era ripreso, continuava a dubitare.

In poco [[motifs/time|tempo]], sarebbe stato molto appropriato dare la risposta giusta. La verità.

Lo stato delle cose tra Willoughby e sua sorella era molto poco noto.

A se stessa, pensò che nel tentativo di spiegarlo, potesse correre lo stesso rischio…

“Dire troppo è come non dire abbastanza… Eppure, essendo convinta che Marianne…”

L'affetto che provava per Willoughby non lasciava alcuna [[concepts/hope|speranza]] che il [[characters/colonel-brandon|-Colonnello Brandon]] potesse.

Successo, qualunque fosse l'esito di quel sentimento, e allo stesso tempo.

[[motifs/time|Tempo]] desiderava proteggere il proprio comportamento dalle critiche; lei riteneva che fosse la cosa più importante.

Sagge e gentile… ma, dopo un po’ di riflessione, forse avrebbe dovuto dire di più di quanto in realtà pensasse.

Conosceva o credeva… Pertanto ammise che, sebbene avesse…

Non sono mai stati informati personalmente sui termini ai quali erano soggetti.

L'uno per l'altro, riguardo al loro affetto reciproco lei non aveva alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], e riguardo a.

Di fronte a quella corrispondenza, non rimase affatto sorpresa.



La ascoltò in silenzio e attenzione; quando lei smise di parlare…

[[motifs/rose|Rose]] si alzò direttamente dal suo posto e, con voce emozionata, disse.

“Per tua sorella desidero tutta la felicità immaginabile; per Willoughby, che…”

“Posso cercare di meritarla, ”, disse, poi si congedò e se ne andò.



Da questa conversazione, Elinor non trasse alcun piacere o sollievo.

Ridurre l’ansia che provava su altri argomenti… Le rimase soltanto…

Al contrario, con un'impressione [[concepts/melancholy|malinconica]] riguardo a [[characters/colonel-brandon|-Colonnello Brandon]].

Infelicità… e lei non poté nemmeno desiderare che scomparisse.

Ansia per l’evento stesso che dovrà confermarlo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_28" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 28" data-chapter="Chapter 28" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/home,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/water,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/honour,concept/hope"></span>


CHAPTER XXVIII.





Nothing occurred during the next three or four days, to make Elinor

regret what she had done, in applying to her mother; for Willoughby

neither came nor wrote. They were engaged about the end of that [[motifs/time|time]] to

attend Lady Middleton to a party, from which Mrs. Jennings was kept

away by the indisposition of her youngest daughter; and for this party,

Marianne, wholly dispirited, careless of her appearance, and seeming

equally indifferent whether she went or staid, prepared, without one

look of [[concepts/hope|hope]] or one expression of pleasure. She sat by the drawing-room

[[motifs/fire|fire]] after tea, till the moment of Lady Middleton’s arrival, without

once stirring from her seat, or altering her attitude, lost in her own

thoughts, and insensible of her sister’s presence; and when at last

they were told that Lady Middleton waited for them at the door, she

started as if she had forgotten that any one was expected.



They arrived in due [[motifs/time|time]] at the place of destination, and as soon as

the string of carriages before them would allow, alighted, ascended the

stairs, heard their names announced from one landing-place to another

in an audible voice, and entered a room splendidly lit up, quite full

of company, and insufferably hot. When they had paid their tribute of

politeness by curtsying to the lady of the house, they were permitted

to mingle in the crowd, and take their share of the heat and

inconvenience, to which their arrival must necessarily add. After some

[[motifs/time|time]] spent in saying little or doing less, Lady Middleton sat down to

Cassino, and as Marianne was not in spirits for moving about, she and

Elinor luckily succeeding to chairs, placed themselves at no great

distance from the table.



They had not remained in this manner long, before Elinor perceived

Willoughby, standing within a few yards of them, in earnest

conversation with a very fashionable looking young woman. She soon

caught his eye, and he immediately bowed, but without attempting to

speak to her, or to approach Marianne, though he could not but see her;

and then continued his discourse with the same lady. Elinor turned

involuntarily to Marianne, to see whether it could be unobserved by

her. At that moment she first perceived him, and her whole countenance

glowing with sudden delight, she would have moved towards him

instantly, had not her sister caught hold of her.



“Good heavens!” she exclaimed, “he is there—he is there—Oh! why does he

not look at me? why cannot I speak to him?”



“Pray, pray be composed,” cried Elinor, “and do not betray what you

feel to every [[concepts/body|body]] present. Perhaps he has not observed you yet.”



This however was more than she could believe herself; and to be

composed at such a moment was not only beyond the reach of Marianne, it

was beyond her wish. She sat in an agony of impatience which affected

every feature.



At last he turned round again, and regarded them both; she started up,

and pronouncing his name in a tone of affection, held out her hand to

him. He approached, and addressing himself rather to Elinor than

Marianne, as if wishing to avoid her eye, and determined not to observe

her attitude, inquired in a hurried manner after Mrs. Dashwood, and

asked how long they had been in town. Elinor was robbed of all presence

of mind by such an address, and was unable to say a word. But the

feelings of her sister were instantly expressed. Her face was crimsoned

over, and she exclaimed, in a voice of the greatest emotion, “Good God!

Willoughby, what is the meaning of this? Have you not received my

letters? Will you not shake hands with me?”



He could not then avoid it, but her touch seemed painful to him, and he

held her hand only for a moment. During all this [[motifs/time|time]] he was evidently

struggling for composure. Elinor watched his countenance and saw its

expression becoming more tranquil. After a moment’s pause, he spoke

with calmness.



“I did myself the [[concepts/honour|honour]] of calling in Berkeley Street last Tuesday,

and very much regretted that I was not fortunate enough to find

yourselves and Mrs. Jennings at [[motifs/home|home]]. My card was not lost, I [[concepts/hope|hope]].”



“But have you not received my notes?” cried Marianne in the wildest

anxiety. “Here is some mistake I am sure—some dreadful mistake. What

can be the meaning of it? Tell me, Willoughby; for heaven’s sake tell

me, what is the matter?”



He made no reply; his complexion changed and all his embarrassment

returned; but as if, on catching the eye of the young lady with whom he

had been previously talking, he felt the necessity of instant exertion,

he recovered himself again, and after saying, “Yes, I had the pleasure

of receiving the information of your arrival in town, which you were so

good as to send me,” turned hastily away with a slight bow and joined

his friend.



Marianne, now looking dreadfully white, and unable to stand, sunk into

her chair, and Elinor, expecting every moment to see her faint, tried

to screen her from the observation of others, while reviving her with

lavender [[motifs/water|water]].



“Go to him, Elinor,” she cried, as soon as she could speak, “and force

him to come to me. Tell him I must see him again—must speak to him

instantly.—I cannot rest—I shall not have a moment’s peace till this is

explained—some dreadful misapprehension or other. Oh, go to him this

moment.”



“How can that be done? No, my dearest Marianne, you must wait. This is

not the place for explanations. Wait only till tomorrow.”



With difficulty however could she prevent her from following him

herself; and to persuade her to check her agitation, to wait, at least,

with the appearance of composure, till she might speak to him with more

privacy and more effect, was impossible; for Marianne continued

incessantly to give way in a low voice to the misery of her feelings,

by exclamations of wretchedness. In a short [[motifs/time|time]] Elinor saw Willoughby

quit the room by the door towards the staircase, and telling Marianne

that he was gone, urged the impossibility of speaking to him again that

evening, as a fresh argument for her to be calm. She instantly begged

her sister would entreat Lady Middleton to take them [[motifs/home|home]], as she was

too miserable to stay a minute longer.



Lady Middleton, though in the middle of a rubber, on being informed

that Marianne was unwell, was too polite to object for a moment to her

wish of going away, and making over her cards to a friend, they

departed as soon as the carriage could be found. Scarcely a word was

spoken during their return to Berkeley Street. Marianne was in a silent

agony, too much oppressed even for [[motifs/tears|tears]]; but as Mrs. Jennings was

luckily not come [[motifs/home|home]], they could go directly to their own room, where

hartshorn restored her a little to herself. She was soon undressed and

in bed, and as she seemed desirous of being alone, her sister then left

her, and while she waited the return of Mrs. Jennings, had leisure

enough for thinking over the past.



That some kind of engagement had subsisted between Willoughby and

Marianne she could not [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], and that Willoughby was weary of it,

seemed equally clear; for however Marianne might still feed her own

wishes, _she_ could not attribute such behaviour to mistake or

misapprehension of any kind. Nothing but a thorough change of sentiment

could account for it. Her indignation would have been still stronger

than it was, had she not witnessed that embarrassment which seemed to

speak a consciousness of his own misconduct, and prevented her from

believing him so unprincipled as to have been sporting with the

affections of her sister from the first, without any design that would

bear investigation. Absence might have weakened his regard, and

convenience might have determined him to overcome it, but that such a

regard had formerly existed she could not bring herself to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]].



As for Marianne, on the pangs which so unhappy a meeting must already

have given her, and on those still more severe which might await her in

its probable consequence, she could not reflect without the deepest

concern. Her own situation gained in the comparison; for while she

could _esteem_ Edward as much as ever, however they might be divided in

future, her mind might be always supported. But every circumstance that

could embitter such an evil seemed uniting to heighten the misery of

Marianne in a final separation from Willoughby—in an immediate and

irreconcilable rupture with him.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_29--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 29 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 29" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/death,motif/fire,motif/love,motif/sleep,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/window,concept/body,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/solitude,concept/suffering,character/bottom"></span>


CHAPTER XXIX.





Before the housemaid had lit their [[motifs/fire|fire]] the next day, or the sun gained

any power over a cold, gloomy morning in January, Marianne, only half

dressed, was kneeling against one of the [[motifs/window|window]]-seats for the sake of

all the little light she could command from it, and writing as fast as

a continual flow of [[motifs/tears|tears]] would permit her. In this situation, Elinor,

roused from [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] by her agitation and sobs, first perceived her; and

after observing her for a few moments with silent anxiety, said, in a

tone of the most considerate gentleness,



“Marianne, may I ask—?”



“No, Elinor,” she replied, “ask nothing; you will soon know all.”



The sort of desperate calmness with which this was said, lasted no

longer than while she spoke, and was immediately followed by a return

of the same excessive affliction. It was some minutes before she could

go on with her letter, and the frequent bursts of grief which still

obliged her, at intervals, to withhold her pen, were proofs enough of

her feeling how more than probable it was that she was writing for the

last [[motifs/time|time]] to Willoughby.



Elinor paid her every quiet and unobtrusive attention in her power; and

she would have tried to sooth and tranquilize her still more, had not

Marianne entreated her, with all the eagerness of the most nervous

irritability, not to speak to her for the world. In such circumstances,

it was better for both that they should not be long together; and the

restless state of Marianne’s mind not only prevented her from remaining

in the room a moment after she was dressed, but requiring at once

[[concepts/solitude|solitude]] and continual change of place, made her wander about the house

till breakfast [[motifs/time|time]], avoiding the sight of every [[concepts/body|body]].



At breakfast she neither ate, nor attempted to eat any thing; and

Elinor’s attention was then all employed, not in urging her, not in

pitying her, nor in appearing to regard her, but in endeavouring to

engage Mrs. Jennings’s notice entirely to herself.



As this was a favourite meal with Mrs. Jennings, it lasted a

considerable [[motifs/time|time]], and they were just setting themselves, after it,

round the common working table, when a letter was delivered to

Marianne, which she eagerly caught from the servant, and, turning of a

[[motifs/death|death]]-like paleness, instantly ran out of the room. Elinor, who saw as

plainly by this, as if she had seen the direction, that it must come

from Willoughby, felt immediately such a sickness at heart as made her

hardly able to hold up her head, and sat in such a general tremour as

made her [[concepts/fear|fear]] it impossible to escape Mrs. Jennings’s notice. That good

lady, however, saw only that Marianne had received a letter from

Willoughby, which appeared to her a very good joke, and which she

treated accordingly, by hoping, with a laugh, that she would find it to

her liking. Of Elinor’s distress, she was too busily employed in

measuring lengths of worsted for her rug, to see any thing at all; and

calmly continuing her talk, as soon as Marianne disappeared, she said,



“Upon my word, I never saw a young woman so desperately in [[motifs/love|love]] in my

life! _My_ girls were nothing to her, and yet they used to be foolish

enough; but as for Miss Marianne, she is quite an altered creature. I

[[concepts/hope|hope]], from the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of my heart, he won’t keep her waiting much

longer, for it is quite grievous to see her look so ill and forlorn.

Pray, when are they to be married?”



Elinor, though never less disposed to speak than at that moment,

obliged herself to answer such an attack as this, and, therefore,

trying to smile, replied, “And have you really, Ma’am, talked yourself

into a persuasion of my sister’s being engaged to Mr. Willoughby? I

thought it had been only a joke, but so serious a question seems to

imply more; and I must beg, therefore, that you will not deceive

yourself any longer. I do assure you that nothing would surprise me

more than to hear of their being going to be married.”



“For shame, for shame, Miss Dashwood! how can you talk so? Don’t we all

know that it must be a match, that they were over head and ears in [[motifs/love|love]]

with each other from the first moment they met? Did not I see them

together in Devonshire every day, and all day long; and did not I know

that your sister came to town with me on purpose to buy wedding

clothes? Come, come, this won’t do. Because you are so sly about it

yourself, you think nobody else has any senses; but it is no such

thing, I can tell you, for it has been known all over town this ever so

long. I tell every [[concepts/body|body]] of it and so does Charlotte.”



“Indeed, Ma’am,” said Elinor, very seriously, “you are mistaken.

Indeed, you are doing a very unkind thing in spreading the report, and

you will find that you have though you will not believe me now.”



Mrs. Jennings laughed again, but Elinor had not spirits to say more,

and eager at all events to know what Willoughby had written, hurried

away to their room, where, on opening the door, she saw Marianne

stretched on the bed, almost choked by grief, one letter in her hand,

and two or three others lying by her. Elinor drew near, but without

saying a word; and seating herself on the bed, took her hand, kissed

her affectionately several times, and then gave way to a burst of

[[motifs/tears|tears]], which at first was scarcely less violent than Marianne’s. The

latter, though unable to speak, seemed to feel all the tenderness of

this behaviour, and after some [[motifs/time|time]] thus spent in joint affliction, she

put all the letters into Elinor’s hands; and then covering her face

with her handkerchief, almost screamed with agony. Elinor, who knew

that such grief, shocking as it was to witness it, must have its

course, watched by her till this excess of [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] had somewhat spent

itself, and then turning eagerly to Willoughby’s letter, read as

CAPITOLO XXIX.





Prima che la cameriera accendesse il loro [[motifs/fire|fuoco]] il giorno dopo, o prima che il sole sorgesse.

“Qualsiasi potere su una fredda e cupa mattina di gennaio… Marianne, solo a metà…”

Vestito, si inginocchiava contro uno dei sedili accanto alla [[motifs/window|finestra]] per.

Utilizzando tutta la luce che riusciva a ottenere da esso, scriveva il più velocemente possibile…

Un flusso continuo di [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] le avrebbe permesso di farlo. In questa situazione, Elinor.

Disturbato dal suo agitamento e dai suoi singhiozzi, la notò per la prima volta; e.

Dopo averla osservata per alcuni momenti con silenziosa ansia, disse…

Tonos di estrema delicatezza e considerazione



“Marianne, posso chiederti…?”



“No, Elinor,” rispose lei, “non chiedere nulla; presto saprai tutto.”



La calma disperata con cui queste parole furono pronunciate non durò a lungo…

Più lungo del tempo impiegato per parlare… e subito dopo seguì un ritorno.

Della stessa eccessiva sofferenza… Passarono alcuni minuti prima che riuscisse a…

Continua con la sua lettera… e con quelle frequenti crisi di dolore che ancora la assalgono.

Costringerla, di tanto in tanto, a trattenere la penna… erano prove sufficienti di…

Il suo sentimento riguardo alla probabilità che stesse scrivendo per…

L’ultima volta a Willoughby.



Elinor le dedicò tutta l’attenzione silenziosa e discreta di cui era capace; e

Avrebbe cercato ancora di calmarla e rassicurarla, se solo…

Marianne la pregò con tutta l’ansia della persona più nervosa…

Irritabilità… per non parlare del fatto che non si voleva assolutamente parlare con lei in quelle circostanze.

Era meglio per entrambi che non trascorressero molto tempo insieme…

Lo stato di agitazione mentale di Marianne le impediva di rimanere ferma…

Nella stanza poco dopo che si era vestita, ma necessario immediatamente…

La [[concepts/solitude|solitudine]] e i continui cambi di luogo la spinsero a vagare per tutta la casa.

Fino all’[[motifs/time|ora]] di colazione, evitando di vedere qualsiasi [[concepts/body|corpo]].



A colazione non mangiò nulla, né tentò nemmeno di mangiare qualcosa; e

L’attenzione di Elinor era completamente assorbita da altro, non nel tentativo di incoraggiarlo, né in…

Comprendendola, senza fingere di prestarle attenzione, ma cercando di…

Attirare completamente l’attenzione della signora Jennings su di sé.



Un pasto preferito dalla signora Jennings…

Dopo un considerevole [[motifs/time|tempo]], stavano appena iniziando a sistemarsi.

Intorno al tavolo da lavoro comune, quando arrivò una lettera

"Marianne, che afferrò con impazienza dalla serva e, girandosi..."

Un pallore simile a quello della [[motifs/death|morte]], uscì immediatamente dalla stanza. Elinor, che vide tutto questo.

Chiaramente, seguendo questa direzione, come se avesse già visto dove sarebbe arrivato…

Un malessere improvviso nel cuore…

A malapena in grado di tenere la testa dritta, sedeva scossa da un tremito generale…

Questo la fece [[concepts/fear|temere]] che fosse impossibile evitare l’attenzione della signora Jennings. Quella brava donna.

La signora, tuttavia, vide solo che Marianne aveva ricevuto una lettera da…

Willoughby… che le sembrava davvero una battuta molto divertente.

trattata di conseguenza, con l’augurio, e ridendo, che lei la trovasse…

A piacimento suo… Di fronte al dolore di Elinor, lei era troppo impegnata per prestare attenzione.
