Una fraintesa che emerge nel giro di uno o due giorni… le carte di…

Un invito per loro, così come per il loro fratello e la loro sorella, a una piccola.

Una festa musicale a casa sua. La conseguenza di ciò fu che la signora.

John Dashwood fu costretto ad accettare non solo l’estrema autorità…

L’inconvenienza di dover inviare la sua carrozza per le signorine Dashwood… ma cosa ancora?

Era ancora peggio: doveva sopportare tutte le sgradevolezze legate alla necessità di comparire in pubblico.

Trattarli con attenzione… E chi avrebbe potuto dire che forse non ne sarebbe valsa la pena?

Aspettarsi di uscire con lei una seconda volta. Il potere del deludere.

“Loro, è vero, dovevano sempre essere suoi… Ma questo non era sufficiente.”

Quando le persone sono decise ad adottare un certo modo di comportarsi, pur sapendo che…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_36--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 36 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 36" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/nature,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/charity,concept/education,concept/nature,setting/london"></span>


wrong, they feel injured by the expectation of any thing better from

them.



Marianne had now been brought by degrees, so much into the habit of

going out every day, that it was become a matter of indifference to

her, whether she went or not: and she prepared quietly and mechanically

for every evening’s engagement, though without expecting the smallest

amusement from any, and very often without knowing, till the last

moment, where it was to take her.



To her dress and appearance she was grown so perfectly indifferent, as

not to bestow half the consideration on it, during the whole of her

toilet, which it received from Miss Steele in the first five minutes of

their being together, when it was finished. Nothing escaped _her_

minute observation and general curiosity; she saw every thing, and

asked every thing; was never easy till she knew the price of every part

of Marianne’s dress; could have guessed the number of her gowns

altogether with better judgment than Marianne herself, and was not

without hopes of finding out before they parted, how much her washing

cost per week, and how much she had every year to spend upon herself.

The impertinence of these kind of scrutinies, moreover, was generally

concluded with a compliment, which though meant as its douceur, was

considered by Marianne as the greatest impertinence of all; for after

undergoing an examination into the value and make of her gown, the

colour of her shoes, and the arrangement of her hair, she was almost

sure of being told that upon “her word she looked vastly smart, and she

dared to say she would make a great many conquests.”



With such encouragement as this, was she dismissed on the present

occasion, to her brother’s carriage; which they were ready to enter

five minutes after it stopped at the door, a punctuality not very

agreeable to their sister-in-law, who had preceded them to the house of

her acquaintance, and was there hoping for some delay on their part

that might inconvenience either herself or her coachman.



The events of this evening were not very remarkable. The party, like

other musical parties, comprehended a great many people who had real

taste for the performance, and a great many more who had none at all;

and the performers themselves were, as usual, in their own estimation,

and that of their immediate friends, the first private performers in

England.



As Elinor was neither musical, nor affecting to be so, she made no

scruple of turning her eyes from the grand pianoforte, whenever it

suited her, and unrestrained even by the presence of a harp, and

violoncello, would fix them at pleasure on any other object in the

room. In one of these excursive glances she perceived among a group of

young men, the very he, who had given them a lecture on toothpick-cases

at Gray’s. She perceived him soon afterwards looking at herself, and

speaking familiarly to her brother; and had just determined to find out

his name from the latter, when they both came towards her, and Mr.

Dashwood introduced him to her as Mr. Robert Ferrars.



He addressed her with easy civility, and twisted his head into a bow

which assured her as plainly as words could have done, that he was

exactly the coxcomb she had heard him described to be by Lucy. Happy

had it been for her, if her regard for Edward had depended less on his

own merit, than on the merit of his nearest relations! For then his

brother’s bow must have given the finishing stroke to what the

ill-humour of his mother and sister would have begun. But while she

wondered at the difference of the two young men, she did not find that

the emptiness and conceit of the one, put her out of all [[concepts/charity|charity]] with

the modesty and worth of the other. Why they _were_ different, Robert

explained to her himself in the course of a quarter of an hour’s

conversation; for, talking of his brother, and lamenting the extreme

_gaucherie_ which he really believed kept him from mixing in proper

society, he candidly and generously attributed it much less to any

natural deficiency, than to the misfortune of a private [[concepts/education|education]];

while he himself, though probably without any particular, any material

superiority by [[concepts/nature|nature]], merely from the advantage of a public school,

was as [[motifs/well|well]] fitted to mix in the world as any other man.



“Upon my [[motifs/soul|soul]],” he added, “I believe it is nothing more; and so I often

tell my mother, when she is grieving about it. ‘My dear Madam,’ I

always say to her, ‘you must make yourself easy. The evil is now

irremediable, and it has been entirely your own doing. Why would you be

persuaded by my uncle, Sir Robert, against your own judgment, to place

Edward under private tuition, at the most critical [[motifs/time|time]] of his life? If

you had only sent him to Westminster as [[motifs/well|well]] as myself, instead of

sending him to Mr. Pratt’s, all this would have been prevented.’ This

is the way in which I always consider the matter, and my mother is

perfectly convinced of her error.”



Elinor would not oppose his opinion, because, whatever might be her

general estimation of the advantage of a public school, she could not

think of Edward’s abode in Mr. Pratt’s family, with any satisfaction.



“You reside in Devonshire, I think,”—was his next observation, “in a

cottage near Dawlish.”



Elinor set him right as to its situation; and it seemed rather

surprising to him that anybody could live in Devonshire, without living

near Dawlish. He bestowed his hearty approbation however on their

species of house.



“For my own part,” said he, “I am excessively fond of a cottage; there

is always so much comfort, so much elegance about them. And I protest,

if I had any money to spare, I should buy a little land and build one

myself, within a short distance of [[settings/london|London]], where I might drive myself

down at any [[motifs/time|time]], and collect a few friends about me, and be happy. I

advise every [[concepts/body|body]] who is going to build, to build a cottage. My friend

Non è giusto… Si sentono offesi dall’aspettativa che venga loro chiesto qualcosa di meglio.

loro.



Marianne ormai si era abituata, gradualmente, a…

Titolo:  
Uscire ogni giorno… fino a quando diventa qualcosa di cui non ci si cura più.

Lei, che andasse o meno… Si preparò in silenzio e con meccanicità.

Per ogni serata di impegni, anche senza aspettarmi nulla in cambio…

Divertimento da parte di chiunque… e spesso senza nemmeno saperlo, fino all’ultimo momento.

Il momento in cui avrebbe dovuto portarla via.



A suo abbigliamento e al proprio aspetto era ormai del tutto indifferente…

Non le dedica nemmeno la metà dell’attenzione che merita, per tutto il tempo…

Bagno, che le fu fornito da Miss Steele nei primi cinque minuti…

Il loro stare insieme, quando tutto fu finito… Niente le sfuggì.

Osservazione attenta e curiosità naturale: vide tutto.

Chiese tutto; non fu mai facile finché non conobbe il prezzo di ogni singola parte.

Il vestito di Marianne… Avrei potuto indovinare quante gonne possedesse.

Con un giudizio molto migliore di quello di Marianne stessa… e non era affatto così.

Senza alcuna speranza di scoprirlo prima della loro separazione… quanto fosse grande il suo amore.

Il costo a settimana, e quanta denaro aveva ogni anno a disposizione per sé stessa.

L’impertinenza di questo tipo di indagini, inoltre, era generalmente…

Si concluse con un complimento, che, sebbene inteso come gesto di gentilezza, in realtà…

Considerato da Marianne come la più grande impertinenza di tutte… perché dopo…

In corso di un esame per valutare il valore e la qualità del suo abito…

“Per il colore delle sue scarpe e l’acconciatura dei suoi capelli, sembrava quasi…”

“Sure of being told that…”

Osò dire che avrebbe ottenuto molti successi.



Con un incoraggiamento del genere, fu congedata sul momento.

"Alla partenza del carrozzone di suo fratello"; erano pronti a salire a bordo."

Cinque minuti dopo essere arrivato alla porta… una puntualità davvero poco…

Piacevole alla loro nuora, che era arrivata prima di loro nella casa di.

La sua conoscente… e si trovava lì nella speranza che loro ritardassero il loro arrivo.

Ciò potrebbe causare disagi sia a lei che al suo cocchiere.



Gli eventi di questa serata non furono particolarmente notevoli. La festa, come…

Altre feste musicali coinvolgevano molte persone che avevano davvero…

Coloro che apprezzavano la qualità delle esibizioni, e molti altri che invece non ne avevano affatto alcuna idea…

E i performer stessi, come al solito, secondo la loro valutazione personale…

E quelli dei loro amici più intimi: i primi artisti che si esibirono in privato

Inghilterra.



As Elinor non era né musicale, né si dava da fare per sembrarlo, non fece nulla al riguardo

Il rimorso di distogliere lo sguardo dal grande pianoforte…

Le si addiceva perfettamente; non veniva nemmeno limitata dalla presenza di un’arpa…

Violoncello: li si potrebbe applicare con piacere su qualsiasi altro oggetto…

Stanza. In uno di questi sguardi fugaci, notò tra un gruppo di…

Gli stessi giovani che avevano ascoltato una sua lezione sui portacarte per stuzzicadenti

Al Gray’s… Poco dopo lo vide guardarla.

Parlando con affetto al fratello, aveva appena deciso di scoprirlo.

Il suo nome dal secondo, quando entrambi si avvicinarono a lei, e il signor.

Dashwood lo presentò a lei come il signor Robert Ferrars.



Le parlò con cortesia e semplicità, poi inclinò leggermente la testa in un inchino.

Titolo:  
Ciò le assicurava, in modo altrettanto chiaro di quanto avrebbero potuto farlo le parole, che lui era…

Esattamente la donnaccia che Lucy aveva descritto come tale… Felice.

Se fosse stato per lei… se il suo affetto per Edward non dipendesse così tanto da lui…

Per il suo merito personale, e non per quello dei suoi parenti più stretti… Allora, infatti, il suo successo sarebbe davvero dovuto solo a lui stesso.

Il colpo di archi del fratello deve aver inflitto il colpo decisivo a ciò che…

L’umore negativo di sua madre e sua sorella sarebbe già iniziato. Ma mentre lei.

Si chiedeva quale fosse la differenza tra quei due giovani uomini, ma non riusciva a individuarla.

Il vuoto e l’arroganza di quella persona la privavano completamente di ogni forma di [[concepts/charity|carità]].

La modestia e il valore dell’altro. Perché erano diversi, Robert

Le spiegò tutto personalmente nel corso di un quarto d’ora…

Conversazione: parlando di suo fratello e lamentandone le condizioni estreme

Goffaggine che, secondo lui, lo impediva di integrarsi correttamente nella società

Titolo:  
Nella società, attribuì onestamente e generosamente tale merito a ben poche persone…

Più che a una carenza naturale, si tratta della sfortuna di un'educazione privata inadeguata.

Mentre lui stesso, probabilmente senza alcun motivo particolare o concreto…

La superiorità derivante dalla [[concepts/nature|natura]], semplicemente dal vantaggio di frequentare una scuola pubblica.

Era altrettanto adatto a integrarsi nel mondo quanto qualsiasi altro uomo.



“Per la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]],” aggiunse, “credo che non sia nient'altro; ed è per questo che spesso, ”

“Dite alla mia madre, quando ne sarà addolorata: ‘Mia cara signora…’”

“Sempre le dì: ‘Devi prenderti cura di te stessa… Il male è ormai qui.’”

Irrimediabile… ed è stato tutto colpa tua. Perché mai dovresti…

Convinto dal mio zio, Sir Robert, contro la tua stessa volontà, ad accettare…

Edward, sotto insegnamento privato, nel momento più critico della sua vita. Se.

Avresti dovuto mandarlo a Westminster solo perché lo volevo io, proprio come me, invece di.

“Se solo lo avessero mandato da Mr. Pratt, tutto questo si sarebbe potuto evitare.”

“È così che io considero sempre la questione, e lo stesso vale per mia madre.”

“Completamente convinta del proprio errore.”



Elinor non avrebbe opposto obiezioni al suo punto di vista, perché, qualunque fosse la sua opinione…

Una valutazione generale dei vantaggi di una scuola pubblica… lei non riusciva a farlo.

Si può considerare con soddisfazione la dimora di Edward all’interno della famiglia del signor Pratt.



“Vive a Devonshire, giusto?”, fu la sua osservazione successiva, “in una…”

“Casa di campagna vicino a Dawlish”.



Elinor gli spiegò chiaramente la situazione; e sembrava piuttosto…

Per lui era sorprendente che qualcuno potesse vivere nel Devonshire senza…

Titolo:  
vicino a Dawlish. Tuttavia, diede loro la sua calorosa approvazione.

Specie di casa.



“Per quanto mi riguarda,” disse, “amo moltissimo le casette di campagna; quelle…

“#Un titolo che trasmette sempre tanto conforto, tanta eleganza… E io protesto.”

Se avessi un po’ di soldi in più, comprerei un pezzo di terra e costruicci sopra una casa.

Io stesso, in breve distanza da [[settings/london|Londra]], dove potrei guidare da solo.

In qualsiasi momento, posso radunare alcuni amici intorno a me e essere felice. Io.

Consiglio a ogni [[concepts/body|persona]] che intenda costruire di costruire una capanna. Mio amico.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_36--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 36 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 36" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/dance,motif/fire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/time,motif/well,concept/conscience,concept/humility,concept/pride,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


Lord Courtland came to me the other day on purpose to ask my advice,

and laid before me three different plans of Bonomi’s. I was to decide

on the best of them. ‘My dear Courtland,’ said I, immediately throwing

them all into the [[motifs/fire|fire]], ‘do not adopt either of them, but by all means

build a cottage.’ And that I fancy, will be the end of it.



“Some people imagine that there can be no accommodations, no space in a

cottage; but this is all a mistake. I was last month at my friend

Elliott’s, near Dartford. Lady Elliott wished to give a [[motifs/dance|dance]]. ‘But how

can it be done?’ said she; ‘my dear Ferrars, do tell me how it is to be

managed. There is not a room in this cottage that will hold ten couple,

and where can the supper be?’ _I_ immediately saw that there could be

no difficulty in it, so I said, ‘My dear Lady Elliott, do not be

uneasy. The dining parlour will admit eighteen couple with ease;

card-tables may be placed in the drawing-room; the library may be open

for tea and other refreshments; and let the supper be set out in the

saloon.’ Lady Elliott was delighted with the thought. We measured the

dining-room, and found it would hold exactly eighteen couple, and the

affair was arranged precisely after my plan. So that, in fact, you see,

if people do but know how to set about it, every comfort may be as [[motifs/well|well]]

enjoyed in a cottage as in the most spacious dwelling.”



Elinor agreed to it all, for she did not think he deserved the

compliment of rational opposition.



As John Dashwood had no more pleasure in music than his eldest sister,

his mind was equally at liberty to fix on any thing else; and a thought

struck him during the evening, which he communicated to his wife, for

her approbation, when they got [[motifs/home|home]]. The consideration of Mrs.

Dennison’s mistake, in supposing his sisters their guests, had

suggested the propriety of their being really invited to become such,

while Mrs. Jennings’s engagements kept her from [[motifs/home|home]]. The expense would

be nothing, the inconvenience not more; and it was altogether an

attention which the delicacy of his [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] pointed out to be

requisite to its complete enfranchisement from his promise to his

father. Fanny was startled at the proposal.



“I do not see how it can be done,” said she, “without affronting Lady

Middleton, for they spend every day with her; otherwise I should be

exceedingly glad to do it. You know I am always ready to pay them any

attention in my power, as my taking them out this evening shows. But

they are Lady Middleton’s visitors. How can I ask them away from her?”



Her husband, but with great [[concepts/humility|humility]], did not see the force of her

objection. “They had already spent a week in this manner in Conduit

Street, and Lady Middleton could not be displeased at their giving the

same number of days to such near relations.”



Fanny paused a moment, and then, with fresh vigor, said,



“My [[motifs/love|love]], I would ask them with all my heart, if it was in my power.

But I had just settled within myself to ask the Miss Steeles to spend a

few days with us. They are very [[motifs/well|well]] behaved, good kind of girls; and I

think the attention is due to them, as their uncle did so very [[motifs/well|well]] by

Edward. We can ask your sisters some other year, you know; but the Miss

Steeles may not be in town any more. I am sure you will like them;

indeed, you _do_ like them, you know, very much already, and so does my

mother; and they are such favourites with Harry!”



Mr. Dashwood was convinced. He saw the necessity of inviting the Miss

Steeles immediately, and his [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] was pacified by the resolution

of inviting his sisters another year; at the same [[motifs/time|time]], however, slyly

suspecting that another year would make the invitation needless, by

bringing Elinor to town as [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s wife, and Marianne as

_their_ visitor.



Fanny, rejoicing in her escape, and proud of the ready wit that had

procured it, wrote the next morning to Lucy, to request her company and

her sister’s, for some days, in Harley Street, as soon as Lady

Middleton could spare them. This was enough to make Lucy really and

reasonably happy. Mrs. Dashwood seemed actually working for her,

herself; cherishing all her hopes, and promoting all her views! Such an

opportunity of being with Edward and his family was, above all things,

the most material to her interest, and such an invitation the most

gratifying to her feelings! It was an advantage that could not be too

gratefully acknowledged, nor too speedily made use of; and the visit to

Lady Middleton, which had not before had any precise limits, was

instantly discovered to have been always meant to end in two days’

[[motifs/time|time]].



When the note was shown to Elinor, as it was within ten minutes after

its arrival, it gave her, for the first [[motifs/time|time]], some share in the

expectations of Lucy; for such a mark of uncommon kindness, vouchsafed

on so short an acquaintance, seemed to declare that the good-will

towards her arose from something more than merely malice against

herself; and might be brought, by [[motifs/time|time]] and address, to do every thing

that Lucy wished. Her flattery had already subdued the [[concepts/pride|pride]] of Lady

Middleton, and made an entry into the close heart of Mrs. John

Dashwood; and these were effects that laid open the probability of

greater.



The Miss Steeles removed to Harley Street, and all that reached Elinor

of their influence there, strengthened her expectation of the event.

Sir John, who called on them more than once, brought [[motifs/home|home]] such accounts

of the favour they were in, as must be universally striking. Mrs.

Dashwood had never been so much pleased with any young women in her

life, as she was with them; had given each of them a needle book made

by some emigrant; called Lucy by her Christian name; and did not know

whether she should ever be able to part with them.



END OF THE SECOND VOLUME


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Un giorno Lord Courtland è venuto da me apposta per chiedermi il mio parere.

Tre diversi progetti di Bonomi mi furono presentati; dovevo decidere quale scegliere.

“Nel migliore dei casi… ‘Mio caro Courtland’, dissi, senza esitazione.”

Metteteli tutti nel [[motifs/fire|fuoco]]; “Non adottatene nessuno, ma assolutamente, ”

“Costruire una capanna, ” E credo che sia proprio questo il finale della storia.



“Alcuni pensano che non possa esserci alcun spazio, alcuna possibilità di accomodamento…”

Casetta… ma tutto questo è un errore. Lo scorso mese ero da mio amico…

La casa degli Elliott, vicino a Dartford. La signora Elliott voleva organizzare una [[motifs/dance|danza]]. “Ma come, ”

“È possibile farlo?”, disse lei; “caro Ferrars, dimmi come si può procedere”.

"Gestito con cura… Non c’è nemmeno una stanza in questa capanna che possa ospitare dieci coppie."

“E dove possiamo mangiare la cena?” Mi resi immediatamente conto che…

“Non c’è alcuna difficoltà in questo, quindi dissi: ‘Mia cara signora Elliott, non si preoccupi…’”

Inquietudine. La sala da pranzo può ospitare facilmente diciotto coppie.

“Le carte da gioco possono essere messe nel salotto; la biblioteca può rimanere aperta.”

“Per il tè e altre bevande rinfrescanti… e che la cena venga servita…”

“Salone…”. Lady Elliott ne fu molto entusiasta. Ne misurammo le dimensioni.

Salone da pranzo, e si scoprì che poteva ospitare esattamente diciotto coppie…

L’intera faccenda fu organizzata esattamente secondo i miei piani. Così che, in realtà…

Se le persone sanno come procedere, ogni comodità potrebbe essere resa disponibile facilmente.

Godersi la vita in una capanna tanto quanto in una dimora spaziosa.



Elinor acconsentì a tutto, perché non pensava che lui meritasse quel trattamento.

Un complimento nato dall’opposizione razionale.



Come John Dashwood non provava alcun piacere nella musica, proprio come sua sorella maggiore…

La sua mente era libera di concentrarsi su qualsiasi altra cosa; e un pensiero…

Gli venne in mente durante la serata e ne parlò con sua moglie.

Il suo consenso, quando tornarono a [[motifs/home|casa]]. La considerazione della signora.

L’errore di Dennison, nel considerare le sue sorelle come ospiti…

Si suggeriva l’opportunità che venissero effettivamente invitati a diventarlo.

Mentre gli impegni della signora Jennings la tenevano lontana da [[motifs/home|casa]], le spese continuavano ad aumentare.

Nessun inconveniente…

Quell’attenzione che la delicatezza della sua [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]] gli faceva notare come necessaria.

Titolo:  
Necessario per il suo completo emancipamento dalla promessa fatta da lui…

Padre. Fanny rimase sorpresa da quella proposta.



“Non vedo come sia possibile farlo“, disse lei, “senza offendere Lady…“.

Middleton, perché passano ogni giorno con lei; altrimenti io…

Molto felice di farlo. Sai che sono sempre pronto a pagarli qualsiasi somma…

L’attenzione è nelle mie mani, come dimostra il fatto che li sto togliendo stasera… Ma

“Sono i visitatori di Lady Middleton… Come posso mandarli via da lei?”



Suo marito, ma con grande [[concepts/humility|umiltà]], non riconobbe la forza di lei.

Obiezione: “Avevano già trascorso una settimana in questo modo a Conduit”.

Via… e Lady Middleton non poteva certo essere scontenta del loro dono

“Lo stesso numero di giorni per parenti così stretti…”



Fanny fece una pausa, poi, con nuovo vigore, disse:



“Mio [[motifs/love|amore]], glielo chiederei con tutto il mio cuore, se fosse nelle mie possibilità.”

Ma proprio in quel momento avevo deciso di chiedere alla signorina Steels di trascorrere del tempo con me…

Qualche giorno con noi. Sono ragazze molto ben educate, gentili. E io.

Pensano che quell’attenzione sia loro dovuta, visto che loro zio l’ha resa possibile in modo davvero eccellente.

Edward… Potremmo chiedere alle tue sorelle un’altra volta, sai… Ma la signorina…

“Gli acciai potrebbero non essere più in città… Sono sicuro che vi piaceranno.”

Infatti, ti piacciono davvero molto, lo sai… E anche a me.

“La madre… e sono davvero i preferiti di Harry!”



Il signor Dashwood era convinto. Riconobbe la necessità di invitare la signorina…

Steeles agì immediatamente, e la sua [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]] fu tranquillizzata da quella decisione.

Di invitare di nuovo le sue sorelle l’anno prossimo; tuttavia, allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]], in modo astuto.

Sospettando che un altro anno rendesse l’invito inutile…

Portando Elinor in città come moglie di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], e Marianne come.

Il loro visitatore.



"Fanny, felice per la propria fuga e orgogliosa dell’ingegno pronto che aveva dimostrato..."

Lo ottenni e il giorno dopo scrissi a Lucy per chiederle di venire da me.

La sorella, per alcuni giorni, in Harley Street… non appena Lady…

“Middleton poteva permetterseli. Questo era sufficiente per far sì che Lucy fosse davvero…”

“Piuttosto felice… Sembra proprio che la signora Dashwood stia facendo del suo meglio per lei.”

Se stessa… custodendo tutte le sue speranze e promuovendo tutte le sue idee! Una persona davvero così…

L’opportunità di trascorrere del tempo con Edward e la sua famiglia era, soprattutto,…

Per lei, l’invito rappresenta ciò che le interessa di più.

Appagante per i suoi sentimenti… Un vantaggio che non poteva essere più grande.

Ringraziato con gratitudine, ma senza utilizzarlo troppo rapidamente… E la visita a…

Lady Middleton, la cui identità fino ad allora non aveva avuto confini precisi, era…

Scoperto immediatamente che era destinato a finire in due giorni…

[[motifs/time|tempo]].



Quando la nota fu mostrata a Elinor, poco più di dieci minuti dopo…

Con il suo arrivo, per la prima [[motifs/time|volta]], le fu concesso un ruolo in questo processo.

Aspettative di Lucy… per un simile segno di straordinaria gentilezza, concessole.

Dopo una conoscenza così breve, sembrava già esserci un sincero affetto reciproco…

Da qualcosa di più della semplice malvagità… si levò verso di lei.

Se stessa. E, con il passare del [[motifs/time|tempo]] e l’uso delle giuste parole, avrebbe potuto essere indotta a fare qualsiasi cosa.

Esattamente ciò che Lucy desiderava. I suoi complimenti avevano già placato l’[[concepts/pride|orgoglio]] di Lady.

Middleton e il suo ingresso nel cuore sincero della signora John

“Dashwood; e questi furono gli eventi che rivelarono la probabilità…”

maggiore.



“The Miss Steeles moved to Harley Street, e tutto ciò che venne a conoscenza di Elinor…”

A causa della loro influenza in quella zona, le sue aspettative riguardo a quell’evento si rafforzarono.

Sir John, che li aveva visitati più volte, portò a casa racconti del genere.

Della favorevole situazione in cui si trovavano, il che deve essere evidente a tutti. La signora.

Dashwood non era mai stata così soddisfatta di nessuna giovane donna prima d’ora…

La vita, così com’era con loro… aveva regalato a ciascuno di loro un album da cucito fatto in casa.

Intitolato da un'emigrata; chiamata Lucy con il suo nome cristiano; e non lo sapeva

Se sarebbe mai riuscita a separarsene.

CHAPTER XXXVII.





Mrs. Palmer was so [[motifs/well|well]] at the end of a fortnight, that her mother felt

it no longer necessary to give up the whole of her [[motifs/time|time]] to her; and,

contenting herself with visiting her once or twice a day, returned from

that period to her own [[motifs/home|home]], and her own habits, in which she found the

Miss Dashwoods very ready to resume their former share.



About the third or fourth morning after their being thus resettled in

Berkeley Street, Mrs. Jennings, on returning from her ordinary visit to

Mrs. Palmer, entered the drawing-room, where Elinor was sitting by

herself, with an air of such hurrying importance as prepared her to

hear something wonderful; and giving her [[motifs/time|time]] only to form that idea,

began directly to justify it, by saying,



“Lord! my dear Miss Dashwood! have you heard the news?”



“No, ma’am. What is it?”



“Something so strange! But you shall hear it all. When I got to Mr.

Palmer’s, I found Charlotte quite in a fuss about the [[archetypes/child|child]]. She was

sure it was very ill—it cried, and fretted, and was all over pimples.

So I looked at it directly, and, ‘Lord! my dear,’ says I, ‘it is

nothing in the world, but the red gum;’ and [[characters/nurse|nurse]] said just the same.

But Charlotte, she would not be satisfied, so Mr. Donavan was sent for;

and luckily he happened to just come in from Harley Street, so he

stepped over directly, and as soon as ever he saw the [[archetypes/child|child]], he said

just as we did, that it was nothing in the world but the red gum, and

then Charlotte was easy. And so, just as he was going away again, it

came into my head, I am sure I do not know how I happened to think of

it, but it came into my head to ask him if there was any news. So upon

that, he smirked, and simpered, and looked [[motifs/grave|grave]], and seemed to know

something or other, and at last he said in a whisper, ‘For [[concepts/fear|fear]] any

unpleasant report should reach the young ladies under your care as to

their sister’s indisposition, I think it advisable to say, that I

believe there is no great reason for alarm; I [[concepts/hope|hope]] Mrs. Dashwood will

do very [[motifs/well|well]].’”



“What! is Fanny ill?”



“That is exactly what I said, my dear. ‘Lord!’ says I, ‘is Mrs.

Dashwood ill?’ So then it all came out; and the long and the short of

the matter, by all I can learn, seems to be this. Mr. [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]],

the very young man I used to joke with you about (but however, as it

turns out, I am monstrous glad there was never any thing in it), Mr.

[[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]], it seems, has been engaged above this twelvemonth to my

cousin Lucy!—There’s for you, my dear! And not a creature knowing a

syllable of the matter, except [[characters/nancy|Nancy]]! Could you have believed such a

thing possible? There is no great [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] in their liking one another;

but that matters should be brought so forward between them, and nobody

suspect it! _That_ is strange! I never happened to see them together,

or I am sure I should have found it out directly. [[motifs/well|Well]], and so this was

kept a great secret, for [[concepts/fear|fear]] of Mrs. Ferrars, and neither she nor your

brother or sister suspected a word of the matter: till this very

morning, poor [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], who, you know, is a [[motifs/well|well]]-meaning creature, but no

conjurer, popt it all out. ‘Lord!’ thinks she to herself, ‘they are all

so fond of Lucy, to be sure they will make no difficulty about it;’ and

so, away she went to your sister, who was sitting all alone at her

carpet-work, little suspecting what was to come—for she had just been

saying to your brother, only five minutes before, that she thought to

make a match between Edward and some Lord’s daughter or other, I forget

who. So you may think what a blow it was to all her [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] and [[concepts/pride|pride]].

She fell into violent hysterics immediately, with such screams as

reached your brother’s ears, as he was sitting in his own dressing-room

down stairs, thinking about writing a letter to his steward in the

country. So up he flew directly, and a terrible scene took place, for

Lucy was come to them by that [[motifs/time|time]], little dreaming what was going on.

Poor [[motifs/soul|soul]]! I pity _her_. And I must say, I think she was used very

hardly; for your sister scolded like any fury, and soon drove her into

a fainting fit. [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], she fell upon her knees, and cried bitterly; and

your brother, he walked about the room, and said he did not know what

to do. Mrs. Dashwood declared they should not stay a minute longer in

the house, and your brother was forced to go down upon _his_ knees too,

to persuade her to let them stay till they had packed up their clothes.

_Then_ she fell into hysterics again, and he was so frightened that he

would send for Mr. Donavan, and Mr. Donavan found the house in all this

uproar. The carriage was at the door ready to take my poor cousins

away, and they were just stepping in as he came off; poor Lucy in such

a condition, he says, she could hardly walk; and [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], she was almost

as bad. I declare, I have no patience with your sister; and I [[concepts/hope|hope]],

with all my heart, it will be a match in spite of her. Lord! what a

taking poor Mr. Edward will be in when he hears of it! To have his [[motifs/love|love]]

used so scornfully! for they say he is monstrous fond of her, as [[motifs/well|well]]

he may. I should not [[concepts/wonder|wonder]], if he was to be in the greatest

passion!—and Mr. Donavan thinks just the same. He and I had a great

deal of talk about it; and the best of all is, that he is gone back

again to Harley Street, that he may be within call when Mrs. Ferrars is

told of it, for she was sent for as soon as ever my cousins left the

house, for your sister was sure _she_ would be in hysterics too; and so

she may, for what I care. I have no pity for either of them. I have no

notion of people’s making such a to-do about money and [[concepts/greatness|greatness]]. There

is no reason on earth why Mr. Edward and Lucy should not marry; for I

CAPITOLO XXXVII.





Dopo quindici giorni, la signora Palmer stava così bene che sua madre ne fu molto sollevata.

Non era più necessario che dedicasse l’intero della sua [[motifs/time|tempo]] a lui; e.

Si accontentava di andarla a trovare una o due volte al giorno, e poi se ne tornava…

Quel periodo le permise di tornare al proprio [[motifs/home|casa]] e alle proprie abitudini, dove trovò il conforto che cercava.

La signorina Dashwood era più che pronta a riprendere il proprio ruolo precedente.



Titolo:  
Intorno al terzo o quarto mattino dopo essere stati così ricollocati…

Berkeley Street, la signora Jennings, al ritorno dalla sua solita visita…

La signora Palmer entrò nel salotto, dove Elinor era seduta

Se stessa, con un’aria di tale urgenza che sembrava prepararla…

Sentire qualcosa di meraviglioso. E darle il tempo necessario per formulare quel pensiero.

“Iniziò subito a giustificarlo, dicendo…”



“Signore mio, cara signorina Dashwood… Avete sentito la notizia?”



"No, signora. Che cosa c’è?"



“Qualcosa di così strano. Ma ascolterete tutto. Quando sono arrivato dal signor, ”

A Palmer’s, ho trovato Charlotte molto preoccupata per il[[archetypes/child|bambino]]. Era.

Certo, stava molto male: piangeva, si preoccupava in continuazione e aveva un sacco di brufoli.

“Ahimè… mio caro”, dissi, “è proprio così”.

Niente al mondo, tranne la gomma rossa. E anche l’[[characters/nurse|infermiera]] disse esattamente lo stesso.

Ma Charlotte non era soddisfatta, quindi chiamarono il signor Donavan.

E per fortuna era appena tornato da Harley Street…

Camminò dritto oltre, e non appena vide il [[archetypes/child|bambino]], disse.

Proprio come abbiamo fatto noi, si è scoperto che non era altro che la gomma rossa…

“Allora Charlotte fu facile da conquistare… E così, proprio mentre stava per andarsene di nuovo…”

Mi è venuto in mente… Sono sicuro di non sapere come abbia fatto a pensarci.

Mi è venuto in mente di chiedergli se ci fossero novità. Quindi…

“Quello, ”, sorrise compiaciuto, fece una smorfia, assunse un’espressione “seria” e sembrava sapere qualcosa.

Qualcosa del genere. E alla fine sussurrò: “Per paura di qualunque cosa, ”

Un rapporto sgradevole dovrebbe raggiungere le giovani signore sotto la tua responsabilità… riguardo a…

"#La malattia di loro sorella… ritengo opportuno dire che io…"

Credo che non ci sia motivo di allarme; spero che la signora Dashwood.

Va molto bene.



“Che cosa? Fanny è malata?”



“Ecco esattamente quello che ho detto, cara mia. ‘Signore!’, dico io, ‘è la signora, ’”

“Dashwood è malato?” E così tutto venne a galla; in breve, la situazione era chiara.

Da quanto ho potuto capire, la situazione sembra essere questa: il signor [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]].

Il giovane di cui spesso scherzavo con te… ma comunque…

A quanto pare, sono estremamente felice che non ci fosse mai nulla dentro. Signore.

Sembra che [[characters/edward-ferrars|Edward Ferrars]] sia stato fidanzato con me già dodici mesi fa.

“Cugina Lucy! Ecco per te, cara… Nessuno lo sa nemmeno.”

La sillaba fondamentale della questione, tranne che per [[characters/nancy|Nancy]]! Avresti mai potuto credere una cosa del genere?

È davvero possibile? Non c’è nulla di straordinario nel fatto che si piacciano a vicenda.

Ma questa questione dovrebbe essere sollevata prima tra loro, e nessuno…

Lo sospetto… È davvero strano! Non ho mai avuto l’occasione di vederli insieme.

O forse avrei dovuto scoprirlo direttamente. [[motifs/well|Beh]], insomma, è stato così.

Teneva un grande segreto, per [[concepts/fear|paura]] di Mrs. Ferrars; né lei né tuo padre ne erano a conoscenza.

Fratello o sorella sospettava qualcosa riguardo alla questione… fino a questo preciso momento.

Mattina, povera [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], che, sapete, è una persona davvero benintenzionata, ma no.

“Mago… fai sì che tutto esca fuori.” “Mio Dio!” pensa tra sé, “sono tutti…”

“Mi piace così tanto Lucy che sicuramente non avranno alcun problema al riguardo…”

Allora, se ne andò dalla tua sorella, che era seduta lì tutta da sola.

“Carpet-work… senza sospettare minimamente ciò che stava per accadere, poiché era appena…”

Titolo:  
Diciendo a tuo fratello, solo cinque minuti prima, che lei pensava…

“Cercare di combinare Edward con la figlia di qualche lord o qualcun altro… Non ricordo esattamente.”

Chi. Potreste pensare quale colpo sia stato per tutta la sua [[concepts/vanity|vanità]] e il suo [[concepts/pride|orgoglio]].

Scoppiò in violente isterie, emettendo urla terribili…

Raggiunsero le orecchie di tuo fratello, mentre lui era seduto nel suo bagno.

Giù per le scale, pensando di scrivere una lettera al proprio maggiordomo…

Paese… Così volò dritto verso l’alto, e si verificò una scena terribile…

A quell’[[motifs/time|ora]], Lucy era già arrivata da loro, senza nemmeno immaginare cosa stesse succedendo.

Povera [[motifs/soul|'anima]]. Mi dispiace per lei. Devo dire che penso sia stata sfruttata molto.

Appena; perché tua sorella l’ha rimproverata con molta durezza e presto l’ha spinta via…

Un attacco di svenimento. [[characters/nancy|Nancy]] cadde in ginocchio e pianse amaramente; e.

“Tuo fratello… camminava avanti e indietro nella stanza e diceva di non sapere cosa fare.”

Titolo:  
“Non possiamo restare un minuto di più…” dichiarò la signora Dashwood.

La casa, e anche tuo fratello fu costretto a mettersi in ginocchio.

Per convincerla a lasciarli restare fino a quando non avessero raccolto i loro vestiti.

Poi ricominciò ad avere attacchi isterici, e lui ne ebbe così paura…

Avrebbe chiamato il signor Donavan, e il signor Donavan trovò la casa in tutto questo disordine.

Trambusto. La carrozza era pronta alla porta, pronta ad accompagnare i miei poveri cugini.

“Lontano… e proprio mentre lui stava scendendo, loro entrarono; povera Lucy…”

Secondo lui, a causa di quella condizione, lei faticava quasi a camminare; e [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], be', era praticamente.

È altrettanto grave. Dichiaro apertamente: non ho alcuna pazienza con tua sorella. E spero davvero che.

Con tutto il mio cuore… sarà una battaglia disperata, nonostante lei. Signore… che situazione terribile.

Povero signor Edward, quando lo scoprirà, ne sarà distrutto! Che cosa significa perdere il proprio [[motifs/love|amore]].

Usato in modo così sprezzante, perché dicono che sia terribilmente innamorato di lei, come è ben noto.

Può farlo. Non dovrei [[concepts/wonder|meravigliarmi]] se dovesse trovarsi nella situazione più difficile.

Passione… E anche il signor Donavan la pensa allo stesso modo. Lui ed io ne abbiamo parlato a lungo.

Molte chiacchiere al riguardo… E la cosa migliore di tutte è che se n’è andato.

Di nuovo in Harley Street, affinché sia reperibile quando la signora Ferrars avrà bisogno di lui…

Si parlò di questo argomento, perché lei fu chiamata non appena i miei cugini se ne andarono.

Casa, perché tua sorella sarebbe sicuramente andata nel panico anche lei. E così.

“Che faccia pure, non mi interessa affatto. Non provo pietà per nessuno dei due… Non ne ho alcuna.”

La nozione che le persone possano creare tanta agitazione riguardo al denaro e alla [[concepts/greatness|grandezza]]. Che strano.

Non esiste alcuna ragione al mondo per cui il signor Edward e Lucy non dovrebbero sposarsi; perché…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_37--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 37 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 37" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/doubt,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/suffering,concept/truth,concept/wonder"></span>


am sure Mrs. Ferrars may afford to do very [[motifs/well|well]] by her son, and though

Lucy has next to nothing herself, she knows better than any [[concepts/body|body]] how to

make the most of every thing; I dare say, if Mrs. Ferrars would only

allow him five hundred a-year, she would make as good an appearance

with it as any [[concepts/body|body]] else would with eight. Lord! how snug they might

live in such another cottage as yours—or a little bigger—with two

maids, and two men; and I believe I could help them to a housemaid, for

my Betty has a sister out of place, that would fit them exactly.”



Here Mrs. Jennings ceased, and as Elinor had had [[motifs/time|time]] enough to collect

her thoughts, she was able to give such an answer, and make such

observations, as the subject might naturally be supposed to produce.

Happy to find that she was not suspected of any extraordinary interest

in it; that Mrs. Jennings (as she had of late often hoped might be the

case) had ceased to imagine her at all attached to Edward; and happy

above all the rest, in the absence of Marianne, she felt very [[motifs/well|well]] able

to speak of the affair without embarrassment, and to give her judgment,

as she believed, with impartiality on the conduct of every one

concerned in it.



She could hardly determine what her own expectation of its event really

was; though she earnestly tried to drive away the notion of its being

possible to end otherwise at last, than in the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] of Edward and

Lucy. What Mrs. Ferrars would say and do, though there could not be a

[[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of its [[concepts/nature|nature]], she was anxious to hear; and still more anxious to

know how Edward would conduct himself. For _him_ she felt much

compassion;—for Lucy very little—and it cost her some pains to procure

that little;—for the rest of the party none at all.



As Mrs. Jennings could talk on no other subject, Elinor soon saw the

necessity of preparing Marianne for its discussion. No [[motifs/time|time]] was to be

lost in undeceiving her, in making her acquainted with the real [[concepts/truth|truth]],

and in endeavouring to bring her to hear it talked of by others,

without betraying that she felt any uneasiness for her sister, or any

resentment against Edward.



Elinor’s office was a painful one.—She was going to remove what she

really believed to be her sister’s chief consolation,—to give such

particulars of Edward as she feared would ruin him for ever in her good

opinion,-and to make Marianne, by a resemblance in their situations,

which to _her_ fancy would seem strong, feel all her own disappointment

over again. But unwelcome as such a task must be, it was necessary to

be done, and Elinor therefore hastened to perform it.



She was very far from wishing to dwell on her own feelings, or to

represent herself as [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] much, any otherwise than as the

[[concepts/self|self]]-command she had practised since her first knowledge of Edward’s

engagement, might suggest a hint of what was practicable to Marianne.

Her narration was clear and simple; and though it could not be given

without emotion, it was not accompanied by violent agitation, nor

impetuous grief. _That_ belonged rather to the hearer, for Marianne

listened with horror, and cried excessively. Elinor was to be the

comforter of others in her own distresses, no less than in theirs; and

all the comfort that could be given by assurances of her own composure

of mind, and a very earnest vindication of Edward from every charge but

of imprudence, was readily offered.



But Marianne for some [[motifs/time|time]] would give credit to neither. Edward seemed

a second Willoughby; and acknowledging as Elinor did, that she _had_

loved him most sincerely, could she feel less than herself! As for Lucy

Steele, she considered her so totally unamiable, so absolutely

incapable of attaching a sensible man, that she could not be persuaded

at first to believe, and afterwards to pardon, any former affection of

Edward for her. She would not even admit it to have been natural; and

Elinor left her to be convinced that it was so, by that which only

could convince her, a better knowledge of mankind.



Her first communication had reached no farther than to state the fact

of the engagement, and the length of [[motifs/time|time]] it had existed.—Marianne’s

feelings had then broken in, and put an end to all regularity of

detail; and for some [[motifs/time|time]] all that could be done was to soothe her

distress, lessen her alarms, and combat her resentment. The first

question on her side, which led to farther particulars, was,—



“How long has this been known to you, Elinor? has he written to you?”



“I have known it these four months. When Lucy first came to Barton Park

last November, she told me in confidence of her engagement.”



At these words, Marianne’s eyes expressed the astonishment which her

lips could not utter. After a pause of [[concepts/wonder|wonder]], she exclaimed—



“Four months!—Have you known of this four months?”



Elinor confirmed it.



“What! while attending me in all my misery, has this been on your

heart? And I have reproached you for being happy!”



“It was not fit that you should then know how much I was the reverse!”



“Four months!” cried Marianne again. “So calm! so cheerful! How have

you been supported?”



“By feeling that I was doing my duty.—My promise to Lucy, obliged me to

be secret. I owed it to her, therefore, to avoid giving any hint of the

[[concepts/truth|truth]]; and I owed it to my family and friends, not to create in them a

solicitude about me, which it could not be in my power to satisfy.”



Marianne seemed much struck.



“I have very often wished to undeceive yourself and my mother,” added

Elinor; “and once or twice I have attempted it;—but without betraying

my trust, I never could have convinced you.”



“Four months! and yet you loved him!”



“Yes. But I did not [[motifs/love|love]] only him; and while the comfort of others was

dear to me, I was glad to spare them from knowing how much I felt. Now,


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Sono sicuro che la signora Ferrars possa permettersi di fare molto per suo figlio, eppure.

Lucy non possiede quasi nulla; lei sa meglio di chiunque altro come fare.

Sfruttare al massimo ogni opportunità… Oserei dire che, se solo la signora Ferrars lo desse il permesso…

Dargli cinquecento all’anno le permetterebbe di mantenere un certo status sociale.

Come qualsiasi altro [[concepts/body|corpo]] lo farebbe con otto, mio Dio, quanto comodi devono essere!

Vivere in una capanna come la tua… o forse un po’ più grande… con due persone…

“Donne di servizio e due uomini… Credo di poterli aiutare a trovare una domestica…”

“La mia Betty ha una sorella che non trova il proprio posto… Quella sorella sarebbe perfetta per loro.”



A questo punto la signora Jennings smise di parlare; Elinor, intanto, aveva avuto abbastanza tempo per riflettere.

“Con i suoi pensieri, riuscì a fornire una risposta del genere e ad agire in quel modo.”

Osservazioni, quelle che si potrebbero naturalmente aspettarsi che il soggetto produca.

Felice di scoprire che non era sospettata di alcun interesse particolare.

In essa; quella signora Jennings… come spesso sperava negli ultimi tempi che potesse diventare…

Non riusciva più nemmeno a immaginare che lei fosse legata a Edward; e felice…

Soprattutto, in assenza di Marianne, si sentiva molto in grado di farcela.

Per parlare dell’argomento senza imbarazzo e per esprimere il proprio parere…

Come lei credeva, giudicando con imparzialità il comportamento di ognuno.

coinvolto in esso.



Non riusciva quasi a capire quali fossero le sue vere aspettative riguardo a quell’evento.

Non riusciva a scacciare quell’idea…

È possibile che alla fine tutto finisca in modo diverso, anziché con il [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] di Edward e.

Lucy… Cosa direbbe e cosa farebbe la signora Ferrars, anche se non potesse esserci alcuna possibilità…

Con [[concepts/doubt|dubbi]] sulla sua [[concepts/nature|natura]], era ansiosa di saperlo, e ancora più desiderosa di.

Sapeva bene come si sarebbe comportato Edward… Per lui, provava qualcosa di molto profondo.

Compassione… per Lucy, quasi nulla; e le costò qualche sforzo ottenerla.

Quello poco, per il resto del gruppo, nessuno affatto.



Come la signora Jennings non parlava d’altro, Elinor presto si rese conto…

Era necessario preparare Marianne per la discussione che avrebbe avuto luogo. Non c'era alcun [[motifs/time|tempo]] da perdere.

Perdutosi nel tentativo di ingannarla, nel farle conoscere la vera [[concepts/truth|_verità]],

E nel tentativo di farle ascoltare altre persone parlare di essa…

Senza mostrare alcun disagio per sua sorella, o nulla del genere…

Rancore verso Edward.



L’ufficio di Elinor era davvero un posto difficile da sopportare… Lei stava per eliminare tutto ciò che vi si trovava.

Considerato davvero il principale conforto per sua sorella… – offrire qualcosa del genere

Dettagli su Edward che, secondo lei, avrebbero potuto rovinarlo per sempre…

Opinione… e per creare un legame tra Marianne, grazie alle somiglianze nelle loro situazioni…

Per quanto a lei sembrasse una scelta decisa e forte, in realtà si ritrovò ad affrontare solo delusione.

Di nuovo… Ma per quanto tale compito fosse sgradito, era necessario farlo.

Era necessario farlo subito, quindi Elinor si affrettò a compiere quel compito.



Non aveva affatto voglia di soffermarsi sui propri sentimenti, o di…

Si presentava come se soffrisse molto, in ogni altro modo che non fosse così.

Quel senso di autocontrollo che aveva sviluppato fin dal momento in cui aveva conosciuto per la prima volta Edward.

L’impegno preso potrebbe suggerire qualcosa di concreto che fosse fattibile per Marianne.

La sua narrazione era chiara e semplice; e sebbene non potesse essere…

Senza emozioni, non fu accompagnato da alcuna agitazione violenta, né…

Impetuoso dolore… Quello apparteneva piuttosto all’ascoltatore, perché Marianne…

Ascoltò con orrore e pianse disperatamente… Elinor sarebbe stata…

Consolatrice degli altri nelle proprie difficoltà, non meno che nelle loro; e…

Tutto il conforto che potesse derivare dalle assicurazioni riguardo alla propria compostezza

Titolo:  
Uno stato d’animo sereno e una difesa appassionata di Edward da ogni accusa…

A causa dell'imprudenza, l'aiuto fu offerto prontamente.



Ma per un certo [[motifs/time|periodo]] di tempo, Marianne non dava credito a nessuno dei due. Edward sembrava.

Un secondo Willoughby; e riconoscendo, come fece Elinor, che lei _aveva_…

Lo amava con tutta la sincerità del cuore… Come avrebbe potuto provare meno di ciò che provava lei? Per quanto riguarda Lucy…

“Acciaio…”, pensò, “una persona così del tutto antipatica, così assolutamente…”

Incapace di attirare un uomo saggio… quindi non poteva essere convinta.

All'inizio è difficile credere, e poi ancora più difficile perdonare qualsiasi affetto passato…

Edward per lei… Lei non avrebbe nemmeno ammesso che fosse qualcosa di naturale…

Elinor rimase convinta che fosse davvero così, da ciò che solo…

Avrei potuto convincerla, grazie a una conoscenza più profonda dell’umanità.



La sua prima comunicazione si limitava semplicemente a enunciare quel fatto.

Dell’impegno, e della durata di [[motifs/time|tempo]] che esisteva, —Di Marianne.

Emozioni si sono scatenate, ponendo fine a ogni regolarità…

I dettagli. E per un po’ di tempo, l’unica cosa che si poteva fare era consolarla.

Distacco, alleviare le sue preoccupazioni e combattere il suo risentimento… Il primo passo.

“Una domanda da parte sua, che portò a ulteriori dettagli, fu…”



“Da quanto tempo lo sai, Elinor? Ti ha scritto qualcosa?”



“Lo so da questi quattro mesi… Quando Lucy è arrivata per la prima volta a Barton Park…”

“Lo scorso novembre, mi confidò in privato del suo fidanzamento.”



A queste parole, lo sguardo di Marianne esprimeva la sorpresa che provava…

Le labbra non riuscivano a pronunciare nulla. Dopo un momento di [[concepts/wonder|stupore]], esclamò.



“Quattro mesi! – Lo sai da quattro mesi?”



Elinor lo confermò.



“Cosa! Mentre mi assistevi in tutta la mia sofferenza, questo era già nei tuoi piani…”

Cuore… E ti ho rimproverato per essere felice!



“Non era giusto che tu sapessi in quel momento quanto fossi l’opposto di ciò che sembravo…”



“Quattro mesi!” esclamò di nuovo Marianne. “Così calma… così serena… Come hai fatto?”

“Hai mai ricevuto sostegno?”



“Sentendo di stare adempiendo al mio dovere… La promessa fatta a Lucy mi obbligava a farlo.”

Resta un segreto. Glielo dovevo, quindi non potevo dare alcun indizio al riguardo.

La [[concepts/truth|verità]]; e la dovevo alla mia famiglia e ai miei amici, non per suscitare in loro.

“Preoccupazioni per me, che non erano affatto nelle mie possibilità di placare.”



Sembrava che Marianne fosse molto colpita.



“Spesso ho desiderato di non ingannare né me stesso né mia madre”, aggiunse.

Elinor; “e una o due volte ci ho provato… ma senza rivelare nulla”

“Mia cara, non sarei mai riuscito a convincerti.”



“Quattro mesi… eppure lo amavi!”



“Sì. Ma non amavo solo lui; e mentre cercavo di confortare gli altri, ”

Per me molto caro… Ero felice di non far loro sapere quanto provassi. Ora…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_37--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 37 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 37" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/silence,motif/spring,motif/storm,motif/time,motif/well,concept/heroism,concept/hope,concept/self,concept/suffering,concept/wonder"></span>


I can think and speak of it with little emotion. I would not have you

suffer on my account; for I assure you I no longer suffer materially

myself. I have many things to support me. I am not conscious of having

provoked the disappointment by any imprudence of my own, I have borne

it as much as possible without spreading it farther. I acquit Edward of

essential misconduct. I wish him very happy; and I am so sure of his

always doing his duty, that though now he may harbour some regret, in

the end he must become so. Lucy does not want sense, and that is the

foundation on which every thing good may be built. And after all,

Marianne, after all that is bewitching in the idea of a single and

constant attachment, and all that can be said of one’s happiness

depending entirely on any particular person, it is not meant—it is not

fit—it is not possible that it should be so. Edward will marry Lucy; he

will marry a woman superior in person and understanding to half her

sex; and [[motifs/time|time]] and habit will teach him to forget that he ever thought

another superior to _her_.”



“If such is your way of thinking,” said Marianne, “if the loss of what

is most valued is so easily to be made up by something else, your

resolution, your [[concepts/self|self]]-command, are, perhaps, a little less to be

wondered at.—They are brought more within my comprehension.”



“I understand you. You do not suppose that I have ever felt much. For

four months, Marianne, I have had all this hanging on my mind, without

being at liberty to speak of it to a single creature; knowing that it

would make you and my mother most unhappy whenever it were explained to

you, yet unable to prepare you for it in the least. It was told me,—it

was in a manner forced on me by the very person herself, whose prior

engagement ruined all my prospects; and told me, as I thought, with

triumph. This person’s suspicions, therefore, I have had to oppose, by

endeavouring to appear indifferent where I have been most deeply

interested; and it has not been only once; I have had her hopes and

exultation to listen to again and again. I have known myself to be

divided from Edward for ever, without hearing one circumstance that

could make me less [[motifs/desire|desire]] the connection. Nothing has proved him

unworthy; nor has anything declared him indifferent to me.  I have had

to contend against the unkindness of his sister, and the insolence of

his mother; and have suffered the punishment of an attachment, without

enjoying its advantages. And all this has been going on at a [[motifs/time|time]],

when, as you know too [[motifs/well|well]], it has not been my only unhappiness. If you

can think me capable of ever feeling, surely you may suppose that I

have suffered _now_. The composure of mind with which I have brought

myself at present to consider the matter, the consolation that I have

been willing to admit, have been the effect of constant and painful

exertion; they did not [[motifs/spring|spring]] up of themselves; they did not occur to

relieve my spirits at first. No, Marianne. _Then_, if I had not been

bound to [[motifs/silence|silence]], perhaps nothing could have kept me entirely—not even

what I owed to my dearest friends—from openly showing that I was _very_

unhappy.”



Marianne was quite subdued.



“Oh! Elinor,” she cried, “you have made me hate myself for ever.—How

barbarous have I been to you!—you, who have been my only comfort, who

have borne with me in all my misery, who have seemed to be only

[[concepts/suffering|suffering]] for me!—Is this my gratitude?—Is this the only return I can

make you?—Because your merit cries out upon myself, I have been trying

to do it away.”



The tenderest caresses followed this confession. In such a frame of

mind as she was now in, Elinor had no difficulty in obtaining from her

whatever promise she required; and at her request, Marianne engaged

never to speak of the affair to any one with the least appearance of

bitterness; to meet Lucy without betraying the smallest increase of

dislike to her; and even to see Edward himself, if chance should bring

them together, without any diminution of her usual cordiality. These

were great concessions; but where Marianne felt that she had injured,

no reparation could be too much for her to make.



She performed her promise of being discreet, to admiration.—She

attended to all that Mrs. Jennings had to say upon the subject, with an

unchanging complexion, dissented from her in nothing, and was heard

three times to say, “Yes, ma’am.”—She listened to her praise of Lucy

with only moving from one chair to another, and when Mrs. Jennings

talked of Edward’s affection, it cost her only a spasm in her

throat.—Such advances towards [[concepts/heroism|heroism]] in her sister, made Elinor feel

equal to any thing herself.



The next morning brought a farther trial of it, in a visit from their

brother, who came with a most serious aspect to talk over the dreadful

affair, and bring them news of his wife.



“You have heard, I suppose,” said he with great solemnity, as soon as

he was seated, “of the very shocking discovery that took place under

our roof yesterday.”



They all looked their assent; it seemed too awful a moment for speech.



“Your sister,” he continued, “has suffered dreadfully. Mrs. Ferrars

too—in short it has been a scene of such complicated distress—but I

will [[concepts/hope|hope]] that the [[motifs/storm|storm]] may be weathered without our being any of us

quite overcome. Poor Fanny! she was in hysterics all yesterday. But I

would not alarm you too much. Donavan says there is nothing materially

to be apprehended; her constitution is a good one, and her resolution

equal to any thing. She has borne it all, with the fortitude of an

angel! She says she never shall think [[motifs/well|well]] of anybody again; and one

cannot [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at it, after being so deceived!—meeting with such

ingratitude, where so much kindness had been shown, so much confidence

had been placed! It was quite out of the benevolence of her heart, that

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_37--part_04" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 37 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 37" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/revenge,concept/wonder,character/lucy_steele"></span>


she had asked these young women to her house; merely because she

thought they deserved some attention, were harmless, [[motifs/well|well]]-behaved

girls, and would be pleasant companions; for otherwise we both wished

very much to have invited you and Marianne to be with us, while your

kind friend there, was attending her daughter. And now to be so

rewarded! ‘I wish, with all my heart,’ says poor Fanny in her

affectionate way, ‘that we had asked your sisters instead of them.’”



Here he stopped to be thanked; which being done, he went on.



“What poor Mrs. Ferrars suffered, when first Fanny broke it to her, is

not to be described. While she with the truest affection had been

planning a most eligible connection for him, was it to be supposed that

he could be all the [[motifs/time|time]] secretly engaged to another person!—such a

suspicion could never have entered her head! If she suspected _any_

prepossession elsewhere, it could not be in _that_ quarter. ‘_There_,

to be sure,’ said she, ‘I might have thought myself safe.’ She was

quite in an agony. We consulted together, however, as to what should be

done, and at last she determined to send for Edward. He came. But I am

sorry to relate what ensued. All that Mrs. Ferrars could say to make

him put an end to the engagement, assisted too as you may [[motifs/well|well]] suppose

by my arguments, and Fanny’s entreaties, was of no avail. Duty,

affection, every thing was disregarded. I never thought Edward so

stubborn, so unfeeling before. His mother explained to him her liberal

designs, in case of his marrying Miss Morton; told him she would settle

on him the Norfolk estate, which, clear of land-tax, brings in a good

thousand a-year; offered even, when matters grew desperate, to make it

twelve hundred; and in opposition to this, if he still persisted in

this low connection, represented to him the certain penury that must

attend the match. His own two thousand pounds she protested should be

his all; she would never see him again; and so far would she be from

affording him the smallest assistance, that if he were to enter into

any profession with a view of better support, she would do all in her

power to prevent him advancing in it.”



Here Marianne, in an ecstasy of indignation, clapped her hands

together, and cried, “Gracious God! can this be possible!”



“[[motifs/well|Well]] may you [[concepts/wonder|wonder]], Marianne,” replied her brother, “at the obstinacy

which could resist such arguments as these. Your exclamation is very

natural.”



Marianne was going to retort, but she remembered her promises, and

forbore.



“All this, however,” he continued, “was urged in vain. Edward said very

little; but what he did say, was in the most determined manner. Nothing

should prevail on him to give up his engagement. He would stand to it,

cost him what it might.”



“Then,” cried Mrs. Jennings with blunt sincerity, no longer able to be

silent, “he has acted like an honest man! I beg your pardon, Mr.

Dashwood, but if he had done otherwise, I should have thought him a

rascal. I have some little concern in the business, as [[motifs/well|well]] as

yourself, for [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]] is my cousin, and I believe there is not a

better kind of girl in the world, nor one who more deserves a good

husband.”



John Dashwood was greatly astonished; but his [[concepts/nature|nature]] was calm, not open

to provocation, and he never wished to offend anybody, especially

anybody of good fortune. He therefore replied, without any resentment,



“I would by no means speak disrespectfully of any relation of yours,

madam. Miss [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]] is, I dare say, a very deserving young woman,

but in the present case you know, the connection must be impossible.

And to have entered into a secret engagement with a young man under her

uncle’s care, the son of a woman especially of such very large fortune

as Mrs. Ferrars, is perhaps, altogether a little extraordinary. In

short, I do not mean to reflect upon the behaviour of any person whom

you have a regard for, Mrs. Jennings. We all wish her extremely happy;

and Mrs. Ferrars’s conduct throughout the whole, has been such as every

conscientious, good mother, in like circumstances, would adopt. It has

been dignified and liberal. Edward has drawn his own lot, and I [[concepts/fear|fear]] it

will be a bad one.”



Marianne sighed out her similar apprehension; and Elinor’s heart wrung

for the feelings of Edward, while braving his mother’s threats, for a

woman who could not reward him.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], sir,” said Mrs. Jennings, “and how did it end?”



“I am sorry to say, ma’am, in a most unhappy rupture:—Edward is

dismissed for ever from his mother’s notice. He left her house

yesterday, but where he is gone, or whether he is still in town, I do

not know; for _we_ of course can make no inquiry.”



“Poor young man!—and what is to become of him?”



“What, indeed, ma’am! It is a [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] consideration. Born to the

prospect of such affluence! I cannot conceive a situation more

deplorable. The interest of two thousand pounds—how can a man live on

it?—and when to that is added the recollection, that he might, but for

his own folly, within three months have been in the receipt of two

thousand, five hundred a-year (for Miss Morton has thirty thousand

pounds,) I cannot picture to myself a more wretched condition. We must

all feel for him; and the more so, because it is totally out of our

power to assist him.”



“Poor young man!” cried Mrs. Jennings, “I am sure he should be very

welcome to bed and board at my house; and so I would tell him if I

could see him. It is not fit that he should be living about at his own

charge now, at lodgings and taverns.”



Elinor’s heart thanked her for such kindness towards Edward, though she

could not forbear smiling at the form of it.



“If he would only have done as [[motifs/well|well]] by himself,” said John Dashwood,

“as all his friends were disposed to do by him, he might now have been

in his proper situation, and would have wanted for nothing. But as it

is, it must be out of anybody’s power to assist him. And there is one

thing more preparing against him, which must be worse than all—his

mother has determined, with a very natural kind of spirit, to settle

_that_ estate upon Robert immediately, which might have been Edward’s,

on proper conditions. I left her this morning with her lawyer, talking

over the business.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]]!” said Mrs. Jennings, “that is _her_ [[concepts/revenge|revenge]]. Everybody has a way

of their own. But I don’t think mine would be, to make one son

independent, because another had plagued me.”



Marianne got up and walked about the room.



“Can anything be more galling to the spirit of a man,” continued John,

“than to see his younger brother in possession of an estate which might

have been his own? Poor Edward! I feel for him sincerely.”



A few minutes more spent in the same kind of effusion, concluded his

visit; and with repeated assurances to his sisters that he really

believed there was no material danger in Fanny’s indisposition, and

that they need not therefore be very uneasy about it, he went away;

leaving the three ladies unanimous in their sentiments on the present

occasion, as far at least as it regarded Mrs. Ferrars’s conduct, the

Dashwoods’, and Edward’s.



Marianne’s indignation burst forth as soon as he quitted the room; and

as her vehemence made reserve impossible in Elinor, and unnecessary in

Mrs. Jennings, they all joined in a very spirited critique upon the

party.

Offrendogli anche la minima assistenza, nel caso in cui dovesse entrare…

Escluso per sempre dall’attenzione di sua madre, lasciò la sua casa.

Ieri… ma dove sia andato, o se sia ancora in città, non lo so.

Benvenuto a casa mia, dove potrai mangiare e dormire; ed è così che glielo avrei detto se.

Il cuore di Elinor le fu grato per tanta gentilezza verso Edward… anche se lei…

"In condizioni appropriate… Questa mattina l’ho lasciata con il suo avvocato, mentre discutevano.”

“Finiamo il lavoro.”

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_38--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 38 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 38" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/grave,motif/home,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/courage,concept/hope,concept/self,character/lucy_steele,character/richard,character/sunday"></span>


CHAPTER XXXVIII.





Mrs. Jennings was very warm in her praise of Edward’s conduct, but only

Elinor and Marianne understood its true merit. _They_ only knew how

little he had had to tempt him to be disobedient, and how small was the

consolation, beyond the consciousness of doing right, that could remain

to him in the loss of friends and fortune. Elinor gloried in his

integrity; and Marianne forgave all his offences in compassion for his

punishment. But though confidence between them was, by this public

discovery, restored to its proper state, it was not a subject on which

either of them were fond of dwelling when alone. Elinor avoided it upon

principle, as tending to fix still more upon her thoughts, by the too

warm, too positive assurances of Marianne, that belief of Edward’s

continued affection for herself which she rather wished to do away; and

Marianne’s [[concepts/courage|courage]] soon failed her, in trying to converse upon a topic

which always left her more dissatisfied with herself than ever, by the

comparison it necessarily produced between Elinor’s conduct and her

own.



She felt all the force of that comparison; but not as her sister had

hoped, to urge her to exertion now; she felt it with all the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of

continual [[concepts/self|self]]-reproach, regretted most bitterly that she had never

exerted herself before; but it brought only the torture of penitence,

without the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of amendment. Her mind was so much weakened that she

still fancied present exertion impossible, and therefore it only

dispirited her more.



Nothing new was heard by them, for a day or two afterwards, of affairs

in Harley Street, or Bartlett’s Buildings. But though so much of the

matter was known to them already, that Mrs. Jennings might have had

enough to do in spreading that knowledge farther, without seeking after

more, she had resolved from the first to pay a visit of comfort and

inquiry to her cousins as soon as she could; and nothing but the

hindrance of more visitors than usual, had prevented her going to them

within that [[motifs/time|time]].



The third day succeeding their knowledge of the particulars, was so

fine, so beautiful a [[characters/sunday|Sunday]] as to draw many to Kensington Gardens,

though it was only the second week in March. Mrs. Jennings and Elinor

were of the number; but Marianne, who knew that the Willoughbys were

again in town, and had a constant dread of meeting them, chose rather

to stay at [[motifs/home|home]], than venture into so public a place.



An intimate acquaintance of Mrs. Jennings joined them soon after they

entered the Gardens, and Elinor was not sorry that by her continuing

with them, and engaging all Mrs. Jennings’s conversation, she was

herself left to quiet reflection. She saw nothing of the Willoughbys,

nothing of Edward, and for some [[motifs/time|time]] nothing of anybody who could by

any chance whether [[motifs/grave|grave]] or gay, be interesting to her. But at last she

found herself with some surprise, accosted by Miss Steele, who, though

looking rather shy, expressed great satisfaction in meeting them, and

on receiving encouragement from the particular kindness of Mrs.

Jennings, left her own party for a short [[motifs/time|time]], to join their’s. Mrs.

Jennings immediately whispered to Elinor,



“Get it all out of her, my dear. She will tell you any thing if you

ask. You see I cannot leave Mrs. Clarke.”



It was lucky, however, for Mrs. Jennings’s curiosity and Elinor’s too,

that she would tell any thing _without_ being asked; for nothing would

otherwise have been learnt.



“I am so glad to meet you;” said Miss Steele, taking her familiarly by

the arm—“for I wanted to see you of all things in the world.” And then

lowering her voice, “I suppose Mrs. Jennings has heard all about it. Is

she angry?”



“Not at all, I believe, with you.”



“That is a good thing. And Lady Middleton, is _she_ angry?”



“I cannot suppose it possible that she should be.”



“I am monstrous glad of it. Good gracious! I have had such a [[motifs/time|time]] of

it! I never saw Lucy in such a rage in my life. She vowed at first she

would never trim me up a new bonnet, nor do any thing else for me

again, so long as she lived; but now she is quite come to, and we are

as good friends as ever. Look, she made me this bow to my hat, and put

in the feather last [[motifs/night|night]]. There now, _you_ are going to laugh at me

too. But why should not I wear pink ribbons? I do not care if it _is_

the Doctor’s favourite colour. I am sure, for my part, I should never

have known he _did_ like it better than any other colour, if he had not

happened to say so. My cousins have been so plaguing me! I declare

sometimes I do not know which way to look before them.”



She had wandered away to a subject on which Elinor had nothing to say,

and therefore soon judged it expedient to find her way back again to

the first.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], but Miss Dashwood,” speaking triumphantly, “people may say what

they chuse about Mr. Ferrars’s declaring he would not have Lucy, for it

is no such thing I can tell you; and it is quite a shame for such

ill-natured reports to be spread abroad. Whatever Lucy might think

about it herself, you know, it was no business of other people to set

it down for certain.”



“I never heard any thing of the kind hinted at before, I assure you,”

said Elinor.



“Oh, did not you? But it _was_ said, I know, very [[motifs/well|well]], and by more

than one; for Miss Godby told Miss Sparks, that nobody in their senses

could expect Mr. Ferrars to give up a woman like Miss Morton, with

thirty thousand pounds to her fortune, for [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]] that had nothing

at all; and I had it from Miss Sparks myself. And besides that, my

cousin [[characters/richard|Richard]] said himself, that when it came to the point he was

afraid Mr. Ferrars would be off; and when Edward did not come near us

for three days, I could not tell what to think myself; and I believe in

my heart Lucy gave it up all for lost; for we came away from your
