“It is hardly worth while, Mr. Willoughby, for you to relate, or for me

to listen any longer. Such a beginning as this cannot be followed by

any thing. Do not let me be pained by hearing any thing more on the

subject.”



“I insist on you hearing the whole of it,” he replied, “My fortune was

never large, and I had always been expensive, always in the habit of

associating with people of better income than myself. Every year since

my coming of age, or even before, I believe, had added to my debts; and

though the [[motifs/death|death]] of my old cousin, Mrs. Smith, was to set me free; yet

that event being uncertain, and possibly far distant, it had been for

some [[motifs/time|time]] my intention to re-establish my circumstances by marrying a

woman of fortune. To attach myself to your sister, therefore, was not a

thing to be thought of; and with a meanness, selfishness, cruelty,

which no indignant, no contemptuous look, even of yours, Miss Dashwood,

can ever reprobate too much,—I was acting in this manner, trying to

engage her regard, without a thought of returning it. But one thing may

be said for me: even in that horrid state of selfish [[concepts/vanity|vanity]], I did not

know the extent of the injury I meditated, because I did not _then_

know what it was to [[motifs/love|love]]. But have I ever known it? [[motifs/well|Well]] may it be

doubted; for, had I really loved, could I have sacrificed my feelings

to [[concepts/vanity|vanity]], to avarice? or, what is more, could I have sacrificed hers?

But I have done it. To avoid a comparative [[concepts/poverty|poverty]], which her affection

and her society would have deprived of all its horrors, I have, by

raising myself to affluence, lost every thing that could make it a

blessing.”



“You did then,” said Elinor, a little softened, “believe yourself at

one [[motifs/time|time]] attached to her?”



“To have resisted such attractions, to have withstood such tenderness!

Is there a man on earth who could have done it? Yes, I found myself, by

insensible degrees, sincerely fond of her; and the happiest hours of my

life were what I spent with her when I felt my intentions were strictly

honourable, and my feelings blameless. Even _then_, however, when fully

determined on paying my addresses to her, I allowed myself most

improperly to put off, from day to day, the moment of doing it, from an

unwillingness to enter into an engagement while my circumstances were

so greatly embarrassed. I will not reason here—nor will I stop for

_you_ to expatiate on the absurdity, and the worse than absurdity, of

scrupling to engage my [[concepts/faith|faith]] where my [[concepts/honour|honour]] was already bound. The

event has proved, that I was a cunning [[archetypes/fool|fool]], providing with great

circumspection for a possible opportunity of making myself contemptible

and wretched for ever. At last, however, my resolution was taken, and I

had determined, as soon as I could engage her alone, to justify the

attentions I had so invariably paid her, and openly assure her of an

affection which I had already taken such pains to display. But in the

interim—in the interim of the very few hours that were to pass, before

I could have an opportunity of speaking with her in private—a

circumstance occurred—an unlucky circumstance, to ruin all my

resolution, and with it all my comfort. A discovery took place,”—here

he hesitated and looked down. “Mrs. Smith had somehow or other been

informed, I imagine by some distant relation, whose interest it was to

deprive me of her favour, of an affair, a connection—but I need not

explain myself farther,” he added, looking at her with an heightened

colour and an enquiring eye,—“your particular intimacy—you have

probably heard the whole story long ago.”



“I have,” returned Elinor, colouring likewise, and hardening her heart

anew against any compassion for him, “I have heard it all. And how you

will explain away any part of your [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] in that dreadful business, I

confess is beyond my comprehension.”



“Remember,” cried Willoughby, “from whom you received the account.

Could it be an impartial one? I acknowledge that her situation and her

character ought to have been respected by me. I do not mean to justify

myself, but at the same [[motifs/time|time]] cannot leave you to suppose that I have

nothing to urge—that because she was injured she was irreproachable,

and because _I_ was a libertine, _she_ must be a saint. If the violence

of her passions, the weakness of her understanding—I do not mean,

however, to defend myself. Her affection for me deserved better

treatment, and I often, with great [[concepts/self|self]]-reproach, recall the tenderness

which, for a very short [[motifs/time|time]], had the power of creating any return. I

wish—I heartily wish it had never been. But I have injured more than

herself; and I have injured one, whose affection for me (may I say it?)

was scarcely less warm than hers; and whose mind—Oh! how infinitely

superior!”



“Your indifference, however, towards that unfortunate girl—I must say

it, unpleasant to me as the discussion of such a subject may [[motifs/well|well]]

be—your indifference is no apology for your cruel neglect of her. Do

not think yourself excused by any weakness, any natural defect of

understanding on her side, in the wanton cruelty so evident on yours.

You must have known, that while you were enjoying yourself in

Devonshire pursuing fresh schemes, always gay, always happy, she was

reduced to the extremest indigence.”



“But, upon my [[motifs/soul|soul]], I did _not_ know it,” he warmly replied; “I did not

recollect that I had omitted to give her my direction; and common sense

might have told her how to find it out.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], sir, and what said Mrs. Smith?”



“She taxed me with the offence at once, and my confusion may be

guessed. The purity of her life, the formality of her notions, her

ignorance of the world—every thing was against me. The matter itself I

could not deny, and vain was every endeavour to soften it. She was

Raggiungendo la prosperità, ho perso tutto ciò che poteva renderla reale.

“Benedizione”.

“Resistere a tali attrazioni, sopportare una tale tenerezza, ”

C’è davvero un uomo al mondo che avrebbe potuto farlo? Sì, mi sono ritrovato io stesso ad essere quel uomo…

Gradi di affetto sincero… e gli istanti più felici della mia vita

La vita che trascorsi con lei quando sentivo che le mie intenzioni erano sincere…

Onorevole… e i miei sentimenti sono senza colpa. Tuttavia, anche allora, quando tutto era chiaro…

Deciso a darle le mie informazioni personali, mi concessi…

Rimandare continuamente, giorno dopo giorno, il momento in cui si dovrebbe agire…

Riluttanza ad impegnarsi in una relazione mentre le mie circostanze erano…

Terribilmente imbarazzato… Non intendo discutere di questo argomento, né mi fermerò ad analizzarlo.

Esplorare l’assurdità… e ciò che è ancora peggio dell’assurdità

Esitavo a mettere alla prova la mia [[concepts/faith|fede]] in un ambito dove la mia [[concepts/honour|'onore]] era già stata messa alla prova.

Gli eventi hanno dimostrato che ero un astuto [[archetypes/fool|idiota]], che avevo previsto tutto con grande precisione.

Prudenza… per cogliere un’eventuale opportunità di rendermi spregevole

“L’attenzione che le ho sempre riservato, e la mia ferma intenzione di continuare a farlo…”

L'affetto che avevo già preso tante precauzioni per dimostrare… Ma nel…

Potrei avere l’opportunità di parlare con lei in privato…

Una sfortunata circostanza… che rovinò tutto per me

“Risoluzione… e con essa tutto il mio conforto. Si verificò una scoperta…”

Titolo:  
Immagino che fosse informato da qualche parente lontano, il cui interesse consisteva nel…

Privatemi della sua simpatia, di una relazione… ma non è necessario.

“Devo spiegarmi meglio”, aggiunse, guardandola con un’espressione più intensa.

Colore e uno sguardo curioso… – “La tua particolare intimità…” – Hai

“Probabilmente avete già sentito tutta questa storia da molto tempo.”



“Lo ho fatto”, rispose Elinor, arrossendo a sua volta e indurendo il proprio cuore.

Senza più alcuna compassione per lui, disse: “L’ho sentito tutto… E come hai fatto…”

Qualsiasi aspetto della tua [[concepts/guilt|colpa]] in quella terribile faccenda potrà essere spiegato. Io.

“Confessare… è al di là della mia comprensione.”



“Ricorda,” gridò Willoughby, “da chi hai ricevuto quel resoconto.”

Potrebbe essere imparziale? Ammetto che la sua situazione…

Quel personaggio avrebbe dovuto essere rispettato da me. Non intendo giustificarmi…

Io stesso, ma allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] non posso lasciarti pensare che io abbia.

Niente da rimproverare… Poiché era ferita, non poteva essere biasimata in alcun modo.

E perché io ero un libertino, lei doveva essere una santa… Se la violenza…

Dei suoi passioni, della debolezza della sua comprensione… Non intendo dire…

"Comunque, per difendermi… Il suo affetto per me meritava di meglio."

Il trattamento. E spesso, con grande [[concepts/self|auto-rimprovero]], ricordo quella tenerezza.

Che, per un brevissimo [[motifs/time|tempo]], aveva il potere di creare qualsiasi tipo di ritorno. Io.

Vorrei con tutto il cuore che non fosse mai successo… Ma ho fatto del male a molte persone.

Se stessa. E ho ferito qualcuno il cui affetto per me. Posso dirlo?

Il calore del suo cuore era quasi altrettanto intenso di quello di lei; e la sua mente… Oh, quanto infinitamente profonda!

“Superiore!”



“Tuttavia, la tua indifferenza verso quella povera ragazza… devo dire…”

Per me è sgradevole, poiché la discussione di un argomento del genere potrebbe [[motifs/well|certamente]].

“La tua indifferenza non è una scusa per la tua crudele negligenza verso di lei.”

Non credere mai di poterti scusare per alcuna debolezza, per alcun difetto naturale…

Comprensione da parte sua, di fronte alla crudeltà spietata che emerge chiaramente da parte tua.

Dovevi saperlo… mentre te la spassavi…

Devonshire, sempre allegra e felice, continuava a intraprendere nuove iniziative…

“Ridotto alla più estrema povertà.”



“Ma, per la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]], non lo sapevo,” rispose calorosamente; “Non lo sapevo davvero.”

“Ricordate che avevo dimenticato di darle le mie indicazioni… e il buon senso…”

“Avrei potuto dirle come scoprirlo.”



“Beh, signore, e cosa ha detto la signora Smith?”



Mi accusò immediatamente dell’offesa, e la mia confusione…

Integrità e formalità…

Ignoranza del mondo… Tutto era contro di me. La stessa questione, in sé…

Non si poteva negare, e ogni tentativo di attenuarne le conseguenze risultava vano. Lei era…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_44--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 44 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 44" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/villain,motif/journey,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/conscience,concept/doubt,concept/faith,concept/friendship,concept/guilt,concept/poverty,concept/pride,concept/self,setting/london"></span>


previously disposed, I believe, to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] the morality of my conduct in

general, and was moreover discontented with the very little attention,

the very little portion of my [[motifs/time|time]] that I had bestowed on her, in my

present visit. In short, it ended in a total breach. By one measure I

might have saved myself. In the height of her morality, good woman! she

offered to forgive the past, if I would marry Eliza. That could not

be—and I was formally dismissed from her favour and her house. The

[[motifs/night|night]] following this affair—I was to go the next morning—was spent by

me in deliberating on what my future conduct should be. The struggle

was great—but it ended too soon. My affection for Marianne, my thorough

conviction of her attachment to me—it was all insufficient to outweigh

that dread of [[concepts/poverty|poverty]], or get the better of those false ideas of the

necessity of riches, which I was naturally inclined to feel, and

expensive society had increased. I had reason to believe myself secure

of my present wife, if I chose to address her, and I persuaded myself

to think that nothing else in common prudence remained for me to do. A

heavy scene however awaited me, before I could leave Devonshire;—I was

engaged to dine with you on that very day; some apology was therefore

necessary for my breaking this engagement. But whether I should write

this apology, or deliver it in person, was a point of long debate. To

see Marianne, I felt, would be dreadful, and I even doubted whether I

could see her again, and keep to my resolution. In that point, however,

I undervalued my own magnanimity, as the event declared; for I went, I

saw her, and saw her miserable, and left her miserable—and left her

hoping never to see her again.”



“Why did you call, Mr. Willoughby?” said Elinor, reproachfully; “a note

would have answered every purpose. Why was it necessary to call?”



“It was necessary to my own [[concepts/pride|pride]]. I could not bear to leave the

country in a manner that might lead you, or the rest of the

neighbourhood, to suspect any part of what had really passed between

Mrs. Smith and myself—and I resolved therefore on calling at the

cottage, in my way to Honiton. The sight of your dear sister, however,

was really dreadful; and, to heighten the matter, I found her alone.

You were all gone I do not know where. I had left her only the evening

before, so fully, so firmly resolved within my [[concepts/self|self]] on doing right! A

few hours were to have engaged her to me for ever; and I remember how

happy, how gay were my spirits, as I walked from the cottage to

Allenham, satisfied with myself, delighted with every [[concepts/body|body]]! But in

this, our last interview of [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], I approached her with a sense

of [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] that almost took from me the power of dissembling. Her sorrow,

her disappointment, her deep regret, when I told her that I was obliged

to leave Devonshire so immediately—I never shall forget it—united too

with such reliance, such confidence in me!—Oh, God!—what a hard-hearted

rascal I was!”



They were both silent for a few moments. Elinor first spoke.



“Did you tell her that you should soon return?”



“I do not know what I told her,” he replied, impatiently; “less than

was due to the past, beyond a [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], and in all likelihood much more

than was justified by the future. I cannot think of it.—It won’t

do.—Then came your dear mother to torture me farther, with all her

kindness and confidence. Thank Heaven! it _did_ torture me. I was

miserable. Miss Dashwood, you cannot have an idea of the comfort it

gives me to look back on my own misery. I owe such a grudge to myself

for the stupid, rascally folly of my own heart, that all my past

sufferings under it are only triumph and exultation to me now. [[motifs/well|Well]], I

went, left all that I loved, and went to those to whom, at best, I was

only indifferent. My [[motifs/journey|journey]] to town—travelling with my own horses, and

therefore so tediously—no creature to speak to—my own reflections so

cheerful—when I looked forward every thing so inviting!—when I looked

back at Barton, the picture so soothing!—oh, it was a blessed [[motifs/journey|journey]]!”



He stopped.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], sir,” said Elinor, who, though pitying him, grew impatient for

his departure, “and this is all?”



“All!—no:—have you forgot what passed in town? That infamous letter?

Did she show it you?”



“Yes, I saw every note that passed.”



“When the first of hers reached me (as it immediately did, for I was in

town the whole [[motifs/time|time]],) what I felt is—in the common phrase, not to be

expressed; in a more simple one—perhaps too simple to raise any

emotion—my feelings were very, very painful.—Every line, every word

was—in the hackneyed metaphor which their dear writer, were she here,

would forbid—a dagger to my heart. To know that Marianne was in town

was—in the same language—a thunderbolt.—Thunderbolts and daggers!—what

a reproof would she have given me!—her taste, her opinions—I believe

they are better known to me than my own,—and I am sure they are

dearer.”



Elinor’s heart, which had undergone many changes in the course of this

extraordinary conversation, was now softened again;—yet she felt it her

duty to check such ideas in her companion as the last.



“This is not right, Mr. Willoughby.—Remember that you are married.

Relate only what in your [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] you think necessary for me to

hear.”



“Marianne’s note, by assuring me that I was still as dear to her as in

former days,—that in spite of the many, many weeks we had been

separated, she was as constant in her own feelings, and as full of

[[concepts/faith|faith]] in the constancy of mine as ever,—awakened all my remorse. I say

awakened, because [[motifs/time|time]] and [[settings/london|London]], business and dissipation, had in

some measure quieted it, and I had been growing a fine hardened

[[archetypes/villain|villain]], fancying myself indifferent to her, and chusing to fancy that

La piccolissima parte del mio [[motifs/time|tempo]] che le avevo dedicato.

La visita attuale… In breve, si è conclusa con un totale fallimento. Secondo uno dei criteri utilizzati…

Avrei potuto salvare me stesso. Nella piena espressione della sua moralità, quella brava donna, lei.

Offerto di perdonare il passato, se avessi sposato Eliza… Ma ciò non era possibile.

Essere. E fui formalmente allontanato dal suo favore e dalla sua casa.

La [[motifs/night|notte]] successiva a questi eventi – dovevo partire il giorno dopo – la trascorsi.

In riflessione su quale dovrebbe essere il mio comportamento futuro… La lotta interiore

“Era fantastico… ma è finito troppo presto. Il mio affetto per Marianne… era davvero profondo.”

La consapevolezza del suo attaccamento per me… nulla di tutto ciò era sufficiente per farle superare questa difficoltà.

Quel terrore della [[concepts/poverty|povertà]], o almeno superare quelle false concezioni riguardo ad essa.

"Necessità della ricchezza: un sentimento che naturalmente provavo..."

La società costosa aveva visto un aumento… Avevo motivo di credere di essere al sicuro.

Di mia attuale moglie, se decidessi di rivolgermi a lei… e se riuscissi a convincermene.

Pensare che non mi restasse altro da fare, se non agire con prudenza…

Una scena drammatica mi aspettava prima che potessi lasciare il Devonshire…

“Impegnato a cenare con te proprio quel giorno… quindi qualche scusa era necessaria.”

“Necessario per rompere questo fidanzamento… Ma se dovrei scrivere o meno…”

Queste scuse, o il fatto di presentarle di persona, sono state oggetto di lunghe debattute.

“Vedere Marianne… sarebbe terribile”, pensai, e dubitavo persino se fosse possibile…

“Potrei rivederla di nuovo, e mantenerò la mia risoluzione… Tuttavia, in quel momento…”

“Non ho mai apprezzato abbastanza la mia magnanimità, come dimostrò quell’evento… perché io andai.”

La vidi, la vidi soffrire, e la lasciai così… ancora sofferente.

“Sperando di non rivederla mai più.”



“Perché ha chiamato, signor Willoughby?”, disse Elinor in tono di rimprovero; “una semplice nota…”

Avrebbe risolto ogni problema… Perché allora era necessario chiamare?



“Era necessario per la mia stessa [[concepts/pride|orgoglio]]. Non riuscivo a sopportare l’idea di andarmene, ”

Un paese che potrebbe condurvi… o condurre gli altri…

**Quartiere… per sospettare qualcosa di ciò che realmente era accaduto tra loro**

La signora Smith ed io, e così ho deciso di fare una visita a.

Casa di campagna… lungo il mio cammino verso Honiton. Ma la vista della tua cara sorella…

Era davvero terribile; e per peggiorare le cose, la trovai da sola.

“Eravate tutti andati… Non so dove. L’avevo lasciata da sola quella sera…”

Prima d’ora, ero davvero deciso, con fermezza e determinazione, nel mio [[concepts/self|interno]], a fare la cosa giusta.

Poche ore avrebbero dovuto legarla a me per sempre; e ricordo come…

Felice… quanto erano allegra la mia anima mentre camminavo dalla capanna…

Allenham, soddisfatto di me stesso, felice con ogni singolo [[concepts/body|-corpo]]. Ma poi.

Questa, l’ultima nostra conversazione riguardo all’[[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], l’ho affrontata con un certo senso.

Di un [[concepts/guilt|senso di colpa]] tale che quasi mi privò della capacità di nascondere le mie emozioni. Il suo dolore.

La sua delusione, il suo profondo rimpianto… quando le dissi che ero costretto a farlo.

“Lasciare immediatamente il Devonshire… Non lo dimenticherò mai… E anche uniti…”

Con tale fiducia, tale affidamento in me… Oh, Dio… che cuore duro.

“Che birichino che ero!”



Rimasero entrambi in silenzio per alcuni momenti. Fu Elinor la prima a parlare.



Hai detto a lei che tornerai presto?



“Non so cosa le abbia detto,” rispose impazientemente; “poco…”.

Doveva essere dovuto al passato, senza alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], e molto probabilmente di più ancora.

“Un atto che in seguito non si rivelò giustificato… Non riesco nemmeno a pensarci… Non succederà.”

E poi arrivò tua cara madre per tormentarmi ancora di più, con tutto il suo…

Bontà e fiducia… Grazie al cielo, mi ha davvero tormentato. Ero…

Miserabile… Signorina Dashwood, non potete nemmeno immaginare quanto conforto possa rappresentare…

Mi costringe a riflettere sulla mia stessa sofferenza… Ho un tale rancore verso me stesso.

Per la stupida e malvagia follia del mio stesso cuore… tutto il mio passato…

Le sofferenze che ne derivano ora sono per me solo trionfo ed esultanza. [[motifs/well|Beh]], io.

Andò via, lasciando tutto ciò che amavo, e si diresse verso coloro per i quali, nel migliore dei casi, non ero altro che…

Solo indifferente. Il mio [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] in città, viaggiando con i miei cavalli, e.

Così noiosamente… senza nessuno con cui parlare, solo i miei stessi pensieri…

Felice… quando tutto sembrava così invitante davanti ai miei occhi… quando guardavo avanti con speranza…

Tornato a Barton, quella scena era davvero rassicurante. Oh, è stata una [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] meravigliosa!



Si fermò.



“Beh, signore,” disse Elinor, che, sebbene provasse compassione per lui, iniziava a diventare impaziente.

La sua partenza… “E questo è tutto?”



“Tutti, no: avete dimenticato ciò che è accaduto in città? Quella famigerata lettera?”

“Te l’ha mostrata?”



“Sì, ho visto ogni nota che è passata.”



"Quando il primo di essi mi raggiunse (e ciò avvenne immediatamente, poiché mi trovavo..."

In tutta la [[motifs/time|tempo]] che sono stato in città, quello che ho provato è, per usare un’espressione comune, non voglio dire che.

Espresso; in modo più semplice… forse troppo semplice per suscitare alcuna reazione.

Emozioni: i miei sentimenti erano davvero molto dolorosi… Ogni riga, ogni parola.

“Era… nella banale metafora che la loro cara scrittrice, se fosse qui…”

Un coltello piantato nel cuore… Sapere che Marianne era in città.

“Fu come un fulmine… Fulmini e pugnali! Che cosa…”

“Una rimprovera mi avrebbe certamente rivolto… i suoi gusti, le sue opinioni… Credo proprio di sì.”

Per me sono più conosciuti di quanto lo siano i miei stessi familiari… E ne sono sicuro.

“Mio caro…”



Il cuore di Elinor, che aveva subito molti cambiamenti nel corso di questo…

Una conversazione straordinaria… che ora tornava ad essere più dolce e gentile; tuttavia lei continuava a sentirne l’impatto su di sé.

Il dovere di verificare tali idee nel proprio compagno veniva considerato l’ultima cosa da fare.



“Non è giusto, signor Willoughby. Ricordi che sei sposato.”

Raccontami soltanto ciò che, secondo la tua [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]], ritieni necessario che io sappia.

"Ascolta."



“La nota di Marianne, nella quale mi assicura che per lei sono ancora tanto caro come prima…”

Titolo:  
Gli anni passati… nonostante le molte, molte settimane trascorse…

Separata, rimase comunque costante nei propri sentimenti e piena di…

La [[concepts/faith|fede]] nella costanza delle mie azioni, come sempre, ha risvegliato in me tutto il rimorso. Lo dico io.

Si svegliò, perché il tempo e Londra, con le loro attività quotidiane e la vita mondana, avevano avuto su di lui un certo effetto.

“Una certa misura di silenzio lo calmò; in quel momento, io stesso stavo diventando sempre più forte e determinato…”

Quel [[archetypes/villain|villain]], fingendo di essere indifferente a lei, preferiva crederlo davvero.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_44--part_04" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 44 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 44" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,archetype/lover,motif/dance,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/time,motif/well"></span>


she too must have become indifferent to me; talking to myself of our

past attachment as a mere idle, trifling business, shrugging up my

shoulders in proof of its being so, and silencing every reproach,

overcoming every scruple, by secretly saying now and then, ‘I shall be

heartily glad to hear she is [[motifs/well|well]] married.’ But this note made me know

myself better. I felt that she was infinitely dearer to me than any

other woman in the world, and that I was using her infamously. But

every thing was then just settled between Miss Grey and me. To retreat

was impossible. All that I had to do, was to avoid you both. I sent no

answer to Marianne, intending by that to preserve myself from her

farther notice; and for some [[motifs/time|time]] I was even determined not to call in

Berkeley Street;—but at last, judging it wiser to affect the air of a

cool, common acquaintance than anything else, I watched you all safely

out of the house one morning, and left my name.”



“Watched us out of the house!”



“Even so. You would be surprised to hear how often I watched you, how

often I was on the point of falling in with you. I have entered many a

shop to avoid your sight, as the carriage drove by. Lodging as I did in

Bond Street, there was hardly a day in which I did not catch a glimpse

of one or other of you; and nothing but the most constant watchfulness

on my side, a most invariably prevailing [[motifs/desire|desire]] to keep out of your

sight, could have separated us so long. I avoided the Middletons as

much as possible, as [[motifs/well|well]] as everybody else who was likely to prove an

acquaintance in common. Not aware of their being in town, however, I

blundered on Sir John, I believe, the first day of his coming, and the

day after I had called at Mrs. Jennings’s. He asked me to a party, a

[[motifs/dance|dance]] at his house in the evening. Had he _not_ told me as an

inducement that you and your sister were to be there, I should have

felt it too certain a thing, to trust myself near him. The next morning

brought another short note from Marianne—still affectionate, open,

artless, confiding—everything that could make _my_ conduct most

hateful. I could not answer it. I tried—but could not frame a sentence.

But I thought of her, I believe, every moment of the day. If you _can_

pity me, Miss Dashwood, pity my situation as it was _then_. With my

head and heart full of your sister, I was forced to play the happy

[[archetypes/lover|lover]] to another woman! Those three or four weeks were worse than all.

[[motifs/well|Well]], at last, as I need not tell you, you were forced on me; and what

a sweet figure I cut! what an evening of agony it was! Marianne,

beautiful as an angel on one side, calling me Willoughby in such a

tone! Oh, God! holding out her hand to me, asking me for an

explanation, with those bewitching eyes fixed in such speaking

solicitude on my face! and Sophia, jealous as the devil on the other

hand, looking all that was—[[motifs/well|Well]], it does not signify; it is over now.

Such an evening! I ran away from you all as soon as I could; but not

before I had seen Marianne’s sweet face as white as [[motifs/death|death]]. _That_ was

the last, last look I ever had of her; the last manner in which she

appeared to me. It was a horrid sight! yet when I thought of her to-day

as really dying, it was a kind of comfort to me to imagine that I knew

exactly how she would appear to those, who saw her last in this world.

She was before me, constantly before me, as I travelled, in the same

look and hue.”



A short pause of mutual thoughtfulness succeeded. Willoughby first

rousing himself, broke it thus:



“[[motifs/well|Well]], let me make haste and be gone. Your sister is certainly better,

certainly out of danger?”



“We are assured of it.”



“Your poor mother, too!—doting on Marianne.”



“But the letter, Mr. Willoughby, your own letter; have you any thing to

say about that?”



“Yes, yes, _that_ in particular. Your sister wrote to me again, you

know, the very next morning. You saw what she said. I was breakfasting

at the Ellisons,—and her letter, with some others, was brought to me

there from my lodgings. It happened to catch Sophia’s eye before it

caught mine—and its size, the elegance of the paper, the hand-writing

altogether, immediately gave her a suspicion. Some vague report had

reached her before of my attachment to some young lady in Devonshire,

and what had passed within her observation the preceding evening had

marked who the young lady was, and made her more jealous than ever.

Affecting that air of playfulness, therefore, which is delightful in a

woman one loves, she opened the letter directly, and read its contents.

She was [[motifs/well|well]] paid for her impudence. She read what made her wretched.

Her wretchedness I could have borne, but her passion—her malice—At all

events it must be appeased. And, in short—what do you think of my

wife’s style of letter-writing?—delicate—tender—truly feminine—was it

not?”



“Your wife!—The letter was in your own hand-writing.”



“Yes, but I had only the credit of servilely copying such sentences as

I was ashamed to put my name to. The original was all her own—her own

happy thoughts and gentle diction. But what could I do!—we were

engaged, every thing in preparation, the day almost fixed—But I am

talking like a [[archetypes/fool|fool]]. Preparation! Day! In honest words, her money was

necessary to me, and in a situation like mine, any thing was to be done

to prevent a rupture. And after all, what did it signify to my

character in the opinion of Marianne and her friends, in what language

my answer was couched? It must have been only to one end. My business

was to declare myself a scoundrel, and whether I did it with a bow or a

bluster was of little importance. ‘I am ruined for ever in their

opinion,’ said I to myself: ‘I am shut out for ever from their society,

they already think me an unprincipled fellow, this letter will only

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_44--part_05" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 44 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 44" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/villain,motif/clock,motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/conscience,concept/forgiveness,concept/guilt,concept/honour,concept/nature,concept/temptation,concept/vanity"></span>


sort of desperate carelessness, I copied my wife’s words, and parted

with the last relics of Marianne. Her three notes,—unluckily they were

all in my pocketbook, or I should have denied their existence, and

hoarded them for ever,—I was forced to put them up, and could not even

kiss them. And the lock of hair—that too I had always carried about me

in the same pocket-book, which was now searched by Madam with the most

ingratiating virulence,—the dear lock,—all, every memento was torn from

me.”



“You are very wrong, Mr. Willoughby, very blamable,” said Elinor, while

her voice, in spite of herself, betrayed her compassionate emotion;

“you ought not to speak in this way, either of Mrs. Willoughby or my

sister. You had made your own choice. It was not forced on you. Your

wife has a claim to your politeness, to your respect, at least. She

must be attached to you, or she would not have married you. To treat

her with unkindness, to speak of her slightingly is no atonement to

Marianne—nor can I suppose it a relief to your own [[concepts/conscience|conscience]].”



“Do not talk to me of my wife,” said he with a heavy sigh; “she does

not deserve your compassion. She knew I had no regard for her when we

married. [[motifs/well|Well]], married we were, and came down to Combe Magna to be

happy, and afterwards returned to town to be gay. And now do you pity

me, Miss Dashwood? Or have I said all this to no purpose? Am I,—be it

only one degree,—am I less guilty in your opinion than I was before? My

intentions were not always wrong. Have I explained away any part of my

[[concepts/guilt|guilt]]?”



“Yes, you have certainly removed something—a little. You have proved

yourself, on the whole, less faulty than I had believed you. You have

proved your heart less wicked, much less wicked. But I hardly know—the

misery that you have inflicted—I hardly know what could have made it

worse.”



“Will you repeat to your sister when she is recovered, what I have been

telling you?—Let me be a little lightened too in her opinion as [[motifs/well|well]] as

in yours. You tell me that she has forgiven me already. Let me be able

to fancy that a better knowledge of my heart, and of my present

feelings, will draw from her a more spontaneous, more natural, more

gentle, less dignified, [[concepts/forgiveness|forgiveness]]. Tell her of my misery and my

penitence—tell her that my heart was never inconstant to her, and if

you will, that at this moment she is dearer to me than ever.”



“I will tell her all that is necessary to what may comparatively be

called, your justification. But you have not explained to me the

particular reason of your coming now, nor how you heard of her

illness.”



“Last [[motifs/night|night]], in Drury Lane lobby, I ran against Sir John Middleton, and

when he saw who I was, for the first [[motifs/time|time]] these two months, he spoke to

me. That he had cut me ever since my [[motifs/marriage|marriage]], I had seen without

surprise or resentment. Now, however, his good-natured, honest, stupid

[[motifs/soul|soul]], full of indignation against me, and concern for your sister,

could not resist the [[concepts/temptation|temptation]] of telling me what he knew ought to,

though probably he did not think it _would_, vex me horridly. As

bluntly as he could speak it, therefore, he told me that Marianne

Dashwood was dying of a putrid fever at Cleveland—a letter that morning

received from Mrs. Jennings declared her danger most imminent—the

Palmers are all gone off in a fright, &c. I was too much shocked to be

able to pass myself off as insensible even to the undiscerning Sir

John. His heart was softened in seeing mine suffer; and so much of his

ill-will was done away, that when we parted, he almost shook me by the

hand while he reminded me of an old promise about a pointer puppy. What

I felt on hearing that your sister was dying, and dying too, believing

me the greatest [[archetypes/villain|villain]] upon earth, scorning, hating me in her latest

moments—for how could I tell what horrid projects might not have been

imputed? _One_ person I was sure would represent me as capable of

anything—What I felt was dreadful! My resolution was soon made, and at

eight o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] this morning I was in my carriage. Now you know all.”



Elinor made no answer. Her thoughts were silently fixed on the

irreparable injury which too early an independence and its consequent

habits of idleness, dissipation, and luxury, had made in the mind, the

character, the happiness, of a man who, to every advantage of person

and talents, united a disposition naturally open and honest, and a

feeling, affectionate temper. The world had made him extravagant and

vain—Extravagance and [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] had made him cold-hearted and selfish.

[[concepts/vanity|Vanity]], while seeking its own guilty triumph at the expense of another,

had involved him in a real attachment, which extravagance, or at least

its offspring, necessity, had required to be sacrificed. Each faulty

propensity in leading him to evil, had led him likewise to punishment.

The attachment, from which against [[concepts/honour|honour]], against feeling, against

every better interest he had outwardly torn himself, now, when no

longer allowable, governed every thought; and the connection, for the

sake of which he had, with little scruple, left her sister to misery,

was likely to prove a source of unhappiness to himself of a far more

incurable [[concepts/nature|nature]]. From a reverie of this kind she was recalled at the

end of some minutes by Willoughby, who, rousing himself from a reverie

at least equally painful, started up in preparation for going, and

said—



“There is no use in staying here; I must be off.”



“Are you going back to town?”



“No—to Combe Magna. I have business there; from thence to town in a day

or two. Good bye.”



He held out his hand. She could not refuse to give him hers;—he pressed

it with affection.



“And you _do_ think something better of me than you did?” said he,

letting it fall, and leaning against the mantel-piece as if forgetting

he was to go.



Elinor assured him that she did;—that she forgave, pitied, wished him

[[motifs/well|well]]—was even interested in his happiness—and added some gentle counsel

as to the behaviour most likely to promote it. His answer was not very

encouraging.



“As to that,” said he, “I must rub through the world as [[motifs/well|well]] as I can.

Domestic happiness is out of the question. If, however, I am allowed to

think that you and yours feel an interest in my fate and actions, it

may be the means—it may put me on my guard—at least, it may be

something to live for. Marianne to be sure is lost to me for ever. Were

I even by any blessed chance at liberty again—”



Elinor stopped him with a reproof.



“[[motifs/well|Well]],”—he replied—“once more good bye. I shall now go away and live in

dread of one event.”



“What do you mean?”



“Your sister’s [[motifs/marriage|marriage]].”



“You are very wrong. She can never be more lost to you than she is

now.”



“But she will be gained by some one else. And if that some one should

be the very he whom, of all others, I could least bear—but I will not

stay to rob myself of all your compassionate goodwill, by showing that

where I have most injured I can least forgive. Good bye,—God bless

you!”



And with these words, he almost ran out of the room.

“La scorsa [[motifs/night|notte]], nell’atrio del Drury Lane, mi sono scontrato con Sir John Middleton, ”

Senza mezzi termini, mi disse che Marianne…

Dashwood stava morendo di febbre putrefica a Cleveland: una lettera quella mattina

Titolo: Ricevuto dalla signora Jennings, si dichiarava che il pericolo fosse imminente…

“Tutti i Palmer sono fuggiti spaventati… Io ero troppo sconvolto per poter reagire.”

Capace di fingermi insensibile anche davanti a un signore inesperto

John: il suo cuore si addolcì vedendo il mio dolore… e molto di lui…

Il rancore svanì; quando ci separammo, quasi mi strinse la mano con affetto

Una promessa d’antico...

Sentii che tua sorella stava morendo… e moriva credendo in qualcosa.

Il più grande [[archetypes/villain|villain]] della terra, che mi disprezza, che mi odia nel suo ultimo messaggio.

Momenti… perché mai avrei dovuto immaginare quali orribili progetti potessero nascondersi dietro di essi?

Imputato? Una persona di cui ero sicura che mi avrebbe rappresentata come capace…

Qualsiasi cosa… Quello che provavo era terribile! La mia decisione fu presa in fretta… e poi…

Alle otto di questa mattina ero nella mia carrozza. Ora sapete tutto.



Elinor non rispose. I suoi pensieri erano fissi, in silenzio, su…

Danno irreparabile causato da un’indipendenza troppo precoce e dalle sue conseguenze

Abitudini di ozio, dissipazione e lusso avevano formato nella mente…

La felicità di un uomo che, nonostante tutti i vantaggi personali…

Abilità e talenti uniti a una natura aperta ed onesta…

Temperamento affettuoso e sensibile… Il mondo lo aveva reso generoso e premuroso.

Inutile. La stravaganza e la [[concepts/vanity|vanità]] lo avevano reso freddo di cuore e egoista.

La [[concepts/vanity|vanità]], nel cercare il proprio trionfo colpevole a scapito di un altro.

Lo aveva coinvolto in un vero legame emotivo… un gesto di eccessiva generosità, o almeno così sembrava.

Il suo prodotto, necessario per certi scopi, doveva essere sacrificato… Ogni elemento difettoso…

La propensione a condurlo verso il male lo aveva ugualmente portato alla punizione.

Quell’attaccamento, che va contro l’[[concepts/honour|'onore]], contro i sentimenti, contro.

“Ogni interesse più nobile che avesse in sé aveva ormai abbandonato, ora che non c’era più nulla…”

Più lungo il tempo consentito… ogni pensiero veniva guidato da quella connessione.

Per questo motivo, senza alcun rimorso, aveva abbandonato sua sorella alla miseria.

Il titolo probabilmente si sarebbe rivelato una fonte di infelicità per lui, in misura molto maggiore…

[[concepts/nature|nature]] incurabile. Fu da un simile sogno che fu richiamata alla realtà.

“La fine di alcuni minuti” di Willoughby, che si risveglia da una specie di trance…

Almeno altrettanto doloroso… Iniziato in preparazione alla partenza…

Disse…



“Non ha senso restare qui; devo andarmene.”



“Tornerai in città?”



“No… verso Combe Magna. Devo sbrigare degli affari lì; da lì tornerò in città entro un giorno.”

“Uno o due… Addio.”



Gli tese la mano. Lei non poté rifiutarsi di stringergliela; lui la strinse forte.

Lo fece con affetto.



“E davvero pensi che io sia migliore di quanto tu credessi in passato?” disse lui.

"Lasciarlo cadere e appoggiarsi al caminetto, come se lo avesse dimenticato..."

Doveva andarsene.



“Elinor gli assicurò che lo faceva; che lo perdonava, provava compassione per lui e gli augurava il meglio.”

[[motifs/well|Ben]] era addirittura interessato alla sua felicità e gli diede alcuni consigli gentili.

Sul comportamento più adatto a promuoverlo… La sua risposta non fu molto chiara.

incoraggiante.



“Per quanto riguarda questo,” disse, “devo viaggiare per il mondo nel modo migliore possibile.”

Felicità domestica è fuori discussione… Tuttavia, se mi fosse permesso…

Credo che voi e quelli a cui tenete abbiate interesse per il mio destino e le mie azioni…

Potrebbe essere un mezzo… potrebbe farmi stare attento… almeno, potrebbe esserlo.

Qualcosa per cui vivere… Marianne, invece, è perduta per sempre per me.

“Anche se per qualche fortunata coincidenza potessi tornare libero…”



Elinor lo fermò con un rimprovero.



“Beh,” rispose, “un altro addio allora. Ora me ne andrò e vivrò, ”

“La paura di un evento specifico”.



“Cosa intendi dire?”



“Il [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] di tua sorella.”



“Ti sbagli di grosso. Non potrebbe mai allontanarsi da te di più di quanto non lo sia già.”

Ora.



“Ma sarà conquistata da qualcun altro… E se quel qualcuno dovesse…”

Quell’uomo che, tra tutti, non potrei sopportare… ma lo farò lo stesso

Rimanere per privarmi della vostra compassione e gentilezza… mostrando così…

Dove ho ferito di più, è lì che riesco meno a perdonare. Addio… Che Dio vi benedica.

“Tu, davvero!”



E con queste parole, quasi corse fuori dalla stanza.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_45--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 45 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 45" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/innocent,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/sleep,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/fear,character/colonel_brandon,character/nurse"></span>


CHAPTER XLV.





Elinor, for some [[motifs/time|time]] after he left her, for some [[motifs/time|time]] even after the

sound of his carriage had died away, remained too much oppressed by a

crowd of ideas, widely differing in themselves, but of which sadness

was the general result, to think even of her sister.



Willoughby, he, whom only half an hour ago she had abhorred as the most

worthless of men, Willoughby, in spite of all his faults, excited a

degree of commiseration for the sufferings produced by them, which made

her think of him as now separated for ever from her family, with a

tenderness, a regret, rather in proportion, as she soon acknowledged

within herself—to his wishes than to his merits. She felt that his

influence over her mind was heightened by circumstances which ought not

in reason to have weight; by that person of uncommon attraction, that

open, affectionate, and lively manner which it was no merit to possess;

and by that still ardent [[motifs/love|love]] for Marianne, which it was not even

[[archetypes/innocent|innocent]] to indulge. But she felt that it was so, long, long before she

could feel his influence less.



When at last she returned to the unconscious Marianne, she found her

just awaking, refreshed by so long and sweet a [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] to the extent of

her hopes. Elinor’s heart was full. The past, the present, the future,

Willoughby’s visit, Marianne’s safety, and her mother’s expected

arrival, threw her altogether into an agitation of spirits which kept

off every indication of fatigue, and made her only fearful of betraying

herself to her sister. Short was the [[motifs/time|time]], however, in which that [[concepts/fear|fear]]

could affect her, for within half an hour after Willoughby’s leaving

the house, she was again called down stairs by the sound of another

carriage.—Eager to save her mother from every unnecessary moment’s

horrible suspense, she ran immediately into the hall, and reached the

outward door just in [[motifs/time|time]] to receive and support her as she entered it.



Mrs. Dashwood, whose terror as they drew near the house had produced

almost the conviction of Marianne’s being no more, had no voice to

inquire after her, no voice even for Elinor; but _she_, waiting neither

for salutation nor inquiry, instantly gave the joyful relief; and her

mother, catching it with all her usual warmth, was in a moment as much

overcome by her happiness, as she had been before by her fears. She was

supported into the drawing-room between her daughter and her friend;

and there, shedding [[motifs/tears|tears]] of joy, though still unable to speak,

embraced Elinor again and again, turning from her at intervals to press

[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s hand, with a look which spoke at once her gratitude,

and her conviction of his sharing with herself in the bliss of the

moment. He shared it, however, in a [[motifs/silence|silence]] even greater than her own.



As soon as Mrs. Dashwood had recovered herself, to see Marianne was her

first [[motifs/desire|desire]]; and in two minutes she was with her beloved [[archetypes/child|child]],

rendered dearer to her than ever by absence, unhappiness, and danger.

Elinor’s delight, as she saw what each felt in the meeting, was only

checked by an apprehension of its robbing Marianne of farther [[motifs/sleep|sleep]]:

but Mrs. Dashwood could be calm, could be even prudent, when the life

of a [[archetypes/child|child]] was at stake, and Marianne, satisfied in knowing her mother

was near her, and conscious of being too weak for conversation,

submitted readily to the [[motifs/silence|silence]] and quiet prescribed by every [[characters/nurse|nurse]]

around her. Mrs. Dashwood _would_ sit up with her all [[motifs/night|night]]; and

Elinor, in compliance with her mother’s entreaty, went to bed. But the

rest, which one [[motifs/night|night]] entirely sleepless, and many hours of the most

wearing anxiety seemed to make requisite, was kept off by irritation of

spirits. Willoughby, “poor Willoughby,” as she now allowed herself to

call him, was constantly in her thoughts; she would not but have heard

his vindication for the world, and now blamed, now acquitted herself

for having judged him so harshly before. But her promise of relating it

to her sister was invariably painful. She dreaded the performance of

it, dreaded what its effect on Marianne might be; doubted whether after

such an explanation she could ever be happy with another; and for a

moment wished Willoughby a widower. Then, remembering [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]],

reproved herself, felt that to _his_ sufferings and _his_ constancy far

more than to his rival’s, the reward of her sister was due, and wished

any thing rather than Mrs. Willoughby’s [[motifs/death|death]].



The shock of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s errand at Barton had been much softened

to Mrs. Dashwood by her own previous alarm; for so great was her

uneasiness about Marianne, that she had already determined to set out

for Cleveland on that very day, without waiting for any further

intelligence, and had so far settled her [[motifs/journey|journey]] before his arrival,

that the Careys were then expected every moment to fetch Margaret away,

as her mother was unwilling to take her where there might be infection.



Marianne continued to mend every day, and the brilliant cheerfulness of

Mrs. Dashwood’s looks and spirits proved her to be, as she repeatedly

declared herself, one of the happiest women in the world. Elinor could

not hear the declaration, nor witness its proofs without sometimes

wondering whether her mother ever recollected Edward. But Mrs.

Dashwood, trusting to the temperate account of her own disappointment

which Elinor had sent her, was led away by the exuberance of her joy to

think only of what would increase it. Marianne was restored to her from

a danger in which, as she now began to feel, her own mistaken judgment

in encouraging the unfortunate attachment to Willoughby, had

contributed to place her;—and in her recovery she had yet another

source of joy unthought of by Elinor. It was thus imparted to her, as

CAPITOLO XLV.





Elinor, per un certo [[motifs/time|tempo]] dopo che lui l'aveva lasciata, per un certo [[motifs/time|tempo]] anche dopo.

Il rumore della sua carrozza si era ormai spento; rimaneva troppo oppresso da…

Una folla di idee, profondamente diverse tra loro… ma tutte caratterizzate dalla tristezza.

Questo era il risultato generale; non si poteva nemmeno pensare a sua sorella.



Willoughby… lui, che soltanto mezz’ora prima lei disprezzava come il più…

“Un uomo senza valore… Nonostante tutti i suoi difetti, Willoughby riusciva comunque ad eccitare…”

Titolo:  
Il grado di compassione per le sofferenze causate da loro…

Lei lo considera ormai separato per sempre dalla sua famiglia…

Tenerezza… un rimpianto, piuttosto proporzionato, come lei stessa ammise presto.

“Within herself… più per volere suo che per meriti suoi. Lei sentiva che…”

L’influenza su la sua mente aumentava a causa di circostanze che non avrebbero dovuto esserci.

Per il suo peso significativo; per quella persona di straordinaria attrattiva…

Un modo aperto, affettuoso e vivace… qualità che non richiedeva alcuno sforzo particolare per essere posseduta.

e per quel sentimento d'amore ancora ardente per Marianne, che anzi non era nemmeno.

Un [[archetypes/innocent|innocente]] che desiderava indulgersi. Ma sentiva che ci sarebbe voluto molto tempo prima che potesse farlo.

Riuscivo a percepire sempre meno la sua influenza su di me.



Quando finalmente tornò da Marianne priva di sensi, la trovò…

Appena sveglio, rinfrescato da un così lungo e dolce [[motifs/sleep|sonno]], al punto che.

Le sue speranze… Il cuore di Elinor era colmo. Il passato, il presente, il futuro…

La visita di Willoughby, la sicurezza di Marianne e le aspettative della sua madre

Arrivo… Un evento che la gettò in uno stato di agitazione totale.

Senza alcun segno di stanchezza, l’unica cosa che la spaventava era il rischio di tradire…

Si rivolse a sua sorella. Tuttavia, il [[motifs/time|tempo]] trascorso fu breve, quel [[concepts/fear|terrore]].

Potrebbe influenzarla: meno di mezz’ora dopo che Willoughby se n’è andato…

Nella casa, fu di nuovo chiamata giù per le scale dal suono di qualcos'altro.

Carriaggio… Desiderosa di salvare sua madre da ogni momento inutile…

Terribile suspense… Corse immediatamente nel corridoio e raggiunse…

La porta d’ingresso era aperta proprio nel [[motifs/time|momento]] giusto per accoglierla e sostenerla non appena lei entrò.



La signora Dashwood, la cui paura aumentava man mano che si avvicinavano alla casa, aveva.

Quasi la certezza che Marianne non esistesse più… non aveva voce per esprimersi.

Chiedere notizie di lei… nemmeno una voce per Elinor; ma lei… non aspettava nulla.

Per saluto o per domanda, immediatamente le diede un sollievo gioioso; e lei…

“Madre, che accolse tutto con la sua solita calore, in un attimo fu completamente…”

Travolta dalla sua felicità, proprio come in passato era stata travolta dalle sue paure…

Portata nella sala da pranzo tra sua figlia e sua amica;

E lì, versando lacrime di gioia, sebbene ancora incapace di parlare.

Abbracciò Elinor ancora e ancora, voltandosi di tanto in tanto per stringerla forte.

La mano di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], accompagnata da uno sguardo che esprimeva al contempo la sua gratitudine.

E la sua convinzione che lui condividesse con lei la gioia di…

In quel momento. Tuttavia, lo condivise in un [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] ancora più profondo del suo.



Non appena la signora Dashwood si fu ripresa, la prima cosa che volle fare fu vedere Marianne.

Prima il [[motifs/desire|desiderio]]; e in due minuti era già con il suo amato [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

Diventò ancora più prezioso per lei a causa dell’assenza, della sfortuna e del pericolo.

La gioia di Elinor, nel vedere ciò che ognuno provava durante quell’incontro, fu davvero immensa…

Il timore che quella situazione potesse privare Marianne di ulteriori momenti di [[motifs/sleep|sonno]] la tormentava.

Ma la signora Dashwood poteva essere calma, anzi persino prudente… quando si trattava della vita…

C'era in gioco la vita di un [[archetypes/child|bambino]], e Marianne, soddisfatta di sapere che sua madre.

Era vicino a lei e si rendeva conto di essere troppo debole per poter conversare.

Si sottomise facilmente al [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] e alla tranquillità prescritti da ogni [[characters/nurse|infermiere]].

Intorno a lei. La signora Dashwood sarebbe rimasta seduta con lei per tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]; e.

Elinor, seguendo l’insistenza di sua madre, andò a letto. Ma…

Restare, una notte intera senza dormire, e molte ore ancora di.

Titolo:  
L’ansia apparentemente necessaria veniva tenuta a bada dall’irritazione…

Spiriti… Willoughby, “povero Willoughby”, come ora si permetteva di chiamarlo

“Chiamarlo…”, quel pensiero non le lasciava mai la mente; avrebbe fatto di tutto per ascoltarlo.

La sua difesa davanti al mondo… ora incolpata, ora assolta.

Per averlo giudicato così severamente in passato… Ma la sua promessa di raccontarlo…

Per sua sorella, quel momento era sempre doloroso. Temeva profondamente l’atto di…

Titolo: Temeva quale potesse essere l’effetto su Marianne; dubitava che, dopo…

Un’esplicazione del genere le avrebbe permesso di essere soddisfatta anche con un’altra… e per sempre.

In quel momento, desiderò che Willoughby diventasse vedovo. Poi, ricordandosi di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]].

Si dimostrò all'altezza delle aspettative; riconobbe che i suoi sacrifici e la sua fedeltà erano davvero significativi per lui…

Più che a quello del suo rivale, spettava a lui il premio dovuto alla sorella di lei… e lo desiderava ardentemente.

Qualsiasi cosa piuttosto che la [[motifs/death|morte]] della signora Willoughby.



Lo shock causato dall'incombenza affidata a [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] a Barton era stato notevolmente attenuato.

All’attenzione della signora Dashwood… per via delle sue stesse precedenti preoccupazioni; infatti, tali erano le sue apprensioni.

Inquietudine riguardo a Marianne… aveva già deciso di partire.

Per Cleveland, proprio in quel giorno, senza aspettare altro

Intelligenza. E aveva già pianificato tutto il suo [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] prima del suo arrivo.

I Carey erano attesi da un momento all’altro per portare via Margaret.

Poiché sua madre non voleva portarla in luoghi dove potesse esserci un rischio di infezione.



Marianne continuava a migliorare giorno dopo giorno, e la sua straordinaria allegria…

Il aspetto e lo spirito della signora Dashwood dimostravano chiaramente che lei era, come ripeteva spesso…

Si dichiarò una delle donne più felici del mondo. Elinor poteva…

Non ascoltare la dichiarazione, né assistere alle sue prove, senza che talvolta…

Chiedendosi se sua madre si fosse mai ricordata di Edward. Ma la signora.

Dashwood, fiduciosa nella descrizione moderata della propria delusione

Il biglietto che Elinor le aveva inviato fu dimenticato, a causa della sua eccessiva gioia…

Titolo:  
Pensa solo a ciò che può aumentarlo… Marianne fu restituita a lui.

Un pericolo nel quale, come iniziava ora a rendersi conto, la sua stessa valutazione errata poteva rivelarsi fatale.

Titolo:  
Nel incoraggiare quell’infelice attaccamento verso Willoughby, aveva…

Contribuì a farla riprendere… e durante il suo recupero ebbe un’altra opportunità.

Fonte di gioia inaspettata per Elinor… Fu così che le fu donata.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_45--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 45 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 45" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/desire,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/time,motif/well,concept/friendship,concept/hope,concept/imagination,concept/wonder,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


soon as any opportunity of private conference between them occurred.



“At last we are alone. My Elinor, you do not yet know all my happiness.

[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] loves Marianne. He has told me so himself.”



Her daughter, feeling by turns both pleased and pained, surprised and

not surprised, was all silent attention.



“You are never like me, dear Elinor, or I should [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at your

composure now. Had I sat down to wish for any possible good to my

family, I should have fixed on [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s marrying one of you as

the object most desirable. And I believe Marianne will be the most

happy with him of the two.”



Elinor was half inclined to ask her reason for thinking so, because

satisfied that none founded on an impartial consideration of their age,

characters, or feelings, could be given;—but her mother must always be

carried away by her [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] on any interesting subject, and

therefore instead of an inquiry, she passed it off with a smile.



“He opened his whole heart to me yesterday as we travelled. It came out

quite unawares, quite undesignedly. I, you may [[motifs/well|well]] believe, could talk

of nothing but my [[archetypes/child|child]];—he could not conceal his distress; I saw that

it equalled my own, and he perhaps, thinking that mere [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], as

the world now goes, would not justify so warm a sympathy—or rather, not

thinking at all, I suppose—giving way to irresistible feelings, made me

acquainted with his earnest, tender, constant, affection for Marianne.

He has loved her, my Elinor, ever since the first moment of seeing

her.”



Here, however, Elinor perceived,—not the language, not the professions

of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], but the natural embellishments of her mother’s

active fancy, which fashioned every thing delightful to her as it

chose.



“His regard for her, infinitely surpassing anything that Willoughby

ever felt or feigned, as much more warm, as more sincere or

constant—which ever we are to call it—has subsisted through all the

knowledge of dear Marianne’s unhappy prepossession for that worthless

young man!—and without selfishness—without encouraging a [[concepts/hope|hope]]!—could he

have seen her happy with another—Such a noble mind!—such openness, such

sincerity!—no one can be deceived in _him_.”



“[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s character,” said Elinor, “as an excellent man, is

[[motifs/well|well]] established.”



“I know it is,”—replied her mother seriously, “or after such a warning,

_I_ should be the last to encourage such affection, or even to be

pleased by it. But his coming for me as he did, with such active, such

ready [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], is enough to prove him one of the worthiest of men.”



“His character, however,” answered Elinor, “does not rest on _one_ act

of kindness, to which his affection for Marianne, were humanity out of

the case, would have prompted him. To Mrs. Jennings, to the Middletons,

he has been long and intimately known; they equally [[motifs/love|love]] and respect

him; and even my own knowledge of him, though lately acquired, is very

considerable; and so highly do _I_ value and esteem him, that if

Marianne can be happy with him, I shall be as ready as yourself to

think our connection the greatest blessing to us in the world. What

answer did you give him?—Did you allow him to [[concepts/hope|hope]]?”



“Oh! my [[motifs/love|love]], I could not then talk of [[concepts/hope|hope]] to him or to myself.

Marianne might at that moment be dying. But he did not ask for [[concepts/hope|hope]] or

encouragement. His was an involuntary confidence, an irrepressible

effusion to a soothing friend, not an application to a parent. Yet

after a [[motifs/time|time]] I _did_ say, for at first I was quite overcome, that if

she lived, as I trusted she might, my greatest happiness would lie in

promoting their [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]; and since our arrival, since our delightful

security, I have repeated it to him more fully, have given him every

encouragement in my power. [[motifs/time|Time]], a very little [[motifs/time|time]], I tell him, will

do everything; Marianne’s heart is not to be wasted for ever on such a

man as Willoughby. His own merits must soon secure it.”



“To judge from the Colonel’s spirits, however, you have not yet made

him equally sanguine.”



“No. He thinks Marianne’s affection too deeply rooted for any change in

it under a great length of [[motifs/time|time]], and even supposing her heart again

free, is too diffident of himself to believe, that with such a

difference of age and disposition he could ever attach her. There,

however, he is quite mistaken. His age is only so much beyond hers as

to be an advantage, as to make his character and principles fixed; and

his disposition, I am [[motifs/well|well]] convinced, is exactly the very one to make

your sister happy. And his person, his manners too, are all in his

favour. My partiality does not blind me; he certainly is not so

handsome as Willoughby; but at the same [[motifs/time|time]], there is something much

more pleasing in his countenance. There was always a something, if you

remember, in Willoughby’s eyes at times, which I did not like.”



Elinor could _not_ remember it; but her mother, without waiting for her

assent, continued,



“And his manners, the Colonel’s manners are not only more pleasing to

me than Willoughby’s ever were, but they are of a kind I [[motifs/well|well]] know to

be more solidly attaching to Marianne. Their gentleness, their genuine

attention to other people, and their manly unstudied simplicity is much

more accordant with her real disposition, than the liveliness, often

artificial, and often ill-timed of the other. I am very sure myself,

that had Willoughby turned out as really amiable, as he has proved

himself the contrary, Marianne would yet never have been so happy with

_him_ as she will be with [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]].”



She paused.—Her daughter could not quite agree with her, but her

dissent was not heard, and therefore gave no offence.



“At Delaford, she will be within an easy distance of me,” added Mrs.

Dashwood, “even if I remain at Barton; and in all probability,—for I

hear it is a large village,—indeed there certainly _must_ be some small

house or cottage close by, that would suit us quite as [[motifs/well|well]] as our

present situation.”



Poor Elinor!—here was a new scheme for getting her to Delaford!—but her

spirit was stubborn.



“His fortune too!—for at my [[motifs/time|time]] of life you know, everybody cares

about _that;_—and though I neither know nor [[motifs/desire|desire]] to know, what it

really is, I am sure it must be a good one.”



Here they were interrupted by the entrance of a third person, and

Elinor withdrew to think it all over in private, to wish success to her

friend, and yet in wishing it, to feel a pang for Willoughby.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Non appena si presentava l’opportunità di un colloquio privato tra loro.



“Finalmente siamo soli. Mia Elinor, tu non conosci ancora tutta la mia felicità.”

Il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] ama Marianne. Me lo ha detto lui stesso.



Sua figlia, provando alternativamente piacere e dolore, sorpresa e…

Nessuna sorpresa; c'era solo un silenzioso attenzionamento da parte di tutti.



“Tu non sei mai come me, cara Elinor. Altrimenti dovrei [[concepts/wonder|chiedermi]] perché, ”

“Composizione, ora… Se solo mi fossi seduto per desiderare qualcosa di buono per me…”

Per quanto riguarda la famiglia, avrei dovuto pensare che il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] sposasse una di voi.

L’oggetto più desiderabile… E credo che Marianne sarà proprio quella.

“Felice con lui dei due.”



Elinor era quasi tentata di chiederle il motivo per cui la pensava così…

"Soddisfatto che nessuno si sia basato su una valutazione imparziale della loro età..."

Personaggi o sentimenti potevano essere attribuiti… ma sua madre doveva sempre rimanere quella.

Trascinata via dalla sua [[concepts/imagination|immaginazione]] su qualsiasi argomento interessante, e

Pertanto, invece di indagare, si limitò ad accettarlo con un sorriso.



“Ieri, mentre viaggiavamo, mi ha aperto completamente il suo cuore… E tutto è venuto fuori.”

Del tutto inaspettatamente, del tutto senza alcuna intenzione premeditata. Potete credermi, io sarei in grado di parlare.

Nient'altro che mio figlio. Non riusciva a nascondere il suo dolore; me ne resi conto.

Era uguale al mio; forse lui pensava che una semplice [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], come.

Il mondo di oggi non giustificherebbe mai un simile calore di solidarietà… o meglio, no.

Immagino che non abbia nemmeno pensato… Le emozioni irresistibili hanno preso il sopravvento su di me.

Conoscendo la sua sincera, tenera, costante affezione per Marianne.

L'ha amata, la mia Elinor, fin dal primo momento in cui l'ha vista.

“Lei.”



Qui, tuttavia, Elinor percepì… non le parole, non le dichiarazioni.

Dell’[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], ma con gli ornamenti naturali ereditati dalla madre.

Fantasia vivace, che trasformava ogni cosa in qualcosa di delizioso per lei…

Scelse.



Il suo affetto per lei superava di gran lunga qualsiasi cosa Willoughby potesse provare…

Mai hai provato o fingito di essere più caloroso, più sincero…

Costante… che nome le diamo, essa è sopravvissuta attraverso tutto…

Conoscenza della triste ossessione di cara Marianne per quell’indesiderabile…

Giovane uomo, e senza egoismo, senza alimentare alcuna [[concepts/hope|speranza]], potrebbe davvero?

Ha visto come fosse felice con un altro… Che nobile anima… Quanta apertura, quanta generosità…

Sincerità! Nessuno può essere ingannato da lui.



“Il carattere di [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]],” disse Elinor, “come uomo eccellente, ”

“Ben radicato.”



“Lo so che è così”, rispose seriamente sua madre, “dopo un avvertimento del genere…”

Non dovrei essere l’ultimo ad incoraggiare un tale affetto, né tantomeno a…

Felice di averlo fatto… Ma il modo in cui è venuto da me, con tanta determinazione e impegno…

Un'amicizia sincera è sufficiente per dimostrare che una persona appartiene ai più preziosi tra gli uomini.



“Tuttavia, il suo carattere non si basa su un singolo atto”, rispose Elinor.

Titolo:  
Della gentilezza… e del sentimento che provava per Marianne… una umanità che trascendeva ogni limite.

Il caso, probabilmente, lo avrebbe spinto ad agire… Verso la signora Jennings, verso i Middleton…

Lo conoscono da tempo e in modo intimo; entrambi lo [[motifs/love|amano]] e lo rispettano.

Conoscenza limitata

Un uomo di notevole valore… E io lo apprezzo e lo stimo così tanto che, se…

“Marianne può essere felice con lui… Anch’io sarò pronto esattamente come te.”

Riteniamo che il nostro legame sia la più grande benedizione della nostra vita. Che cosa…

“Gli hai dato una risposta? Gli hai permesso di [[concepts/hope|sperare]]?”



“Oh, mio [[motifs/love|amore]], in quel momento non potevo parlare di [[concepts/hope|speranza]] né con lui né con me stessa.”

In quel momento, Marianne poteva anche essere in punto di morte. Ma lui non chiese né [[concepts/hope|speranza]] né, altro.

Incoraggiamento. Era una fiducia involontaria, irrefrenabile…

Un messaggio di conforto rivolto a un amico fidato… non certo una richiesta ai genitori. Eppure…

Dopo un po’ di tempo, alla fine dissi sì, perché all’inizio ero davvero sopraffatto dall’emozione.

Titolo:  
Viveva… come speravo che facesse; la mia più grande felicità consisteva nel…

Promuovere il loro [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]]; e da quando siamo arrivati, da quando tutto è stato così piacevole.

"Segurança", gliel'ho ripetuto più volte in modo chiaro e dettagliato, gli ho fornito tutte le informazioni necessarie."

Un incoraggiamento è nel mio potere. [[motifs/time|Tempo]],] molto poco [[motifs/time|tempo]], gli dico io, e tutto sarà risolto.

Fai di tutto… Ma il cuore di Marianne non deve essere sprecato per sempre in qualcosa del genere

“L’uomo come Willoughby: i suoi meriti personali ne garantiranno presto il successo.”



“A giudicare dall’umore del colonnello, però, sembra che non siate ancora riusciti…”

“Altrettanto ottimista su di lui.”



"No. Ritiene che l’affetto di Marianne sia troppo radicato per poter subire alcun cambiamento."

Dopo un lungo periodo di tempo, anche ammettendo che il suo cuore potesse nuovamente.

Libero… ma troppo insicuro di sé per credere che, con qualcosa del genere…

Differenza d’età e temperamento: un legame impossibile da creare. Lì…

Tuttavia, si sbaglia di grosso: la differenza d’età tra loro è davvero minima.

Per essere un vantaggio, affinché il suo carattere e i suoi principi rimangano saldi e immutabili…

Sono assolutamente convinto che il suo carattere sia proprio quello adatto per fare.

“Tua sorella è felice… E anche la sua persona, i suoi modi… tutto è davvero a posto.”

Favore… La mia preferenza non mi acceca: di certo lui non è così.

Attraente quanto Willoughby, ma allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]], c’è qualcosa di molto diverso.

Il suo volto appariva più piacevole da vedere… C’era sempre qualcosa, se si vuole…

“Ricorda… a volte, negli occhi di Willoughby, qualcosa che non mi piaceva affatto.”



Elinor non riusciva a ricordarlo; ma sua madre, senza aspettare che lei rispondesse…

Assenso continuato



“E i modi del Colonnello… non sono solo più piacevoli da osservare…”

Non sono mai state come quelle di Willoughby, ma appartengono a quel tipo che io conosco molto bene.

“Legarsi sempre di più a Marianne… La loro dolcezza, la loro sincerità…”

Attenzione verso gli altri e la loro semplicità naturale, senza alcuna affettazione… molto importante.

Un titolo più in linea con la sua vera natura, piuttosto che quella vivacità… spesso presente.

“Artificiale, e spesso inopportuno… Ne sono assolutamente convinto.”

Willoughby si rivelò davvero affabile, come aveva dimostrato di essere.

Al contrario, Marianne non sarebbe mai stata così felice se…

_lui_, così come lei sarà con [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]].”



Si fermò un attimo… Sua figlia non era del tutto d’accordo con lei, ma…

Non si udì alcuna voce di dissenso, quindi non ci fu alcun offesa.



“A Delaford, sarà a poca distanza da me,” aggiunse la signora.

Dashwood: “Anche se rimarrò a Barton… e con ogni probabilità…”

Un villaggio grande… di certo devono esserci anche dei piccoli luoghi…

Una casa o una capanna nelle vicinanze, che ci andasse altrettanto bene quanto la nostra.

“La situazione attuale”.



Povera Elinor!… Ecco un nuovo piano per farla andare a Delaford… Ma lei…

Lo spirito era testardo.



Anche la sua fortuna! – perché alla mia età, come sai, a tutti importa.

Riguardo a _quello_; e anche se non so né desidero sapere cosa sia.

“Deve davvero essere un bel libro, ne sono sicuro.”



Qui furono interrotti dall’ingresso di una terza persona.

Elinor si ritirò per riflettere su tutto in privato, per augurare il proprio successo a ciò che stava facendo.

Amico. Eppure, nel desiderarlo, provavo un senso di malinconia per Willoughby.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_46--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 46 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 46" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/journey,motif/nature,motif/road,motif/well,motif/window,concept/body,concept/courage,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/suffering,concept/wonder,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER XLVI.





Marianne’s illness, though weakening in its kind, had not been long

enough to make her recovery slow; and with youth, natural strength, and

her mother’s presence in aid, it proceeded so smoothly as to enable her

to remove, within four days after the arrival of the latter, into Mrs.

Palmer’s dressing-room. When there, at her own particular request, for

she was impatient to pour forth her thanks to him for fetching her

mother, [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] was invited to visit her.



His emotion on entering the room, in seeing her altered looks, and in

receiving the pale hand which she immediately held out to him, was

such, as, in Elinor’s conjecture, must arise from something more than

his affection for Marianne, or the consciousness of its being known to

others; and she soon discovered in his [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] eye and varying

complexion as he looked at her sister, the probable recurrence of many

past scenes of misery to his mind, brought back by that resemblance

between Marianne and Eliza already acknowledged, and now strengthened

by the hollow eye, the sickly skin, the posture of reclining weakness,

and the warm acknowledgment of peculiar obligation.



Mrs. Dashwood, not less watchful of what passed than her daughter, but

with a mind very differently influenced, and therefore watching to very

different effect, saw nothing in the Colonel’s behaviour but what arose

from the most simple and [[concepts/self|self]]-evident sensations, while in the actions

and words of Marianne she persuaded herself to think that something

more than gratitude already dawned.



At the end of another day or two, Marianne growing visibly stronger

every twelve hours, Mrs. Dashwood, urged equally by her own and her

daughter’s wishes, began to talk of removing to Barton. On _her_

measures depended those of her two friends; Mrs. Jennings could not

quit Cleveland during the Dashwoods’ stay; and [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] was soon

brought, by their united request, to consider his own abode there as

equally determinate, if not equally indispensable. At his and Mrs.

Jennings’s united request in return, Mrs. Dashwood was prevailed on to

accept the use of his carriage on her [[motifs/journey|journey]] back, for the better

accommodation of her sick [[archetypes/child|child]]; and the Colonel, at the joint

invitation of Mrs. Dashwood and Mrs. Jennings, whose active good-[[concepts/nature|nature]]

made her friendly and hospitable for other people as [[motifs/well|well]] as herself,

engaged with pleasure to redeem it by a visit at the cottage, in the

course of a few weeks.



The day of separation and departure arrived; and Marianne, after taking

so particular and lengthened a leave of Mrs. Jennings, one so earnestly

grateful, so full of respect and kind wishes as seemed due to her own

heart from a secret acknowledgment of past inattention, and bidding

[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] farewell with a cordiality of a friend, was carefully

assisted by him into the carriage, of which he seemed anxious that she

should engross at least half. Mrs. Dashwood and Elinor then followed,

and the others were left by themselves, to talk of the travellers, and

feel their own dullness, till Mrs. Jennings was summoned to her chaise

to take comfort in the gossip of her maid for the loss of her two young

companions; and [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] immediately afterwards took his

solitary way to Delaford.



The Dashwoods were two days on the [[motifs/road|road]], and Marianne bore her [[motifs/journey|journey]]

on both, without essential fatigue. Every thing that the most zealous

affection, the most solicitous care could do to render her comfortable,

was the office of each watchful companion, and each found their reward

in her bodily ease, and her calmness of spirits. To Elinor, the

observation of the latter was particularly grateful. She, who had seen

her week after week so constantly [[concepts/suffering|suffering]], oppressed by anguish of

heart which she had neither [[concepts/courage|courage]] to speak of, nor fortitude to

conceal, now saw with a joy, which no other could equally share, an

apparent composure of mind, which, in being the result as she trusted

of serious reflection, must eventually lead her to contentment and

cheerfulness.



As they approached Barton, indeed, and entered on scenes of which every

field and every tree brought some peculiar, some painful recollection,

she grew silent and thoughtful, and turning away her face from their

notice, sat earnestly gazing through the [[motifs/window|window]]. But here, Elinor could

neither [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] nor blame; and when she saw, as she assisted Marianne

from the carriage, that she had been crying, she saw only an emotion

too natural in itself to raise any thing less tender than pity, and in

its unobtrusiveness entitled to praise. In the whole of her subsequent

manner, she traced the direction of a mind awakened to reasonable

exertion; for no sooner had they entered their common sitting-room,

than Marianne turned her eyes around it with a look of resolute

firmness, as if determined at once to accustom herself to the sight of

every object with which the remembrance of Willoughby could be

connected.—She said little, but every sentence aimed at cheerfulness,

and though a sigh sometimes escaped her, it never passed away without

the atonement of a smile. After dinner she would try her piano-forte.

She went to it; but the music on which her eye first rested was an

opera, procured for her by Willoughby, containing some of their

favourite duets, and bearing on its outward leaf her own name in his

hand-writing.—That would not do.—She shook her head, put the music

aside, and after running over the keys for a minute, complained of
