Si era trasferita con la madre di lui, e quando quel momento decisivo fu passato…

Avrebbe voluto anche lei stringergli la mano… Ma ormai era troppo tardi.

In ritardo, e con un’espressione che sembrava voler essere aperta e sincera, si sedette di nuovo.

Parlarono del tempo.



Marianne si era ritirata il più possibile fuori dalla vista, per nascondersi.

Distress… e Margaret, che ne comprendeva una parte, ma non tutta intera…

Il caso… Pensò che fosse suo dovere comportarsi con dignità, e quindi…

Si sedette il più lontano possibile da lui e mantenne una distanza rigorosa.

[[motifs/silence|silenzio]].



Quando Elinor smise di godersi la secchezza di quella stagione…

Si verificò un terribile silenzio… Fu interrotto da Madame Dashwood, la quale provava…

Era costretto ad [[concepts/hope|sperare]] che avesse lasciato la signora Ferrars in ottime condizioni. In fretta e furia.

In quel modo, rispose affermativamente.



Un’altra pausa.



Elinor si decide a impegnarsi, nonostante tema il suono della propria voce

Voce… ora pronunciata.



“La signora Ferrars è a Longstaple?”



“Ad Longstaple!”, rispose lui, con un tono di sorpresa. “No, mia madre è…”

“In città”.



“Volevo dire…”, disse Elinor, prendendo alcuni lavori dal tavolo, “che volevo chiedere…”

“Per la signora Edward Ferrars.”



Non osava alzare lo sguardo; ma sia sua madre che Marianne girarono entrambe la testa verso di lei

Gli occhi di tutti fissi su di lui… Arrossì, sembrava perplesso, guardava con scetticismo…

Dopo un po’ di esitazione, disse:—



“Forse intendi… mio fratello… intendi la signora… la signora Robert Ferrars.”



“Signora Robert Ferrars!”, ripeterono insieme Marianna e sua madre.

Un’espressione di estrema meraviglia; e sebbene Elinor non riuscisse a parlare, nemmeno…

I suoi occhi erano fissi su di lui con lo stesso impaziente [[concepts/wonder|stupore]]. Lui si [[motifs/rose|alzò]].

Dalla sua sedia, si avvicinò alla [[motifs/window|finestra]], evidentemente perché non lo sapeva.

Cosa fare… Prese un paio di forbici che erano lì e, mentre…

Rovinando sia loro che il loro “ fodero” tagliandolo in pezzi…

“Parlò, disse, con voce affrettata…”



“Forse non lo sai… Forse non hai mai sentito dire che mio fratello…”

Di recente sposato con, la più giovane, la signorina [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]].”



Le sue parole suscitarono un’indescrivibile meraviglia in tutti, tranne che in Elinor.

Chi sedeva con la testa china sul proprio lavoro, in uno stato del genere…

L’agitazione la rendeva quasi incapace di capire dove si trovasse.



“Sì,” disse lui, “si sono sposati la scorsa settimana e ora si trovano a Dawlish.”



Elinor non riusciva più a trattenersi; uscì di corsa dalla stanza…

Non appena la porta si chiuse, scoppiò in [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] di gioia, che all’inizio.

Una sofferenza che sembrava non avrebbe mai fine… Edward, che fino ad allora aveva mostrato…

Dove, piuttosto che accanto a lei, la vide allontanarsi di fretta… e forse anche vide… o addirittura…

Sentì la sua emozione; perché subito dopo cadde in una sorta di trance.

Nessun commento, nessuna domanda, nessuna parola affettuosa da parte della signora.

Titolo:  
Dashwood riuscì a penetrare, e alla fine, senza dire una parola, se ne andò.

La stanza… e uscì verso il villaggio, lasciando gli altri lì dentro.

La più grande meraviglia e perplessità di fronte al cambiamento della sua situazione…

“Meraviglioso e così improvviso… Una situazione di perplessità dalla quale non avevano alcun modo per uscire.”

Riducendola, ma solo attraverso le loro stesse congetture.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_49--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 49 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 49" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/clock,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/night,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/despair,concept/doubt,concept/freedom,concept/hope,concept/truth,setting/oxford"></span>


CHAPTER XLIX.





Unaccountable, however, as the circumstances of his release might

appear to the whole family, it was certain that Edward was free; and to

what purpose that [[concepts/freedom|freedom]] would be employed was easily pre-determined

by all;—for after experiencing the blessings of _one_ imprudent

engagement, contracted without his mother’s consent, as he had already

done for more than four years, nothing less could be expected of him in

the failure of _that_, than the immediate contraction of another.



His errand at Barton, in fact, was a simple one. It was only to ask

Elinor to marry him;—and considering that he was not altogether

inexperienced in such a question, it might be strange that he should

feel so uncomfortable in the present case as he really did, so much in

need of encouragement and fresh air.



How soon he had walked himself into the proper resolution, however, how

soon an opportunity of exercising it occurred, in what manner he

expressed himself, and how he was received, need not be particularly

told. This only need be said;—that when they all sat down to table at

four o’[[motifs/clock|clock]], about three hours after his arrival, he had secured his

lady, engaged her mother’s consent, and was not only in the rapturous

profession of the [[archetypes/lover|lover]], but, in the reality of reason and [[concepts/truth|truth]], one

of the happiest of men. His situation indeed was more than commonly

joyful. He had more than the ordinary triumph of accepted [[motifs/love|love]] to swell

his heart, and raise his spirits. He was released without any reproach

to himself, from an entanglement which had long formed his misery, from

a woman whom he had long ceased to [[motifs/love|love]];—and elevated at once to that

security with another, which he must have thought of almost with

[[concepts/despair|despair]], as soon as he had learnt to consider it with [[motifs/desire|desire]]. He was

brought, not from [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] or suspense, but from misery to happiness;—and

the change was openly spoken in such a genuine, flowing, grateful

cheerfulness, as his friends had never witnessed in him before.



His heart was now open to Elinor, all its weaknesses, all its errors

confessed, and his first boyish attachment to Lucy treated with all the

philosophic dignity of twenty-four.



“It was a foolish, idle inclination on my side,” said he, “the

consequence of ignorance of the world, and want of employment. Had my

mother given me some active profession when I was removed at eighteen

from the care of Mr. Pratt, I think, nay, I am sure, it would never

have happened; for though I left Longstaple with what I thought, at the

[[motifs/time|time]], a most unconquerable preference for his niece, yet had I then had

any pursuit, any object to engage my [[motifs/time|time]] and keep me at a distance

from her for a few months, I should very soon have outgrown the fancied

attachment, especially by mixing more with the world, as in such case I

must have done. But instead of having any thing to do, instead of

having any profession chosen for me, or being allowed to chuse any

myself, I returned [[motifs/home|home]] to be completely idle; and for the first

twelvemonth afterwards I had not even the nominal employment, which

belonging to the university would have given me; for I was not entered

at [[settings/oxford|Oxford]] till I was nineteen. I had therefore nothing in the world to

do, but to fancy myself in [[motifs/love|love]]; and as my mother did not make my [[motifs/home|home]]

in every respect comfortable, as I had no friend, no companion in my

brother, and disliked new acquaintance, it was not unnatural for me to

be very often at Longstaple, where I always felt myself at [[motifs/home|home]], and

was always sure of a welcome; and accordingly I spent the greatest part

of my [[motifs/time|time]] there from eighteen to nineteen: Lucy appeared everything

that was amiable and obliging. She was pretty too—at least I thought so

_then;_ and I had seen so little of other women, that I could make no

comparisons, and see no defects. Considering everything, therefore, I

[[concepts/hope|hope]], foolish as our engagement was, foolish as it has since in every

way been proved, it was not at the [[motifs/time|time]] an unnatural or an inexcusable

piece of folly.”



The change which a few hours had wrought in the minds and the happiness

of the Dashwoods, was such—so great—as promised them all, the

satisfaction of a sleepless [[motifs/night|night]]. Mrs. Dashwood, too happy to be

comfortable, knew not how to [[motifs/love|love]] Edward, nor praise Elinor enough, how

to be enough thankful for his release without wounding his delicacy,

nor how at once to give them leisure for unrestrained conversation

together, and yet enjoy, as she wished, the sight and society of both.



Marianne could speak _her_ happiness only by [[motifs/tears|tears]]. Comparisons would

occur—regrets would arise; and her joy, though sincere as her [[motifs/love|love]] for

her sister, was of a kind to give her neither spirits nor language.



But Elinor—how are _her_ feelings to be described? From the moment of

learning that Lucy was married to another, that Edward was free, to the

moment of his justifying the hopes which had so instantly followed, she

was every thing by turns but tranquil. But when the second moment had

passed, when she found every [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], every solicitude removed, compared

her situation with what so lately it had been,—saw him honourably

released from his former engagement,—saw him instantly profiting by the

release, to address herself and declare an affection as tender, as

constant as she had ever supposed it to be,—she was oppressed, she was

overcome by her own felicity; and happily disposed as is the human mind

to be easily familiarized with any change for the better, it required

several hours to give sedateness to her spirits, or any degree of

tranquillity to her heart.



Edward was now fixed at the cottage at least for a week;—for whatever

other claims might be made on him, it was impossible that less than a

Incomprensibile, tuttavia, le circostanze della sua liberazione…

A tutta la famiglia sembrava certo che Edward fosse libero; e…

Lo scopo per cui quella [[concepts/freedom|libertà]] sarebbe stata utilizzata era facilmente prevedibile.

Per tutti… perché dopo aver sperimentato i benefici di un’azione imprudente…

Impegno contratto senza il consenso di sua madre, poiché egli lo aveva già fatto…

Dopo più di quattro anni… non si poteva certo aspettarsi nulla di meno da lui.

Il fallimento di _quello_, piuttosto che la contrazione immediata di un altro.



Il suo compito a Barton, in realtà, era molto semplice: doveva soltanto chiedere…

Elinor lo sposerà… ma considerando che lui non era del tutto…

Inesperto in una questione del genere, potrebbe sembrare strano che lui…

Si sente davvero a disagio in questa situazione, molto di più di quanto non si possa immaginare.

Necessità di incoraggiamento e aria fresca.



Ma quanto in fretta riuscì ad arrivare alla giusta decisione…

Ben presto si presentò l’opportunità di metterlo in pratica, e in che modo lo fece…

Il modo in cui si è espresso e il modo in cui è stato accolto non hanno bisogno di essere descritti in dettaglio…

Detto questo, basta aggiungere che quando tutti si sedettero a tavola…

La signorina ottenne il consenso di sua madre e non era affatto solo…

La dichiarazione d'amore di uno [[archetypes/lover|innamorato]], ma nella realtà della ragione e della [[concepts/truth|verità]], tutto è diverso.

Il più felice degli uomini… La sua situazione, infatti, era davvero insolita rispetto alla norma.

Felice. Provava una gioia più grande di quella derivante dal normale trionfo di un amore accettato e condiviso.

Riscaldare il suo cuore e sollevargli lo spirito… Fu rilasciato senza alcuna rimprovera.

Per sé stesso, per liberarsi da un intrigo che da tempo costituiva la sua sofferenza…

Una donna che da tempo aveva smesso di [[motifs/love|_amare]], e che improvvisamente fu elevata a quel livello.

La sicurezza con un altro… qualcosa che sicuramente aveva già preso in considerazione.

La [[concepts/despair|disperazione]], non appena imparò a considerarla con [[motifs/desire|desiderio]]. Lui era.

Portato non dalla [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] o dall'incertezza, ma dalla sofferenza alla felicità;—e

La modifica fu discussa apertamente in modo così sincero, fluido e grato…

Allegria, come i suoi amici non l'avevano mai visto prima in lui.



Il suo cuore era ora aperto a Elinor, con tutte le sue debolezze, tutti i suoi errori.

Confessato… e il suo primo sentimento infantile per Lucy fu affrontato con tutto il dovuto rigore.

La dignità filosofica di ventiquattro anni.



“È stata una debolezza sciocca e inutile da parte mia,” disse. “La…”

"Conseguenza dell’ignoranza del mondo e della mancanza di lavoro… Avevo il mio“

Una professione attiva mi fu data da mia madre quando avevo diciotto anni

Dalla cura del signor Pratt, penso… no, ne sono sicuro: mai.

Titolo:  
Anche se sono partito da Longstaple con certe convinzioni…

Nel [[motifs/time|tempo]] passato, provavo un'affetto insuperabile per mia nipote; tuttavia, se allora avessi avuto.

Qualsiasi attività, qualsiasi obiettivo che possa occupare il mio [[motifs/time|tempo]] e tenermi impegnato.

Per alcuni mesi… avrei presto superato quella fantasia.

Titolo:  
“Attaccamento, soprattutto attraverso l’integrazione con il mondo esterno… come in questo caso.”

Deve averlo fatto… Ma invece di fare qualcosa, invece di…

Essere costretti ad adottare una professione scelta per me, o essere lasciati liberi di sceglierne qualsiasi

Io stesso tornai a [[motifs/home|casa]] per poter stare completamente a riposo; ed era la prima volta.

Dodici mesi dopo, non possedevo nemmeno un lavoro nominale…

Appartenenza all'università avrebbe potuto darmelo… poiché non ero stato ammesso.

A [[settings/oxford|Oxford]], fino ai diciannove anni. Quindi, non avevo nulla al mondo.

Lo faccio, ma immaginare di essere innamorata. E poiché mia madre non ha creato per me un vero e proprio “casa”.

In ogni senso confortevole… poiché non avevo amici, nessuno con cui condividere quel momento.

“Fratello… e un nuovo conoscente che non mi piaceva: non era affatto strano che io…”

Ero molto spesso a Longstaple, dove mi sentivo sempre come a [[motifs/home|casa]], e.

Sempre sicuro di essere accolto con favore; e così trascorsi la maggior parte del tempo…

Del mio [[motifs/time|periodo]] lì, tra gli diciotto e i diciannove anni: Lucy rappresentava tutto per me.

“Era davvero gentile e premurosa… E anche carina, almeno così pensavo.”

Poi… e avendo visto così poche altre donne, non riuscivo proprio a fare nulla.

“Confronti e nessun difetto evidente… Pertanto, considerando tutto ciò…”

La [[concepts/hope|speranza]], per quanto sciocca fosse la nostra promessa, per quanto sciocca sia rimasta da allora.

Essendo stato dimostrato in modo incontrovertibile, non si trattava all’[[motifs/time|epoca]] di un comportamento innaturale o inescusabile.

“Un’azione davvero stupida.”



Il cambiamento che poche ore avevano apportato nelle menti e nella felicità…

Il titolo dei Dashwood era davvero tale – così straordinario – come tutti avevano sperato.

Il riposo dopo una [[motifs/night|notte]] insonne. La signora Dashwood, troppo felice per poter essere altrimenti.

Comoda com'era, non sapeva come [[motifs/love|amare]] Edward, né come lodare abbastanza Elinor, come?

Essere sufficientemente grato per la sua liberazione, senza ferire la sua sensibilità…

Come poter loro concedere subito il tempo necessario per conversare liberamente

Insieme, eppure potendo godere, come desiderava lei, sia della vista che della compagnia di entrambi.



Marianne poteva esprimere la propria felicità soltanto attraverso le [[motifs/tears|lacrime]]; qualsiasi paragone sarebbe stato inutile.

Se fosse accaduto, sarebbero sorti rimpianti; e la sua gioia, sebbene sincera quanto il suo [[motifs/love|amore]] per.

Sua sorella era il tipo di persona che non le dava né energia né parole per esprimersi.



Ma Elinor… come possono essere descritti i suoi sentimenti? Dal momento in cui…

Scoprendo che Lucy era sposata con un altro e che Edward era libero…

Il momento in cui realizzò di aver giustificato le speranze che erano nate immediatamente dopo…

Il secondo momento non fu affatto tranquillo…

Passò il tempo; quando tutte le sue [[concepts/doubt|dubbi]] furono dissipate, ogni preoccupazione scomparve, e tutto sembrò più chiaro.

La sua situazione, rispetto a ciò che era accaduto di recente, lo vedeva comportarsi onorevolmente.

Rilasciato dal suo precedente impegno… lo vide immediatamente trarne beneficio

"Libera te stessa e dichiara un affetto così tenero..."

Costante, proprio come aveva sempre immaginato che fosse… Era oppressa.

Sopraffatta dalla propria felicità; e con un animo sereno, come è tipico dell’essere umano…

Per potersi abituare facilmente a qualsiasi cambiamento positivo, era necessario…

“Diverse ore sono necessarie per calmare i suoi spiriti, o almeno per ottenere un certo grado di tranquillità…”

La tranquillità tornò nel suo cuore.



Edward sarebbe rimasto nella capanna per almeno una settimana… per qualsiasi motivo fosse.

Altri diritti potrebbero essere rivendicati su di lui, ma era impossibile che ne venissero meno di uno…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_49--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 49 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 49" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/marriage,motif/road,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/doubt,concept/imagination,concept/jealousy,concept/vanity,concept/wonder,setting/london,setting/oxford,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


week should be given up to the enjoyment of Elinor’s company, or

suffice to say half that was to be said of the past, the present, and

the future;—for though a very few hours spent in the hard labor of

incessant talking will despatch more subjects than can really be in

common between any two rational creatures, yet with lovers it is

different. Between _them_ no subject is finished, no communication is

even made, till it has been made at least twenty times over.



Lucy’s [[motifs/marriage|marriage]], the unceasing and reasonable [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] among them all,

formed of course one of the earliest discussions of the lovers;—and

Elinor’s particular knowledge of each party made it appear to her in

every view, as one of the most extraordinary and unaccountable

circumstances she had ever heard. How they could be thrown together,

and by what attraction Robert could be drawn on to marry a girl, of

whose [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] she had herself heard him speak without any admiration,—a

girl too already engaged to his brother, and on whose account that

brother had been thrown off by his family—it was beyond her

comprehension to make out. To her own heart it was a delightful affair,

to her [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] it was even a ridiculous one, but to her reason, her

judgment, it was completely a puzzle.



Edward could only attempt an explanation by supposing, that, perhaps,

at first accidentally meeting, the [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] of the one had been so worked

on by the flattery of the other, as to lead by degrees to all the rest.

Elinor remembered what Robert had told her in Harley Street, of his

opinion of what his own mediation in his brother’s affairs might have

done, if applied to in [[motifs/time|time]]. She repeated it to Edward.



“_That_ was exactly like Robert,” was his immediate observation. “And

_that_,” he presently added, “might perhaps be in _his_ head when the

acquaintance between them first began. And Lucy perhaps at first might

think only of procuring his good offices in my favour. Other designs

might afterward arise.”



How long it had been carrying on between them, however, he was equally

at a loss with herself to make out; for at [[settings/oxford|Oxford]], where he had

remained for choice ever since his quitting [[settings/london|London]], he had had no means

of hearing of her but from herself, and her letters to the very last

were neither less frequent, nor less affectionate than usual. Not the

smallest suspicion, therefore, had ever occurred to prepare him for

what followed;—and when at last it burst on him in a letter from Lucy

herself, he had been for some [[motifs/time|time]], he believed, half stupified between

the [[concepts/wonder|wonder]], the horror, and the joy of such a deliverance. He put the

letter into Elinor’s hands.



“DEAR SIR,

“Being very sure I have long lost your affections, I have thought

myself at liberty to bestow my own on another, and have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of

being as happy with him as I once used to think I might be with

you; but I scorn to accept a hand while the heart was another’s.

Sincerely wish you happy in your choice, and it shall not be my

fault if we are not always good friends, as our near relationship

now makes proper. I can safely say I owe you no ill-will, and am

sure you will be too generous to do us any ill offices. Your

brother has gained my affections entirely, and as we could not live

without one another, we are just returned from the altar, and are

now on our way to Dawlish for a few weeks, which place your dear

brother has great curiosity to see, but thought I would first

trouble you with these few lines, and shall always remain,





“Your sincere [[motifs/well|well]]-wisher, friend, and sister,

“LUCY FERRARS.





“I have burnt all your letters, and will return your picture the first

opportunity. Please to destroy my scrawls—but the ring with my hair you

are very welcome to keep.”



Elinor read and returned it without any comment.



“I will not ask your opinion of it as a composition,” said Edward.—“For

worlds would not I have had a letter of hers seen by _you_ in former

days.—In a sister it is bad enough, but in a wife!—how I have blushed

over the pages of her writing!—and I believe I may say that since the

first half year of our foolish—business—this is the only letter I ever

received from her, of which the substance made me any amends for the

defect of the style.”



“However it may have come about,” said Elinor, after a pause,—“they are

certainly married. And your mother has brought on herself a most

appropriate punishment. The independence she settled on Robert, through

resentment against you, has put it in his power to make his own choice;

and she has actually been bribing one son with a thousand a-year, to do

the very deed which she disinherited the other for intending to do. She

will hardly be less hurt, I suppose, by Robert’s marrying Lucy, than

she would have been by your marrying her.”



“She will be more hurt by it, for Robert always was her favourite.—She

will be more hurt by it, and on the same principle will forgive him

much sooner.”



In what state the affair stood at present between them, Edward knew

not, for no communication with any of his family had yet been attempted

by him. He had quitted [[settings/oxford|Oxford]] within four and twenty hours after Lucy’s

letter arrived, and with only one object before him, the nearest [[motifs/road|road]]

to Barton, had had no leisure to form any scheme of conduct, with which

that [[motifs/road|road]] did not hold the most intimate connection. He could do

nothing till he were assured of his fate with Miss Dashwood; and by his

rapidity in seeking _that_ fate, it is to be supposed, in spite of the

[[concepts/jealousy|jealousy]] with which he had once thought of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], in spite of

the modesty with which he rated his own deserts, and the politeness

with which he talked of his doubts, he did not, upon the whole, expect

a very cruel reception. It was his business, however, to say that he

La conoscenza tra loro iniziò così… E forse, all’inizio, Lucy…

Pensare solo a ottenere il suo aiuto a mio favore… Altri scopi nascosti.

“Potrebbero sorgere problemi in seguito.”



Da quanto tempo andava avanti tra loro…

Imbarazzata nel non riuscire a capire; perché a [[settings/oxford|Oxford]], dove lui si trovava.

Di lei si sentiva parlare solo da parte sua, e attraverso le sue lettere, fino all’ultima.

Lo [[concepts/wonder|stupore]], l’orrore e la gioia di una tale liberazione. Lui mise.

La lettera finì nelle mani di Elinor.



Caro Signore,

“Essendo assolutamente certo di aver perso da tempo il tuo affetto, ho pensato…”

Ho la libertà di donare il mio affetto a un altro, e non ho alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] al riguardo.

Essere felice con lui proprio come un tempo pensavo di poter essere…

Tu, ma disprezzo l’idea di accettare un aiuto quando il cuore appartiene a qualcun altro.

Auguro sinceramente che tu sia felice nella tua scelta… e che questa non sia una mia decisione.

Se non siamo sempre buoni amici, è colpa nostra, data la nostra stretta relazione…

Ora tutto è a posto. Posso dire con certezza di non provare alcun rancore verso di te, e…

"Certo che sarete troppo generosi per farci del male..."

Il fratello ha conquistato completamente il mio affetto, e poiché non potevamo vivere insieme…

Senza di noi stessi, siamo come se fossimo appena tornati dall’altare… e basta.

Ora siamo in viaggio verso Dawlish per alcune settimane… un luogo che, ne sono sicura, piacerà molto a te.

“Mio fratello ha una grande curiosità di vedere… ma ho pensato che fosse meglio farlo prima io.”

Vi disturbo con queste poche righe, ma rimarrò sempre al vostro fianco.





“Il tuo sincero desideroso di il meglio, amico e sorella, ”

“LUCY FERRARS.”





“Ho bruciato tutte le tue lettere e ti restituirò la tua foto il prima…”

Opportunità… Per favore, distruggi i miei scarabocchi… Ma quel anello con i miei capelli…

“Siete molto i benvenuti a tenerlo.”



Elinor lo lesse e lo restituì senza fare alcun commento.



“Non chiederò mai la tua opinione su questo lavoro letterario,” disse Edward. “Perché…”

Titolo: “Avrei voluto che tu vedessi una sua lettera… in passato”

Giorni… In una sorella è già abbastanza grave, ma in una moglie… Come ho potuto arrossire così!

Tra le pagine delle sue opere… e credo di poter dire che da allora…

Prima metà dell’anno del nostro folle progetto… Questa è l’unica lettera che abbia mai scritto

Titolo:  
Ricevuto da lei… il cui contenuto mi ha permesso di rimediare in qualche modo alle mie colpe.

“Defetto dello stile”.



“Comunque sia successo,” disse Elinor dopo una pausa, “loro sono…”

Punizione adeguata. L’indipendenza che scelse di concedere a Robert…

Rancore verso di te gli ha dato il potere di fare la sua scelta.

E in realtà ha corrotto uno dei suoi figli offrendogli mille sterline all’anno, affinché facesse ciò che voleva…

L’atto stesso per cui lei lo diseredò, proprio perché intendeva compiere quel gesto.

Credo che Robert non rimarrà certo meno ferito dal fatto che sposi Lucy…

“Se solo l’avessi sposata…”



“Le farà ancora più male, perché Robert è sempre stato il suo preferito… Lei.”

Sarà più ferita a causa di questo, e per lo stesso principio gli perdonerà

“Molto prima.”



Titolo:  
In quale stato si trovava attualmente la loro relazione, Edward lo sapeva bene.

Non c’era ancora stata alcuna tentativa di comunicare con la sua famiglia.

Da parte sua. Aveva lasciato [[settings/oxford|Oxford]] entro ventiquattro ore dopo la partenza di Lucy.

Arrivò la lettera; davanti a lui c'era solo un oggetto: la strada più vicina.

A Barton non era stato concesso il tempo di elaborare alcun piano d’azione.

Quella [[motifs/road|strada]] non rappresentava il legame più profondo per lui; poteva comunque.

“Niente, finché non fosse stato certo del proprio destino con la signorina Dashwood…”

La fretta nell’inseguire quel destino… nonostante tutto

La [[concepts/jealousy|invidia]] che un tempo aveva provato per [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]], nonostante.

La modestia con cui valutava i propri meriti, e la cortesia…

Con cui esprimeva i suoi dubbi, in realtà non si aspettava nulla di particolare…

Una accoglienza molto crudele. Tuttavia, spettava a lui decidere cosa dire.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_49--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 49 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 49" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/garden,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/education,concept/friendship,concept/honour,concept/imagination,concept/nature,concept/self,concept/vanity,character/colonel_brandon,character/lucy_steele"></span>


_did_, and he said it very prettily. What he might say on the subject a

twelvemonth after, must be referred to the [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] of husbands and

wives.



That Lucy had certainly meant to deceive, to go off with a flourish of

malice against him in her message by Thomas, was perfectly clear to

Elinor; and Edward himself, now thoroughly enlightened on her

character, had no scruple in believing her capable of the utmost

meanness of wanton ill-[[concepts/nature|nature]]. Though his eyes had been long opened,

even before his acquaintance with Elinor began, to her ignorance and a

want of liberality in some of her opinions—they had been equally

imputed, by him, to her want of [[concepts/education|education]]; and till her last letter

reached him, he had always believed her to be a [[motifs/well|well]]-disposed,

good-hearted girl, and thoroughly attached to himself. Nothing but such

a persuasion could have prevented his putting an end to an engagement,

which, long before the discovery of it laid him open to his mother’s

anger, had been a continual source of disquiet and regret to him.



“I thought it my duty,” said he, “independent of my feelings, to give

her the option of continuing the engagement or not, when I was

renounced by my mother, and stood to all appearance without a friend in

the world to assist me. In such a situation as that, where there seemed

nothing to tempt the avarice or the [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] of any living creature, how

could I suppose, when she so earnestly, so warmly insisted on sharing

my fate, whatever it might be, that any thing but the most

disinterested affection was her inducement? And even now, I cannot

comprehend on what motive she acted, or what fancied advantage it could

be to her, to be fettered to a man for whom she had not the smallest

regard, and who had only two thousand pounds in the world. She could

not foresee that [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] would give me a living.”



“No; but she might suppose that something would occur in your favour;

that your own family might in [[motifs/time|time]] relent. And at any rate, she lost

nothing by continuing the engagement, for she has proved that it

fettered neither her inclination nor her actions. The connection was

certainly a respectable one, and probably gained her consideration

among her friends; and, if nothing more advantageous occurred, it would

be better for her to marry _you_ than be single.”



Edward was, of course, immediately convinced that nothing could have

been more natural than Lucy’s conduct, nor more [[concepts/self|self]]-evident than the

motive of it.



Elinor scolded him, harshly as ladies always scold the imprudence which

compliments themselves, for having spent so much [[motifs/time|time]] with them at

Norland, when he must have felt his own inconstancy.



“Your behaviour was certainly very wrong,” said she; “because—to say

nothing of my own conviction, our relations were all led away by it to

fancy and expect _what_, as you were _then_ situated, could never be.”



He could only plead an ignorance of his own heart, and a mistaken

confidence in the force of his engagement.



“I was simple enough to think, that because my _faith_ was plighted to

another, there could be no danger in my being with you; and that the

consciousness of my engagement was to keep my heart as safe and sacred

as my [[concepts/honour|honour]]. I felt that I admired you, but I told myself it was only

[[concepts/friendship|friendship]]; and till I began to make comparisons between yourself and

Lucy, I did not know how far I was got. After that, I suppose, I _was_

wrong in remaining so much in Sussex, and the arguments with which I

reconciled myself to the expediency of it, were no better than

these:—The danger is my own; I am doing no injury to anybody but

myself.”



Elinor smiled, and shook her head.



Edward heard with pleasure of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s being expected at the

Cottage, as he really wished not only to be better acquainted with him,

but to have an opportunity of convincing him that he no longer resented

his giving him the living of Delaford—“Which, at present,” said he,

“after thanks so ungraciously delivered as mine were on the occasion,

he must think I have never forgiven him for offering.”



_Now_ he felt astonished himself that he had never yet been to the

place. But so little interest had he taken in the matter, that he owed

all his knowledge of the house, [[motifs/garden|garden]], and glebe, extent of the

parish, condition of the land, and rate of the tithes, to Elinor

herself, who had heard so much of it from [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], and heard it

with so much attention, as to be entirely mistress of the subject.



One question after this only remained undecided, between them, one

difficulty only was to be overcome. They were brought together by

mutual affection, with the warmest approbation of their real friends;

their intimate knowledge of each other seemed to make their happiness

certain—and they only wanted something to live upon. Edward had two

thousand pounds, and Elinor one, which, with Delaford living, was all

that they could call their own; for it was impossible that Mrs.

Dashwood should advance anything; and they were neither of them quite

enough in [[motifs/love|love]] to think that three hundred and fifty pounds a-year

would supply them with the comforts of life.



Edward was not entirely without hopes of some favourable change in his

mother towards him; and on _that_ he rested for the residue of their

income. But Elinor had no such dependence; for since Edward would still

be unable to marry Miss Morton, and his chusing herself had been spoken

of in Mrs. Ferrars’s flattering language as only a lesser evil than his

chusing [[characters/lucy-steele|Lucy Steele]], she feared that Robert’s offence would serve no

other purpose than to enrich Fanny.



About four days after Edward’s arrival [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] appeared, to

complete Mrs. Dashwood’s satisfaction, and to give her the dignity of

having, for the first [[motifs/time|time]] since her living at Barton, more company

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_49--part_04" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 49 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 49" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/night,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/body,concept/fear,concept/friendship,concept/honour,concept/humility,concept/reconciliation,concept/wonder,setting/london,setting/oxford,character/colonel_brandon,character/nancy"></span>


with her than her house would hold. Edward was allowed to retain the

privilege of first comer, and [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] therefore walked every

[[motifs/night|night]] to his old quarters at the Park; from whence he usually returned

in the morning, early enough to interrupt the lovers’ first tête-à-tête

before breakfast.



A three weeks’ residence at Delaford, where, in his evening hours at

least, he had little to do but to calculate the disproportion between

thirty-six and seventeen, brought him to Barton in a temper of mind

which needed all the improvement in Marianne’s looks, all the kindness

of her welcome, and all the encouragement of her mother’s language, to

make it cheerful. Among such friends, however, and such flattery, he

did revive. No rumour of Lucy’s [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] had yet reached him:—he knew

nothing of what had passed; and the first hours of his visit were

consequently spent in hearing and in wondering. Every thing was

explained to him by Mrs. Dashwood, and he found fresh reason to rejoice

in what he had done for Mr. Ferrars, since eventually it promoted the

interest of Elinor.



It would be needless to say, that the gentlemen advanced in the good

opinion of each other, as they advanced in each other’s acquaintance,

for it could not be otherwise. Their resemblance in good principles and

good sense, in disposition and manner of thinking, would probably have

been sufficient to unite them in [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], without any other

attraction; but their being in [[motifs/love|love]] with two sisters, and two sisters

fond of each other, made that mutual regard inevitable and immediate,

which might otherwise have waited the effect of [[motifs/time|time]] and judgment.



The letters from town, which a few days before would have made every

nerve in Elinor’s [[concepts/body|body]] thrill with transport, now arrived to be read

with less emotion than mirth. Mrs. Jennings wrote to tell the wonderful

tale, to vent her honest indignation against the jilting girl, and pour

forth her compassion towards poor Mr. Edward, who, she was sure, had

quite doted upon the worthless hussy, and was now, by all accounts,

almost broken-hearted, at [[settings/oxford|Oxford]]. “I do think,” she continued, “nothing

was ever carried on so sly; for it was but two days before Lucy called

and sat a couple of hours with me. Not a [[motifs/soul|soul]] suspected anything of the

matter, not even [[characters/nancy|Nancy]], who, poor [[motifs/soul|soul]]! came crying to me the day

after, in a great fright for [[concepts/fear|fear]] of Mrs. Ferrars, as [[motifs/well|well]] as not

knowing how to get to Plymouth; for Lucy it seems borrowed all her

money before she went off to be married, on purpose we suppose to make

a show with, and poor [[characters/nancy|Nancy]] had not seven shillings in the world; so I

was very glad to give her five guineas to take her down to Exeter,

where she thinks of staying three or four weeks with Mrs. Burgess, in

hopes, as I tell her, to fall in with the Doctor again. And I must say

that Lucy’s crossness not to take them along with them in the chaise is

worse than all. Poor Mr. Edward! I cannot get him out of my head, but

you must send for him to Barton, and Miss Marianne must try to comfort

him.”



Mr. Dashwood’s strains were more solemn. Mrs. Ferrars was the most

unfortunate of women—poor Fanny had suffered agonies of sensibility—and

he considered the existence of each, under such a blow, with grateful

[[concepts/wonder|wonder]]. Robert’s offence was unpardonable, but Lucy’s was infinitely

worse. Neither of them were ever again to be mentioned to Mrs. Ferrars;

and even, if she might hereafter be induced to forgive her son, his

wife should never be acknowledged as her daughter, nor be permitted to

appear in her presence. The secrecy with which everything had been

carried on between them, was rationally treated as enormously

heightening the crime, because, had any suspicion of it occurred to the

others, proper measures would have been taken to prevent the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]];

and he called on Elinor to join with him in regretting that Lucy’s

engagement with Edward had not rather been fulfilled, than that she

should thus be the means of spreading misery farther in the family. He

thus continued:—



“Mrs. Ferrars has never yet mentioned Edward’s name, which does not

surprise us; but, to our great astonishment, not a line has been

received from him on the occasion. Perhaps, however, he is kept silent

by his [[concepts/fear|fear]] of offending, and I shall, therefore, give him a hint, by a

line to [[settings/oxford|Oxford]], that his sister and I both think a letter of proper

submission from him, addressed perhaps to Fanny, and by her shown to

her mother, might not be taken amiss; for we all know the tenderness of

Mrs. Ferrars’s heart, and that she wishes for nothing so much as to be

on good terms with her children.”



This paragraph was of some importance to the prospects and conduct of

Edward. It determined him to attempt a [[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]], though not

exactly in the manner pointed out by their brother and sister.



“A letter of proper submission!” repeated he; “would they have me beg

my mother’s pardon for Robert’s ingratitude to _her_, and breach of

[[concepts/honour|honour]] to _me?_ I can make no submission. I am grown neither humble nor

penitent by what has passed. I am grown very happy; but that would not

interest. I know of no submission that _is_ proper for me to make.”



“You may certainly ask to be forgiven,” said Elinor, “because you have

offended;—and I should think you might _now_ venture so far as to

profess some concern for having ever formed the engagement which drew

on you your mother’s anger.”



He agreed that he might.



“And when she has forgiven you, perhaps a little [[concepts/humility|humility]] may be

convenient while acknowledging a second engagement, almost as imprudent

in _her_ eyes as the first.”



He had nothing to urge against it, but still resisted the idea of a

letter of proper submission; and therefore, to make it easier to him,

as he declared a much greater willingness to make mean concessions by

word of mouth than on paper, it was resolved that, instead of writing

to Fanny, he should go to [[settings/london|London]], and personally intreat her good

offices in his favour. “And if they really _do_ interest themselves,”

said Marianne, in her new character of candour, “in bringing about a

[[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]], I shall think that even John and Fanny are not entirely

without merit.”



After a visit on [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]’s side of only three or four days, the

two gentlemen quitted Barton together. They were to go immediately to

Delaford, that Edward might have some personal knowledge of his future

[[motifs/home|home]], and assist his patron and friend in deciding on what improvements

were needed to it; and from thence, after staying there a couple of

nights, he was to proceed on his [[motifs/journey|journey]] to town.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_50--part_01" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 50 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 50" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/autumn,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/marriage,motif/time,motif/well,concept/honour,concept/humility,concept/truth,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


CHAPTER L.





After a proper resistance on the part of Mrs. Ferrars, just so violent

and so steady as to preserve her from that reproach which she always

seemed fearful of incurring, the reproach of being too amiable, Edward

was admitted to her presence, and pronounced to be again her son.



Her family had of late been exceedingly fluctuating. For many years of

her life she had had two sons; but the crime and annihilation of Edward

a few weeks ago, had robbed her of one; the similar annihilation of

Robert had left her for a fortnight without any; and now, by the

resuscitation of Edward, she had one again.



In spite of his being allowed once more to live, however, he did not

feel the continuance of his existence secure, till he had revealed his

present engagement; for the publication of that circumstance, he

feared, might give a sudden turn to his constitution, and carry him off

as rapidly as before. With apprehensive caution therefore it was

revealed, and he was listened to with unexpected calmness. Mrs. Ferrars

at first reasonably endeavoured to dissuade him from marrying Miss

Dashwood, by every argument in her power;—told him, that in Miss Morton

he would have a woman of higher rank and larger fortune;—and enforced

the assertion, by observing that Miss Morton was the daughter of a

nobleman with thirty thousand pounds, while Miss Dashwood was only the

daughter of a private gentleman with no more than _three;_ but when she

found that, though perfectly admitting the [[concepts/truth|truth]] of her representation,

he was by no means inclined to be guided by it, she judged it wisest,

from the experience of the past, to submit—and therefore, after such an

ungracious delay as she owed to her own dignity, and as served to

prevent every suspicion of good-will, she issued her decree of consent

to the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] of Edward and Elinor.



What she would engage to do towards augmenting their income was next to

be considered; and here it plainly appeared, that though Edward was now

her only son, he was by no means her eldest; for while Robert was

inevitably endowed with a thousand pounds a-year, not the smallest

objection was made against Edward’s taking orders for the sake of two

hundred and fifty at the utmost; nor was anything promised either for

the present or in future, beyond the ten thousand pounds, which had

been given with Fanny.



It was as much, however, as was desired, and more than was expected, by

Edward and Elinor; and Mrs. Ferrars herself, by her shuffling excuses,

seemed the only person surprised at her not giving more.



With an income quite sufficient to their wants thus secured to them,

they had nothing to wait for after Edward was in possession of the

living, but the readiness of the house, to which [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]], with

an eager [[motifs/desire|desire]] for the accommodation of Elinor, was making

considerable improvements; and after waiting some [[motifs/time|time]] for their

completion, after experiencing, as usual, a thousand disappointments

and delays from the unaccountable dilatoriness of the workmen, Elinor,

as usual, broke through the first positive resolution of not marrying

till every thing was ready, and the ceremony took place in Barton

church early in the [[motifs/autumn|autumn]].



The first month after their [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] was spent with their friend at the

Mansion-house; from whence they could superintend the progress of the

Parsonage, and direct every thing as they liked on the spot;—could

chuse papers, project shrubberies, and invent a sweep. Mrs. Jennings’s

prophecies, though rather jumbled together, were chiefly fulfilled; for

she was able to visit Edward and his wife in their Parsonage by

Michaelmas, and she found in Elinor and her husband, as she really

believed, one of the happiest couples in the world. They had in fact

nothing to wish for, but the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] and Marianne,

and rather better pasturage for their cows.



They were visited on their first settling by almost all their relations

and friends. Mrs. Ferrars came to inspect the happiness which she was

almost ashamed of having authorised; and even the Dashwoods were at the

expense of a [[motifs/journey|journey]] from Sussex to do them [[concepts/honour|honour]].



“I will not say that I am disappointed, my dear sister,” said John, as

they were walking together one morning before the gates of Delaford

House, “_that_ would be saying too much, for certainly you have been

one of the most fortunate young women in the world, as it is. But, I

confess, it would give me great pleasure to call [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]]

brother. His property here, his place, his house, every thing is in

such respectable and excellent condition! And his woods,—I have not

seen such timber any where in Dorsetshire, as there is now standing in

Delaford Hanger! And though, perhaps, Marianne may not seem exactly the

person to attract him, yet I think it would altogether be advisable for

you to have them now frequently staying with you, for as Colonel

Brandon seems a great deal at [[motifs/home|home]], nobody can tell what may happen;

for, when people are much thrown together, and see little of anybody

else,—and it will always be in your power to set her off to advantage,

and so forth. In short, you may as [[motifs/well|well]] give her a chance: you

understand me.”



But though Mrs. Ferrars _did_ come to see them, and always treated them

with the make-believe of decent affection, they were never insulted by

her real favour and preference. _That_ was due to the folly of Robert,

and the cunning of his wife; and it was earned by them before many

months had passed away. The selfish sagacity of the latter, which had

at first drawn Robert into the scrape, was the principal instrument of

his deliverance from it; for her respectful [[concepts/humility|humility]], assiduous

attentions, and endless flatteries, as soon as the smallest opening was

given for their exercise, reconciled Mrs. Ferrars to his choice, and


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO L.





Dopo una decisa resistenza da parte della signora Ferrars… davvero molto violenta.

E così ferma da evitare quella critica che lei temeva sempre…

Sembrava temere di incorrere nella rimprovera di essere troppo affabile, Edward.

Fu ammesso alla sua presenza e dichiarato nuovamente suo figlio.



La sua famiglia, negli ultimi tempi, aveva subito notevoli cambiamenti. Per molti anni…

La sua vita: aveva avuto due figli; ma il crimine e la distruzione di Edward…

“Qualche settimana fa, le era stato rubato uno di quegli oggetti… Una distruzione simile…”

Robert l’aveva lasciata per due settimane senza alcuna spiegazione… E ora, finalmente…

Con la risurrezione di Edward, lei ebbe un’altra opportunità.



Nonostante gli fosse stato permesso di vivere ancora una volta, egli non lo fece.

Sentire la continuità della propria esistenza al sicuro, finché non avesse rivelato ciò che aveva in mente…

Titolo: Impegno attuale; per la pubblicazione di tale circostanza, lui…

Si temeva che potesse verificarsi un improvviso cambiamento nel suo stato di salute, portandolo alla morte.

Con la stessa rapidità di prima. Pertanto, con cautela e apprensione…

Rivelato… e fu ascoltato con una calma inaspettata. La signora Ferrars

All’inizio si cercò in modo ragionevole di dissuaderlo dal sposare la signorina…

Titolo:  
“Con ogni argomento a sua disposizione, Dashwood gli spiegò che riguardo alla signorina Morton…”

Avrebbe avuto una donna di rango più elevato e con maggiori ricchezze… e l’avrebbe costretta ad accettare.

L'affermazione, basata sul fatto che la signorina Morton era figlia di…

Un nobile con trentamila sterline, mentre la signorina Dashwood… solo…

Figlia di un gentiluomo privato che non aveva più di tre figli… ma quando lei…

Scoprì che, sebbene ammettesse perfettamente la [[concepts/truth|verità]] di quanto lei aveva descritto,

“Non era affatto disposto ad seguirne i consigli; lei riteneva che fosse la cosa più saggia da fare.”

Dalla esperienza del passato… per sottomettersi – e quindi, dopo tutto ciò…

Un ritardo ingiusto, dovuto alla sua stessa dignità… e che serviva soltanto a…

Per evitare qualsiasi sospetto di buone intenzioni, emise il suo decreto di consenso.

al [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] di Edward ed Elinor.



Titolo:  
Quello che era disposta a fare per aumentare il loro reddito…

Da prendere in considerazione; e qui risultava chiaramente che, sebbene Edward ora…

Il suo unico figlio… ma di certo non il maggiore; infatti, mentre Robert era…

Inevitabilmente dotato di mille sterline all’anno… nemmeno la minima quantità.

Fu sollevata obiezione al fatto che Edward accettasse ordini per il bene di due persone.

Cento cinquanta al massimo; e non fu promesso nulla nemmeno in merito ad altro.

Il presente o il futuro… al di là delle diecimila sterline che aveva…

È stato dato a Fanny.



Era esattamente ciò che si desiderava, e anche di più di quanto si fosse previsto.

Edward ed Elinor; e la stessa signora Ferrars, con le sue scuse evasive

Sembrava l’unica persona sorpresa dal fatto che lei non avesse dato di più.



Con un reddito più che sufficiente a soddisfare le loro esigenze,

Non c’era nulla da aspettare una volta che Edward ne aveva preso possesso

Vivendo lì, ma grazie alla disponibilità della casa, dove [[characters/colonel-brandon|-Colonnello Brandon]], insieme ad altri.

Un ardente [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di ospitare Elinor lo spingeva a farlo.

Miglioramenti considerevoli; e dopo aver aspettato per un certo [[motifs/time|tempo]].

Completamento, dopo aver vissuto, come al solito, mille delusioni

"Elinor e i ritardi causati dall’incomprensibile lentezza dei lavoratori"

Come al solito, ha infranto la prima decisione positiva di non sposarsi.

Fino a quando tutto non fu pronto e la cerimonia ebbe luogo a Barton

Andò in chiesa all’inizio dell’[[motifs/autumn|autunno]].



Il primo mese dopo il loro [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] lo trascorsero con un loro amico.

Mansione-casa; da dove potevano seguire lo svolgimento dei lavori.

“Parsonage: dirigere tutto secondo i loro desideri, sul momento stesso…”

Documenti scelti, arbusti piantati e un sistema di pulizia ideato… La signora Jennings

Le profezie, sebbene piuttosto disordinate, si avverarono per lo più; infatti…

Riuscì a visitare Edward e sua moglie nella loro canonica.

Michaelmas… e scoprì in Elinor e suo marito ciò che realmente cercava

Si diceva che fossero una delle coppie più felici del mondo… Infatti lo erano davvero.

Niente di cui desiderare, se non il [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] tra [[characters/colonel-brandon|-Colonnello Brandon]] e Marianne.

E inoltre pascoli molto migliori per le loro mucche.



Durante il loro primo periodo di insediamento, furono visitati da quasi tutti i loro parenti.

E amici… La signora Ferrars venne a verificare se quella felicità esistesse davvero.

Quasi imbarazzato per aver dato il permesso… E anche i Dashwood erano…

A spese di un [[motifs/journey|Viaggio]] dal Sussex per onorarli.



“Non direi di essere deluso, mia cara sorella”, disse John.

Camminavano insieme una mattina, davanti ai cancelli di Delaford

House, “Quello significherebbe dire troppo, perché sicuramente tu hai già, ”

“Una delle giovani donne più fortunate del mondo… almeno per ora.”

Confessa. Mi darebbe grande piacere chiamare il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]].

Fratello. La sua proprietà qui, il suo posto, la sua casa. Tutto è lì.

In condizioni così rispettabili ed eccellenti! E i suoi boschi… non ne ho ancora parlato.

Non ho mai visto in tutto il Dorsetshire legname del genere, come quello che ora si trova lì.

Delaford Hanger! E anche se forse Marianne non sembra esattamente…

Personaggio in grado di attirarlo… Tuttavia, penso che sarebbe assolutamente consigliabile…

“Perché ora quegli oggetti rimangono spesso con te, proprio come il Colonnello…”

A casa, Brandon sembra davvero fantastico. Nessuno può prevedere cosa possa succedere.

Perché, quando le persone sono costrette a stare insieme per molto tempo e vedono poco chiunque altro…

Altrimenti… e sarà sempre nelle tue possibilità far sì che lei abbia successo.

E così via. In breve, potreste benissimo darle una possibilità.

“Capiscimi.”



Ma sebbene la signora Ferrars venisse davvero a trovarli e li trattasse sempre con gentilezza…

Con l’illusione di un affetto sincero, non furono mai offesi…

La sua vera preferenza e predilezione… Questo era dovuto alla follia di Robert.

E l’astuzia di sua moglie; qual merito conquistato da loro molto tempo prima…

Erano passati molti mesi… La saggezza egoistica di quest’ultimo…

Il primo ad attirare Robert in quella situazione complicata fu, in realtà, l’elemento principale che ne determinò lo sviluppo…

La sua liberazione da esso; per la sua rispettosa [[concepts/humility|umiltà]], per il suo impegno costante.

“Attenzioni e lusinghe infinite, non appena si presentava la minima opportunità…”

Per motivi legati all’esercizio richiesto, riuscì a far ragionare la signora Ferrars riguardo alla scelta fatta da lui…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_50--part_02" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 50 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 50" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/home,motif/marriage,motif/time,motif/well,concept/conscience,concept/forgiveness,concept/friendship,concept/humility,concept/self,character/colonel_brandon,character/marianne_dashwood"></span>


re-established him completely in her favour.



The whole of Lucy’s behaviour in the affair, and the prosperity which

crowned it, therefore, may be held forth as a most encouraging instance

of what an earnest, an unceasing attention to [[concepts/self|self]]-interest, however

its progress may be apparently obstructed, will do in securing every

advantage of fortune, with no other sacrifice than that of [[motifs/time|time]] and

[[concepts/conscience|conscience]]. When Robert first sought her acquaintance, and privately

visited her in Bartlett’s Buildings, it was only with the view imputed

to him by his brother. He merely meant to persuade her to give up the

engagement; and as there could be nothing to overcome but the affection

of both, he naturally expected that one or two interviews would settle

the matter. In that point, however, and that only, he erred; for though

Lucy soon gave him hopes that his eloquence would convince her in

_time_, another visit, another conversation, was always wanted to

produce this conviction. Some doubts always lingered in her mind when

they parted, which could only be removed by another half hour’s

discourse with himself. His attendance was by this means secured, and

the rest followed in course. Instead of talking of Edward, they came

gradually to talk only of Robert,—a subject on which he had always more

to say than on any other, and in which she soon betrayed an interest

even equal to his own; and in short, it became speedily evident to

both, that he had entirely supplanted his brother. He was proud of his

conquest, proud of tricking Edward, and very proud of marrying

privately without his mother’s consent. What immediately followed is

known. They passed some months in great happiness at Dawlish; for she

had many relations and old acquaintances to cut—and he drew several

plans for magnificent cottages;—and from thence returning to town,

procured the [[concepts/forgiveness|forgiveness]] of Mrs. Ferrars, by the simple expedient of

asking it, which, at Lucy’s instigation, was adopted. The [[concepts/forgiveness|forgiveness]],

at first, indeed, as was reasonable, comprehended only Robert; and

Lucy, who had owed his mother no duty and therefore could have

transgressed none, still remained some weeks longer unpardoned. But

perseverance in [[concepts/humility|humility]] of conduct and messages, in [[concepts/self|self]]-condemnation

for Robert’s offence, and gratitude for the unkindness she was treated

with, procured her in [[motifs/time|time]] the haughty notice which overcame her by its

graciousness, and led soon afterwards, by rapid degrees, to the highest

state of affection and influence. Lucy became as necessary to Mrs.

Ferrars, as either Robert or Fanny; and while Edward was never

cordially forgiven for having once intended to marry her, and Elinor,

though superior to her in fortune and birth, was spoken of as an

intruder, _she_ was in every thing considered, and always openly

acknowledged, to be a favourite [[archetypes/child|child]]. They settled in town, received

very liberal assistance from Mrs. Ferrars, were on the best terms

imaginable with the Dashwoods; and setting aside the jealousies and

ill-will continually subsisting between Fanny and Lucy, in which their

husbands of course took a part, as [[motifs/well|well]] as the frequent domestic

disagreements between Robert and Lucy themselves, nothing could exceed

the harmony in which they all lived together.



What Edward had done to forfeit the right of eldest son, might have

puzzled many people to find out; and what Robert had done to succeed to

it, might have puzzled them still more. It was an arrangement, however,

justified in its effects, if not in its cause; for nothing ever

appeared in Robert’s style of living or of talking to give a suspicion

of his regretting the extent of his income, as either leaving his

brother too little, or bringing himself too much;—and if Edward might

be judged from the ready discharge of his duties in every particular,

from an increasing attachment to his wife and his [[motifs/home|home]], and from the

regular cheerfulness of his spirits, he might be supposed no less

contented with his lot, no less free from every wish of an exchange.



Elinor’s [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] divided her as little from her family as could [[motifs/well|well]]

be contrived, without rendering the cottage at Barton entirely useless,

for her mother and sisters spent much more than half their [[motifs/time|time]] with

her. Mrs. Dashwood was acting on motives of policy as [[motifs/well|well]] as pleasure

in the frequency of her visits at Delaford; for her wish of bringing

Marianne and [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] together was hardly less earnest, though

rather more liberal than what John had expressed. It was now her

darling object. Precious as was the company of her daughter to her, she

desired nothing so much as to give up its constant enjoyment to her

valued friend; and to see Marianne settled at the mansion-house was

equally the wish of Edward and Elinor. They each felt his sorrows, and

their own obligations, and Marianne, by general consent, was to be the

reward of all.



With such a confederacy against her—with a knowledge so intimate of his

goodness—with a conviction of his fond attachment to herself, which at

last, though long after it was observable to everybody else—burst on

her—what could she do?



[[characters/marianne-dashwood|Marianne Dashwood]] was born to an extraordinary fate. She was born to

discover the falsehood of her own opinions, and to counteract, by her

conduct, her most favourite maxims. She was born to overcome an

affection formed so late in life as at seventeen, and with no sentiment

superior to strong esteem and lively [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], voluntarily to give

her hand to another!—and _that_ other, a man who had suffered no less

than herself under the event of a former attachment, whom, two years

before, she had considered too old to be married,—and who still sought

the constitutional safeguard of a flannel waistcoat!



But so it was. Instead of falling a sacrifice to an irresistible


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Lo ristabilì completamente a suo favore.



L’intero comportamento di Lucy in questa vicenda, e la prosperità che ne è derivata…

Un esempio particolarmente incoraggiante

di quell’attenzione sincera e incessante verso gli interessi personali, comunque sia.

Chiedendolo, e su istigazione di Lucy, questa proposta fu accettata. La [[concepts/forgiveness|perdono]], quindi.

All’inizio, infatti, come era logico, solo Robert riuscì a comprenderlo; e…

Perseveranza nell’[[concepts/humility|umiltà]] nel comportamento e nelle parole, nonché nella [[concepts/self|autocondanna]].

Per l’offesa fatta a Robert… e per la gratitudine verso quella cattiveria che le è stata inflitta.

Con quel modo, le procurò in tempo quella notifica arrogante che la sopraffisse con il suo contenuto.

Gentilezza e nobiltà d’animo, che in breve tempo portarono alle più alte vette.

Uno stato di affetto e influenza reciproco. Lucy divenne indispensabile per la signora.

Ferrars, sia come Robert che come Fanny; e mentre Edward mai…

“Perdonato cordialmente per aver un tempo intenzione di sposarla… e anche Elinor.”

Sebbene superiore a lei per fortuna e nascita, veniva considerato…

L'intrusa… in ogni senso del termine, e sempre in modo palese.

Riconosciuto come il loro preferito tra i bambini, si stabilirono in città e ricevettero.

Un aiuto molto generoso da parte della signora Ferrars… in ottimi rapporti.

“Immaginabile con i Dashwoods… E mettendo da parte le gelosie…”

Malanimo che persiste costantemente tra Fanny e Lucy…

Naturalmente anche i mariti partecipavano, così come le frequenti attività domestiche.

Disaccordi tra Robert e Lucy stessi… nulla poteva superarli.

L’armonia con cui vivevano tutti insieme.



Cosa avesse fatto Edward per perdere il diritto di essere il figlio maggiore… forse avrebbe potuto evitare tutto ciò.

Molte persone rimasero perplesse nel cercare di capire… E cosa avesse fatto Robert per riuscirci.

Forse avrebbe confuso ancora di più loro… Comunque, si trattava di un accordo.

Giustificato nei suoi effetti, se non nella sua causa… perché nulla mai avviene senza motivo.

Del suo rammarico per l’entità dei propri guadagni, come se lasciare…

Troppo poco fratello, o troppo di sé stesso… E se Edward potesse…

A causa di un legame sempre più forte con sua moglie e la sua [[motifs/home|casa]], e anche a causa del.

Data la sua solita allegria d’animo, si potrebbe pensare che anche in questo caso…

Risolto con la propria sorte, privo di ogni desiderio di cambiamento.



Il matrimonio di Elinor non la allontanò affatto dalla sua famiglia, anzi, le permise di mantenere un legame stretto con loro.

“Deve essere realizzato in modo da non rendere del tutto inutilizzabile la capanna di Barton.”

Perché sua madre e sue sorelle trascorrevano molto più della metà del loro [[motifs/time|tempo]] con.

La signora Dashwood agiva sia per motivi politici che per piacere personale.

Un caro amico. E vedere Marianne sistemata in quella dimora, era davvero meraviglioso.

Anche il desiderio di Edward ed Elinor era lo stesso: entrambi condividevano le sue sofferenze.

Le proprie responsabilità… e Marianne, per consenso generale, avrebbe dovuto essere…

La ricompensa di tutti.



Con una tale alleanza contro di lei… con una conoscenza così intima di lui…

Bontà… con una profonda consapevolezza del proprio affetto per lei, che…

Solo dopo che ormai tutti gli altri se ne erano accorti, finalmente esplose…

Lei, cosa poteva fare?



[[characters/marianne-dashwood|Marianne Dashwood]] nacque destinata a un destino straordinario. Fu concepita in una famiglia.

Scoprire l’infondatezza delle proprie opinioni e agire di conseguenza…

Conducere secondo i suoi principi preferiti… È nata per superare ogni ostacolo.

Affetto nato così tardi nella vita, a diciassette anni, e privo di qualsiasi sentimento reale

Superiore a un profondo rispetto e a una vivace [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], disposto volontariamente a donare.

Mettere la propria mano su un altro… e quell’“altro”, un uomo che aveva sofferto altrettanto.

“Più di se stessa… in caso di un legame passato… con qualcuno che, due anni fa…”

Prima, riteneva di essere troppo vecchia per sposarsi… eppure qualcuno continuava a cercarla.

La tutela costituzionale del gilet di flanella.



Ma così fu. Invece di diventare vittima di qualcosa di irresistibile…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_50--part_03" data-title="Sense and Sensibility — Chapter 50 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 50" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/home,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/time,concept/beauty,concept/forgiveness,concept/honour,character/colonel_brandon"></span>


passion, as once she had fondly flattered herself with

expecting,—instead of remaining even for ever with her mother, and

finding her only pleasures in retirement and study, as afterwards in

her more calm and sober judgment she had determined on,—she found

herself at nineteen, submitting to new attachments, entering on new

duties, placed in a new [[motifs/home|home]], a wife, the mistress of a family, and the

patroness of a village.



[[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] was now as happy, as all those who best loved him,

believed he deserved to be;—in Marianne he was consoled for every past

affliction;—her regard and her society restored his mind to animation,

and his spirits to cheerfulness; and that Marianne found her own

happiness in forming his, was equally the persuasion and delight of

each observing friend. Marianne could never [[motifs/love|love]] by halves; and her

whole heart became, in [[motifs/time|time]], as much devoted to her husband, as it had

once been to Willoughby.



Willoughby could not hear of her [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] without a pang; and his

punishment was soon afterwards complete in the voluntary [[concepts/forgiveness|forgiveness]] of

Mrs. Smith, who, by stating his [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] with a woman of character, as

the source of her clemency, gave him reason for believing that had he

behaved with [[concepts/honour|honour]] towards Marianne, he might at once have been happy

and rich. That his repentance of misconduct, which thus brought its own

punishment, was sincere, need not be doubted;—nor that he long thought

of [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonel Brandon]] with envy, and of Marianne with regret. But that he

was for ever inconsolable, that he fled from society, or contracted an

habitual gloom of temper, or died of a broken heart, must not be

depended on—for he did neither. He lived to exert, and frequently to

enjoy himself. His wife was not always out of humour, nor his [[motifs/home|home]]

always uncomfortable; and in his breed of horses and dogs, and in

sporting of every kind, he found no inconsiderable degree of domestic

felicity.



For Marianne, however, in spite of his incivility in surviving her

loss, he always retained that decided regard which interested him in

every thing that befell her, and made her his secret standard of

perfection in woman; and many a rising [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] would be slighted by him

in after-days as bearing no comparison with Mrs. Brandon.



Mrs. Dashwood was prudent enough to remain at the cottage, without

attempting a removal to Delaford; and fortunately for Sir John and Mrs.

Jennings, when Marianne was taken from them, Margaret had reached an

age highly suitable for dancing, and not very ineligible for being

supposed to have a [[archetypes/lover|lover]].



Between Barton and Delaford, there was that constant communication

which strong family affection would naturally dictate; and among the

merits and the happiness of Elinor and Marianne, let it not be ranked

as the least considerable, that though sisters, and living almost

within sight of each other, they could live without disagreement

between themselves, or producing coolness between their husbands.



THE END


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Passione… proprio come un tempo si era lusingata dolcemente pensando…

Aspettando… invece di rimanere per sempre con sua madre.

Titolo: Trovando i suoi unici piaceri nella pensione e nello studio…

Con la sua mente più calma e sobria, aveva preso una decisione… e l’aveva attuata.

A diciannove anni, si sottomette a nuovi legami, inizia una nuova fase della sua vita…

Doveri, un nuovo [[motifs/home|casa]], una moglie, la padrona di casa, e il resto.

Patronessa di un villaggio.



Il [[characters/colonel-brandon|Colonnello Brandon]] era ora altrettanto felice quanto tutte le persone che lo amavano di più.

Si credeva che meritasse di essere così; in Marianne trovava conforto per tutto ciò che era accaduto in passato.

Afflizione… il suo affetto e la sua compagnia riuscirono a restituirgli la serenità.

E il suo spirito tornò alla gioia… E Marianna trovò ciò che cercava

La felicità nel formare il proprio essere era allo stesso tempo la convincenza e il piacere di.

Ogni amico che osservava la situazione. Marianne non avrebbe mai potuto [[motifs/love|amare]] a metà; e lei.

Con tutto il suo cuore, in quel [[motifs/time|periodo]], lei si dedicò a suo marito con la stessa intensità di prima.

Una volta sono stato a Willoughby.



Willoughby non poteva pensare al suo [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] senza provare un dolore profondo; e lui.

La punizione fu presto completata attraverso il volontario [[concepts/forgiveness|perdono]] di.

La signora Smith, che, dichiarando il suo [[motifs/marriage|mattrimono]] con una donna di carattere.

Il motivo della sua clemenza gli diede motivo di credere che, se avesse…

Se si fosse comportato con [[concepts/honour|onore]] verso Marianne, avrebbe potuto essere felice immediatamente.

E ricco… Il suo pentimento per i comportamenti scorretti, che così hanno portato alle loro conseguenze…

Titolo:  
La punizione era sincera, non c’è motivo di dubitarne; né si può negare che ci abbia pensato a lungo…

Guardava con invidia il colonnello Brandon e con rimorso Marianne. Ma lui.

Per sempre inconsolabile… fuggì dalla società, o si isolò completamente…

“La cupa malinconia abituale del carattere… o la morte per un cuore spezzato… non devono essere ignorati.”

Dipendeva da… perché lui non faceva nulla di entrambi. Viveva per esercitare il proprio potere, e spesso anche per…

Si divertisse pure. Sua moglie non era sempre di umore allegro, e nemmeno la sua [[motifs/home|casa]] lo era.

Sempre a disagio. E nei suoi cavalli, nei suoi cani, e in tutto ciò che riguardava quel genere di animali.

Ogni tipo di sport… ma non trovò nulla di trascurabile nel contesto domestico

Felicità.



Per Marianna, tuttavia, nonostante la sua scortesia nel sopravviverle…

Perdita… ma egli conservò sempre quell’interesse deciso che lo attirava verso di essa.

Tutto ciò che le accadde e che la rese il suo standard segreto…

La perfezione in una donna. E molte giovani bellezze, che stanno emergendo, verrebbero da lui trascurate.

Negli anni successivi, non poteva essere paragonata a Madame Brandon.



La signora Dashwood fu abbastanza saggia da rimanere nella capanna…

Cercando di trasferirsi a Delaford; e fortunatamente per Sir John e la signora.

Jennings: quando Marianne fu portata via da loro, Margaret aveva raggiunto…

Adatta in età per ballare, e non del tutto inadeguata per…

Si diceva che avesse un [[archetypes/lover|amante]].



Tra Barton e Delaford esisteva quella costante comunicazione.

Un affetto familiare profondo che, naturalmente, avrebbe dovuto guidarli… e tra loro…

I meriti e la felicità di Elinor e Marianne… che non vengano giudicati in modo superficiale

Senza dubbio, anche se sorelle e vivendo quasi insieme…

A portata di vista l’uno dall’altro, potrebbero vivere senza conflitti

Tra loro stesse, o generando freddezza nei loro mariti.



La fine
